audit.headline: Hobart Hurricanes bolster WBBL squad with Chamari
audit.summary: The Hurricanes have secured one of the world's most destructive batters for WBBL|12, with Sri Lankan captain Chamari Athapaththu joining the club as an overseas replacement player. Athapaththu, currently ranked sixth in the ICC Women's T20I batting rankings, joins the Hurricanes as an overseas replacement for England international Danni Wyatt-Hodge, who has unfortunately been ruled out of the tournament through injury. Emerging wicketkeeper-batter Kate Pelle has also been rewarded for her impressive Spring Challenge campaign with a contract for the upcoming season. The dual signings provide the reigning champions with a timely boost ahead of their season opener against the Melbourne Stars on Thursday (29).
audit.body: The Hurricanes have secured one of the world's most destructive batters for WBBL|12, with Sri Lankan captain Chamari Athapaththu joining the club as an overseas replacement player. Athapaththu, currently ranked sixth in the ICC Women's T20I batting rankings, joins the Hurricanes as an overseas replacement for England international Danni Wyatt-Hodge, who has unfortunately been ruled out of the tournament through injury. Emerging wicketkeeper-batter Kate Pelle has also been rewarded for her impressive Spring Challenge campaign with a contract for the upcoming season. The dual signings provide the reigning champions with a timely boost ahead of their season opener against the Melbourne Stars on Thursday (29). One of the most influential figures in Sri Lankan cricket history, Athapaththu brings a wealth of international experience and an imposing WBBL record to Hobart, having featured in the past seven editions of the competition across 69 matches with the Perth Scorchers, Melbourne Renegades and Sydney Thunder. The 36-year-old enjoyed a remarkable campaign with the Thunder in WBBL|09, amassing 552 runs at an average of 42.46, including five half-centuries, to claim Player of the Tournament honours. She also collected nine wickets during that campaign, underlining her ability to influence matches with both bat and ball. Hurricanes Head of High Performance Salliann Beams said while the club was disappointed to lose Wyatt-Hodge, securing a player of Athapaththu's calibre was an outstanding outcome. "We're obviously incredibly disappointed for Danni, who has been such an important part of our group and was influential in our maiden championship last year,” Beams said. “We wish her all the very best with her recovery. To be able to bring in someone of Chamari's quality and experience is a fantastic result for the Hurricanes. “She's one of the most dangerous batters in world cricket, she's a proven performer in the WBBL and she brings enormous leadership experience as captain of Sri Lanka. “We saw just how influential she can be during her Player of the Tournament campaign with the Thunder, and we're really excited about what she can bring to our group. “Chamari plays an aggressive, fearless brand of cricket that fits perfectly with the way we want to play, and we're looking forward to welcoming her to Hobart.” Chamari Athapaththu (O/S), Nicola Carey, Heather Graham, Ella Hayward, Chinelle Henry (O/S), Ruth Johnston, Lizelle Lee, Kate Pelle, Hayley Silver-Holmes, Amy Smith, Lauren Smith, Linsey Smith (O/S), Molly Strano, Rachel Trenaman, Callie Wilson

audit.headline: Is SL failing its injured elephants?
audit.summary: 28 Oct 2026 | By Venessa Anthony As another of Sri Lanka's iconic tuskers battles serious health complications, conservationists question whether lessons have been learned from previous tragedies, and whether the country's wildlife veterinary services have the resources to respond. The plight of Kawanthissa, one of Sri Lanka's most celebrated wild tuskers, has once again brought the country's elephant conservation efforts under scrutiny, raising difficult questions about veterinary care, institutional accountability and the effectiveness of measures intended to protect the island's dwindling number of iconic tuskers.
audit.body: 28 Oct 2026 | By Venessa Anthony As another of Sri Lanka's iconic tuskers battles serious health complications, conservationists question whether lessons have been learned from previous tragedies, and whether the country's wildlife veterinary services have the resources to respond. The plight of Kawanthissa, one of Sri Lanka's most celebrated wild tuskers, has once again brought the country's elephant conservation efforts under scrutiny, raising difficult questions about veterinary care, institutional accountability and the effectiveness of measures intended to protect the island's dwindling number of iconic tuskers. Just over a year after the death of Bhathiya, another well-known tusker whose injuries and subsequent treatment sparked widespread concern, Kawanthissa's death has reignited a familiar debate: are Sri Lanka's wildlife authorities doing enough to save injured elephants, or are the same systemic shortcomings continuing to place their lives at risk? Known for his exceptional height and magnificent tusks, Kawanthissa, who was estimated to be approximately 50 to 60 years old, has long been a familiar presence in the Galgamuwa landscape, particularly around Usgala and Siyambalangamuwa. However, following a gunshot injury to his right foreleg, the tusker required veterinary intervention. Although initial reports suggested signs of recovery, his condition subsequently deteriorated and he passed away, with reports of diarrhoea and other complications prompting further treatment. For conservationists, the situation is an unsettling reminder of the circumstances surrounding Bhathiya's death in July 2025, following severe injuries that included gunshot wounds. Environmental activist and conservationist Supun Lahiru Prakash, who has raised concerns about the treatment of both elephants, believes the recurring incidents demand a closer examination of Sri Lanka's wildlife management system. Prakash questioned whether the authorities have adequately addressed the concerns raised following previous elephant deaths. "We cannot continue to mourn these magnificent animals, raise questions after their suffering and deaths, and then allow the same concerns to emerge again," he said. Following Bhathiya's death, allegations of veterinary negligence prompted calls for investigations into whether the elephant received timely and appropriate medical attention. Questions were raised about the assessment of his injuries, the treatment administered and the response of the relevant authorities. Now, with Kawanthissa’s passing, conservationists are asking whether those investigations resulted in meaningful procedural improvements. Prakash also pointed to the deaths of other prominent tuskers, including Thekka Raja and the Siyambalangamuwa Tusker, the latter having died during a translocation attempt. Together, these cases raise broader concerns about how conservation interventions are planned, implemented and monitored, particularly when dealing with large, injured or distressed wild elephants. When treatment becomes another concern One of the central questions surrounding Kawanthissa's treatment and passing relates to the possible effects of repeated antibiotic treatment following his gunshot injury. Elephants are hindgut fermenters, meaning they rely on a complex community of microorganisms within their digestive systems to break down fibrous plant material. Certain antibiotics can disrupt this microbial balance, potentially resulting in diarrhoea, digestive disturbances and other complications. Prakash raised concerns that repeated antibiotic administration may have contributed to Kawanthissa's deteriorating condition, although the precise cause of his illness would require independent veterinary assessment. "If repeated antibiotic use contributed to Kawanthissa's condition, serious questions must be asked about whether his treatment was appropriately managed and monitored," he noted. However, the development of complications does not necessarily establish veterinary negligence. Treating gunshot injuries in free-ranging elephants involves considerable challenges, including difficulties in administering medication, monitoring responses and conducting repeated examinations. Establishing whether Kawanthissa's treatment was appropriate would require access to his medical records, the medications administered, their dosages and the clinical reasoning behind the treatment decisions. These are questions that extend beyond the circumstances of one elephant and into the protocols governing wildlife emergency care. While allegations of negligence have dominated parts of the public discussion, conservationists have also highlighted the difficult conditions under which Sri Lanka's wildlife veterinarians operate. According to Prakash, the Department of Wildlife Conservation currently has only 17 veterinarians serving across field stations and headquarters, despite an approved cadre of 35 positions. If accurate, this would mean that fewer than half the approved positions are filled, placing considerable pressure on a relatively small number of professionals responsible for wildlife emergencies across the country. The challenges reportedly extend beyond staffing shortages. Wildlife veterinarians must travel considerable distances, work irregular hours and carry out potentially dangerous procedures in remote environments, often with limited facilities and logistical support. Prakash also highlighted the lack of clear career progression pathways, inadequate allowances for hazardous fieldwork and limited professional recognition as factors that may discourage veterinarians from remaining in the service. These conditions raise an important question: can individual veterinarians reasonably be expected to deliver consistent emergency care without sufficient institutional support? One of Sri Lanka’s leading authorities on the Asian elephant, habitat preservation, and the mitigation of the human-elephant conflict (HEC) Dr Sumith Pilapitiya said, "The discussion should not be limited to whether an individual veterinarian made the right decision. We also need to examine whether the system provides veterinarians with the resources, personnel and support necessary to respond effectively. Accountability is important, but so is ensuring that the institutions responsible for wildlife conservation are equipped to fulfil their mandate." The distinction between individual responsibility and institutional failure is particularly important in a country where injured elephants may be located far from veterinary facilities and require specialised equipment, personnel and prolonged monitoring. What has changed since Bhathiya? The Department of Wildlife Conservation remains the principal authority responsible for protecting Sri Lanka's wild elephants and coordinating veterinary interventions. However, the recurrence of high-profile cases has raised questions about whether existing protocols are sufficient and whether recommendations arising from previous investigations have been implemented. Among the issues requiring clarification are the findings of investigations into Bhathiya's death, any subsequent changes to emergency treatment procedures, and the mechanisms available for independent review when concerns about veterinary care arise. Director General, Department of Wildlife Conservation Ranjan Marasinghe noted, "The Department recognises the importance of ensuring that injured elephants receive timely and appropriate treatment. Wildlife veterinary interventions are complex, particularly when treating free-ranging animals under difficult field conditions. We are committed to reviewing treatment procedures, strengthening veterinary capacity and addressing any shortcomings identified through the appropriate investigations." Beyond official assurances, conservationists argue that measurable improvements are necessary to restore public confidence. This could include transparent reporting on investigations, filling vacant veterinary positions, establishing standardised emergency response protocols and ensuring that treatment decisions are adequately documented and reviewed. Although the suffering of prominent tuskers such as Bhathiya and Kawanthissa attracts considerable public attention, the underlying problems affect the country's wider elephant population. Female elephants, calves and tuskless males are equally vulnerable to gunshot injuries, electrocution, explosive bait and other threats associated with human–elephant conflict. Prakash acknowledged that conservation efforts must extend beyond individual animals, noting that all elephants play important roles in maintaining viable populations. Nevertheless, the repeated injuries and deaths of highly recognisable tuskers have become powerful symbols of the challenges facing Sri Lanka's conservation system. Their cases also highlight the tension between population-level conservation strategies and the immediate welfare needs of individual animals. While the protection of habitats and ecosystems remains essential, the effectiveness of conservation policy must also be assessed through its ability to prevent avoidable injuries and respond when elephants are in distress. A system in need of answers Ultimately, Kawanthissa's death raises questions that cannot be answered through public concern alone. The circumstances surrounding his treatment require careful examination, as do the findings of earlier investigations and the broader challenges facing the Department of Wildlife Conservation. Any assessment must recognise the dedication of wildlife veterinarians working under difficult conditions while also ensuring that concerns about treatment standards are investigated transparently and fairly. For Prakash, the issue is not simply whether another celebrated tusker can be saved, but whether Sri Lanka is prepared to confront the recurring shortcomings that threaten its elephants. "The question is no longer simply whether anything has changed. It is whether the authorities are prepared to act before history repeats itself once more," he said. The responsibility now falls on the authorities to demonstrate that the lessons of Bhathiya's death and now, Kawanthissa’s, have not been forgotten. Without meaningful institutional reform, transparent accountability and adequate support for the professionals entrusted with wildlife care, Sri Lanka risks confronting the same questions each time another elephant is injured, and another life hangs in the balance.

audit.headline: Landslide preparedness needs urgency
audit.summary: With the first anniversary of Cyclone Ditwah approaching fast, the risk of landslides in the hill country remains a matter of serious concern. The National Building Research Institute (NBRI) has warned repeatedly this year that slopes weakened during the cyclone could fail even under moderate rainfall. The scale of the problem is not in doubt. During Cyclone Ditwah , some mountainous areas received over 500 mm of rain within 24 hours, against the 150 mm threshold at which landslides are considered likely. Rainfall in some areas approached 1,000 mm over 10 days. NBRO officials at the time described the situation as unprecedented. Satellite assessments by the Arthur C Clarke Institute later identified approximately 4,800 landslides, a figure considerably higher than earlier reported.
audit.body: With the first anniversary of Cyclone Ditwah approaching fast, the risk of landslides in the hill country remains a matter of serious concern. The National Building Research Institute (NBRI) has warned repeatedly this year that slopes weakened during the cyclone could fail even under moderate rainfall. The scale of the problem is not in doubt. During Cyclone Ditwah , some mountainous areas received over 500 mm of rain within 24 hours, against the 150 mm threshold at which landslides are considered likely. Rainfall in some areas approached 1,000 mm over 10 days. NBRO officials at the time described the situation as unprecedented. Satellite assessments by the Arthur C Clarke Institute later identified approximately 4,800 landslides, a figure considerably higher than earlier reported. By mid-December, over 70,000 people were still housed in relief centres, the majority in the Kandy, Nuwara Eliya and Badulla Districts. In September, NBRI Senior Geologist Dr Wasantha Senadheera stated that 16,793 families had been identified as being at high risk following Ditwah . This is in addition to approximately 15,000 families identified over the past 15 years, of whom around 5,000 are being resettled. In effect, more than 30,000 families are now considered to be at high risk. According to the NBRI, soil and rock displaced during the cyclone may give way during further heavy rain, and areas previously considered safe may no longer be so. The Government has taken a number of steps. In March, the Cabinet approved an increase in the financial assistance provided under the resettlement programme for families in landslide-prone areas, from Rs. 1.6 million to Rs 2.5 million per house. The Sri Lanka Army has been engaged in constructing interim shelters for displaced persons in the Kegalle, Kandy, Nuwara Eliya and Badulla Districts, and construction of 237 new houses commenced in the Badulla District this month. In December, the Deputy Minister of Housing, Construction and Water Supply told this newspaper that resettlement would be completed within one to two years. The Cabinet has also approved the preparation of a National Building Code, which Sri Lanka does not currently have. These measures are necessary. However, they do not yet amount to a comprehensive response. The first concern is hazard mapping. As this newspaper reported, the National Audit Office (NAO) has found that the country's landslide-prone zones have not been adequately mapped. The NBRI has stated that detailed maps at a scale of 1:10,000 require extensive field data, funds and time, and has attributed the delays to insufficient funding and staff shortages. Mapping has been under way since 1985. With approximately 30% of the country's land area across 14 districts classified as landslide-prone, this work cannot be delayed further. The NAO's recommendation that the NBRI expedite mapping and fully utilise allocated funds must be acted upon. The second concern is enforcement. Since 2011, construction in landslide-prone areas has required NBRO recommendations, and landslide risk assessment reports are mandatory for building permits in high-risk districts. Unauthorised construction on slopes has nevertheless continued. The proposed amendments to empower Local Government authorities to intervene before such structures are completed are a step in the right direction, but they will be effective only if local bodies are prepared to enforce them consistently. The third concern is the pace of resettlement. Identifying suitable land remains difficult, and families are understandably reluctant to relocate where doing so affects their livelihoods or their children's access to schools. These are legitimate considerations and must be addressed in planning. At the same time, every delay leaves families exposed to a risk that has already been identified by the State's own technical agency. Several measures are therefore required. The Government should publish district-level data on the number of high-risk families notified, the number relocated, and the funds allocated and spent on resettlement. The NBRI should be provided with the resources required to complete detailed hazard mapping within a fixed timeframe. The National Building Code should be finalised and given legal effect without further delay. Local authorities must also be held accountable for approvals granted, or construction permitted, in areas designated as high risk. Residents in landslide-prone areas continue to be advised to remain vigilant and to move to safer locations during heavy rain. Such advice is essential, but it cannot substitute for a sustained and adequately funded programme of risk reduction. A year after Ditwah , the authorities must ensure that the lessons of that disaster are reflected in action, and not merely in warnings.

audit.headline: Maritime: ‘Digital capabilities must be prioritised with port infra’
audit.summary: 28 Oct 2026 | By Sulochana Ramiah Mohan Sri Lanka must strengthen its technological capabilities alongside physical infrastructure development to consolidate its position as a regional maritime and logistics hub, Deputy Minister of Ports and Civil Aviation Janitha Kodithuwakku said yesterday (27). Addressing the ‘Regional Port Community System and Maritime Single Windows Workshop’ organised by the US Embassy, Kodithuwakku said the adoption of advanced digital technologies was essential to maximising investments in port infrastructure and responding to the evolving demands of international trade. “Modern ports require more than expanded terminals and improved physical facilities. They also depend on efficient information management, streamlined regulatory procedures and effective coordination among the many stakeholders involved in maritime operations,” he said.
audit.body: 28 Oct 2026 | By Sulochana Ramiah Mohan Sri Lanka must strengthen its technological capabilities alongside physical infrastructure development to consolidate its position as a regional maritime and logistics hub, Deputy Minister of Ports and Civil Aviation Janitha Kodithuwakku said yesterday (27). Addressing the ‘Regional Port Community System and Maritime Single Windows Workshop’ organised by the US Embassy, Kodithuwakku said the adoption of advanced digital technologies was essential to maximising investments in port infrastructure and responding to the evolving demands of international trade. “Modern ports require more than expanded terminals and improved physical facilities. They also depend on efficient information management, streamlined regulatory procedures and effective coordination among the many stakeholders involved in maritime operations,” he said. He highlighted the importance of Maritime Single Windows (MSWs) and Port Community Systems (PCSs) in modernising port operations, improving efficiency and strengthening competitiveness. A Maritime Single Window enables the electronic submission of required information through a single point of entry, simplifying regulatory formalities for ships and their agents. A Port Community System, meanwhile, facilitates information exchange among stakeholders, helping reduce delays, lower operating costs and improve coordination. Kodithuwakku said these digital solutions could contribute to a more efficient and reliable maritime transport system while strengthening Sri Lanka’s integration into regional and global supply chains.

audit.headline: Namal indicted in Airbus case
audit.summary: The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) informed the Colombo Magistrate’s Court (MC) yesterday (27) that indictments have been filed before a Permanent Trial-at-Bar against Opposition Parliamentarian Namal Rajapaksa and several other defendants in connection with the controversial Airbus deal. Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara, appearing on behalf of the CIABOC, informed the Court that the indictments comprise 24 charges against the defendants. Rajapaksa was brought to the Hulftsdorp Courts Complex (Aluthkade) yesterday in connection with the controversial Airbus deal. When the case was taken up on 13 October, the Court ordered that Rajapaksa be remanded until yesterday after considering the facts presented.
audit.body: The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) informed the Colombo Magistrate’s Court (MC) yesterday (27) that indictments have been filed before a Permanent Trial-at-Bar against Opposition Parliamentarian Namal Rajapaksa and several other defendants in connection with the controversial Airbus deal. Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara, appearing on behalf of the CIABOC, informed the Court that the indictments comprise 24 charges against the defendants. Rajapaksa was brought to the Hulftsdorp Courts Complex (Aluthkade) yesterday in connection with the controversial Airbus deal. When the case was taken up on 13 October, the Court ordered that Rajapaksa be remanded until yesterday after considering the facts presented. The order was issued by Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga S Bodaragama after considering submissions made by officers of the CIABOC and the suspect’s lawyers. Rajapaksa, who is currently in remand custody in connection with the controversial Airbus deal, has been ordered to be produced before the Colombo Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar today (28). Chief Magistrate Bodaragama also ordered that a report on the matter be submitted to the MC on 30 October. The Chief Magistrate further directed that the suspect remain in custody until he is produced before the said Court. Meanwhile, the Colombo MC has directed the CIABOC to present its submissions today regarding the bail application filed on behalf of Rajapaksa, who is currently in remand custody over the controversial Krrish deal. President’s Counsel M.U.M. Ali Sabry, appearing on behalf of Rajapaksa, filed a motion seeking bail. The CIABOC subsequently requested additional time to present its submissions on the bail application. Rajapaksa has been further remanded until today by the Colombo MC in connection with an alleged bribery case involving the Krrish Group.

audit.headline: Over 21,000 affected by adverse weather in 17 districts
audit.summary: 28 Oct 2026 | By Staff Writer A total of 21,218 people belonging to 5,696 families have been affected by prevailing adverse weather conditions across the country, according to the Disaster Management Centre (DMC). The latest situation report issued by the DMC stated that residents in 109 Divisional Secretariat divisions across 17 districts have been affected by heavy rains and gusty winds. The adverse weather conditions have claimed one life and left five people injured, while three others remain missing, the DMC noted. Two houses have been completely destroyed, while a further 462 houses have sustained damage due to weather-related incidents. Meanwhile, 173 families affected by the adverse weather have been relocated to safety shelters. The DMC said authorities continue to monitor the situation as adverse weather conditions affect several parts of the country.
audit.body: 28 Oct 2026 | By Staff Writer A total of 21,218 people belonging to 5,696 families have been affected by prevailing adverse weather conditions across the country, according to the Disaster Management Centre (DMC). The latest situation report issued by the DMC stated that residents in 109 Divisional Secretariat divisions across 17 districts have been affected by heavy rains and gusty winds. The adverse weather conditions have claimed one life and left five people injured, while three others remain missing, the DMC noted. Two houses have been completely destroyed, while a further 462 houses have sustained damage due to weather-related incidents. Meanwhile, 173 families affected by the adverse weather have been relocated to safety shelters. The DMC said authorities continue to monitor the situation as adverse weather conditions affect several parts of the country. Moreover, the influence of very severe cyclonic storm “Arnab” on Sri Lanka’s weather has gradually weakened as the system makes landfall along the coast of Andhra Pradesh, India, the Department of Meteorology stated. According to the Met. Department, several spells of showers are expected in the Western and Sabaragamuwa provinces and in the Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Galle and Matara districts today (28). Showers or thundershowers are also likely at a few places in the Uva Province and in the Batticaloa and Ampara districts after 1.00 p.m. Meanwhile, strong winds reaching speeds of 40–50 kmph may occur at times over the western slopes of the Central Hills, the Northern, North-Central and North-Western provinces, and the Trincomalee and Hambantota districts, the Met. Department warned. The Department also urged the general public to take adequate precautions against possible damage caused by temporary, localized strong winds and lightning during thundershowers. Although the influence of the cyclone on Sri Lanka is easing, the public has been advised to remain cautious in areas likely to experience adverse weather conditions.

audit.headline: Pardon for Gnanasara Thera: No request to Govt from Chief Prelates
audit.summary: 28 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya CPRP to complain to HRCSL on Gnanasara Thera's rights The Chief Prelates have so far not made a request to the Government seeking the release of the Bodu Bala Sena organisation’s General Secretary, Ven. Galagodaaththe Gnanasara Thera, according to the Cabinet of Ministers Spokesperson Dr Nalinda Jayatissa. He made these remarks yesterday (27) in response to a question raised at the weekly Cabinet media briefing. However, he stressed that even if such a request were made by the Chief Prelates, the Government would act in accordance with the existing law and had no intention of overriding a judicial decision. He also explained that the Government had amended the Standing Orders (SOs) of the Prisons Department following a letter sent to the Prisons Commissioner General by the four Chief Prelates of the Buddhist Chapters of the Buddhist Sects.
audit.body: 28 Oct 2026 | BY Dhanushka Dharmapriya CPRP to complain to HRCSL on Gnanasara Thera's rights The Chief Prelates have so far not made a request to the Government seeking the release of the Bodu Bala Sena organisation’s General Secretary, Ven. Galagodaaththe Gnanasara Thera, according to the Cabinet of Ministers Spokesperson Dr Nalinda Jayatissa. He made these remarks yesterday (27) in response to a question raised at the weekly Cabinet media briefing. However, he stressed that even if such a request were made by the Chief Prelates, the Government would act in accordance with the existing law and had no intention of overriding a judicial decision. He also explained that the Government had amended the Standing Orders (SOs) of the Prisons Department following a letter sent to the Prisons Commissioner General by the four Chief Prelates of the Buddhist Chapters of the Buddhist Sects. According to him, following the receipt of the letter, discussions were held with representatives of the Chief Prelates, including Anunayake Theras and senior officials pertaining to the matter. The discussions resulted in an agreement to amend the relevant Prison regulations. He said that the authorities would proceed in accordance with the amended SOs and noted that the Government had acted on the matters raised by the Chief Prelates. “The Government operates on the basis that everyone is subject to the law,” he said, reiterating that there was no intention to change a decision delivered by a court by placing the Government above the Judiciary. Dr Jayatissa emphasised that the Government would continue to act within the framework of the law regarding matters concerning Gnanasara Thera. Meanwhile, the Committee for Protecting the Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) organisation plans to file a complaint with the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka (HRCSL) today (28), alleging that the rights of the imprisoned Gnanasara are being violated. It says that prison authorities are preventing its representatives from meeting him in order to submit an appeal to the United Nations (UN). Speaking to The Daily Morning , CPRP Convenor Sudesh Nandimal Silva said that the monk has expressed his wish to submit a special appeal to the UN, but that the prison authorities and the Justice Ministry are standing in the way. “Any prisoner has the right to file an appeal if they are willing to. But the prison officials are obstructing us for days from going to the monk to get the necessary documents signed,” he said.

audit.body: 28 Oct 2026 | By Nethmi Rajawasam Though Sri Lanka has made progress on realising transition towards renewable energy, transmission capacity, market design, financing channels and digital infrastructure have not kept pace with the ongoing renewable energy (RE) capacity additions; necessitating an integrated system to absorb RE additions, Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) Research Fellow Dr Erandathie Pathiraja said. Presenting a chapter in the IPS State of the Economy report titled; ‘Renewable Energy Transition: A Strategic Imperative for Energy Security, Economic Resilience and Durable Growth’, Dr Pathiraja compared the distributed generation of solar panels with the centralised model: “In centralised systems the power plant and transmissions lines are built, but when it comes to renewable energy generation, the renewable sources are scattered.” “For example when you take roof top solar producers, the system should be capable of absorbing that. Right now, generation is everywhere, it’s an increasing business. The generation has exceeded the capacity of the system,” Dr Pathiraja said, speaking to The Daily Morning Business on the sidelines of the discussion. Calling for grid modernisation, she added: “That rate of energy generation is not parallel to the transmission and other systems’ development speed. A system needs to be developed to absorb that.” Sri Lankan Energy Minister Anura Karunathilaka, speaking to French news agency AFP last week (25) said that Sri Lanka has the capacity to exceed the 2030 70% national renewable energy target, amid rising global fuel costs. However, the Minister also added that the Government faces major technical, financial and social challenges in relation to the transition. In line with the broader aspiration, the Sri Lankan Government plans to expand solar power capacity to nearly 4,400 megawatts by 2029 and add five major transmission lines from 2027 to strengthen the national grid. The Government is also considering a new pricing model for privately generated solar electricity and plans to expand battery storage to improve grid stability. Karunathilaka, as quoted by the foreign news agency, said that in order for Sri Lanka to reach its long-term goal of generating 90-95% of electricity from renewable energy, it may require substantial investment in generation, transmission infrastructure and energy storage. Dr Pathiraja, acknowledging the ongoing progress in energy sector reforms, said that Sri Lanka’s wholesale market is yet to follow a model of its own, which can enable connectivity with scattered energy generators.

audit.body: 28 Oct 2026 | By Sindy Fernando Sri Lanka must strengthen public-private partnerships and expand its maritime services to attract more business from ships passing its waters, Admiral Jayantha Perera said at the ICCSL’s 50th webinar on Saturday (24). Perera said: “Our port is going very well, and Sri Lanka must encourage public-private partnerships with more than the Government to go ahead with expanding maritime services and to ensure that all the ships passing by become customers of Sri Lanka,” emphasising the need to turn the country’s strategic location into greater economic opportunities. He added: “Any ship coming from the Strait of Hormuz and also from the Red Sea, has to pass through towards the Strait of Malacca or to South China via Sri Lanka. There are more than 300-400 merchant ships passing Sri Lanka daily.” “There are over 500 shipping agents registered with Sri Lanka’s Ministry of Shipping, providing services and assistance, including bunkering, to vessels operating along international shipping routes,” Perera said. He identified Colombo, Hambantota, Trincomalee and Kankesanthurai as important ports in Sri Lanka’s maritime network, describing Colombo as a major container transshipment hub. “We have major ports: Colombo, Hambantota, Trincomalee, and Kankesanthurai. Colombo is globally a transshipment hub and is in the top 20 globally for container transshipment. And we do about 9.9 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) and also expect to increase capacity to 11.1 million TEUs through the development of the East and West terminals and to about 15 million TEUs by 2028,” he noted. “However, at the moment, all the ships passing here are taking ship husbandry, all the logistics and channelling and crew changes, everything from Sri Lanka, when they pass Galle, Colombo, or maybe Hambantota,” Perera said. “Now shipping density has increased due to the Middle East conflict, with some vessels having to wait offshore.” Sri Lanka has also taken steps to improve its bunkering infrastructure. In August 2025, a new pipeline system and oil-loading facility were introduced at Colombo Port’s South Jetty, according to the Ministry of Energy. “Sri Lankan ship repairs and Colombo hub are doing well, and there’s no competition as we are a transshipment hub. Sri Lanka should build on Colombo’s transshipment business and strengthen cooperation with India, which accounts for about 80% of the port’s transshipment cargo,” Perera further stated. “We have to cooperate with India, and we must improve our levels,” he said, adding that better service standards were necessary to gain the confidence of international shipping companies.

audit.headline: SL's geopolitical reality: No way out
audit.summary: 28 Oct 2026 | BY A JATHINDRA No discussion about foreign policy is complete without acknowledging geopolitical realities. audit.body: 28 Oct 2026 | BY A JATHINDRA No discussion about foreign policy is complete without acknowledging geopolitical realities. The world is entering an era often described as the "great fragmentation", creating growing uncertainty and instability in international affairs. Recently, at the Bay of Bengal Conversation in Bangladesh, several geopolitical experts discussed the major crises shaping global politics today. The event was organised by the Centre for Governance Studies. Among the speakers, the former Maldivian President Mohamed Nasheed particularly impressed. He spoke with the clarity and strategic understanding expected from the leader of a small State. He explained: "We have greater rivalry in the Indian Ocean again, with big powers wanting to establish a foothold. We have always understood India as our biggest neighbour. We have always had a foreign policy that places India first. If we try to disrupt that, it might be difficult for us to maintain our sovereignty." He added: "I’m not a non-aligned person. I believe that there should be alignment in your ideology and in the way that you want to develop your country. I wouldn’t go for non-alignment." The question of what kind of foreign policy that a country like Sri Lanka should pursue remains a subject of debate. This is partly because Sri Lanka continues to rely on Cold War-era concepts such as "non-alignment", "neutrality", and "balancing" when framing its foreign policy. In reality, these concepts were designed as strategies to avoid becoming entangled in the rivalries of major powers. As President Anura Kumara Dissanayake has stated, Sri Lanka would not become a "sandwich" between India and China. However, maintaining such a position is not easy amid the intensifying United States (US)-China great-power competition. It is an extremely difficult balancing act in which even a small mistake can have serious consequences. Sri Lanka has experienced this before. President Junius Richard Jayewardene arguably overestimated Sri Lanka's strategic autonomy, and the country ultimately paid the price. Colombo faced a similar challenge when President Percy Mahendra Mahinda Rajapaksa deepened ties with China. Given these historical experiences, it is worth questioning whether the current international environment still allows countries to remain genuinely non-aligned or neutral. The controversy surrounding the Iranian vessels stranded just outside Sri Lanka's 12-nautical-mile territorial waters off Galle provides a useful example. If Sri Lanka was fully committed to neutrality, one could argue that assistance should have been provided on humanitarian grounds. However, concerns over possible repercussions from the US significantly limited Colombo's room for manoeuvre. Washington had warned countries and service providers against supplying food, water, fuel, medicines, or other forms of support to sanctioned Iranian vessels. The practical viability of neutrality This episode raises serious questions about the practical viability of neutrality in today's geopolitical environment. The Sri Lankan Government could justifiably argue that it did not wish to become involved in a Middle Eastern conflict. Yet, others might contend that humanitarian considerations should transcend geopolitical disputes. Viewed through the lens of great-power rivalry, the costs of antagonising the US may outweigh the benefits of adhering to a strict interpretation of neutrality. In this sense, neutrality increasingly appears less like a genuine policy option and more like a constrained choice shaped by the interests and influence of powerful states. Small states often speak of "strategic autonomy" and "independent decision-making". While such language may be appealing in domestic politics, it carries far less weight when dealing with powerful nations. Viewed through a geopolitical lens, the sovereignty of smaller states is often constrained by the interests, security concerns, and strategic calculations of great powers. Sri Lanka itself provides a clear example. Several years ago, the Chinese firm Sinosoar-Etechwin secured a contract to build hybrid renewable energy systems on islands off the Jaffna coast. Although concerns were raised about the procurement process, the projects were later cancelled by the Sri Lankan Government. China subsequently alleged that a third party had influenced Colombo's decision, a clear reference to India. The episode demonstrated how geopolitical considerations can override purely economic decisions in small states caught between competing powers. In theory, Sri Lanka has every sovereign right to choose its economic partners. In practice, however, geopolitical realities place limits on that freedom. If a particular project is viewed by India as a threat to its national security, Sri Lanka's sovereignty alone cannot shield it. As a small State located just off India's Southern coast, Sri Lanka lacks the military capability to provide credible assurances against potential security risks to India. From this perspective, China's growing presence near India's southern coastline, even under the banner of economic investment, can be viewed by New Delhi (India) as a national security concern. Consequently, when Sri Lanka makes decisions that India perceives as strategically harmful, diplomatic, economic, or political pressure from India, as both a regional power and immediate neighbour, becomes difficult to avoid. China is a global power whose influence increasingly extends through economic engagement. The US has identified China as its “near peer competitor”. Against this backdrop, it is reasonable to ask why a major power such as China would devote attention to Sri Lanka's Northern Province, particularly Jaffna, a region that offers limited economic returns. What economic benefit does China gain from operating small ice cream businesses in Jaffna? Why is Beijing interested in establishing a foothold in the region? The explanation may be less economic than strategic. The strategic importance of Jaffna lies in its proximity to India. While India prioritises connectivity and engagement with Northern Sri Lanka, China may see long-term geopolitical value in expanding its presence there. Additionally, South India, particularly Tamil Nadu, occupies a unique place in India's domestic politics, making it a region of considerable strategic interest. Many in Sri Lanka paid little attention to a job advertisement published by the Law Faculty at The Chinese University of Hong Kong for a postdoctoral research position linked to a project conducted in collaboration with the Transnational Government of Tamil Eelam organisation. The project proposed examining political and legal debates surrounding the establishment of an independent Tamil state and the relevant international legal frameworks. Regardless of one's interpretation, such developments inevitably raise geopolitical questions that deserve closer examination. If China seeks a greater presence in Sri Lanka's Northern and Eastern Provinces, what are Beijing's long-term motivations? In international politics, countries can never be entirely certain of another state's future intentions. As a result, they tend to prepare for worst-case scenarios rather than best-case assumptions. If India views China's presence in Sri Lanka's Northern and Eastern Provinces as a potential long-term strategic challenge, such concerns cannot simply be dismissed. Nor can Sri Lanka afford to ignore them, given the realities of geography and its proximity to India. The same logic helps explain China's acquisition of a 99-year lease over the Hambantota Port. The Port's strategic location, rather than its immediate commercial performance, appears to have been the primary attraction. In this sense, Sri Lanka has already become entangled in a major geopolitical competition from which it may find it difficult to disengage. Likewise, as Sri Lanka's closest neighbour and natural partner, India's interest in Sri Lanka's Northern and Eastern Provinces is driven not only by strategic considerations but also by deep historical, cultural, and people-to-people ties. Geography ensures that these realities cannot be ignored, regardless of the Government in power in Colombo. The writer is a political analyst and the founding Director of the think tank based in Trincomalee, the Trinco Centre for Strategic Studies The views and opinions expressed in this column are those of the writer, and do not necessarily reflect those of this publication

audit.headline: SLC to prioritise representing the nation: Sidath
audit.summary: 28 Oct 2026 | BY JATILA KARAWITA Restrictions imposed on playing franchise leagues Eran optimistic of adoption of new Constitution before year end Fitness and discipline also given special attention Sri Lanka Cricket’s (SLC) Transformation Committee is set to prioritise representing the country for the national team with the drastic restriction of taking part in global franchise competitions, ahead of the signing of new player contracts. This was revealed jointly by the CTC Cricket Committee head Sidath Wettimuny and its member Roshan Mahanama, during a press briefing convened at SLC headquarters at Maitland Place last morning.
audit.body: 28 Oct 2026 | BY JATILA KARAWITA Restrictions imposed on playing franchise leagues Eran optimistic of adoption of new Constitution before year end Fitness and discipline also given special attention Sri Lanka Cricket’s (SLC) Transformation Committee is set to prioritise representing the country for the national team with the drastic restriction of taking part in global franchise competitions, ahead of the signing of new player contracts. This was revealed jointly by the CTC Cricket Committee head Sidath Wettimuny and its member Roshan Mahanama, during a press briefing convened at SLC headquarters at Maitland Place last morning. Wettimuny, 70, said it has reached the stage where the sport’s domestic controlling body has had to put their foot down and force players to draw the line, when it comes to turning out for the country as opposed to the preference shown for franchise cricket in the recent past. “One reason we have brought this restriction is, when we were in England quite recently, we found four players walking into the team from franchise leagues, just four days before the tour,” the former opener said. “That kind of thing can’t happen. I am sure Roshan (Mahanama) is aware of some of those player contracts that take place abroad. And our (SLC) legal team is also looking at it. But, when it comes to the next term or when they sign fresh contracts, this will hopefully be part of it.” Ex-captain Mahanama, 60, who faced the press for the first time since being named to the CTC six months ago, concurred with the sentiments aired by his erstwhile colleague. He noted that they had studied contracts implemented in this regard by ‘two or three big countries.’ “If you notice recently, I think two or three big countries said that they were not going to issue NOCs (No Objection Certificates) for players who were going to be included in the Afghanistan Premier League (APL),” he pointed out. He continued to shed further light on the vexed issue. “What we have said is three, including the LPL, out of the top eight franchise leagues. Also there is a clause to say that we will consider them, only if they get clearance from the Sports Science Medicine Unit.” The former batter-a 1996 World Cup winner, asserted that another core reason for the restrictions imposed on franchise cricket is to manage the already heavy workload of the national players. “What we seek to have is more control over the smaller tournaments,” Mahanama elaborated. “The assignments are increasing by the day for the players. I went and officiated in a tournament in the Cayman Islands. For an official, if the ICC confirmed it's okay. But for a player, I don’t think it’s ideal. I think that is then more towards players who have either finished playing or on the threshold of finishing. But we don’t want any of our youngsters to go and play in such tournaments.” He averred that the decision to this effect was being taken with the best interests of the game and players and vowed that there was no other ulterior motive behind it. Wettimuny butted in and insisted that the CTC was out to rationalise the process of playing for the country being the priority, with some fine tuning to be done moving forward. Both further affirmed that aspects of fitness and discipline will also be prioritised for the national team henceforth. Meanwhile, the CTC head Eran Wickramaratne stated that there was no hindrance to funds being allocated to Sri Lanka by the global body, although there was a change in the method of it being released, due to the presence of an interim administration. He added that his Committee was focussed on waste management and basically on saving every single rupee which would enable them to channel funds to school cricket, to women’s cricket and to the sport in general. Asked for a summation on the state of the gazetted SLC Bill, the ex-lawmaker opined the Supreme Court will hopefully provide its final determination on the Bill this week, ahead of its tabling in the Legislature next week. He expressed optimism that following the adherence to the requisite Parliamentary procedure, the new Constitution for SLC could become law before the end of the year.

audit.headline: Secures SL's entry into final: Madushanka skittles Pakistan for 110
audit.summary: Dilshan Madushanka's career-best ODI figures of 5 for 34 set up a dominant eight-wicket win in Lahore, as Sri Lanka snapped a five-game losing streak against Pakistan, and with it, secured a final clash with the same opponents. The result left England mathematically eliminated from final contention, rendering their match against Sri Lanka on Thursday a dead rubber. Having skittled Pakistan out for just 110, Sri Lanka knocked off the target in 18.1 overs - the match itself lasted a total of 43.4 overs and finished not long after the floodlights had been fired up. This was Pakistan's second-lowest total on home turf, and their third-lowest against Sri Lanka – Sri Lanka are also responsible for their lowest total at home.
audit.body: Dilshan Madushanka's career-best ODI figures of 5 for 34 set up a dominant eight-wicket win in Lahore, as Sri Lanka snapped a five-game losing streak against Pakistan, and with it, secured a final clash with the same opponents. The result left England mathematically eliminated from final contention, rendering their match against Sri Lanka on Thursday a dead rubber. Having skittled Pakistan out for just 110, Sri Lanka knocked off the target in 18.1 overs - the match itself lasted a total of 43.4 overs and finished not long after the floodlights had been fired up. This was Pakistan's second-lowest total on home turf, and their third-lowest against Sri Lanka – Sri Lanka are also responsible for their lowest total at home. Kamindu Mendis finished unbeaten on 62 off 60 as he spearheaded the chase, while Pavan Rathnayake cut one away in front of square to wrap up the win; he finished on 23 off 26. Fortune too was certainly in Sri Lanka's favour, with Kamindu being dropped behind the stumps early by Saad Baig. Later, he holed out at deep backward square leg trying to reach his fifty, only for the fielder to tread on the boundary skirting after completing the catch. That said, the two wickets to fall in the Lankan innings were largely against the run of play, as Pakistan struggled for penetration on a pretty placid surface. For Pakistan, Babar Azam top scored with 29 off 33, but only three other batters managed double digits as Sri Lanka's bowlers ran through the Pakistan batting. Sahan Arachchige, who has had a quiet series thus far, finally sunk his teeth into the contest picking up two wickets, while there was a wicket each for Asitha Fernando, Eshan Malinga and Dunith Wellalage. But it was the lively Madushanka who caused all manner of trouble for the hosts, extracting menacing bounce on an otherwise decent batting track, despite clocking speeds in the mid-130s. It was just his second five-for in ODIs, his last coming against India in the 2023 World Cup. There he was among the tournaments top wicket-takers but injuries derailed his progress in the years since, so Sri Lanka will be pleased to see him returning close to his best in a World Cup year. It was a game in which Sri Lanka were in control from start to finish, and one Pakistan would do well to take note of ahead of their rematch in the final. Pakistan 110 all out in 25.3 overs (Babar Azam 29, Dilshan Madushanka 5/34, Sahan Arachchige 2/24) Sri Lanka 114/2 wkts in 18.1 overs (Kamindu Mendis 62 not out, Pavan Rathnayake 23 not out)

audit.headline: Tourism: SL sees 262% surge in searches among Indians
audit.summary: As Indian travellers seek intentional and culturally rich getaways during the October to November festive period, Sri Lanka has emerged as a top international destination, recording a massive 262% year-on-year growth in searches. Driven by an increasing preference for cultural, culinary, and leisure experiences alongside major celebrations like Dussehra, Durga Puja, and Diwali, the island nation leads search growth among top global travel choices for Indian explorers. For Indian travellers, the October to November festive period is increasingly becoming an opportunity to combine celebrations with a change of scene. With Dussehra, Durga Puja, and Diwali approaching, accommodation search trends on digital travel platform Agoda show travellers looking at a mix of international experiences and domestic leisure breaks.
audit.body: As Indian travellers seek intentional and culturally rich getaways during the October to November festive period, Sri Lanka has emerged as a top international destination, recording a massive 262% year-on-year growth in searches. Driven by an increasing preference for cultural, culinary, and leisure experiences alongside major celebrations like Dussehra, Durga Puja, and Diwali, the island nation leads search growth among top global travel choices for Indian explorers. For Indian travellers, the October to November festive period is increasingly becoming an opportunity to combine celebrations with a change of scene. With Dussehra, Durga Puja, and Diwali approaching, accommodation search trends on digital travel platform Agoda show travellers looking at a mix of international experiences and domestic leisure breaks. Based on searches made between 1 August and 30 September, for stays between 15 October and 30 November, Bangkok, Phuket and Tokyo emerged as the top three international cities searched by Indian travellers, while Goa, Puri, and Udaipur were the most popular domestic destinations. International travel interest for Indian travellers is led by destinations across Asia, with Thailand, Vietnam, and Japan emerging among the most searched countries recording 55%, 86% and 125% growth in searches respectively compared to last year. Sri Lanka on the other hand recorded an almost 262% year-on-year growth in searches among the top international destinations, followed by Hong Kong SAR, China at nearly 138% indicating growing interest across a mix of destinations that offer cultural, culinary, and leisure experiences. At the city level, Bangkok and Phuket in Thailand recorded 65% and 51% growth in searches, respectively, offering travellers a combination of cultural landmarks such as the Grand Palace and Wat Pho along with local food and coastal experiences. In Vietnam, Phu Quoc recorded 124% growth in searches by Indian travellers, with its beaches, island-hopping experiences, and night markets offering a mix of leisure and local experiences. Hanoi recorded a 94% increase, with attractions such as the Old Quarter and Hoan Kiem Lake offering a glimpse of the city’s heritage. Tokyo also recorded 109% growth in searches from India, with the October to November travel window coinciding with its autumn foliage season, when spots such as Shinjuku Gyoen become popular for Kōyō , Japan’s tradition of enjoying the changing colours of the leaves. Within India, festive travel trends reflect a mix of leisure, cultural and nature-led getaways. Goa saw nearly 43% year-over-year growth in searches, while Udaipur grew by nearly 29%, reflecting continued interest in established leisure and heritage destinations. Puri recorded 318% growth in searches, followed by Ooty at 166% and Munnar at 107%, pointing to interest in coastal, hill and nature-focused breaks. Varanasi also recorded 92% year-over-year growth, adding to interest in destinations associated with India’s cultural and spiritual heritage. Agoda Country Director, Indian Subcontinent and Indian Ocean Islands Gaurav Malik shared: “The festive period has traditionally been when travel and celebration come together, but the destinations people are considering reveal that there are now various ways to spend this time. We are seeing interest spanning beach holidays, city breaks, cultural destinations and hill station escapes, suggesting that travellers are choosing destinations around the experience they want to have, rather than simply following a conventional itinerary. For Agoda, this also means helping people discover the right stay and experiences around increasingly diverse ways of travelling.” As travellers increasingly shape festive getaways around the experiences they want to discover, Agoda brings stays, flights, and activities together in one place, giving travellers access to more than 6 million holiday properties, over 130,000 flight routes and more than 300,000 activities worldwide through its website and mobile app.

audit.headline: Tourist arrivals in October top 135,000
audit.summary: 28 Oct 2026 | By Staff Writer The number of tourists that have arrived in Sri Lanka so far this month has surpassed 135,000. Sri Lanka welcomed 136,096 international tourists in the first 25 days of October, with India continuing to dominate the tourism market, according to the latest figures released by the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA). India accounted for 51,424 arrivals, representing around 38% of all tourists who visited Sri Lanka during the month. The United Kingdom was the second-largest source market, recording 10,117 arrivals, while China ranked third with 9,411 visitors. Australia and Germany rounded out the top five markets, with 6,844 and 6,269 arrivals respectively. The October figures pushed Sri Lanka’s cumulative tourist arrivals for 2026 to 1,829,772.

audit.headline: Cabinet approves special compensation and reforms following Negombo prison clashes
audit.summary: The Cabinet of Ministers has approved implementing recommendations to provide special compensation and relief to prison officers, who lost their lives or were injured on duty during the clashes at the Negombo Prison on 5 and 6 July 2026. On 3 August 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers decided to appoint a committee headed by the Justice and National Integration Ministry Secretary to make recommendations on compensation and relief for the affected officers. The committee has since submitted its report, which was presented to the Cabinet by the Justice and National Integration Minister Harshana Nanayakkara. “As per the approved recommendations, special compensation will be paid in addition to the compensation already provided under Public Administration Circular No. 22/93,” Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said at the weekly post-Cabinet meeting media briefing yesterday.
audit.body: The Cabinet of Ministers has approved implementing recommendations to provide special compensation and relief to prison officers, who lost their lives or were injured on duty during the clashes at the Negombo Prison on 5 and 6 July 2026. On 3 August 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers decided to appoint a committee headed by the Justice and National Integration Ministry Secretary to make recommendations on compensation and relief for the affected officers. The committee has since submitted its report, which was presented to the Cabinet by the Justice and National Integration Minister Harshana Nanayakkara. “As per the approved recommendations, special compensation will be paid in addition to the compensation already provided under Public Administration Circular No. 22/93,” Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said at the weekly post-Cabinet meeting media briefing yesterday. A sum of Rs. 5 million will be paid to each officer, who died and to each officer who became completely disabled. An officer who has become partially disabled, with a maximum earning capacity of 100%, will receive Rs. 4 million, while an officer who became temporarily partially disabled will receive Rs. 3 million, the Government said. The Cabinet of Ministers also approved a series of measures to strengthen the Prison Tactical Force. These include amending the Prisons Ordinance to grant the force legal status, recruiting an adequate number of suitable officers, and providing formal training in relevant fields along with the necessary modern equipment. “Steps will also be taken to establish a Prison Tactical Force Headquarters at a suitable location,” he added.

audit.headline: CanCham Sri Lanka leads business delegation to Canada to connect investors and unlock new markets
audit.summary: The Business Promotion Mission of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Sri Lanka (CanCham Sri Lanka) is creating opportunities for its member companies to connect with Canadian investors, explore commercial partnerships and expand their reach to international markets. Running from 18 October to 1 November 2026, the mission travels across Vancouver, Toronto, Ottawa and Montréal, with a focus on sectors such as tourism, real estate and infrastructure, AgriTech, green housing, healthcare and wellness, education, IT and Fintech, with Women in Development and Empowerment identified as a special area of interest.
audit.body: The Business Promotion Mission of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Sri Lanka (CanCham Sri Lanka) is creating opportunities for its member companies to connect with Canadian investors, explore commercial partnerships and expand their reach to international markets. Running from 18 October to 1 November 2026, the mission travels across Vancouver, Toronto, Ottawa and Montréal, with a focus on sectors such as tourism, real estate and infrastructure, AgriTech, green housing, healthcare and wellness, education, IT and Fintech, with Women in Development and Empowerment identified as a special area of interest. Building a Canada–Sri Lanka–Indo-Pacific business corridor At a business conclave and networking session in Vancouver hosted by Surrey Board of Trade former President and CEO Anita Huberman, CanCham Sri Lanka Co-Founder and Board Director Mohamed Hameez outlined the Chamber’s proposed Canada–Sri Lanka–Indo-Pacific Corridor Initiative. “Our proposed initiative seeks to connect Canadian expertise, capital and innovation with Sri Lanka’s capabilities and commercial opportunities. At a time of changing global trade dynamics, market diversification is increasingly important. Sri Lanka’s strategic location at the crossroads of South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Middle East, together with its position along major maritime routes, presents opportunities for Canadian businesses seeking to expand their reach into regional markets,” he said. The initiative is intended to link Canadian investment and expertise with Sri Lankan businesses and resources, providing a framework for exploring commercial cooperation across the two countries and the wider Indo-Pacific. Connecting member companies with Canadian investors Representing a range of sectors including property development, education, telecommunications, tourism and manufacturing, the delegation comprises members of Home Lands Skyline, Port City Colombo, Horizon Campus, Horizon College International, Hutch Sri Lanka, ECD Global, AmmA Mega Industries Ltd., Thames International Educational Consultancy and Spillburg Vacation Ltd. The Vancouver program included meetings with colleges and universities, as well as Sri Lankan university student groups from British Columbia and Alberta, opening discussions on educational links and potential areas of collaboration. At the Port City Colombo Investment Forum – Metro Vancouver, Hameez highlighted Port City Colombo’s potential to attract regional business operations and investment. The forum connected Canadian investors with Sri Lankan business leaders to explore prospects in the country’s flagship Special Economic Zone. Former Surrey Councillor Linda Annis was also appointed CanCham Sri Lanka’s Honorary Brand Ambassador, which strengthens a further link between the Chamber and the Canadian community as it develops its international business network. Advancing the mission across Canada Following the Vancouver program, the delegation continues its mission in Toronto, Ottawa and Montréal, with further business, investment, institutional and tourism-related engagements planned across the three cities. CanCham Sri Lanka is also connected to investment-promotion initiatives in Sri Lanka, including the Northern Investment Summit and Sri Lanka Expo 2027. These platforms promote the Chamber’s international outreach by strengthening links between local enterprises and overseas investors. Through its involvement, CanCham Sri Lanka aims to build on its international business network and expand opportunities for international commercial cooperation.

audit.headline: FASL outlines contributions since 2018; seeks clarity on AFA membership selection
audit.summary: FASL Founding President Rajkumar Kanagasingam (second from left) and then Singapore FinTech Association President Chia Hock Lai exchange an MoU in April 2019, witnessed by the then Central Bank of Sri Lanka Assistant Governor R. A. Ananda Jayalath and other representatives The Fintech Association of Sri Lanka (FASL) has issued the following statement in response to comments by LankaPay CEO and FinTech Forum Sri Lanka Chairman Channa de Silva in the Daily FT interview published on 22 October 2026, “FinTech Forum to connect fintechs, build trust and open doors abroad.” In the interview, Channa de Silva states that AFA selected FinTech Forum as its sole member association from Sri Lanka. He also says the Forum provides fintech companies with a channel to engage the Central Bank and Government that they previously lacked.
audit.body: FASL Founding President Rajkumar Kanagasingam (second from left) and then Singapore FinTech Association President Chia Hock Lai exchange an MoU in April 2019, witnessed by the then Central Bank of Sri Lanka Assistant Governor R. A. Ananda Jayalath and other representatives The Fintech Association of Sri Lanka (FASL) has issued the following statement in response to comments by LankaPay CEO and FinTech Forum Sri Lanka Chairman Channa de Silva in the Daily FT interview published on 22 October 2026, “FinTech Forum to connect fintechs, build trust and open doors abroad.” In the interview, Channa de Silva states that AFA selected FinTech Forum as its sole member association from Sri Lanka. He also says the Forum provides fintech companies with a channel to engage the Central Bank and Government that they previously lacked. Although FASL is not named, the interview indirectly questions the achievements of earlier association initiatives. FASL therefore provides context on its contributions and the outstanding AFA membership questions. Contributions since 2018 Established and incorporated in 2018, FASL has developed regional partnerships, supported entrepreneurs, contributed to research and education, and advanced international engagement. In April 2019, FASL signed an MoU with the Singapore FinTech Association at Mandarin Oriental, Singapore. In June 2019, FASL signed an MoU with the FinTech Association of Hong Kong. Signatories included its then General Manager Syed Musheer Ahmed, with Professor Douglas W. Arner, Kerry Holdings Professor in Law at the University of Hong Kong, among the witnesses. FASL’s partnerships also include fintech associations in Japan and the Philippines. In March 2024, it signed an MoU with the Indonesian Fintech Association (AFTECH), in Colombo. FASL’s Singapore FinTech Festival Community Partner role dates back to 2019, while supporting engagement with Hong Kong FinTech Week is documented from 2020. FASL was named a Community Partner of Seamless Middle East in 2020, with engagement through 2024 encompassing institutional support, speaking contributions and participation on judging panels. It has also served as an Association Partner of the Dubai FinTech Summit for the 2024, 2025 and 2026 editions. Wider engagements include Global FinTech Fest in Mumbai and platforms in Vietnam, Shanghai and Hong Kong. Supporting ventures and innovation As a collaborating partner of the 2019 FinX Awards in Dubai, FASL helped connect Sri Lankan startups with international opportunities. Helios P2P participated in the Al Baraka challenge, while iLoan was selected for the Emirates NBD challenge. In 2020, FASL became a strategic partner of HatchX, the fintech accelerator launched by Hatch and the Lankan Angel Network with Ford Foundation support and Central Bank endorsement. In April 2021, FASL signed an MoU with the ASEAN Financial Innovation Network to promote fintech development through APIX. Further collaboration was announced in 2026. FASL initiated a report on enhancing Port City Colombo as a leading South Asian fintech hub, with Professor Arner as Chief Consultant. An interim report was presented in 2024 to then Commission Chairman Dinesh Weerakkody and then Monetary Authority of Singapore Chief FinTech Officer Sopnendu Mohanty. FASL organised FinTech World Cup Regional Competitions at Port City Colombo in 2025 and 2026. AnybanQ.lk progressed to the 2025 Dubai global final; RealX and NanoSoft Global jointly won the 2026 regional competition. FASL’s knowledge activities include awareness workshops and contributions acknowledged in the 2022 Global COVID-19 Fintech Market Impact and Industry Resilience Study, jointly published by the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, the World Bank and the World Economic Forum. It served as Knowledge Partner for the Asian Digital Finance Forum & Awards in 2022 and 2023 and as co-organiser in 2025. AFA’s clarification and outstanding questions Following private correspondence, FASL published its representation query on 6 October 2026. On 13 October, AFA Chairwoman Jaclyn Tsai confirmed its one-member-association-per-jurisdiction framework and FinTech Forum Sri Lanka’s membership. She clarified that membership does not designate an association as the sole or exclusive representative of an entire national fintech ecosystem, nor diminish other associations’ standing. FASL welcomes this clarification. Its separate selection questions remain outstanding: What eligibility and assessment criteria applied? Was FASL’s institutional record considered? How could established associations submit credentials before the membership position was filled? Is a review mechanism or alternative participation pathway available? The Daily FT interview identifies capability, membership, constitution and governance as factors in AFA’s membership assessment. However, FASL was neither approached nor invited to submit its credentials before the Sri Lankan member was selected. FASL has therefore asked AFA how potential associations were identified, how these criteria were applied and whether FASL’s record was considered. These questions remain unanswered at the time of this statement. Sri Lanka’s fintech development reflects contributions from multiple institutions. Public discussion should recognise those contributions and distinguish membership of a private alliance from an exclusive national mandate.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka to host World Buddhist Sangha Council’s 60th anniversary
audit.summary: Sri Lanka will host the 60th anniversary celebrations of the World Buddhist Sangha Council from 28 November to 2 December, 2026, with more than 600 delegates expected to attend. The conference will open at the Nagananda International Institute for Buddhist Studies in Kelaniya under the patronage of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, and several events will also be held in Anuradhapura and Kandy. Preparations were reviewed at the Presidential Secretariat on 26 October. The meeting was led by World Buddhist Sangha Council Organising Committee Chairman Ven. Dr. Bodagama Chandima Thera, World Buddhist Sangha Council Secretary-General Ven. Dr. Maitipe Wimalasara Maha Thera and Secretary to the President Dr. Nandika Sanath Kumanayake.
audit.body: Sri Lanka will host the 60th anniversary celebrations of the World Buddhist Sangha Council from 28 November to 2 December, 2026, with more than 600 delegates expected to attend. The conference will open at the Nagananda International Institute for Buddhist Studies in Kelaniya under the patronage of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, and several events will also be held in Anuradhapura and Kandy. Preparations were reviewed at the Presidential Secretariat on 26 October. The meeting was led by World Buddhist Sangha Council Organising Committee Chairman Ven. Dr. Bodagama Chandima Thera, World Buddhist Sangha Council Secretary-General Ven. Dr. Maitipe Wimalasara Maha Thera and Secretary to the President Dr. Nandika Sanath Kumanayake. The delegates will include Buddhist monks representing Buddhist countries around the world, about 250 Sri Lankans living overseas and about 250 Sri Lankan Buddhist monks. The meeting noted that the arrival of a large number of foreign participants would help increase foreign exchange earnings and promote tourism. The Council also plans to donate Rs. 500,000 to each of 15 Buddhist temples damaged by Cyclone Ditwah to support their restoration. Discussions also covered security for all participating monks, including foreign monks and delegation members, along with medical facilities, first aid and other infrastructure. Infrastructure and decorations at the conference venues and in the surrounding cities were also discussed. Other participants included World Buddhist Sangha Council Assistant Secretary Ven. Dr. Rambukewela Gnanaseeha Thera, along with other Buddhist monks. Senior Additional Secretary to the President Roshan Gamage also attended. So did Buddhasasana, Religious and Cultural Affairs Ministry Secretary Prince Senadheera and Commissioner-General of Buddhist Affairs R.M.G. Senaratne. Deputy Inspector General of Police Kalinga Jayasinghe was present, as was Sri Lanka Army Headquarters Personnel Administration Director Brigadier A.P.A.D.D. Dharmakeerthi. Government officials and heads of security agencies also took part.

audit.headline: CSE ends six-session slump closing 0.27% on the up
audit.summary: The Colombo stock market yesterday ended a six-session losing streak to end on the up. The ASPI ended up 0.27% or 52.11 points at 19,692.67 and the S&P SL20 gained 0.19% or 10.44 points to 5,612.31. Market turnover was nearly Rs. 549.4 million on over 34 million shares traded and Foreign investors were net buyers on a net inflow of Rs. 35.12 million. With 125 counters ending on the up against 75 that declined, the top contributors to the ASPI gain were DIAL, CARS, CCS, SEMB and LGL. NDB Securities said high net worth and institutional investor participation was noted in Softlogic Life Insurance, CIC Holdings and John Keells Holdings. Mixed interest was observed in Panasian Power, Haycarb and Prime Lands Residencies whilst retail interest was noted in Browns Investments, LOLC Finance and Ceylon Land & Equity.
