audit.headline: Following TISL’s contempt application, SC sets deadline for Rs. 275 m payment in medical procurement case
audit.summary: Following an application for contempt of court filed by Transparency International Sri Lanka (TISL) on 12 October 2026, the Supreme Court made directions on the failure of respondents in a medical procurement case to comply with its judgment requiring payment of Rs. 275 million in total, to the State. The proceedings arise from the Supreme Court’s judgment delivered in case SC/FR/65/2023 on the 27 of March 2026, which found that five respondents; including former Health Minister Keheliya Rambukwella, former Health Secretary S. J. S. Chandraguptha, and three other senior officials had infringed the fundamental right to equal protection of the law guaranteed under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Court ordered the former Minister to pay Rs. 75 million to the State and each of the other four respondents to pay Rs. 50 million.
audit.body: Following an application for contempt of court filed by Transparency International Sri Lanka (TISL) on 12 October 2026, the Supreme Court made directions on the failure of respondents in a medical procurement case to comply with its judgment requiring payment of Rs. 275 million in total, to the State. The proceedings arise from the Supreme Court’s judgment delivered in case SC/FR/65/2023 on the 27 of March 2026, which found that five respondents; including former Health Minister Keheliya Rambukwella, former Health Secretary S. J. S. Chandraguptha, and three other senior officials had infringed the fundamental right to equal protection of the law guaranteed under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Court ordered the former Minister to pay Rs. 75 million to the State and each of the other four respondents to pay Rs. 50 million. TISL subsequently moved the Supreme Court for contempt proceedings, alleging wilful disobedience of the judgment and seeking appropriate action since the payments remained outstanding seven months after the judgement was delivered. At the hearing on Monday, the third respondent, former National Medicines Regulatory Authority (NMRA) Chairman Prof. S. D. Jayaratne submitted to Court that the payment of Rs. 50 million has been made on 22 October, following the filing of TISL’s contempt application. The remaining respondents undertook to make payments in the following manner: *The first respondent, Rambukwella, made a payment of Rs. 20 million on 23 October 2026 and gave an undertaking to pay the outstanding balance of Rs. 55 million within two weeks. *The second respondent, Chandraguptha, gave an undertaking to pay Rs. 5 million within a week and to settle the remaining Rs. 45 million within three months. *The fourth respondent, former Chief Executive Officer of the NMRA Dr. Vijith Gunasekara gave an undertaking to pay Rs. 20 million within two weeks and the remaining Rs. 30 million within three months. *The fifth respondent, former Medical Supplies Division Director Dr. A. Thusitha Sudharshana gave an undertaking to pay all his savings amounting to approximately Rs. 2 million within this week and to settle the outstanding balance of Rs. 48 million within three months. The Supreme Court, while directing the first, second, fourth and fifth respondents to pay the total amounts due within three months, imposed travel bans on all four respondents. The Court ordered that they be enlarged on bail with each subject to a cash bond of Rs. 50 million and two sureties who must establish their capacity to pay the specified amount. The respondents were directed to fulfil the bail conditions within one week. By bringing the non-compliance with the Supreme Court’s payment order before the Court, TISL sought to ensure that the Court’s orders were respected and that appropriate action was taken in response to their continued failure to be held accountable. TISL emphasises that compliance with judicial orders is fundamental to the rule of law and constitutional accountability. Such compliance must not be dependent on the petitioner’s ability to initiate further proceedings in Court. TISL further emphasises the following realities to those in positions of public power; their actions carry ethical and legal obligations towards the public they serve. Consequences of corruption carries long-term legal ramifications and permanent reputational harm. Civil Society Organisations and accountability actors will continue to actively monitor decisions to ensure strict adherence to legal frameworks and accountability standards. Senior Counsel Senany Dayaratne with Attorneys-at-Law Lasanthika Hettiarachchi, Nishadi Wickramasinghe, Janani Abeywickrema and Maheshika Bandara appeared for TISL, instructed by Attorney-at-Law Thushari Jayawardena. The matter is fixed to be taken up on 15 February 2027.

audit.headline: WNPS goes to Court over guns for civilians as elephant killings rise
audit.summary: The Wildlife and Nature Protection Society (WNPS), Sri Lanka’s oldest and leading conservation organisation, had initiated legal action in the Court of Appeal to halt the State-issuance of firearms to civilians, which is driving an unprecedented surge in the slaughter of the country’s wild elephants. The writ application seeks urgent judicial intervention to stop the escalating killing of elephants both within and outside protected reservations. WNPS argued in its Petition that the crisis had intensified following the relevant public authorities’ decision to issue firearms to civilians for the purpose of protecting crops from wild animals. The legal challenge was filed in August 2025, over a year before the tragic and widely publicised killing of the iconic tusker ‘Kavantissa’.
audit.body: The Wildlife and Nature Protection Society (WNPS), Sri Lanka’s oldest and leading conservation organisation, had initiated legal action in the Court of Appeal to halt the State-issuance of firearms to civilians, which is driving an unprecedented surge in the slaughter of the country’s wild elephants. The writ application seeks urgent judicial intervention to stop the escalating killing of elephants both within and outside protected reservations. WNPS argued in its Petition that the crisis had intensified following the relevant public authorities’ decision to issue firearms to civilians for the purpose of protecting crops from wild animals. The legal challenge was filed in August 2025, over a year before the tragic and widely publicised killing of the iconic tusker ‘Kavantissa’. WNPS contends that this legal action should have served as a stark warning to the Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC), the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Environment, and other state authorities that placing firearms in civilian hands would inevitably result in the death of wild elephants, which are strictly protected under Sri Lankan law. In its petition, WNPS highlighted the agonising death of another iconic tusker, ‘Bathiya’, who succumbed to multiple gunshot wounds after prolonged suffering in a pool of mud. The petition noted that Bathiya’s slow death exposed severe resource shortages and a critical lack of capacity within the DWC and local veterinary services to handle such wildlife emergencies. Strikingly, just a year later, the nation and the global conservation community witnessed the majestic tusker ‘Kavantissa’ perish under identical, preventable circumstances. To underscore the staggering scale of the risk, the petition cited a statement made in Parliament on March 18, 2025, by MP Namal Karunaratne, revealing that the Government had distributed 13,207 firearms to farmers under the scheme. Subsequent court disclosures indicated that an extremely large number of these State-issued weapons remained entirely unlicensed, and unaccounted for, presenting an existential threat to Sri Lanka’s endangered wildlife and national heritage. Demonstrating a clear link between the distribution of weapons and rising violence against wild elephants, WNPS cited official figures published by the State, including the statement made by the Minister of Environment that 21 wild elephants had been shot in various locations within seven months in the period January to July, 2025, with most struck below the knee. The petition emphasised that shootings account for approximately 20% of annual elephant deaths in Sri Lanka, pushing the endangered species closer to extinction. The Petition quotes the following profound observation made by His Lordship, Justice N.E. Dissanayake, Retired Supreme Court Judge in an in an inquiry report: “When the birth rate of elephants is considered with the annual rate of death of elephants it is clear that there is a grave threat of depletion of its numbers. You need not be a great mathematician to conclude that the day will not be too far away for our elephants to become extinct”. WNPS further argued that releasing over 13,000 firearms to civilians (including where a large volume thereof remained unlicensed and unaccounted for), was an irrational and short-sighted measure, that directly contradicts the Government’s own law enforcement initiatives to seize illegal weapons and combat underworld crime. WNPS maintains that the indiscriminate distribution of firearms undermines the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance (FFPO), transforms a conservation crisis into a public safety hazard, and threatens the survival of Sri Lanka’s natural heritage. In 2020, WNPS challenged the Sri Lankan Government’s issuance of 6,000 firearms to Civil Defence Forces to combat human-elephant conflict. This legal action led to the Hon. Attorney General representing the relevant public authorities, furnishing a formal undertaking before the Court of Appeal that the weapons would be recalled and the management of wildlife transferred to the Department of Wildlife Conservation. Despite this court undertaking and formal commitment, the relevant public authorities have repeatedly recycled this failed action, resulting in a continuous cycle of weapon distribution and escalating elephant fatalities. Through this application, WNPS has urgently invited and moved for judicial intervention to protect Sri Lanka’s iconic national heritage from an unprecedented existential threat. The Sri Lankan elephant is now listed as endangered by the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, and faces imminent extinction. The Parliament of Sri Lanka has explicitly declared the Sri Lankan Elephant as Protected Public Property in terms of the provisions of the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance, rendering any harm caused to this national heritage a serious criminal offense met with the absolute harshest legal penalties. WNPS remains steadfastly committed to safeguarding Sri Lanka’s majestic wild elephants and ensuring their survival for generations to come. WNPS is represented by President’s Counsel Sanjeewa Jayawardane, with Attorneys-at-Law Prashanthi Mahindaratne and Dilumi de Alwis, and instructed by Attorney-at-Law Amila Kumara.

audit.headline: Apparel exports grow in Sept., YTD picture remains cautious: JAAF
audit.summary: Sri Lanka’s apparel exports returned to growth in September 2026, an encouraging sign for the sector. Although the nine-month total is still behind last year, the Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF) sees the latest result as a positive step. Apparel exports for the month came to $ 416.99 million, up 3.47% from $ 403.01 million in September 2025. The United States and the European Union, the sector’s two largest markets, led the gain. Exports to the US grew 7.17% to $ 172.03 million, and exports to the EU (excluding the UK) grew 6.5% to $ 132.46 million. Performance across markets was mixed. Exports to the UK fell 5.92% to $ 47.33 million, and exports to other destinations slipped 3.89% to $ 65.17 million. The cumulative figures tell a more sobering story.
audit.body: Sri Lanka’s apparel exports returned to growth in September 2026, an encouraging sign for the sector. Although the nine-month total is still behind last year, the Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF) sees the latest result as a positive step. Apparel exports for the month came to $ 416.99 million, up 3.47% from $ 403.01 million in September 2025. The United States and the European Union, the sector’s two largest markets, led the gain. Exports to the US grew 7.17% to $ 172.03 million, and exports to the EU (excluding the UK) grew 6.5% to $ 132.46 million. Performance across markets was mixed. Exports to the UK fell 5.92% to $ 47.33 million, and exports to other destinations slipped 3.89% to $ 65.17 million. The cumulative figures tell a more sobering story. Between January and September 2026, apparel exports totalled $ 3,588.46 million, a decline of 5.52% from $ 3,798.25 million in the same period last year. That is a shortfall of roughly $ 210 million. One strong month, welcome as it is, does not close a gap of that size. The decline runs across all major markets over the nine months. The UK saw the steepest fall at 10.85%, followed by the EU at 5.44% and other markets at 5.43%. The US fell 3.69%, the smallest drop among the major markets. Changing trade flows of major trading countries, are also shaping the global picture. Chinese apparel shipments to the United States were around 34% lower in the first seven months of 2026, according to US import data. Industry representatives in competing countries note that China and India have been turning more of their attention to Europe following higher US tariffs, which has made the market more price-competitive. China’s share of EU apparel imports edged up from 26.9% to 28.6% between January and April 2026. For Sri Lankan manufacturers, this points to a busier European market at a time when overall demand remains soft, and it underlines the importance of competitiveness, reliability and diversification. JAAF Secretary General Yohan Lawrence said: “September’s growth in the US and EU is encouraging, and it shows our manufacturers can compete when demand is there. We’re still more than five percent behind where we were this time last year. What the industry needs now is steady, competitively priced energy and a supportive policy environment, so that this momentum lasts beyond a single month”. JAAF sees September as an encouraging sign, particularly with the US and EU both growing, but not yet a turnaround. The industry will be watching closely whether this momentum carries through the remaining months of the year, and whether markets such as the UK can recover.

audit.headline: Skyscrapers on a quagmire
audit.summary: On 21 October, the developers of PHP – the engine behind around 70% of the world’s websites – disclosed 2 severe flaws, since nicknamed PHP2Shell, that could let a stranger with no password take control of the computer behind a website. The US National Security Agency then told organisations unable to fix their systems to take them offline, and the South African Presidency, the Finnish Government and the UK Government did exactly that within hours, if not days. Sri Lankans got a general advisory from SL-CERT the same day, naming no institution. Not a single site was taken offline. Over next 3 days that followed I checked around 640 live gov.lk sites I could discover. I was searching for critical PHP vulnerabilities, but came back with a far more disturbing picture of, and appreciation for the incredible fragility of our public digital, and critical national infrastructure.
audit.body: On 21 October, the developers of PHP – the engine behind around 70% of the world’s websites – disclosed 2 severe flaws, since nicknamed PHP2Shell, that could let a stranger with no password take control of the computer behind a website. The US National Security Agency then told organisations unable to fix their systems to take them offline, and the South African Presidency, the Finnish Government and the UK Government did exactly that within hours, if not days. Sri Lankans got a general advisory from SL-CERT the same day, naming no institution. Not a single site was taken offline. Over next 3 days that followed I checked around 640 live gov.lk sites I could discover. I was searching for critical PHP vulnerabilities, but came back with a far more disturbing picture of, and appreciation for the incredible fragility of our public digital, and critical national infrastructure. 80 vulnerable sites, and likely much more At least 80 websites run by the state, or by the utilities and companies it owns, run vulnerable versions of PHP, and 61 of them run versions so old that the makers stopped fixing them years ago, which means they carry every flaw discovered since and have no official repair available. This isn’t a complete number since for a lot of technical reasons, including by measures established to thwart potential hackers, it’s often impossible to determine specific vulnerabilities that exist within websites as an outsider. Accordingly, I could only count sites that announced their software version. The list reads like an organisational chart of the state, running from the Ceylon Electricity Board and the Disaster Management Centre, both on a version released in June 2013, through LECO, the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, SLT Mobitel, the Telecommunications Regulatory Commission, the National Transport Commission, the Sri Lanka Air Force and the Department for Registration of Persons, which holds the national identity card registry, to the Ministries of Health, Mass Media and Justice, a Prime Minister’s Office system, the Bribery Commission, the Department of Government Information, the National Police Commission, 8 of the 9 provinces, 3 municipal councils and several Pradeshiya Sabhas. These are not random or peripheral sites. Worse still, the Ministry of Health’s human resources systems, which handle transfers, post-intern appointments and appeals for health workers, run on a version released in July 2010, while a ministry portal asks doctors to log in with their national identity card numbers, and the Bribery Commission takes complaints from the public, so NIC numbers, employment records and the details of those who report corruption all sit behind architectures no one has updated or maintained in years. It truly beggars belief. The rot beyond PHP Updating PHP won’t fix what ails many official websites. 9 state sites, including the CEB and the Air Force, publish diagnostic pages that display their entire server configuration to anyone who looks, and the login pages of database administration tools, which are by definition doors to databases, are reachable on the Sri Lanka Police, Ministry of Defence, Disaster Management Centre and LECO sites, with LECO’s dating from 2017. The Railway Department, the Auditor General’s Department and the Director General of Merchant Shipping share a server whose public status page leaks the address of a machine inside the Government network, while a Pradeshiya Sabha site briefly exposed the kind of file that typically holds passwords and keys. The Auditor General’s Department, whose job is to hold the rest of the state to account, is amongst them. Other countries try their best to secure this sensitive information by layer upon layer of safeguards, including regular updates to the underlying code. The situation in Sri Lanka is vastly different, and stolen data held to crypto-currency ransoms we simply can’t afford to pay may actually be the least of our worries. In a country with a long and recent history of disinformation driving offline violence, a compromised official website is the most credible vehicle for falsehood imaginable. A forged flood warning on the Disaster Management Centre’s site during a cyclone, or a false tariff notice on the CEB’s, would be believed precisely because of where it appeared. Nor do attackers usually stop at the website. Once they control it, they can use it as a way into the databases and internal Government networks that sit behind it. Gmail, the Fuel Pass and a culture of convenience The state of our servers are a symptom of absolutely rotten institutional cultures decades in the making. In March I wrote about the National Fuel Pass, whose rollout failed to recognise newly issued NIC numbers, sent one-time passwords after they had expired and showed second-hand vehicles under their previous owners, while for over 48 hours no ministry or development team said anything online, leaving Asela Waidyalankara, an independent cybersecurity expert, to field public complaints on Twitter/X, and act as a conduit to the authorities. You couldn’t make it up. Earlier this month, I went through the first 500 search results for gmail.com (the commercial Gmail domain) on official gov.lk domains. I found state bodies advertising consumer Gmail addresses for right-to-information requests, procurement, health appointments and child protection, with the Department of Census and Statistics directing confidential survey returns to district addresses, many of them Gmail, and the Registrar General’s website displaying an official address whose link opens a Gmail one. Consumer Gmail accounts leave citizens’ identity, health and bank details dependent on whoever holds the password, with no institutional control over custody, retention or continuity when staff move on. All this, with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) becoming fully operational on 1 January 2027. I have yet to hear the President, or Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya as Chief Presidential Adviser on Digital Economy, speak to any of it. Photo-opportunities vs ground realities The public are regularly shown photographs of meetings with the Indian High Commissioner, the UN system, the World Bank and other bilateral and multilateral partners about funding or supporting digitalisation, from the Sri Lanka Unique Digital Identity scheme to GovPay, whereas the rot in the foundations these platforms are being retrofitted onto, and the cultures that produced it, never feature. Nor does the fact that no single body is mandated to keep the state’s systems current, since SL-CERT can advise institutions but cannot compel them, as Deputy Minister of Digital Economy Eranga Weeraratne told Parliament in March 2025, and as late as May 2026 no law required institutions to report incidents to it. Countries that have more successfully address this Gordian Knot of issues have established a dedicated institution, with a clear mandate for 5 years or more, with the people, processes and regulatory authority to build what was missing, and not just by issuing advisories. The expertise to help exists, including within the UN system, if the Government asks for it directly, and means it. It may be that the President, Deputy Minister Weeraratne, and Dr. Wijayasuriya somewhat grasp the problem. But the true state of even critical national infrastructure suggests they may under-appreciate how fundamentally flawed the foundations really are, including beyond Government. Infrastructure this brittle can quickly turn any small, sustained shock into a major socio-economic, and political crisis – and we are sitting ducks. Parliament’s blind spot Earlier this month, I published a report on a study of 173 Hansards, from January 2025 to September 2026, focussing on digitalisation, and AI. MPs did discuss cybersecurity, and often in ways that bear out what I found last week. Ajith P. Perera pressed for cybersecurity legislation in drafting since 2019, Chathura Galappaththi urged a security framework and bug-bounty testing before any biometric data is collected, and Ravi Karunanayake sought a forensic audit after the October 2025 Lanka Government Cloud disruption, which the Deputy Minister attributed to a full disk on a platform with no centralised backup. The Deputy Minister later told the House that the 2023 ransomware attack permanently erased emails linked to around 5,000 Government addresses because institutions lacked offline backups, and in August 2026 the Leader of the Opposition cited weak passwords and missing multi-factor authentication behind the US$2.5 million lost during a debt repayment to Australia. The floor debate, though, was around fraud, deepfakes and online harms rather than the upkeep of the state’s own systems. MPs need to better understand ground realities – software unpatched for decades, exposed private data – as well as emergent developments, where AI makes finding, and exploiting vulnerabilities cheaper, faster, more automated, and available to anyone, anywhere. The resulting risks, threats, and harms to Sri Lanka will grow exponentially. Foundations before facades We are being promised skyscrapers built on quagmires. The fixes are unglamorous, but urgent. They include, but aren’t limited to a complete inventory of state systems with a named official accountable for each, and a binding rule that institutions run only supported software. Every second more with foundations this fragile, and institutional cultures this frightful invites a collective national grief we can ill afford after 2022.

audit.headline: From street Bhandiwalla to $ 624 b Circular Economy: How South Asian tradition can power sustainable growth
audit.summary: - Rooted in ancient philosophies of non-wastage and pioneered by historic trade communities, South Asia's circular ethos offers a powerful blueprint for economic resilience and urban sustainability Addressing the Regional Forum on Circular Economy – South Asia, jointly organised by SAARC and the Federation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Sri Lanka (FCCISL) with support from the Institute for Global Environmental Strategies (IGES), brought back a vivid memory from my childhood in Mumbai. Echoing down the street outside our apartment, a vendor carrying a large basket on his head would call out: “Bhandiwalla, Bhandiwalla!” Once or twice a year, my mother would call him upstairs. He would unload his basket to reveal sparkling stainless-steel utensils. My mother would bring out a stack of old, worn-out family clothes, and the bargaining would begin.
audit.body: - Rooted in ancient philosophies of non-wastage and pioneered by historic trade communities, South Asia's circular ethos offers a powerful blueprint for economic resilience and urban sustainability Addressing the Regional Forum on Circular Economy – South Asia, jointly organised by SAARC and the Federation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Sri Lanka (FCCISL) with support from the Institute for Global Environmental Strategies (IGES), brought back a vivid memory from my childhood in Mumbai. Echoing down the street outside our apartment, a vendor carrying a large basket on his head would call out: “Bhandiwalla, Bhandiwalla!” Once or twice a year, my mother would call him upstairs. He would unload his basket to reveal sparkling stainless-steel utensils. My mother would bring out a stack of old, worn-out family clothes, and the bargaining would begin. Eventually, they would settle on a fair barter—a gleaming steel plate, bowl, or glass in exchange for a pile of discarded garments. That street vendor was a key operator in a thriving, decentralised circular economy. He took those old clothes and systematically repurposed them. Usable garments were cleaned, ironed, and resold in smaller towns and villages. Hardware like buttons and zips were salvaged and sold to local tailors. Nothing was wasted; everything was reused, repurposed, or recycled. Landfills simply did not factor into the equation. A philosophy embedded in cultural DNA This informal barter system was not merely a survival tactic; it was the practical manifestation of an ancient South Asian worldview. The Indian philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (“the world is one family”) highlights the intrinsic interdependence of all living beings. Similarly, the concept of Ahimsa—practiced so powerfully by Mahatma Gandhi—demands non-violence not only toward human beings but also implicitly toward the natural environment. At South Asian dining tables, children are raised with a fundamental command: never waste a single morsel of food. In our culture, squandering resources is viewed almost as a moral failing. While the modern global economy operates largely on a linear “take-make-dispose” model, the circular economy focuses on “use, repurpose, renew, and recycle.” It ensures materials remain continuously within the economic loop rather than ending up as toxic land contamination. Entrepreneurial communities: South Asia’s original circular pioneers While India’s current position as one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies is frequently attributed to its demographic dividend, its bedrock lies in entrenched entrepreneurial communities. Long before modern sustainability frameworks were codified, these merchant networks jumpstarted trade by operationalising zero-waste principles: The Marwaris (Rajasthan) and operational efficiency: Marwari trade culture was built on eliminating operational leakage (kasar). In early merchant supply chains, packaging materials—dunnage, burlap sacks, wooden crates, and metal bindings—were systematically harvested, graded, and resold across secondary commodity markets. Machinery in Marwari-run mills was continuously repaired, retrofitted, and downgraded through secondary manufacturing tiers before final scrap recovery. Furthermore, through community banking instruments (Hundis), financial capital circulated internally, minimising interest leakage to external institutions. Nattukottai Chettiars (Tamil Nadu) and cross-border loops: As maritime merchant bankers operating across South and Southeast Asia, the Chettiars optimised cross-border shipping networks. Vessels exporting spices or textiles never returned empty; they brought back timber, stone, and raw materials as structural ballast, which were immediately converted into construction materials upon arrival. Gujaratis and Jains (Western India) and material valorisation: Guided by Ahimsa, these trading guilds prioritised resource stewardship. Gujarati networks pioneered secondary textile markets by collecting cotton mill waste (ru) and processing short-staple fibers into coarse industrial cloth, paper, or stuffing. This ethos also built major industrial salvage hubs like Alang in Gujarat, where decommissioned ships are systematically stripped down to re-roll structural steel and re-introduce every component back into the industrial supply chain. Parsis (Mumbai and Gujarat) and extended lifespan design: Industrial pioneers like the Tata and Godrej families rejected planned obsolescence. Heavy consumer products—from steel cabinetry and locks to industrial machinery—were engineered for multi-generational durability, modular repair, and high residual scrap value. Moreover, industrial profits were systematically reinvested into urban green belts, housing trusts, and civic infrastructure. Bunts (Coastal Karnataka) and integrated agro-hospitality loops: In traditional Bunt-run restaurant networks (such as Udupi eateries), organic kitchen waste was redirected to coastal dairy farms or converted into agricultural compost. In native Canara agricultural estates, every component of coconut and arecanut cultivation was monetised—husks became coir fiber, fronds were woven into roofing, shells were converted into activated carbon, and fallen leaves served as biodegradable serving plates (patravali). Modern start-ups harnessing waste for wealth This ancestral ingenuity is currently experiencing a high-tech revival across South Asia’s start-up ecosystem: Chakr Innovation has developed the “Chakr Shield,” a technology that captures particulate matter emissions from diesel generators and converts it into high-grade industrial ink—now purchased by global tech firms like Dell. Boson White Water addresses industrial water security by treating sewage effluent from large apartment complexes to potable standards for use in IT parks and industrial facilities. In an era of booming data center expansion, such liquid waste innovations are vital. The scale of the crisis Despite these deep-rooted traditions and promising innovations, South Asia faces an unprecedented environmental challenge driven by rapid urbanisation: 1. Surging Solid Waste: India’s urban population is projected to reach 600 million (40%) by 2030 and 800 million by 2050. Consequently, annual municipal solid waste (MSW) generation will surge from roughly 62 million tons today to 165 million tons by 2030, and 436 million tons by 2050. 2. Urban Land Loss: Unmanaged dumping currently locks up over 10,000 hectares of prime urban land across 2,100+ legacy dumpsites (such as Delhi’s Ghazipur and Okhla mounds), posing serious public health hazards. 3. Unused Liquid Waste: India generates 112 billion litres of domestic wastewater daily (the 3rd largest volume globally), but only ~28% undergoes treatment. Monetising treated urban wastewater for industrial and agricultural reuse represents a potential ₹3.04 trillion market opportunity by 2047. 4. Resource Dependencies: Urban material consumption is set to more than double—from 40 billion tons in 2010 to 90 billion tons by 2050. Heavily reliant on imported critical minerals for electronics, electric vehicles (EVs), and heavy manufacturing, the region urgently requires urban mining and closed-loop recycling networks to secure strategic supply chain autonomy. The macroeconomic opportunity Where there is a resource crisis, there is tremendous macroeconomic potential. Joint research by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and NITI Aayog reveals that transitioning to a circular economy could unlock ₹40 lakh crore ($624 billion) in annual value for India by 2050—equivalent to 30% of its current GDP. In the near term, adopting circular practices across construction, agriculture, mobility, and manufacturing could yield ₹14 lakh crore ($218 billion) in annual material cost savings by 2030, lowering production costs by 11% while creating millions of skilled and semi-skilled green jobs across formal and informal sectors. Bridging tradition and tomorrow The path forward for South Asia does not require importing alien economic philosophies. The core tenets of the circular economy are already encoded in our cultural history, our childhood memories of the bhandiwalla, and our traditional business networks. By combining modern technology and regulatory frameworks with our ancestral values of resource stewardship and non-wastage, South Asia can transform its urban waste challenges into a powerful engine for job creation, sustainable growth, and long-term economic prosperity. (The author is the President of the Lanka India Business Association (LIBA). He can be reached at [email protected])

audit.headline: Lula seeks deeper Sri Lanka trade ties as $ 1 b target looms
audit.summary: Anura Kumara Dissanayake (left) with Lula da Silva at the AI Impact 2026 Summit in New Delhi in February 2026 Newly elected for a fourth term, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has expressed hope of deepening bilateral trade and technical cooperation with Sri Lanka, as the two countries work towards elevating bilateral trade to $ 1 billion by 2030. “I hope we can deepen technical cooperation and bilateral trade between our countries,” Lula said in a post on X, responding to President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s message congratulating him on his election victory. Lula also recalled meeting Dissanayake in India in February this year. The $ 1 billion trade target was agreed at the Second Round of Bilateral Political Consultations, held in Colombo on 20 March, 2026.
audit.body: Anura Kumara Dissanayake (left) with Lula da Silva at the AI Impact 2026 Summit in New Delhi in February 2026 Newly elected for a fourth term, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has expressed hope of deepening bilateral trade and technical cooperation with Sri Lanka, as the two countries work towards elevating bilateral trade to $ 1 billion by 2030. “I hope we can deepen technical cooperation and bilateral trade between our countries,” Lula said in a post on X, responding to President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s message congratulating him on his election victory. Lula also recalled meeting Dissanayake in India in February this year. The $ 1 billion trade target was agreed at the Second Round of Bilateral Political Consultations, held in Colombo on 20 March, 2026. At the talks, both sides acknowledged steady growth in economic cooperation and stressed the importance of broadening engagement in response to evolving global economic dynamics. Under the technical cooperation framework, the Dairy Livestock Project and the Sugarcane Project have been finalised and are expected to be signed in the near future, with support from the Brazilian Cooperation Agency (ABC). The parties also committed to finalising outstanding legal instruments on defence, law enforcement, countering human smuggling and transnational organised crime, traditional and Ayurvedic medicine, and diplomatic training. New avenues for cooperation were identified in agriculture, animal husbandry, agricultural research, ports and shipping, and sports. Both sides agreed to continue close collaboration in bilateral and multilateral forums. In his post, Lula said Brazilians had shown that democracy could be defended against disinformation and extremism. In an earlier post on X, Dissanayake described Lula’s win as historic, saying it showed that people could not be misled by political dynasties and forces of the past. “Today, the people of Brazil did not just win an election; they defeated the forces of corruption, division and political lies,” Dissanayake said. The target requires roughly a five-fold increase on current levels. Two-way trade was $ 199.5 million in 2025, according to Export Development Board (EDB) data. Sri Lanka’s exports to Brazil fell 13.2% to $ 73.5 million, while imports from Brazil surged 77.5% to $ 126 million, leaving a deficit of $ 52.5 million. Sri Lanka had run a surplus with Brazil every year from 2018 to 2024, according to Sri Lanka Customs data published by the Sri Lankan Embassy in Brasilia. Exports peaked at $ 84.6 million in 2024, led by apparel, new pneumatic tyres, fuel oil and retreaded or used rubber tyres. Synthetic rubber, sugar and paper were the main imports. The Embassy says there were no recorded significant Brazilian investments in Sri Lanka as of 2023. It lists light vessels, animal feed preparations, rubber gloves, new pneumatic tyres, desiccated coconut, cinnamon and solid or cushion tyres as having strong export potential in Brazil. Trade under the Global System of Trade Preferences among Developing Countries (GSTP), to which both countries belong, remains negligible: Sri Lanka’s exports under the scheme were $ 80,000 in 2022.

audit.headline: Cabinet approves $ 100 m ADB loan to support Sri Lanka’s economic recovery
audit.summary: - Facility comprises equal $ 50 m policy-based and investment loans - Financing falls under ADB’s $ 620 m Macro-Recovery Sectoral Development Program - Cabinet Spokesman says Govt. to assess need for fresh IMF deal in early 2027 amid global uncertainties The Cabinet of Ministers has approved a $ 100 million loan agreement with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) to support Sri Lanka’s economic recovery and reform agenda. The approval follows the conclusion of formal loan negotiations between the Department of External Resources and the ADB. The proposal was submitted by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in his capacity as Finance, Planning and Economic Development Minister.
audit.body: - Facility comprises equal $ 50 m policy-based and investment loans - Financing falls under ADB’s $ 620 m Macro-Recovery Sectoral Development Program - Cabinet Spokesman says Govt. to assess need for fresh IMF deal in early 2027 amid global uncertainties The Cabinet of Ministers has approved a $ 100 million loan agreement with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) to support Sri Lanka’s economic recovery and reform agenda. The approval follows the conclusion of formal loan negotiations between the Department of External Resources and the ADB. The proposal was submitted by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in his capacity as Finance, Planning and Economic Development Minister. “The financing will be provided from the ADB’s regular general capital resources and will consist of two equal components; a policy-based loan of $ 50 million and an investment loan of $ 50 million,” Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said at the weekly post-Cabinet meeting media briefing yesterday. The facility forms part of the Macro-Recovery Sectoral Development Program, which the Cabinet approved for implementation on 7 September 2026. The program draws on $ 100 million from a broader $ 620 million ADB policy-based loan facility. The wider facility, approved by the Cabinet on 16 March 2026, covers five sub-programs and is intended to advance Sri Lanka’s reform agenda in line with the IMF’s Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program. The Cabinet had also authorised negotiations with the ADB at that time. The latest approval comes as the Government considers whether Sri Lanka will require a fresh IMF arrangement after the current EFF program expires in March 2027. Dr. Jayatissa said the question of a new IMF facility had not been discussed at Monday’s Cabinet meeting. He noted that the evolving international situation, particularly tensions in the Middle East, would influence the Government’s assessment of the economy’s ability to withstand further external shocks without additional support. “No one can predict what will happen amidst the ongoing Middle East tensions and if the Government is considering a fresh deal with the IMF, it would only be discussed in the early months of 2027,” he said, adding the Government was balancing its growth ambitions against the need to preserve economic stability. At the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026, President Dissanayake said discussions were underway on the possibility of a new agreement with the IMF that would shift the emphasis from crisis recovery towards economic growth without reversing gains achieved under the existing program. “We are at a mid-level and open about it,” the President said during a fireside chat at the summit, adding that the Government would use the remaining six months of the current arrangement to assess its options before deciding on the future of its engagement with the IMF (https://www.ft.lk/front-page/President-keeps-door-open-to-fresh-IMF-deal/44-798601).

audit.headline: Why Sri Lanka needs Singapore Temasek-style holding model for SOEs
audit.summary: Rethinking role of State in business State-owned enterprises (SOEs) play a significant role in Sri Lanka’s economy. They provide essential services, support national development, generate employment, and manage important public assets. However, the performance of many SOEs has raised serious concerns about financial sustainability, operational efficiency, accountability, and the effective use of public resources. The International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its Country Report No. 23/116, issued in March 2023, identified substantial scope for improving the operational efficiency of Sri Lanka’s State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs). The fundamental question is not whether the State should own businesses rather than whether the State has the right institutional structure to manage its commercial investments effectively.
audit.body: Rethinking role of State in business State-owned enterprises (SOEs) play a significant role in Sri Lanka’s economy. They provide essential services, support national development, generate employment, and manage important public assets. However, the performance of many SOEs has raised serious concerns about financial sustainability, operational efficiency, accountability, and the effective use of public resources. The International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its Country Report No. 23/116, issued in March 2023, identified substantial scope for improving the operational efficiency of Sri Lanka’s State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs). The fundamental question is not whether the State should own businesses rather than whether the State has the right institutional structure to manage its commercial investments effectively. Sri Lanka needs to move beyond treating SOEs as extensions of Government ministries and begin managing them as professionally governed business enterprises. One possible approach is to establish a Sri Lankan State-owned holding company inspired by Singapore’s Temasek Holdings. The objective should not be to copy Singapore blindly but it should be to adapt the principles that make the Temasek model valuable pillars of professional ownership, independent boards, commercial discipline, transparent reporting, and long-term value creation. Sri Lanka needs a Government that acts as a responsible owner of businesses, rather than a Government that attempts to run every business through the machinery of administration. 1. Understanding Singapore Temasek model Temasek Holdings was established in 1974 to own and commercially manage investments and assets previously held by the Singapore Government. Its creation helped separate the Government’s role as a policymaker from its role as a shareholder in commercial enterprises. Today, Temasek is wholly owned by the Singapore Ministry of Finance but operates through its own board and professional management structure. Under the Temasek model, the Government establishes the overall ownership objectives and appoints a competent board. The board, in turn, oversees the company’s strategy, risk management, investments, and senior management. Individual businesses are responsible for their own operational and commercial decisions. The Government does not ordinarily direct individual investment decisions. In simple terms, the model creates a clear separation between three functions: - Government: Develops national policy, establishes the legal framework, and defines the State’s ownership objectives. - Holding company: Manages the State’s commercial investment portfolio, appoints and evaluates subsidiary boards, and monitors performance. - Individual Enterprise Units: Manage daily operations, employees, customers, costs, investments, and business performance. This arrangement allows commercial enterprises units to operate with greater professional independence while remaining accountable for their results. Temasek is not simply a fund into which the Government deposits money. It owns investments and manages a portfolio of companies with a long-term commercial orientation. It also distributes dividends to its shareholder and publishes information about its performance. The central lesson for Sri Lanka is that public ownership and professional business management do not have to be competing objectives. 2. Why Sri Lanka needs a different approach Sri Lanka has established numerous public enterprises to support economic development, provide essential services, and protect national interests. Some perform important commercial functions, while others deliver services that the private sector may not provide adequately or affordably. Nevertheless, the performance of SOEs cannot be judged solely by their size, number of employees, or importance to the economy. They must also be evaluated according to their financial results, service quality, productivity, governance, and contribution to national development. Several structural challenges make reform necessary. 2.1 Political interference in commercial decisions One of the major challenges faced by SOEs was the potential influence of short-term political priorities on long-term business decisions. Frequent changes in leadership, politically influenced appointments, and decisions that do not adequately consider commercial consequences can weaken institutional stability. When business decisions depend on political relationships rather than professional judgement, accountability becomes difficult to establish. A Temasek-style holding company could reduce this risk by introducing transparent board selection criteria, competency-based appointments, fixed performance expectations, and clearly defined responsibilities. Political leaders would retain responsibility for national policy and public ownership objectives, but ordinary commercial decisions would be delegated to professionally appointed boards and management teams. 2.2 Financial losses and the burden on taxpayers When an SOE repeatedly incurs losses, the consequences extend beyond the enterprise itself. The Government may need to provide additional capital, settle outstanding obligations, restructure debt, or finance essential operations. These resources have an opportunity cost. Money used to support inefficient operations cannot be used for other priorities such as education, healthcare, infrastructure, and social protection. However, not every loss indicates poor management. An enterprise may be required to provide services below commercial cost for legitimate social or economic reasons. The real problem arises when the Government does not clearly distinguish between commercial losses and the cost of fulfilling public-service obligations. Under a reformed model, every enterprise should have an agreed financial and operational mandate. If the Government requires an enterprise to provide a socially necessary service at a loss, the obligation and its cost should be explicitly identified, budgeted, and transparently financed. This would allow management to be held accountable for controllable business performance without unfairly penalising enterprises for Government-imposed obligations. 2.3 Weak accountability and fragmented ownership SOEs are often subject to multiple layers of oversight involving boards, ministries, departments, Treasury officials, and other public institutions. Although oversight is necessary, fragmented responsibilities can make it difficult to determine who is ultimately accountable for poor performance. A holding company could create a clearer ownership structure. It would establish measurable performance targets, appoint competent boards, monitor results, and take corrective action when enterprises fail to meet agreed objectives. The objective would not be to eliminate public accountability. Instead, it would be to make accountability more meaningful by linking authority, responsibility, and measurable results. 2.4 Limited transparency and inconsistent performance information Effective reform requires reliable information. The Government, Parliament, investors, employees, and citizens should be able to understand the financial position of major SOEs, their liabilities, government support, operational performance, and contributions to the economy. Sri Lanka has previously pursued performance-management initiatives, including Statements of Corporate Intent for selected SOEs. However, a stronger and more consistent ownership framework is needed to make performance monitoring a regular institutional practice rather than an isolated reform exercise. A holding company should therefore publish audited consolidated financial statements, enterprise-level results, board information, key performance indicators, and details of material Government support. Transparency should be a foundational requirement from the first day of operation. 3. The Proposed solution: Establish “Lanka Holdings” Sri Lanka could establish a State-owned holding company under a new State Business Enterprises Management Act. For the purposes of this proposal, the institution may be called Lanka Holdings. It would be a public limited company wholly owned by the State, with the Treasury acting as its shareholder. Its principal responsibility would be to manage designated Government-owned commercial investments professionally and maximise their sustainable long-term value. The proposed company should not become another ministry, a regulatory authority, or a central body that micromanages every subsidiary. Instead, it should operate as a professional shareholder with a clear mandate. Its principal functions would include: 1. Holding the State’s shares in designated commercial enterprises. 2. Appointing qualified and independent boards through a transparent selection process. 3. Providing authority to take operational and administrative decisions. 4. Establishing measurable financial, operational, and governance targets. 5. Monitoring the performance and financial risks of subsidiaries. 6. Allocating capital according to commercial viability and national priorities. 7. Publishing audited consolidated accounts and regular performance reports. 8. Receiving dividends and distributing an agreed portion to the treasury. 9. Recommending restructuring, mergers, partnerships, listings, or divestments where appropriate. The holding company should be subject to parliamentary oversight, independent audit, applicable public disclosure requirements, and clearly defined statutory responsibilities. Its independence must not become an excuse for secrecy or the avoidance of public accountability. 4. Three-tier structure for Sri Lankan SOEs Sri Lanka should not place every State-owned institution under the same commercial model. Enterprises have different purposes, risks, and obligations. A more practical approach would classify them into three broad categories. Tier 1: Commercial enterprises This category would include commercially oriented businesses such as telecommunications, airlines, hotels, plantations, and selected financial or other business enterprises, subject to legal, regulatory, and strategic considerations. Their principal objective should be to generate sustainable financial returns, improve productivity, serve customers, and protect the value of public assets. Each enterprise should operate under a professionally approved business plan with measurable targets for profitability, cash flow, productivity, customer satisfaction, and investment. Where an enterprise is commercially viable, the holding company should support expansion, innovation, partnerships, and access to capital. Where an enterprise remains unviable despite reasonable restructuring, options such as mergers, strategic partnerships, minority listings, or divestment should be evaluated transparently and on their merits. The objective is not to sell public assets indiscriminately. It is to ensure that the State retains ownership where justified and uses its capital efficiently. Tier 2: Strategic utilities and essential services Some enterprises provide services that are essential to national security, economic stability, or public welfare. Examples may include Electricity, Petroleum, Railway, and port-related enterprises. These businesses should not be evaluated exclusively on short-term profitability. Their performance should be assessed against a dual mandate of financial sustainability and the delivery of clearly defined public-service obligations. For example, if the Government requires an enterprise to maintain an uneconomic service for social reasons, the cost should be separately calculated and financed through an approved mechanism. This would prevent hidden subsidies from distorting financial results and would help the public understand the true cost of Government policy. Commercial discipline and social responsibility can coexist, provided that both are clearly defined. Tier 3: Non-core and persistently unviable entities Sri Lanka should undertake a comprehensive review of smaller, overlapping, inactive, and persistently unviable State-owned entities. Depending on their functions and legal obligations, these enterprises could be merged, consolidated, restructured, transferred, or wound up. A dedicated restructuring unit could coordinate this process using transparent criteria, independent financial assessments, and clearly defined timelines. Before making any decision, the Government must assess employment consequences, contractual commitments, public-service requirements, and the interests of affected stakeholders. Restructuring should be evidence-based, not an automatic exercise in closure or privatisation. 5. Independent Boards and professional leadership The success of Lanka Holdings would depend less on its name or legal structure than on the quality of its governance. An institution that is formally independent but remains vulnerable to political appointments and informal interference would reproduce the same weaknesses it was designed to address. The holding company should therefore have a predominantly independent board with expertise in finance, corporate governance, strategy, law, risk management, technology, and relevant industry expertise. Board members should be selected through a transparent, competency-based process, with published eligibility criteria, declarations of interests, and safeguards against conflicts of interest. Ministers should not sit on the holding company’s board or the boards of its commercial subsidiaries. Their role should be exercised through the Government’s ownership policy and lawful shareholder mechanisms. The CEO should be appointed through a professional process, with clearly defined responsibilities, an appropriate term of office, and performance-linked remuneration. Appointments and removals should follow established legal procedures, with protection against arbitrary political interference. Each subsidiary board should have genuine authority to supervise its management and make business decisions. The holding company should set strategic expectations and assess results, rather than interfere in routine operational matters. This is the essential difference between a professional holding company and a centralised administrative department. 6. Financial discipline, dividends, and reinvestment A well-designed holding company should improve the way the State manages the financial resources invested in its enterprises. First, all participating companies should prepare reliable financial statements and disclose material liabilities, guarantees, subsidies, and related-party transactions. Second, the holding company should establish a transparent dividend policy. Profitable enterprises would contribute dividends according to their financial capacity, capital requirements, investment plans, and long-term sustainability. These dividends could provide a more predictable return to the treasury and, ultimately, the public. However, the Government should not extract excessive dividends from enterprises that need capital to maintain infrastructure, modernise operations, or remain competitive. Dividend decisions should balance current public revenue with future enterprise value. Third, capital should be allocated according to transparent investment criteria. Enterprises with credible business plans and strong prospects should be able to compete for investment on merit. Fourth, public enterprises should not be encouraged to accumulate hidden liabilities under the assumption that the treasury will always rescue them. Government guarantees, where justified, should be explicitly authorised, disclosed, and assessed for fiscal risk. The long-term objective should be to create a cycle in which commercially sound enterprises generate returns, retain sufficient funds for sustainable growth, and contribute appropriately to public finances. 7. Listing on CSE: Option, not objective in itself A Temasek-style holding structure could create opportunities for carefully selected SOEs to access the capital market. A minority listing could introduce additional disclosure requirements, independent scrutiny, market-based valuation, and broader investor participation. It could also help enterprises raise capital for expansion without relying entirely on Government funding. Nevertheless, listing should not be treated as a substitute for governance reform. An enterprise should not be listed merely to raise immediate revenue or transfer financial risks to private investors. It should first demonstrate credible accounts, appropriate governance, a viable business strategy, and a clear ownership and regulatory framework. Where national interests require the State to retain control, a minority listing could be considered. Where listing is unsuitable, the enterprise could remain wholly State-owned while operating under professional commercial governance. The principle should be simple “Reform governance first, establish credibility next, and consider market participation when the conditions are right.” 8. Lessons from SEMA and previous reform attempts Sri Lanka’s previous institutional reform experiences offer an important warning. The establishment of another authority or restructuring institution does not, by itself, guarantee sustainable reform. An institution may lose effectiveness if it lacks a clear mandate, consistent political support, operational independence, or the authority needed to implement its responsibilities. The proposed Lanka Holdings must therefore be designed to avoid becoming another institution that exists on paper but has limited influence over actual SOE performance. Its mandate should be established by legislation, with clear limits on political intervention and transparent rules governing board appointments, reporting, capital allocation, and restructuring decisions. The law should also define the circumstances in which the Government can issue lawful directions and require such directions to be documented and disclosed, subject to legitimate confidentiality and national-security requirements. At the same time, no statutory arrangement can eliminate political interference entirely. Strong institutions require enforcement, a professional public service, independent oversight, and sustained public commitment. Sri Lanka should learn from earlier reform attempts by building safeguards into the institutional design rather than relying on assurances of good intentions. 9. Protecting public assets and workers’ interests SOE reform must be approached as a national economic and governance reform, not simply as a cost-cutting programme. Employees have legitimate concerns about job security, working conditions, statutory payments, career development, and fair treatment. These concerns should be addressed through consultation, transparent restructuring plans, skills development, redeployment where feasible, and legally compliant employment arrangements. Workers’ retirement savings, including the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) and Employees’ Trust Fund (ETF), should not be treated as a convenient source of capital for the holding company. Any involvement of these funds in investment activities must remain subject to their own legal mandates, fiduciary duties, and independent governance. Similarly, public assets should not be transferred or sold without proper valuation, due diligence, disclosure, and safeguards against conflicts of interest. A successful reform programme must demonstrate that better governance benefits the country as a whole, not only investors or the treasury. 10. Practical five-year implementation roadmap Sri Lanka should introduce the proposed model gradually, with measurable milestones and independent evaluation. Years 1–2: Establish the foundations - Enact the necessary legislation and establish Lanka Holdings. - Complete an inventory and financial assessment of State-owned enterprises. - Select an initial group of approximately 10–15 commercially oriented enterprises, subject to due diligence and legal requirements. - Appoint professional boards and establish performance agreements. - Publish audited financial statements and baseline performance indicators. - Establish clear rules on appointments, disclosure, dividends, and conflicts of interest. Years 3–4: Expand and strengthen - Evaluate the performance of the first group and correct weaknesses. - Consider transferring additional commercial enterprises into the holding structure. - Introduce a transparent framework for the public-service obligations of strategic utilities. - Evaluate suitable minority listings and strategic partnerships. - Publish consolidated reports on financial performance, public support, liabilities, and governance. Year 5 onwards: Consolidate and create long-term value - Expand the portfolio only when governance and reporting standards are demonstrably effective. - Restructure or consolidate persistently unviable enterprises where justified. - Reinvest capital in commercially sound opportunities and national development priorities. - Assess whether a separate savings or investment is appropriate, but only if fiscal conditions and genuine sustainable surpluses support it. Progress should be measured through improvements in financial sustainability, productivity, service quality, transparency, capital efficiency, and the reduction of unjustified fiscal risks not simply by the number of enterprises transferred or privatised. 11. Can Sri Lanka replicate Singapore’s success? Sri Lanka should recognise that Temasek operates within a different institutional and economic environment. Singapore’s experience cannot be separated from its governance arrangements, professional capabilities, regulatory framework, and long-term policy consistency. Consequently, establishing a holding company will not automatically make Sri Lankan SOEs profitable. If the same political appointment practices, weak reporting systems, and informal interventions continue under a new institutional name, the reform will achieve little. Sri Lanka must first establish credible ownership rules, independent boards, transparent accounts, enforceable performance targets, and effective oversight. It must also accept that some enterprises may require fundamental restructuring, while others may be commercially viable if their governance and operating arrangements improve. The objective should not be to promise that every SOE will generate profits. It should be to ensure that every SOE has a clearly justified purpose, an accountable management structure, a transparent financial position, and a measurable contribution to the country. Conclusion: From political ownership to professional stewardship Sri Lanka’s SOE challenge is fundamentally a governance challenge. The country needs to move from fragmented administrative control towards professional, transparent, and accountable ownership of its commercial public assets. A Singapore Temasek-style holding company could provide an institutional framework for this transformation. By separating policymaking from commercial ownership, strengthening independent boards, introducing financial discipline, and making performance visible to the public, Sri Lanka could improve the management of its State-owned businesses and reduce unnecessary fiscal pressures. However, the proposed model should not be regarded as a shortcut to economic recovery. It must be supported by sound legislation, credible institutions, professional leadership, transparent financial reporting, and consistent implementation. The ultimate purpose is not merely to increase profits or collect dividends. It is to protect the value of public assets, improve the quality of essential services, encourage productive investment, and ensure that the State’s commercial resources contribute more effectively to national development. (The author holds a DBA (Reading), MBA in HRM, Pg Dip in HRM, Pg Dip in Def.Mgt, BBA in HRM, Assoc CIPD(UK), AMCIPM(SL) and was Deputy General Manager (HR & Administration) at Sri Lanka State Plantations Corporations)

audit.headline: AG indicts Namal Rajapaksa on 24 charges over Airbus deal
audit.summary: Namal Rajapaksa - Indictment filed before Colombo Permanent Trial-at-Bar, with 59 witnesses listed - Chief Magistrate orders MP kept in custody until produced before Trial-at-Bar today The Attorney General has filed an indictment comprising 24 charges against Parliamentarian Namal Rajapaksa before the Colombo Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar, over alleged bribery in connection with the Airbus transaction, the Colombo Chief Magistrate’s Court was informed yesterday. Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara told Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga S. Bodaragama that the indictment lists 59 witnesses. The Chief Magistrate ordered that Rajapaksa be kept in custody until he is produced before the Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar today (28).

Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara told Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga S. Bodaragama that the indictment lists 59 witnesses. The Chief Magistrate ordered that Rajapaksa be kept in custody until he is produced before the Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar today (28). AG indicts Delivering the order, the Magistrate said that since the indictment had already been filed before the Trial-at-Bar, the Magistrate’s Court could no longer issue any judicial order concerning the suspect in the case, including one granting bail or remanding him. The Magistrate added that no exceptional circumstances had been presented to justify releasing Rajapaksa on bail.

audit.headline: Beyond promises on paper: Sri Lanka must deliver on investments it wins
audit.summary: In January 2025, Sri Lanka signed an agreement with Sinopec for a $ 3.7 billion refinery project in Hambantota, which remains on paper Several years have passed since Sri Lanka faced the most severe economic crisis in its history. Macroeconomic stability has largely been restored, and the country is now nearing the end of its current IMF program, which has required strict fiscal discipline. Whether Sri Lanka will need to return to the IMF remains an open question. However, the next stage of recovery cannot rely on austerity measures and support from multilateral institutions alone. Of these, FDI has become especially pressing in light of recent events.
audit.body: In January 2025, Sri Lanka signed an agreement with Sinopec for a $ 3.7 billion refinery project in Hambantota, which remains on paper Several years have passed since Sri Lanka faced the most severe economic crisis in its history. Macroeconomic stability has largely been restored, and the country is now nearing the end of its current IMF program, which has required strict fiscal discipline. Whether Sri Lanka will need to return to the IMF remains an open question. However, the next stage of recovery cannot rely on austerity measures and support from multilateral institutions alone. The key growth reforms include liberalising trade and diversifying the export base, making the tax system more efficient and fair, addressing labour market rigidities, and improving and streamlining FDI regulations. Of these, FDI has become especially pressing in light of recent events. Much of the policy discussion centres on attracting new investors through roadshows, investment forums and incentive packages. However, less attention is given to an equally important aspect of the FDI story, retaining the investments already secured. Every project that is withdrawn, delayed or stalled sends a powerful signal to the wider market, often speaking far louder than any promotional campaign. Two recent cases make the point. China Merchants Port Holdings (CMPort) withdrew from its planned $ 392 million logistics hub project at the Port of Colombo in October. Meanwhile, Sinopec’s proposed $ 3.7 billion refinery project in Hambantota, considered the largest FDI commitment in Sri Lanka’s history, remains at a standstill despite the signing of the MoU. Lost opportunity at Colombo Port On 15 October CMPort exited the commercial and logistics hub project following a mutually agreed settlement with its Sri Lankan partners, Access Engineering, and the Sri Lanka Ports Authority. Established through a joint venture company, the South Asia Commercial and Logistics Hub was envisaged as South Asia’s largest integrated commercial and logistics hub, aimed at strengthening Sri Lanka’s position as a regional trade and maritime centre. In 2023, an agreement was signed for the construction and operation of the facility under a 50 year Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) arrangement. Under the agreement, CMPort held a 70% stake in the project, while the Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Access Engineering each held 15%. The decision to withdraw from the investment was driven by concerns relating to the project’s implementation environment, timelines and commercial considerations while some local observers attribute the withdrawal to broader geopolitical pressures. Following the project’s termination, the Sri Lanka Ports Authority has announced plans to develop a new logistics hub through a competitive public private partnership (PPP) model. It is important to emphasise that CMPort is not leaving Sri Lanka. The company continues to operate the container terminal at the Port of Colombo and remains involved in the Hambantota Port. However, that is precisely the point, when an investor that has already established a long term presence in the country decides to withdraw from a new project, potential investors take notice. Sinopec’s Hambantota refinery: Biggest deal still on paper In January 2025, Sri Lanka signed an agreement with Sinopec for a $ 3.7 billion refinery project in Hambantota with a planned processing capacity of 200,000 barrels per day, a significant portion of which is intended for export market. The project is set to represent the largest FDI commitment in the country’s history. For context, Sri Lanka’s only existing refinery at Sapugaskanda has a processing capacity of just 50,000 barrels of crude oil per day. Despite its scale and strategic significance, the project has made little progress amid a series of unresolved concerns. Mainly the disagreement over market access, with Sinopec seeking unrestricted access to sell its refined products in the local market, while the Government has limited domestic sales to 20% of total output. Additional points of contention include requests for more land, the fiscal concessions available to the investor, and concerns regarding long term water availability in the Hambantota region. On the issue of local market access, in early 2026, Ministry of Energy stated that Sinopec agreed to proceed with the project under the Government’s 20% cap on domestic fuel sales. At the time, authorities expressed confidence that construction would commence sooner, while also indicating willingness to consider Sinopec’s request for more access to the local fuel market. However, the project remains on paper, with no clear implementation timeline in place. As a result, the economic benefits associated with the investment continue to be delayed. What these cases tell us The two projects differ significantly in scale and sector, yet they share a common pattern. Both were announced with headlines on papers, both encountered obstacles, and both have remained stalled long enough to erode investor confidence. Getting the fundamentals right from the beginning is essential. The disagreements over land allocation, regulatory clearances and market access surfaced only after agreements had been signed. These are issues that should have been resolved during negotiations. Once a project is announced, investors should have confidence that its core terms and conditions are settled and will not be subject to renegotiation. Delay carries a cost of its own. Projects that spend years waiting for land allocation, regulatory approvals or final agreements risk losing momentum, missing financing opportunities and weakening internal support from investor’s side. More often than not, prolonged delays inflict more damage on a project than any single obstacle. By the time outstanding issues are resolved, the original investment rationale may no longer exist. Sri Lanka’s investment story is not written on a paper or promotional campaigns. It is written in the fate of the projects already on the table. A completed refinery in Hambantota or a fully operational logistics hub in Colombo would do far more to attract the next wave of investors than any investment forum or overseas roadshows. The priority now should be not only to attract new investment opportunities but also to strengthen investor aftercare. This requires a robust framework centred on a single point of accountability for approved projects, time bound approval processes, and the early and transparent resolution of land, regulatory and policy related issues. Attracting investment is only half the challenge. Retaining it, implementing it and converting commitments into successful projects are what ultimately build a country’s reputation as a credible investment destination. (The author is a researcher in a leading private investment research firm in Sri Lanka, whose primary focus is researching broader economic issues, including geopolitical/technological developments, and their implications across various sectors with special focus and interest on related developments in China)

audit.headline: Cabinet approves amendment regulations on licensing of tea brokers
audit.summary: The Cabinet of Ministers has approved submitting to Parliament amendment regulations relating to the grant of licenses to tea brokers. The amendments were published in Gazette Extraordinary No. 2501/68 dated 12 August 2026, following the approval given by the Cabinet at its meeting held on 22 June 2026. The regulations amend the Regulations for the Grant of Licences to Producers (Tea) Brokers, 1979, which were made under the provisions of the Producers (Legalisation) of Producers Act, No. 9 of 1979. The amendment regulations will now be placed before Parliament for approval. The proposal to this effect was submitted by Plantations and Community Infrastructure Minister Samantha Viddyarathna.
