The decision was taken on a proposal submitted by the Plantations and Community Infrastructure Minister Samantha Viddyarathna, following recommendations made by the High Level Procurement Committee after evaluating the proposals received. The Cabinet had previously approved inviting expressions of interest (EOIs) from investors to lease out underutilised land and property managed by the three entities, with the aim of ensuring their optimal utilisation. Announcing the decision at the weekly post-Cabinet meeting media briefing yesterday, Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said under the first phase, EOIs were invited for 1,514 hectares of land, 10 tourist bungalows and scenic spots, and 15 inactive factories. He said a total of 470 interested investors responded. Requests for proposals were then invited from shortlisted investors, and 44 proposals were received for 30 plots of land and property. “These were evaluated by the High Level Procurement Committee, whose recommendations formed the basis of the Cabinet’s decision,” he added.

audit.headline: From consumption to capacity: Taxing those who can pay
audit.summary: The World Bank has said what many Sri Lankan taxpayers have long felt. In a recent interview, World Bank Senior Economist Jakob Engel said Sri Lanka’s tax system should be progressive and simple, and focused primarily on taxing those who can most afford to pay. He also called for broadening the base, widening the tax net, and moving from indirect taxes towards direct taxes. The timing matters. As Budget 2027 approaches, the question is no longer whether Sri Lanka needs more revenue. The question now is who should pay it, and how. First phase was necessary In 2022, Sri Lanka was collecting only around 7–8% of GDP in revenue, while even low-income countries were moving towards 15%. Under the IMF-backed reform program. VAT and income taxes were raised and exemptions were cut back. These measures were painful, but they were needed to restore fiscal stability.
audit.body: The World Bank has said what many Sri Lankan taxpayers have long felt. In a recent interview, World Bank Senior Economist Jakob Engel said Sri Lanka’s tax system should be progressive and simple, and focused primarily on taxing those who can most afford to pay. He also called for broadening the base, widening the tax net, and moving from indirect taxes towards direct taxes. The timing matters. As Budget 2027 approaches, the question is no longer whether Sri Lanka needs more revenue. The question now is who should pay it, and how. First phase was necessary In 2022, Sri Lanka was collecting only around 7–8% of GDP in revenue, while even low-income countries were moving towards 15%. Under the IMF-backed reform program. VAT and income taxes were raised and exemptions were cut back. These measures were painful, but they were needed to restore fiscal stability. The results are clear in the Finance Ministry’s Final Budget Position Report 2025. Tax revenue rose to Rs. 5,049.2 billion in 2025, or 15.4% of GDP, up from 12.3% in 2024. The World Bank accepts this. It also makes the more important point: revenue has risen very quickly, and the task now is to make it sustainable. Revenue that depends on squeezing the same compliant taxpayers is not sustainable. It is borrowed time. Imbalance we cannot ignore Indirect taxes still account for the bulk of collections, and the Ministry’s own figures show the gap is widening rather than narrowing. Direct taxes made up 33.5% of total tax revenue in 2023. That fell to 27.7% in 2024 and to just 22.6% in 2025, leaving indirect taxes with 77.4% of the total. The composition tells the same story. In 2025, income tax brought in Rs. 1,139.4 billion, or 3.5% of GDP. Taxes on goods and services brought in Rs. 3,198.1 billion, or 9.8% of GDP, almost three times as much. VAT alone raised Rs. 1,746.9 billion, well above total income tax collections. Part of the 2025 shift reflects one-off factors such as excise duty on motor vehicles, which rose to Rs. 471.8 billion from Rs. 58.6 billion in 2024 as vehicle imports resumed. Even so, the long-term direction is clear: revenue growth is coming mainly from consumption. VAT and similar levies are paid by every consumer at the same rate, whatever their income. A daily wage earner buying essentials and a high-net-worth individual buying luxuries add to the same pool, but the burden weighs far more heavily on the first. Indirect taxes are efficient to collect, and no modern system can do without them. But when a tax system leans too heavily on consumption, it becomes regressive almost by default. It also weakens something harder to measure but essential to revenue: public trust. Real gap is compliance, not rates Perhaps the most telling part of the World Bank’s comments is the observation that a large number of people are not complying, and that significant leakages remain in the base, in compliance, and in administration. This is the heart of the matter. Sri Lanka does not mainly have a rate problem; it has a coverage problem. The number of registered taxpayers grew to around 1.3 million in 2025, which is real progress. But registration is not the same as contribution. Salaried employees have tax deducted at source. Registered businesses file, pay, and get audited. Meanwhile, a significant share of people with real economic capacity, such as owners of multiple properties, high-value professionals operating informally, and those whose lifestyles clearly exceed their declared income, remain partly or entirely outside the net. The burden falls on registered businesses too as reflected in the World Bank’s Sri Lanka Enterprise Survey 2025, 27.5% of business owners and top managers of 607 firms reported competing against unregistered or informal firms. When the compliant few carry the load for the non-compliant many, every further rate increase deepens the unfairness. Taxing those who can pay is not about raising rates. It is about finding those who should already be paying. Practical steps for next phase Several measures could turn the World Bank’s principle into practice. Use the data that already exists Land registries, motor vehicle registrations, bank interest records, high-value transactions and foreign travel data together show a great deal about economic capacity. Systematically matching this information against tax filings would identify people who can pay but do not file, without adding any new tax. Link the TIN to economic activity The Government has already introduced the process requiring a Taxpayer Identification Number for major transactions, such as property transfers, high-value vehicle purchases and large investments, which would steadily draw capacity into the net and leaves an audit trail. Shift the mix gradually Moving from indirect to direct taxation should be sequenced, not sudden. With indirect taxes now making up more than three-quarters of tax revenue, a sharp cut in VAT or other consumption taxes would put the hard-won fiscal gains at risk. The shift should instead be tied to results. As income tax compliance improves and the base widens, the extra revenue should be used to ease the burden on consumption, for example by reviewing levies on essential goods or gradually phasing out overlapping taxes such as the SSCL which is a cascading tax in nature. Announcing this link in advance would make the commitment credible. That way, honest taxpayers see that compliance brings relief, not just more obligations. Remove taxes that hold back growth The World Bank has again called for moving away from distortionary taxes, especially para-tariffs, towards taxes that do not hold back private sector activity. A cleaner, simpler tax structure is both a growth measure and a compliance measure. Make administration easier In the World Bank’s Sri Lanka Enterprise Survey 2025, which interviewed business owners and top managers of 607 firms, tax rates ranked as the single biggest obstacle to doing business cited by 19.3%. Tax administration came third at 12.3%, nearly three times the South Asian average of 4.6%. Together, almost one in three named tax as their biggest constraint. Much of this burden can be eased without giving up revenue. Simplified returns, using shorter or pre-filled forms for both individuals and SMEs, would reduce compliance costs and honest errors. Predictable rulings, published on time, would give businesses certainty and prevent disputes. Faster refunds within set timelines, with interest paid on delays, would show that obligations run both ways. Consistent assessments would ensure compliant taxpayers are not targeted simply because they are easy to reach. None of these costs much in revenue, yet each does a great deal for the willingness to comply. The need for Tax Ombudsman The steps above, particularly data matching and TIN linkage, will give the Inland Revenue Department far greater visibility and reach. As the Government tightens tax administration and the Department is given stronger powers to access data, assess and collect, there must be an equally strong safeguard for taxpayers. An independent Tax Ombudsman would provide that. It would give taxpayers an accessible, low-cost avenue to raise complaints about delays, unfair treatment or the improper use of powers, without having to resort to lengthy appeals or litigation. Enhanced powers are necessary to reach those outside the net, but they must be applied consistently and within their intent, so that the honest taxpayers already in the net do not bear the cost of reaching those outside it. A Tax Ombudsman would bring transparency and accountability to the process and reassure taxpayers that stronger enforcement will be matched by fair treatment. As the system becomes stricter, an ombudsman is needed more than ever before. Protect taxpayer data The approach outlined above depends on the tax administration holding more information about taxpayers than ever before. Returns capture details of assets and liabilities, bank balances are reported through banking channels, and property ownership and transfers are drawn from the land registry etc. This is highly sensitive information, and the Government must ensure that it is protected with the same seriousness with which it is collected. Strong data privacy measures are needed, including strict controls on who can access taxpayer information and for what purpose, secure systems, clear audit trails of access, and meaningful consequences for any unauthorised use or disclosure. Taxpayers must be able to trust that the information they provide will be used only for tax purposes and kept secure. That trust is what will allow them to rely on the system. Without it, the very data that is meant to widen the net may instead drive people further away from it. The Government’s new Medium-Term Revenue Strategy, which aims to close compliance gaps in VAT, income tax and other areas, provides the framework. What matters now is whether it is implemented consistently. Fairness as revenue strategy Tax morale, meaning a citizen’s willingness to pay, is shaped by what people see. When people see that those with visible wealth are paying their share, compliance rises. When they see the opposite, even honest taxpayers begin to question why they should stay in the system. That is why the World Bank’s message goes beyond economic advice. A progressive, simple tax system focused on capacity to pay is fairer. It is also more resilient, because it rests on a broad base rather than on the patience of a narrow one. Road ahead Sri Lanka has done the hard part of raising revenue in a crisis. The next phase is harder in a different way. It requires data, administrative discipline and political will to reach those who have stayed outside the net. Budget 2027 is an opportunity to signal that change, from taxing what people consume to taxing what they can afford. If we get this right, the reward will be more than revenue. It will be a tax system that citizens see as fair and are therefore more willing to support. (This article draws on the recent interview given by World Bank Senior Economist Jakob Engel, World Bank’s Sri Lanka Enterprise Survey 2025 (country profile) published in April 2026 and on the Ministry of Finance’s Final Budget Position Report 2025. The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author in her personal capacity)

audit.headline: APG opens Sri Lanka’s third AML/CFT evaluation
audit.summary: Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe (left) with Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya - PM says financial system strength rests on effectiveness, not just laws and institutions - Corruption, eroding trust in State financial institutions flagged as threat to economic, political stability - Evaluation to test progress against financial crime and alignment with international standards - Govt. pledges full engagement with assessors to retain confidence of international partners, investors The Asia/Pacific Group on Money Laundering (APG) yesterday held the inaugural meeting of Sri Lanka’s Third Mutual Evaluation on Anti-Money Laundering, Countering the Financing of Terrorism and Countering Proliferation Financing (AML/CFT/CPF), with Prime Minister Dr.
audit.body: Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe (left) with Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya - PM says financial system strength rests on effectiveness, not just laws and institutions - Corruption, eroding trust in State financial institutions flagged as threat to economic, political stability - Evaluation to test progress against financial crime and alignment with international standards - Govt. pledges full engagement with assessors to retain confidence of international partners, investors The Asia/Pacific Group on Money Laundering (APG) yesterday held the inaugural meeting of Sri Lanka’s Third Mutual Evaluation on Anti-Money Laundering, Countering the Financing of Terrorism and Countering Proliferation Financing (AML/CFT/CPF), with Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya stressing that the credibility of the country’s financial system would be judged on how its safeguards work in practice. A mutual evaluation is a peer review of how effectively a country prevents its financial system from being used to launder money and to finance terrorism and the spread of weapons of mass destruction. “The strength of a country’s financial system depends not only on the institutions and regulations it puts in place, but also on how effectively they work together in practice,” Dr. Amarasuriya said. She said the evaluation provided an important opportunity for Sri Lanka to demonstrate its progress in combating financial crime, identify areas requiring further improvement and strengthen alignment with international standards. Dr. Amarasuriya warned that corruption and the erosion of public trust in State institutions, particularly financial institutions, posed significant challenges to economic and political stability. Addressing these through transparency, accountability, strong institutional coordination and effective enforcement was essential to safeguarding financial integrity, restoring public confidence and strengthening the country’s economic resilience, she said. She reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to working constructively with the assessment team and all relevant stakeholders to strengthen Sri Lanka’s AML/CFT/CPF framework, address emerging risks and uphold the confidence of international partners and investors, the Prime Minister’s Media Division said. The meeting was attended by Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eranga Weeraratne, Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe, the Secretary to the Minister of Justice and National Integration, members of the Financial Intelligence Unit and members of the assessment team.

audit.headline: A crossing too far
audit.summary: N obody has the right to take our lives unless a court of law sentences us to death and the President signs the death warrant. Other than that, no one has the right to kill us. But what if the drivers of passenger buses we board put our lives at risk by driving onto railway tracks and allowing oncoming trains to crash into their vehicles? What if they keep doing this, time and again? What punishment would you propose for such drivers? We might forgive them once or twice, but what about the 10th or 15th time? On Sunday, 10 students were admitted to the Karapitiya National Hospital after a bus carrying tuition class students collided with a train travelling from Matara to Colombo near the Martin Wickramasinghe Folk Museum in Koggala.
audit.body: N obody has the right to take our lives unless a court of law sentences us to death and the President signs the death warrant. Other than that, no one has the right to kill us. But what if the drivers of passenger buses we board put our lives at risk by driving onto railway tracks and allowing oncoming trains to crash into their vehicles? What if they keep doing this, time and again? What punishment would you propose for such drivers? We might forgive them once or twice, but what about the 10th or 15th time? On Sunday, 10 students were admitted to the Karapitiya National Hospital after a bus carrying tuition class students collided with a train travelling from Matara to Colombo near the Martin Wickramasinghe Folk Museum in Koggala. The incident (not an accident) occurred when a private bus carrying around 60 students from a tuition class in Kottawa was returning after a visit to the museum. Ironically, the bus was named Visekaraya (an undisciplined person). A student on board said that as the bus left the cultural centre and approached the railway crossing, the students inside the bus and bystanders shouted at the driver to stop because a train was approaching. However, the driver ignored their warnings and continued forward, causing the train to hit the rear of the bus. The Habaraduwa Police have taken the driver into custody. But what if the train had struck the middle of the bus? What would have happened to the precious lives of those children? Some of the most serious train–bus collisions in Sri Lanka have occurred at railway level crossings, often when buses have entered the tracks despite warning signals or closed gates. Three particularly significant incidents were the 1989 Ahungalla disaster, the 2005 Polgahawela collision and the 2009 Welikanda collision. The Ahungalla incident occurred in January 1989, when a train travelling towards Galle struck a school bus at an unmanned railway crossing in southern Sri Lanka. Many of those killed were schoolchildren. With 40 deaths and 80 injuries, it was the deadliest of the three collisions mentioned here. The disaster prompted calls for better protection at unattended railway crossings and remains one of the most widely discussed train–bus collisions in Sri Lanka. The second similar incident occurred at Polgahawela (Yangalmodara) on 26 April 2005, claiming 37 lives and leaving many others injured. An intercity train travelling from Colombo to Kandy collided with a crowded passenger bus at a railway crossing near Polgahawela. Reports indicated that the bus had attempted to cross despite the warning gate being closed, possibly while racing another bus. In fact, it is the people who continue to remember this tragedy, not the reckless drivers whose actions put their lives at risk. It remains one of Sri Lanka’s best-known fatal bus–train collisions. The next tragedy occurred at Sevanapitiya, Welikanda, in the Polonnaruwa District, on 16 May 2009. Fifteen people were reported killed, while around 40 others sustained serious injuries. The disaster occurred when a private bus carrying approximately 70 passengers collided with a train at a railway crossing. Reports said the driver had attempted to bypass the railway gate. The incident remained in the news years later when the bus driver was arrested in February 2024 after evading court proceedings. He had been sentenced to death in 2023. The latest ‘accident’ occurred in Koggala on 25 October 2026 (last Sunday), injuring 13 children. Two of them were critically injured and received treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU). The tragedy occurred when a bus carrying students returning from an excursion to the Martin Wickramasinghe Memorial Museum collided with a train travelling from Beliatta to Maradana at a railway crossing near Koggala. According to the police, the bus crossed the railway line despite the warning signals being activated. The driver and his assistant were arrested, and the bus was scheduled for inspection. Both should be banned from driving for the rest of their lives. Such a penalty is not without precedent, as the judiciary in Sri Lanka has already imposed lifetime driving bans on reckless drivers. Several recurring risk factors emerge from these incidents. The first is the disregard for warning signals. Entering a railway crossing while warning lights are flashing or gates are closed, even when bystanders are shouting warnings, is all too common in Sri Lanka. Perhaps these drivers mistake recklessness for bravery. The second factor is bypassing railway barriers. Attempting to cross the tracks through an open lane or by going around a barrier is a common practice among drivers, regardless of who they are. Unprotected railway crossings are another contributing factor. Crossings without adequate barriers or functioning warning systems still exist in the country, leaving road users exposed to the risk of such tragedies. In 2024, Sri Lanka Railways recorded 65 collisions between road vehicles and trains at level crossings, compared with 76 in 2023. A National Audit Office report recorded 1,501 railway-crossing accidents involving road traffic between 2000 and 2022. It is high time the country put an end to these recurring tragedies by imposing lifetime driving bans on those found guilty of recklessly endangering lives at railway crossings.

audit.headline: Taliban rejects Pakistan’s terrorism allegations
audit.summary: The Taliban has rejected Pakistan’s accusations that militants use Afghanistan territory to launch attacks, saying instability in its neighbouring country would harm Afghanistan and the wider region. Zabihullah Mujahid, spokesperson for the Taliban administration, said the authorities lacked the capacity to create or finance insecurity in other countries. He argued that instability in Pakistan would have economic, social and humanitarian consequences for Afghanistan. “We do not have the means to create insecurity in other countries or finance it,” Mujahid said, according to his statement. Mujahid accused Pakistani military and security institutions of blaming Afghanistan when they failed to contain violence at home. He also alleged that Pakistan was spending resources to destabilise Afghanistan but did not provide evidence to support the claim.

His remarks followed statements by Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif at a high-level security meeting in Peshawar, where he accused militants operating from Afghanistan of carrying out repeated attacks against Pakistani security personnel and civilians. (Khaama Press)

audit.headline: Israelis vote for first time since October 2025 Hamas attack
audit.summary: Voter turnout in the first three hours of the Israeli General Election was the highest in decades, Israel’s Central Elections Committee said yesterday (27). According to the committee, nationwide turnout by mid-morning was already at 16.68 percent, the highest at this stage of the vote since 1981 and up from 15.9 percent at the same time in the 2022 election. “By 10 a.m., more than 1,200,000 Israelis had voted,” said the committee’s acting Director General Dean Livne. Total voter turnout in Israeli general elections approached 80 percent the 1990s but hasn’t been higher than 72.3 percent since the turn of the century. Turnout at the last general election in 2022 was 70.6 percent. Turnout among Arab Israelis is expected to be particularly important given the role Arab parties could play as potential kingmakers in coalition talks.

Arabs in Israel make up about 18 percent of the electorate, and pre-election surveys have suggested a sharp increase in voter participation. Data from the Midgam Research Institute cited by the Qatar-owned The New Arab indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62 percent and 63 percent, up from approximately 53 percent in previous elections. The National , based in the United Arab Emirates, said its sources were predicting an “astronomical” Arab turnout. (DW)

audit.headline: Bangladesh measles crisis ‘warning sign’ of other outbreaks
audit.summary: Experts have warned Bangladesh that deadly outbreaks of diphtheria, whooping cough and polio could follow an ongoing measles epidemic that has already killed over 1,200 children, according to a report seen by AFP yesterday. “The measles outbreak is a litmus test and a warning sign of a deteriorating immunisation system,” said the report by an independent committee of national and international experts, which carried out its research earlier in October. Bangladesh has struggled since March to contain the outbreak, which has killed more than 1,200 children and infected 220,000 people, making it the country’s deadliest in decades, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).

Bangladesh has struggled since March to contain the outbreak, which has killed more than 1,200 children and infected 220,000 people, making it the country’s deadliest in decades, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). “If no urgent mitigation measures are taken, it is only a matter of time before there are large outbreaks of pertussis (whooping cough), diphtheria and even vaccine-derived poliovirus,” added the report, which has been submitted to the government. The Health Ministry pledged action yesterday. (FMT)

audit.headline: Bodybuilder Rajkumar shines at LYFT Oman Pro 2026 in Muscat
audit.summary: Sri Lankan bodybuilder Madhavan Rajkumar, professionally known as R.K. Rajakumaran, has achieved a significant milestone by winning the prestigious IFBB Pro Card at the LYFT Oman Pro 2026, bringing pride to Sri Lanka. Hailing from Labukale in the Nuwara Eliya District, Rajakumaran began his bodybuilding journey at the age of 16. Despite facing numerous defeats, hardships and humiliating experiences, he remained committed to his ambition. His latest success is the result of nearly a decade of dedication, disciplined training and perseverance. The international championship was held on October 22 and 23 at the Oman Convention and Exhibition Centre in Muscat, Oman. It attracted more than 150 athletes from over 20 countries, with 32 contests conducted across categories including Bodybuilding, Classic Physique and Men’s Physique.
audit.body: Sri Lankan bodybuilder Madhavan Rajkumar, professionally known as R.K. Rajakumaran, has achieved a significant milestone by winning the prestigious IFBB Pro Card at the LYFT Oman Pro 2026, bringing pride to Sri Lanka. Hailing from Labukale in the Nuwara Eliya District, Rajakumaran began his bodybuilding journey at the age of 16. Despite facing numerous defeats, hardships and humiliating experiences, he remained committed to his ambition. His latest success is the result of nearly a decade of dedication, disciplined training and perseverance. The international championship was held on October 22 and 23 at the Oman Convention and Exhibition Centre in Muscat, Oman. It attracted more than 150 athletes from over 20 countries, with 32 contests conducted across categories including Bodybuilding, Classic Physique and Men’s Physique. Rajkumar impressed the judges with his muscular development, physical conditioning and body symmetry, earning the coveted professional qualification. Educated at Pussellawa Hindu National School, Rajkumar began establishing his reputation in bodybuilding in 2015, winning a silver medal at the Central Province Bodybuilding Championship and a gold medal at the All-Island Schools Games Bodybuilding Championship. These early achievements laid the foundation for his subsequent international success. In 2018, he won a gold medal at the South Asian Bodybuilding Championship in Nepal. He continued his impressive performance in 2019, winning a bronze medal in the men’s 60kg category at the 53rd IFBB Asian Bodybuilding and Fitness Championship in Harbin, China, followed by a silver medal in the men’s 65kg category at the IFBB World Bodybuilding Championship in Fujairah, the United Arab Emirates. His achievement at the World Championship, alongside that of his teammate Amila Gedara, who won a gold medal, contributed to Sri Lanka securing ninth place in the overall team standings. In 2024, Rajkumar also won a gold medal at the United Arab Emirates Bodybuilding Championship. Rajkumar’s latest triumph marks another important chapter in his bodybuilding career. Having earned his professional status, he now hopes to compete against the world’s leading professional bodybuilders, with the ultimate ambition of reaching the prestigious Mr Olympia stage. His journey from a young aspiring bodybuilder in the up-country to an international achiever stands as a testament to the value of determination, sacrifice and consistent training.

audit.headline: NESTOMALT and Ogilvy Digital win Gold at Dragons of Asia Awards
audit.summary: Nestlé Lanka’s flagship malted food drink brand, NESTOMALT, together with Ogilvy Digital, has won a Gold Dragon at the Dragons of Asia Awards 2026 for its Avurudu campaign, (Our Very Own New Year Filled with Power, Strength and Energy). The campaign reimagined NESTOMALT’s enduring values of Power, Strength and Energy for a new generation, celebrating everyday Sri Lankans who embody these qualities and giving the brand a distinctive way to connect during Avurudu , one of the country’s most competitive marketing periods. Presented at the 2026 awards night held in Malaysia, the recognition comes from the Dragons of Asia platform, one of the region’s leading programmes for marketing communications effectiveness, with entries judged on strategy, originality, execution and measurable results.
audit.body: Nestlé Lanka’s flagship malted food drink brand, NESTOMALT, together with Ogilvy Digital, has won a Gold Dragon at the Dragons of Asia Awards 2026 for its Avurudu campaign, (Our Very Own New Year Filled with Power, Strength and Energy). The campaign reimagined NESTOMALT’s enduring values of Power, Strength and Energy for a new generation, celebrating everyday Sri Lankans who embody these qualities and giving the brand a distinctive way to connect during Avurudu , one of the country’s most competitive marketing periods. Presented at the 2026 awards night held in Malaysia, the recognition comes from the Dragons of Asia platform, one of the region’s leading programmes for marketing communications effectiveness, with entries judged on strategy, originality, execution and measurable results. Nestlé Lanka Senior Brand Manager-NESTOMALT Keashan Wijayasinghe said; “ Avurudu has long been a defining moment for NESTOMALT to celebrate the power, strength and energy that have connected the brand with Sri Lankans for generations. Drawing on this long-standing association, the campaign reimagined these enduring brand values as a contemporary celebration of the resilience and determination of the Sri Lankan people, recognising those who embody them through their everyday actions. For a brand that has been part of the nation’s life for over six decades, recognition at the Dragons of Asia is especially meaningful. It is a testament to NESTOMALT’s ability to remain true to its heritage while continually evolving the way it connects with and inspires new generations of Sri Lankans.” The campaign placed fishermen, farmers, tea pluckers, tuk-tuk drivers, municipal workers, security personnel, and many other communities who keep Sri Lanka moving at the heart of NESTOMALT’s Avurudu celebrations. Their unique skills and expertise inspired a fresh interpretation of familiar Avurudu traditions. Ogilvy Digital Director – Digital Rohan Perera said; “The opportunity was to take a brand truth that Sri Lankans have known for generations and find a fresh, culturally relevant way to bring it to life. We realised that Power, Strength and Energy were already all around us in the people whose skills and effort keep the country moving every day. By making them the focus of the idea, we could move beyond simply communicating the brand promise and let people experience it for themselves. For us, that is where creativity becomes most valuable, when a strong idea builds relevance for the brand, connects meaningfully with people and ultimately delivers results for the client.”

audit.headline: Janashakthi Life recognised among Lanka’s Top 20 Great Workplaces for Young Talent

The DPMC Workshop Madapatha, the vehicle servicing, maintenance and repairing centre achieved Gold after progressing from a Merit Award in 2024 to Bronze in 2025.
audit.body: David Pieris Group of Companies has secured two Gold Awards and one Silver Award at the Presidential Environment Awards 2026, recognising its continued commitment to environmental sustainability, innovation and responsible business practices. The awards recognise the environmental initiatives implemented at the DPMC Workshop Madapatha and Matara run by David Pieris Motor Company (Private) Limited and the Assembly Plant in Ranna Manufacturing Complex of David Pieris Motor Company (Lanka) Limited. The DPMC Workshop Madapatha, the vehicle servicing, maintenance and repairing centre achieved Gold after progressing from a Merit Award in 2024 to Bronze in 2025. This consecutive improvement reflects its commitment to enhancing environmental performance through rainwater harvesting, wastewater treatment and reuse, renewable energy utilisation, responsible waste management and resource conservation. Winning Gold in its first participation, the Assembly Plant of the Ranna Manufacturing Complex was recognised for its integrated environmental management practices, including rainwater harvesting, on-site lakes supporting water management, renewable energy projects, systematic waste management and carbon and water footprint assessments. Its Net Zero Energy Certification further demonstrates its commitment to resource efficiency and sustainable industrial operations. The DPMC Workshop Matara secured Silver in its first participation. Its environmental initiatives include rooftop solar power, wastewater treatment and reuse systems that recycle approximately 95% of treated water for vehicle washing, improved resource efficiency and measures to minimise hazardous waste and environmental pollution. These achievements demonstrate the Group’s commitment to integrating environmental considerations into its business operations. Through investments in renewable energy, water conservation, wastewater treatment and responsible waste management, the Group continues to minimise the environmental impact of its activities. For customers, these awards provide added confidence that the facilities involved in the Group’s automotive operations are implementing recognised environmental management practices. While the awards recognise the environmental performance of the respective facilities rather than individually certifying every product, they reflect the Group’s commitment to responsible manufacturing, assembly and vehicle servicing. The achievements align with DPG STEP (Sustain, Track, Empower, Progress), the Group’s sustainability strategy, which promotes measurable environmental improvements and responsible business practices across its companies. David Pieris Group remains committed to strengthening environmental performance, conserving resources and contributing towards a cleaner, greener and more sustainable Sri Lanka.

audit.headline: Nawaloka Hospitals Colombo, strengthens digital healthcare position with Doc990
audit.summary: Nawaloka Hospitals PLC, Colombo, has strengthened its strategic investment in Doc990, increasing its shareholding from 8.8% to 12.1% and reinforcing its commitment to more accessible, digitally connected healthcare in Sri Lanka. The additional stake was acquired after Nawaloka exercised its right of first refusal under the existing shareholders’ agreement. By expanding its ownership, Nawaloka has reinforced an established investment in digital healthcare and its involvement in the development of more convenient access to medical services. Doc990 enables patients to book doctor appointments, access digital consultations and make payments through mobile, web and telephone channels. These services connect the hospital experience with the convenience of digital access, helping patients organise their healthcare needs before arriving at a hospital.
audit.body: Nawaloka Hospitals PLC, Colombo, has strengthened its strategic investment in Doc990, increasing its shareholding from 8.8% to 12.1% and reinforcing its commitment to more accessible, digitally connected healthcare in Sri Lanka. By expanding its ownership, Nawaloka has reinforced an established investment in digital healthcare and its involvement in the development of more convenient access to medical services. Doc990 enables patients to book doctor appointments, access digital consultations and make payments through mobile, web and telephone channels. These services connect the hospital experience with the convenience of digital access, helping patients organise their healthcare needs before arriving at a hospital. For Nawaloka Hospitals PLC, Colombo, the significance extends beyond an increased shareholding. Participation in digital healthcare complements its hospital services, creating opportunities to bring clinical expertise and technology closer together. As patients increasingly seek simpler ways to find doctors and arrange consultations, digital platforms can play an important role in connecting them with appropriate services. The transaction takes place alongside changes in Digital Health’s ownership, including the entry of Sunshine Healthcare as an investor. Dialog Axiata retains a substantial interest through its investment entities, maintaining a strong telecommunications and technology presence within the business. Within this shareholder network, Nawaloka brings the perspective of a hospital service provider. Its practical understanding of patient expectations, appointment coordination and hospital operations offers a relevant foundation for participation in the digital healthcare sector. The increased investment also highlights the importance of continuity between online access and services delivered within the hospital. Convenient bookings are one part of the patient journey; clear communication, reliable coordination and efficient service delivery remain essential to the overall experience. Nawaloka’s larger holding provides a stronger basis for its continued participation as Digital Health develops. Potential opportunities include supporting closer connections between patients and providers and contributing a hospital perspective to the evolution of digital services. Specific developments will depend on the platform’s plans and implementation.

audit.headline: India, Sri Lanka Navies jointly clean up Galle Face beach
audit.summary: Personnel from the Indian Navy and Sri Lanka Navy carried out a joint beach cleanup drive along the Galle Face coastline in Colombo yesterday (27). The initiative involved crew members and Officer under-trainees from the Indian Navy’s First Training Squadron (1TS), comprising INS Tir, INS Sujata and ICGS Sarathi, which arrived in Sri Lanka on an official visit, alongside personnel from the Sri Lanka Navy’s Western Naval Command. During the programme, Naval personnel collected a significant volume of solid waste, including plastic and polythene debris, scattered across the Galle Face shore. The collected waste was subsequently disposed of in a responsible manner.

audit.headline: ‘Innovate today to feed tomorrow’ by New Anthoney’s Farms
audit.summary: Every year on October 16, World Food Day asks the world to look at its plates and at the people who fill them. This year’s theme, ‘Innovate today to feed tomorrow’, is a useful prompt for a sector that often talks about innovation in terms of machines and prices. For poultry producers in Sri Lanka, innovation has a more practical meaning. It is the way a bird is raised, what it eats and whether a family can trust the label on the pack. The scale of the challenge The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) estimates that about 673 million people were undernourished in 2024, equal to 8.2 per cent of the world’s population. In Southern Asia, the prevalence of undernourishment fell from 7.9 per cent in 2022 to 6.7 per cent in 2024. That is real progress, but it still leaves a very large number of people in a region of nearly two billion without enough to eat.
audit.body: Every year on October 16, World Food Day asks the world to look at its plates and at the people who fill them. This year’s theme, ‘Innovate today to feed tomorrow’, is a useful prompt for a sector that often talks about innovation in terms of machines and prices. For poultry producers in Sri Lanka, innovation has a more practical meaning. It is the way a bird is raised, what it eats and whether a family can trust the label on the pack. The scale of the challenge The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) estimates that about 673 million people were undernourished in 2024, equal to 8.2 per cent of the world’s population. In Southern Asia, the prevalence of undernourishment fell from 7.9 per cent in 2022 to 6.7 per cent in 2024. That is real progress, but it still leaves a very large number of people in a region of nearly two billion without enough to eat. For many households, affordable and nutritious food remains a daily concern. Animal protein is one of the most efficient ways to deliver essential nutrients in a modest serving and chicken and eggs are among the most accessible sources for families on tight budgets. That is why the way poultry is produced matters beyond the farm gate. What matters is not only how much food reaches the market, but what that food is made of and how it was raised. Sri Lanka’s poultry sector has grown. According to the Department of Animal Production and Health (DAPH), poultry meat production rose from about 236,110 tonnes in 2023 to about 258,540 tonnes in 2024. Egg output increased from about 2,044 million eggs to about 2,953 million over the same period. Growth in volume is welcome, but it does not settle whether the industry can keep producing reliably, or how the food is raised. Innovation starts with the feed Feed sits behind those numbers. Government estimates published in 2022 put annual maize requirements for animal feed at about 700,000 tonnes. Domestic maize output across the two cultivation seasons of 2024 totalled 223,497 tonnes, according to DAPH, so imports fill much of the gap. Their timing, permits and cost shape what a farmer pays for every bag, and what a consumer pays for every kilogram of chicken. Innovation in poultry is often measured by speed and cost. We think it should also be measured by what goes into the bird. New Anthoney’s Farms raises its birds without antibiotics, a choice that has forced the team to work harder on housing, biosecurity and nutrition. It is slower and more demanding than the conventional route. It also reduces pressure on a public health system already dealing with antimicrobial resistance, which the World Health Organisation has described as a serious global threat. Feed is where that discipline has to start. Our milling operation, Anthoney’s Feeds, sits at the centre of how we think about quality. In 2023 the company was awarded rights to the Sustainable U.S. Soy logo, verified under the U.S. Soy Sustainability Assurance Protocol, and several other Sri Lankan producers and feed millers now carry the same standard. A label is only useful when it is trusted, so we treat it as a commitment to be audited, not a badge to display. Innovation is also about who gets to take part. Smallholder farmers already supply around 40 per cent of New Anthoney’s production through contract farming and outgrower partnerships. For a small farm, a known buyer, agreed terms and technical advice on biosecurity and flock management are as valuable as any new housing system. They help a family farm plan, invest and stay in the business through a difficult year. That model also protects the wider industry. A farm that can plan its season is less likely to leave the sector when feed prices spike, and a supply base built on stable partners is easier to trace, audit and rely on. For a company that wants its label to mean something, those are the foundations, not side benefits. South Asia shares the same exposure. Poultry industries across the region depend on imported feed ingredients, so price shocks move quickly across borders, and no single company can solve that alone. What can spread faster is a set of practices more producers adopt: traceable feed, responsible antibiotic use, fair terms for farmers and honest labelling for buyers. We would welcome more competition on those terms, because a more trusted category helps every producer in the market, including us. Consumers are asking sharper questions than they were a few years ago. Where did this come from? What was it fed? Was anything added to make it grow faster? Those questions are reasonable, and younger households in particular are making purchasing decisions for their children on the strength of the answers. A producer that can answer plainly, with records behind the answer, earns a place on the shelf that price alone cannot secure. World Food Day is an easy day to make commitments, so we would rather show our work. That means being clear about how birds are raised, what they are fed, where the feed comes from and how many farmers are part of the supply base. It also means accepting that a claim is only as strong as the evidence behind it, and being ready to be checked. Innovate today to feed tomorrow is not a slogan for one factory or one season. It is a test for the whole sector. The people who will eat the food produced over the next decade are already here, in Colombo, in the regional towns and in the homes where a chicken dinner is the most affordable way to feed a family well. The producers who will still be trusted when the next shock arrives are the ones taking the harder path now: cleaner feed, fewer shortcuts, fair partnerships with farmers and labels that can stand up to scrutiny. New Anthoney’s is committed to that work, and we hope the rest of the industry will join us.

audit.headline: AMW authorised distributor for Nissan, unveils Tekton expands SUV range
audit.summary: Associated Motorways (AMW), Nissan’s authorised distributor in Sri Lanka, unveiled the Nissan Tekton at its Union Place showroom in Colombo on Thursday, adding a new model to the country’s Nissan SUV range. The launch comes as Nissan marks 75 years of SUV production. AMW Group Managing Director Jawahar Ganesh said the company has a long standing partnership with the Japanese carmaker and aimed to strengthen Nissan’s presence in the market. The Tekton, which carries a five-star safety rating from Bharat NCAP, will be offered in four variants with turbocharged engines and a choice of transmissions. The event was attended by media representatives and AMW executives, including Sales Director Prasanna de Silva and Nissan Head Jagath Wijesekera.

AMW Group Managing Director Jawahar Ganesh said the company has a long standing partnership with the Japanese carmaker and aimed to strengthen Nissan’s presence in the market. The Tekton, which carries a five-star safety rating from Bharat NCAP, will be offered in four variants with turbocharged engines and a choice of transmissions. The event was attended by media representatives and AMW executives, including Sales Director Prasanna de Silva and Nissan Head Jagath Wijesekera. AMW also signalled plans to bring the Nissan Navara pickup to Sri Lanka in the near future, though the company said any introduction remains subject to further evaluation and confirmation. Founded in 1949, AMW has been part of the Al-Futtaim Group since 2008.

audit.headline: Fiery action, borrowed flames, but fights that win hearts

At a time when Sinhala cinema is in search of fresh faces and stories that speak to the younger generation, Agni Jaya attempts to fill that gap by telling the story of a young man who dares to stand against the evils of society. The film revolves around Manchana, the only son born into an upper middle class family. His father is a well known businessman, his mother a devoted housewife, and he has an elder sister who deeply cares for him. The much awaited Sinhala film Agni Jaya , which marks the first directorial and production venture of popular actor, model and dancer Manchana Tharaka Peiris, has finally arrived on the silver screen with the promise of youth, romance, action and a strong social message. At a time when Sinhala cinema is in search of fresh faces and stories that speak to the younger generation, Agni Jaya attempts to fill that gap by telling the story of a young man who dares to stand against the evils of society. The film revolves around Manchana, the only son born into an upper middle class family. His father is a well known businessman, his mother a devoted housewife, and he has an elder sister who deeply cares for him. From childhood, Manchana has nurtured the ambition of becoming a doctor and is currently pursuing his higher studies at a private university. He is not an ordinary student who merely attends lectures and returns home. He is portrayed as a courageous, active and outspoken young man who cannot tolerate corruption, irregularities, illegal and unrighteous acts that have become common in society. Whether it is at home or within the university premises, he always takes the lead in demanding a law-abiding and respectful environment, making him both loved and hated. Into this principled life enters love. Manchana finds himself drawn towards Meera, a beautiful and intelligent university student who becomes the centre of his affection. Their campus romance brings a soft and emotional touch to the otherwise intense narrative, giving the audience a much needed romantic relief. The director has tried to balance action with emotion through this track, showing how even a fearless youth can become vulnerable when it comes to love. The film takes a dark and serious turn when the drug menace that is silently spreading inside the university comes to light. A student who becomes addicted to drugs commits suicide, shaking the entire university. This tragic incident becomes the turning point in Manchana’s life. His attention is now drawn to Rex, the powerful and cunning drug trafficker who operates his network with the help of his henchmen. Manchana decides to confront this evil directly. His first major clash is with Dhana, Rex’s main disciple, right on the university grounds. This explosive confrontation is one of the highlights of the first half and from here onward Manchana’s life is constantly under threat from various types of thugs and criminals who will go to any extent to silence him. Parallel to the campus underworld story, the film weaves in a family drama that adds another layer of suspense. When Manchana’s parents return home after a long-distance trip, they are shocked to discover that their house has been burgled and valuable items are missing. With the help of a few close friends, Manchana begins to investigate the theft and identifies a broker named Riya as the person behind the crime. The investigation brings him face to face with a different kind of criminal world, one that deals in stolen property and black market dealings. As the story progresses, the greed and power struggle within the criminal world itself leads to Rex being killed by his own trusted man Dhana, who now emerges as the main antagonist. This leads the audience to the final and most awaited part of the film, the deadly fight between Mangwana and Dhana. Who will win this battle between good and evil, what will be the ultimate fate of Riya, and will Manchana’s sincere hopes for Meera be fulfilled or shattered, is what Agni Jaya finally reveals on screen with a dramatic climax. When it comes to performances, one actor who stands out remarkably is Bimal Jayakodi. He is doing great justice to his character as the Underworld Big Boss. With his powerful screen presence, controlled aggression and cold-blooded dialogue delivery, Bimal brings a chilling authenticity to the role of the drug lord. His performance is layered and menacing without being over-the-top, which makes his character truly fearsome. In fact, watching him in certain scenes reminds one of some intense scenes from the film Pravegaya, where the late veteran actor Jackson Anthony played the lead villain with such brilliance. Bimal Jayakodi follows that same lineage of powerful villainy, and his portrayal will surely be remembered as one of the major pillars of Agni Jaya . As a film, Agni Jaya has many strengths that deserve appreciation, but it also carries some clear flaws that cannot be ignored by a discerning viewer. The biggest strength of the film is undoubtedly its action. The fight scenes of the movie are fantastic. They are raw, fast paced, energetic and shot with a sense of style that keeps the audience engaged. From the hand to hand combat in the university canteen to the final showdown in a dark warehouse, every action block is executed with intensity. Full credit should go to the stunt director who has done a truly commendable job. He has choreographed the fights with precision, realism and cinematic flair, proving that Sinhala cinema is capable of delivering high quality action when given to the right technicians. His work lifts the entire film and saves it from many of its narrative weaknesses. However, on the other side, the film suffers from issues of logic and originality. One of the most unrealistic sequences in the entire film is the house theft scene. The film shows a thief entering a house and stealing everything, including cash, jewelry and even large household items like televisions, cassette players, fridges, washing machines and other heavy items. This entire act is shown to have happened within a timeframe of just two hours, which is truly unrealistic and practically impossible. A thief cannot completely empty a house of its belongings in such a short period without being noticed. This sequence breaks the realism the film tries to establish and leaves the audience questioning the script. Furthermore, the film clearly bears a strong South Indian influence throughout. From its dialogue delivery, background music, slow motion hero elevations and over stylized fight build-ups, watching certain scenes might even lead one to wonder if it is a copy of a Hindi or Tamil movie rather than an original Sinhala film. This constant deja vu feeling of watching a dubbed South Indian action film takes away the authentic local identity that Agni Jaya could have had, especially when it was dealing with a very real Sri Lankan social issue like university drugs. Despite these flaws, Agni Jaya remains a watchable and honest first attempt by a new filmmaker who has shown great dedication. Manchana Tharaka Peiris, who made his debut in the arts by appearing in a television commercial when he was just eight years old, has come a long way. He has contributed to many commercials, appeared in lyric videos like Sahat Pabeysekara’s Kandulin and Theekshana Anuradha’s Pama Vu Kotche, and has been part of over fifteen songs and films including Sajith Nuwan’s Heenay Vela and Me May Gaha Yata. Excelling in both dance and modeling, he won the Sri Lankan crown in the Man Hunt competition along with Best Photogenic and Mr. Popular titles, earning the chance to represent Sri Lanka at Mr. Universe in America. He studied acting and cinematography under film director and cinema professor Mr. Sarvan and has acted in films like Sihinayaki Adare and Madhura Charika and teledrama Mandakini. Today, as a businessman by profession, he has taken a bold step to direct and produce his first feature film. For a debutant, his effort, his choice of a socially relevant subject and his courage to invest in commercial cinema must be appreciated, even if the execution needs more maturity and originality in the future.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka, Türkiye hold discussions to strengthen bilateral cooperation
audit.summary: Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra held bilateral discussions with Ambassador A. Berris Ekinci, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye, in Ankara yesterday (27), as part of his official visit to Türkiye. The meeting focused on strengthening the longstanding friendship between Sri Lanka and Türkiye and advancing bilateral cooperation across key areas of mutual interest, including trade, investment, foreign employment, agriculture, tourism, education, renewable energy and defence. Both sides explored opportunities to expand bilateral trade, improve market access for Sri Lankan products, particularly Ceylon Tea, and encourage increased Turkish investment in key sectors of Sri Lanka’s economy. Agricultural cooperation featured prominently in the discussions, with particular attention to the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)on Agricultural Cooperation.
audit.body: Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra held bilateral discussions with Ambassador A. Berris Ekinci, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Türkiye, in Ankara yesterday (27), as part of his official visit to Türkiye. The meeting focused on strengthening the longstanding friendship between Sri Lanka and Türkiye and advancing bilateral cooperation across key areas of mutual interest, including trade, investment, foreign employment, agriculture, tourism, education, renewable energy and defence. Both sides explored opportunities to expand bilateral trade, improve market access for Sri Lankan products, particularly Ceylon Tea, and encourage increased Turkish investment in key sectors of Sri Lanka’s economy. Agricultural cooperation featured prominently in the discussions, with particular attention to the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)on Agricultural Cooperation. The two sides discussed opportunities to enhance collaboration in modern agricultural technologies, research, knowledge sharing, capacity building, agricultural productivity and food security. The discussions also covered strengthening air connectivity under the Air Transport Agreement, identifying suitable employment opportunities for skilled Sri Lankan workers, and promoting people-to-people ties through tourism, education, cultural exchanges and institutional partnerships. Climate change, sustainable development, disaster preparedness and resilience were also discussed as important areas for enhanced cooperation in addressing emerging global challenges. On diplomatic and international affairs, the two sides exchanged views on strengthening parliamentary diplomacy, defence cooperation and engagement in regional and multilateral forums. They underscored the importance of a rules-based international order, respect for international law, national sovereignty, the principles of the United Nations Charter and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Deputy Minister Hemachandra expressed Sri Lanka’s appreciation for Türkiye’s longstanding friendship and continued support, reaffirming Sri Lanka’s commitment to further strengthening bilateral relations and translating the outcomes of the engagement into tangible benefits for the peoples of both countries. The meeting marked an important opportunity to deepen bilateral engagement and advance a forward-looking partnership encompassing economic cooperation, institutional ties and people-to-people relations. Sri Lanka’s Ambassador to Türkiye, Niluka Kadurugamuwa, and Minister at the Sri Lankan Embassy in Ankara, Nilusha Dilmini, also participated in the meeting.

audit.headline: Pakistan Embassy commemorates ‘Kashmir Black Day’
audit.summary: The High Commission of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan in Colombo hosted a Seminar and Photo Exhibition yesterday (27) at the Embassy premises, to commemorate ‘Kashmir Black Day’. The Seminar featured an address by Political Activist Shiraz Yoonus, who illuminated the difficulties faced by people in the Indian ruled Jammu and Kashmir. High Commissioner of Pakistan to Sri Lanka Major General (Rtd) Dr. Nayyar Naseer, HI (M), paid tribute to the resilience and just struggle of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. In his address, the High Commissioner reiterated Pakistan’s steadfast moral, political and diplomatic support for the Kashmiris’ right to Self-determination.
audit.body: The High Commission of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan in Colombo hosted a Seminar and Photo Exhibition yesterday (27) at the Embassy premises, to commemorate ‘Kashmir Black Day’. The Seminar featured an address by Political Activist Shiraz Yoonus, who illuminated the difficulties faced by people in the Indian ruled Jammu and Kashmir. High Commissioner of Pakistan to Sri Lanka Major General (Rtd) Dr. Nayyar Naseer, HI (M), paid tribute to the resilience and just struggle of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. In his address, the High Commissioner reiterated Pakistan’s steadfast moral, political and diplomatic support for the Kashmiris’ right to Self-determination. He emphasised that Pakistan consistently advocates for a peaceful resolution of the Kashmir dispute, in accordance with the aspirations of the Kashmiri people and in line with the relevant United Nations Security Council Resolutions. The event saw participation from diverse segments of the community, including Sri Lanka Pakistan Business Council President Wasantha De Silva, members of the Pakistani diaspora in Sri Lanka, journalists, writers, and friends of Kashmir. Messages from the President and Prime Minister of Pakistan were read out, underscoring Pakistan’s unwavering support for the Kashmiri people.

audit.headline: Key female murder suspect ‘Achini’ arrested in Dubai and repatriated
audit.summary: Anusha Lakmali alias ‘Achini’, a key female suspect wanted on Red notice by the INTERPOL, in connection with the shooting murder of Aruna Vidanagamage alias ‘Kajja’ and his two children, was arrested in Dubai and repatriated early yesterday (27) morning. The Police Media Division stated that the 34-year-old suspect, a resident of Katuwana area in Middeniya, wanted for aiding and abetting the shooting and murder of Aruna Vidanagamage alias ‘Kajja’ and his two children in Hungama area of Middeniya on 08.02.2025, has been arrested upon arrival at the Katunayake Airport yesterday morning at 5:20 am, aboard SriLankan Airlines flight UL-226, by the officers of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID).
audit.body: Anusha Lakmali alias ‘Achini’, a key female suspect wanted on Red notice by the INTERPOL, in connection with the shooting murder of Aruna Vidanagamage alias ‘Kajja’ and his two children, was arrested in Dubai and repatriated early yesterday (27) morning. The Police Media Division stated that the 34-year-old suspect, a resident of Katuwana area in Middeniya, wanted for aiding and abetting the shooting and murder of Aruna Vidanagamage alias ‘Kajja’ and his two children in Hungama area of Middeniya on 08.02.2025, has been arrested upon arrival at the Katunayake Airport yesterday morning at 5:20 am, aboard SriLankan Airlines flight UL-226, by the officers of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID). Police investigations revealed that the suspect who is wanted on open warrant by the Walasmulla Magistrate’s Court for the ongoing case on the murder of ‘Kajja’ and his two children in Middeniya, had maintained a close relationship with the victim, ‘Kajja’. Investigations have further disclosed that this suspect was the person who made the final phone call and sent the last text message to ‘Kajja’, shortly before the murder took place. Also, it has been revealed that acting on instructions from a notorious criminal known as ‘Backhoe Saman’, she had lured “Kajja” and his two children to the restaurant where the shooting occurred. The shooting took place while the victims were there to have a meal. A special team of Police Officers traveled to Dubai to bring back the female suspect, who had been arrested and imprisoned by local security forces while in hiding there. Upon her arrival at the Katunayake Airport, officers from the CID recorded her initial statement. She was subsequently transported to CID headquarters in Colombo under heavy security and has been handed over to the Homicide Investigation Division of the CID for further investigations.

audit.headline: Explorations in a 1 × 1 Box
audit.summary: T he second edition of ‘ArtnArtist’ brings together nine Sri Lankan artists whose diverse practices explore themes of memory, nature, cultural identity, social realities, imagination, and humanity’s relationship with the world around us. A defining feature of this edition is its shared 1 × 1-foot format, with each artist creating work within the same dimensions while maintaining a distinct artistic language, medium, and perspective. Painting, printmaking, ceramics, metalwork, and sculpture come together to create a dialogue between varied approaches to contemporary art. ‘ArtnArtist’ highlights both the individuality of each artist and the creative possibilities that emerge through their collective presence. The exhibition is curated by Mandira Ranathunga and programme managed by Gayan Hemarathne. When describing the art works, Gayan repeatedly uses the word –“Explores”.
audit.body: T he second edition of ‘ArtnArtist’ brings together nine Sri Lankan artists whose diverse practices explore themes of memory, nature, cultural identity, social realities, imagination, and humanity’s relationship with the world around us. A defining feature of this edition is its shared 1 × 1-foot format, with each artist creating work within the same dimensions while maintaining a distinct artistic language, medium, and perspective. Painting, printmaking, ceramics, metalwork, and sculpture come together to create a dialogue between varied approaches to contemporary art. ‘ArtnArtist’ highlights both the individuality of each artist and the creative possibilities that emerge through their collective presence. The exhibition is curated by Mandira Ranathunga and programme managed by Gayan Hemarathne. When describing the art works, Gayan repeatedly uses the word –“Explores”. It is a word that is very close to my heart as I believe that we are all explorers in this world. Every exhibition is some place new. That is the power of exhibitions- taking the viewer into a world he or she has not been to before. A world he or she has not seen before. A world he or she has never experienced before. A place. Chammika Jayawardena’s Camouflage Landscape explores themes of landscape, memory, history, power, and perception, moving beyond the conventional representation of place. Jayawardena approaches landscape as a constructed and shifting terrain where personal and collective histories intersect with the ways in which places are experienced and remembered. The landscape becomes a living entity, transformed by the presence, experiences, and memories of those who encounter it. Through this approach, Camouflage Landscape invites viewers to reconsider what a landscape can conceal, reveal, and preserve. Memory is something that is truly remarkable. Every day we gather memories. It is a never- ending process. Each day is an accumulation of memories and yet we have the power of retention. No matter how many memories are stored in our brains, the memories that gathered before remain. Memories are part of our identity. Some people have a sharper recollection of certain events, and others have a sharper recollection of other events. Different recollections. Perception is another way that we experience the world around us. Why do we connect with different characters? It could be a book, a movie or even a Netflix series. Why do we as individuals connect with different characters? It is because of what we have gone through in life. To me, Jayawardena’s creations are all about the connection of the world inside of us and the world outside. Prabath Samaranayaka’s Questioning Human Supremacy explores themes of human supremacy, animal ethics, sacrifice, and humanity’s relationship with other living beings. Samaranayaka questions the assumption that human life should automatically be valued above all other forms of existence, examining how animals and other sentient beings are sacrificed and reduced to commodities for human consumption, luxury, and desire. Referencing the ancient symbol of the Agnus Dei, the innocent lamb becomes a metaphor for sacrifice that continues in contemporary laboratories, slaughterhouses, and disappearing forests. Through this work, Samaranayaka challenges viewers to reconsider humanity’s ethical responsibility towards other forms of life. This is a timeless topic. Egocentrism vs Nature Centrism. The web of life. Man is just a strand in the web, whatever he does to the web he does to himself. Anthropocentrism vs Nature Centrism. We know that today because of the actions of human beings, animals go through terrible suffering. The dog is considered a pet, while equally intelligent animals like pigs and cows are slaughtered in slaughter houses. Our intelligence is a curse to other animals. These animals feel pain and terror just like us human beings. We certainly have an ethical responsibility to other forms of life. Chandani Bandara’s Third Class Pressure explores themes of social realities, human experience, and the invisible pressures of everyday life through the expressive language of woodcut printmaking. Bandara’s practice examines the social conditions and inequalities that influence individual and collective experiences. The physical process of printmaking becomes a means of translating these pressures into a direct and compelling visual language. Through Third Class Pressure, she draws attention to the tensions and realities that often remain unseen within everyday life. The world outside. The invisible pressures of everyday life. Reality is such that we must get comfortable with discomfort. We must not sugarcoat reality or social conditions. Dillai Joseph’s Toxic Beauty explores themes of beauty, contradiction, everyday experience, and a constantly changing world. Joseph’s practice is centered on an ongoing exploration of the human spirit and the world around her, drawing inspiration from fleeting expressions, quiet landscapes, ordinary moments, and unexpected encounters. Rather than following a fixed subject or theme, she allows each work to respond intuitively to whatever captures her attention at a particular moment. In Toxic Beauty, this openness becomes an exploration of the contradictions between beauty, discomfort, uncertainty, and the inherent chaos of everyday existence. I often ask myself – truly is there anything as deceptive as beauty? The beautiful things we want to do, are they at odds with what others consider to be beautiful? Eade Kunst’s IMNUVORA explores themes of imagined nature, transformation, memory, and possibility, creating a world that exists somewhere between reality and imagination. Working with metal sculpture, Kunst creates forms that do not attempt to imitate nature as we know it, but instead suggest what nature might become beyond the boundaries of familiar reality. The resulting forms occupy a space between the organic and the imagined, encouraging viewers to consider alternative environments and possibilities of existence. Through IMNUVORA, sculpture becomes a medium for imagining what lies beyond the natural world as we understand it. A world that exists between reality and imagination! What a theme to explore! The realm of imagination! It exists in our minds. And what exists in the mind can take shape and form in reality. Could it sometimes be an extension of the mind? But we know that imagination can be a double -edged sword! Ishara Madushanka’s Guardian of the Forgotten Land explores themes of nature, memory, Sri Lankan folklore, and the female figure through a practice grounded in symbolism and cultural remembrance. Working on copper plate, Madushanka uses the female figure as a significant symbolic presence, connecting human experience with the natural environment and inherited cultural narratives. The work reflects on forgotten landscapes and stories while considering the fragile relationship between humanity and nature. Guardian of the Forgotten Land creates a contemplative dialogue between folklore, memory, identity, and the Sri Lankan landscape. Connecting the human experience with cultural narratives while highlighting the fragile relationship between humanity and nature is fascinating. Isuru Niranga’s Currency explores themes of cultural memory, value, identity, and traditional visual language through a personal reinterpretation of currency notes. Drawing loose inspiration from the historic wood carvings of Embekke, Niranga does not seek to reproduce these traditional forms directly but instead reimagines their visual and cultural references through a contemporary perspective. The work brings together ideas of money, history, cultural heritage, and personal identity, questioning how value is constructed and understood. Through Currency, familiar symbols are transformed into a new and personal artistic vocabulary. This is innovation at its best. The concept seems to me to be very original. It is a refreshing idea. Lahiru Lakshan’s Karam Koku explores themes of childhood memory, nature, sensory experience, and personal recollection through an abstract ceramic narrative. The work draws from Lakshan’s childhood experiences of gathering Karam Koku, also known as Bara Koku, an activity that required navigating sharp leaves and the hidden dangers of venomous creatures. Despite these challenges, the experience remains connected to vivid memories of color, form, texture, rhythm, and the anticipation of a cherished meal. Through ceramics, Lakshan transforms this personal recollection into a tactile exploration of memory, nature, and childhood. Childhood memories associated with adventure have been made the subject matter here. Sachira Lakshan’s Nature and Modern Society explores themes of nature, human perception, modernity, and co-existence through realistic sculpture. His practice focuses on lifelike details, textures, and the inherent qualities of raw materials, allowing each sculpture to retain a strong sense of physical presence. Through Nature and Modern Society, Lakshan reflects on the delicate balance between humanity and the natural environment within an increasingly modernized world. Lakshan approaches sculpture as a bridge between the natural world and contemporary human experience, examining how nature and modern society coexist, interact, and collide. There certainly is a delicate balance between humanity and the natural environment which we need to be mindful of. The venue is Harold Peiris Gallery, Lionel Wendt Art Centre, and the opening preview will be on Friday, 30 October from 6:00pm to 8:00pm and the public exhibition will be from 31st October to 1st November 2026, 9:00am– 7:00pm.

audit.headline: Rs. 2,200 Mn allocated for construction, modernisation of post offices – Minister
audit.summary: Health and Mass Media Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa stated that by restarting the construction of postal buildings that had been halted for 10 years, the Government has allocated Rs. 1,000 million for the construction of new post offices and Rs. 1,200 million for the modernisation and repair of post offices over the past two years alone. The Minister made these remarks while attending the foundation laying ceremony for the new sub-post office building in Pimbura, Agalawatta yesterday (27). The construction of this sub-post office, built at a cost of Rs. 6.63 million, is scheduled to be completed within three months, directly serving 2,600 families. Emphasising that the Pimbura area should be developed as an advanced region, the Minister noted that when developing it as a sub-town, hospitals and other public buildings must also be developed accordingly.

The Minister made these remarks while attending the foundation laying ceremony for the new sub-post office building in Pimbura, Agalawatta yesterday (27). The construction of this sub-post office, built at a cost of Rs. 6.63 million, is scheduled to be completed within three months, directly serving 2,600 families. Emphasising that the Pimbura area should be developed as an advanced region, the Minister noted that when developing it as a sub-town, hospitals and other public buildings must also be developed accordingly. He stated that steps were taken to construct this new sub-post office with focus on those urban development needs. He pointed out that the Government has taken steps to revive the postal sector, which had been neglected in the recent past. The construction of 13 post offices and three sub-post offices has already been completed, while construction work on another six post offices has commenced. The Minister stated that this is the seventh post office for which the foundation stone has been laid for construction within this year. There are 34 post offices and 130 sub-post offices in the Kalutara district.
