audit.headline: Government’s vision to reform prisoners as upright citizens – Minister
audit.summary: Our Government’s vision is to provide opportunities for wrongdoers to transform their lives and rejoin society as good citizens while enforcing the Law, which is the true meaning of rehabilitation, Justice and National Integration Minister Harshana Nanayakkara stated. He said that a Prison is not a separate world isolated from society, but a reflection of the country’s own society and the Government’s goal is to build a Prison system that upholds the Rule of Law, public safety, and the Human Rights and dignity of inmates. The Minister expressed these views yesterday (27) morning at the Diyatha Uyana premises in Battaramulla, while participating as the Chief Guest at the opening ceremony of the “Sirasara Shilpa 2026” Industry and Sales Exhibition, organised to bring the creative skills and talents of Prison inmates to the National platform.
audit.body: Our Government’s vision is to provide opportunities for wrongdoers to transform their lives and rejoin society as good citizens while enforcing the Law, which is the true meaning of rehabilitation, Justice and National Integration Minister Harshana Nanayakkara stated. He said that a Prison is not a separate world isolated from society, but a reflection of the country’s own society and the Government’s goal is to build a Prison system that upholds the Rule of Law, public safety, and the Human Rights and dignity of inmates. The Minister expressed these views yesterday (27) morning at the Diyatha Uyana premises in Battaramulla, while participating as the Chief Guest at the opening ceremony of the “Sirasara Shilpa 2026” Industry and Sales Exhibition, organised to bring the creative skills and talents of Prison inmates to the National platform. “Today, I did not come here merely to attend a product sales event. I see this occasion as one of much deeper significance. Today, we are not just seeing a few goods. Behind every single product, there is someone’s hard work, a new learning experience, and an effort to rebuild the belief that they too are capable of achieving something. I must say that this is extremely important. When we usually talk about Prisons, we think about the mistakes committed by the people inside and the punishment they deserve. But within that narrative, there is another side we often forget: the people inside these Prisons are also human beings who once lived in our own society. They have families too; a mother, a father, a wife, a husband, a child, or a sibling. There are people who hold expectations for them and among them are those who wish to reform their lives. Therefore, we must look at this issue not only from the perspective of the Law, but also from the perspective of humanity. It is our Government’s vision that while enforcing the Law, we must also provide opportunities for wrongdoers to transform their lives and rejoin society as good citizens. That is what rehabilitation means. I believe we must understand the true meaning of the word rehabilitation. It is not merely giving an inmate a task to pass the time; it is making them feel valued, giving them the opportunity to learn something new, and helping them foster hope for their future. Today, what we are selling here is one of the results of that hope. When a person manufacturing a product creates something with their own hands, we should be able to understand the feeling they experience. The feeling that they too can accomplish something, learn something new, and produce something valuable through their own hard work becomes a very vital part of rehabilitation. Therefore, these programmes must be further strengthened. There must also be opportunities to sell these products after manufacturing them. The quality of the products must be improved, new markets must be identified, and pathways must be established so that even after gaining freedom, they can earn a livelihood using the skills they have learned. Then, these programmes will not remain confined within the Prison walls, but will connect to the future lives of the inmates. Ensuring justice for victims of crime is essential. At the same time, providing a society where crimes do not recur is equally crucial. Providing opportunities for rehabilitation can be cited as a vital step in achieving that second objective. A fair share of the product sales revenue should be allocated to the workers. As you visit and purchase these products today, I urge you to think about this. You are not just buying a good product; you are giving value to someone’s hard work, recognising their capability, and encouraging their endeavour to rebuild a good life. Whatever their past may be, do not give up on their potential to do good things in the future. What they learn today, the hard work they put in today, and the self-belief they build today can be vital for their life tomorrow. As a government, we are committed to providing the necessary support for that journey. Not only State institutions, but families and society as a whole must join hands in this effort. The true strength of a society is shown not only by how it treats successful people, but also by how it provides an opportunity for someone who has failed in life to rise again. Prison is not a place isolated from us; the people inside it are part of our society. The opportunities we provide to improve their lives ultimately contribute to bettering the future of our entire society. Therefore, let us work together to build a Prison system that upholds the Rule of Law, while leaving room for humanity, carrying punishment and rehabilitation forward hand in hand,” the Minister stated. The Minister and other guests also inspected the exhibition stalls of Sirasara Shilpa 2026, which showcase the creative talents of inmates from 28 Prisons across the country. The Sirasara Shilpa 2026 creative exhibition and sales outlet will be held today (28) and tomorrow (29) from 9 am to 9 pm at the Diyatha Uyana premises, Battaramulla. Acting Commissioner General of Prisons Gamini B. Dissanayake and Commissioner of Prisons (Industries) Sujeewa Wijesekara also addressed the gathering. Minister of Public Security and Parliamentary Affairs Ananda Wijeapala, Mayor of Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte Municipal Council Arosha Atapattu, along with officials from the Ministry of Justice and National Integration and the Department of Prisons, participated in the event. Items turned out by inmates during their rehabilitation period are available for purchase at the venue.

audit.headline: Court orders recall of arrest warrant issued for Diana Gamage
audit.summary: The Colombo High Court yesterday ordered the recall of the arrest warrant issued for former State Minister Diana Gamage over a case filed for allegedly forging a birth certificate to obtain a National Identity Card. The case was taken up yesterday before Colombo High Court Judge Nadee Aparna Suwadurugoda through a motion, and the defence informed court the accused was unable to appear at the last occasion due to an urgent matter. The defence therefore sought permission from court to withdraw the arrest warrant issued against the accused. Considering the facts, the Colombo High Court Judge ordered the recall of the arrest warrant. Gamage was released by the Colombo High Court on cash bail of Rs. 25, 000 and two sureties of Rs. 1 million after she was served with an indictment.
audit.body: The Colombo High Court yesterday ordered the recall of the arrest warrant issued for former State Minister Diana Gamage over a case filed for allegedly forging a birth certificate to obtain a National Identity Card. The case was taken up yesterday before Colombo High Court Judge Nadee Aparna Suwadurugoda through a motion, and the defence informed court the accused was unable to appear at the last occasion due to an urgent matter. The defence therefore sought permission from court to withdraw the arrest warrant issued against the accused. Considering the facts, the Colombo High Court Judge ordered the recall of the arrest warrant. Gamage was released by the Colombo High Court on cash bail of Rs. 25, 000 and two sureties of Rs. 1 million after she was served with an indictment. The Attorney General had filed indictment in the Colombo High Court against Gamage on three charges of allegedly forging or abetting the forging of a birth certificate to deceive officials of the Department of Registration of Persons to get a National Identity Card issued to her in the name of “Diana Gamage” when her name was not legally amended. The alleged offence had been committed between October 09, 2004, and December 01, 2004. The Attorney General also listed 14 productions and 23 prosecution witnesses in the case.

audit.summary: Worldwide, there are more than 12,000 reptile species, including approximately 4,100 species of snakes. audit.body: Worldwide, there are more than 12,000 reptile species, including approximately 4,100 species of snakes. The first international congress on amphibians and reptiles was held in England in 1989, and the 10th edition of that conference has since been successfully concluded.Commenting on Sri Lanka’s snake diversity, Dr Nimal D Ratnayake, Secretary-General of the 1st World Congress on Snakes, said the country had recorded 113 snake species belonging to 11 families, of which 64 were endemic. S ri Lanka is endowed with exceptional biodiversity and has earned international recognition for its contribution to herpetology, the study of reptiles and amphibians. The recently held 1st World Congress on Snakes – 2026 in Kandy, under the auspices of Environment Minister Dr Dammika Patabandige, once again highlighted the country’s role in advancing scientific research and the conservation of snakes. Scientists, researchers and conservationists from 44 countries attended the gathering. The congress was brought to Sri Lanka through the efforts of Dr Anslem de Silva. Its organisation was overseen by Dr Nimal D Ratnayake, World Congress on Snakes – 2026, Secretary-General, Dr. Nimal D. Ratnayake committee member Suranjan Karunarathna, Dr Kanishka Ukuwela of Rajarata University and committee member Nayana Daundasekara. Worldwide, there are more than 12,000 reptile species, including approximately 4,100 species of snakes. The first international congress on amphibians and reptiles was held in England in 1989, and the 10th edition of that conference has since been successfully concluded. Commenting on Sri Lanka’s snake diversity, Dr Nimal D Ratnayake, Secretary-General of the 1st World Congress on Snakes, said the country had recorded 113 snake species belonging to 11 families, of which 64 were endemic. The latest addition to the national list is Thasun’s bronze-back (Thasunge Haldanda), discovered on Maragala Mountain in 2025 by Anusha Attanagoda and his team. Dr Ratnayake explained that Sri Lankan snakes were classified into four main categories, based on their medical significance. The classification takes into account the frequency of bites by each species, the proportion of the human population exposed to risk given the snake’s geographical distribution, the prevalence of local and systemic toxic effects, and the number of fatalities resulting from bites. These criteria help determine the medical importance of different snake species in Sri Lanka and guide the assessment of the risks they pose to human health. Official snakebite statistics in Sri Lanka are based primarily on cases in which victims are admitted to hospital for treatment. However, many bites across the island go unrecorded, largely because some victims turn to traditional herbal remedies, occult practices known as kem , and various chants and incantations rather than seeking hospital care. Sri Lanka records approximately 30,000 to 40,000 snakebites annually, with reported fatalities remaining below 100. Unofficial estimates, however, suggest that the actual number of bites could be around 80,000 a year, resulting in approximately 400 deaths. Although snakes are often regarded primarily as venomous creatures to be feared, they are essential to the health and stability of ecosystems. As both predators and prey in the natural food web, they help maintain ecological balance by controlling populations of rodents, snails, cockroaches and insects that damage agricultural crops and can pose risks to human health. Although snake venom is widely regarded as deadly, it also has considerable value in modern medicine and traditional healing practices. Antivenom, used to treat potentially fatal snakebites, is produced using venom extracted from snakes. Dr Nimal D Ratnayake proposed establishing a dedicated hotline, similar to Sri Lanka’s 1990 Suwa Seriya ambulance service, to report snakes spotted in residential areas and other human-occupied spaces. “Instead of killing snakes out of fear or ignorance, people should be encouraged to report sightings immediately through a dedicated hotline. A trained team with experience in safely capturing snakes could respond to these calls. Equipped with appropriate uniforms and modern equipment, such a service could eventually be developed into a formal nationwide operation. This would help protect both people and snakes while contributing to environmental conservation,” he said. Urbanisation and deforestation have severely reduced the natural habitats of snakes, bringing them into closer contact with human settlements and heightening public fears about encounters with them. Yet it is worth remembering that, in many cases, it is humans who have encroached on snake habitats, rather than snakes invading human territory. The successful conclusion of the 1st World Congress on Snakes in Kandy offers an opportunity to encourage schoolchildren and younger generations in Sri Lanka to view snakes from a fresh environmental perspective. Dr Nimal D Ratnayake stressed the need to educate the public about snakebites and promote a more informed understanding of snakes. “Rather than killing a snake as soon as it is spotted, we must improve public awareness and understanding of these creatures. Institutions such as the Department of Wildlife Conservation, the Young Zoologists’ Association of Sri Lanka and the Amphibian and Reptile Research Organisation have a significant responsibility to fulfil in this regard. I also urge the public never to attempt to capture snakes without the necessary training and experience,” he said. Few creatures inspire as much irrational fear and hostility as snakes. Yet science reveals a different picture: these animals play a vital role in maintaining ecological balance, protecting agriculture by controlling pest populations and contributing to research that could advance medical science. This is the message the 1st World Congress on Snakes brought into focus. Sri Lanka is home to a remarkable diversity of snakes, including many species found nowhere else in the world. Protecting this natural heritage and preserving it for future generations is therefore a responsibility we cannot afford to neglect. The challenge is to move beyond the instinct to kill snakes on sight and foster a culture of informed co-existence and conservation. Recognising their ecological value is not merely a matter of protecting wildlife; it is also an investment in the health of our environment and the future we leave to those who follow us.

audit.headline: BASL concerned over death in Homagama police custody
audit.summary: The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) yesterday expressed grave concern over the death of 29-year-old Ishara Harshakumara, a father of two from Kiriwaththuduwa, while in the custody of the Homagama Police Station following his arrest on October 25. Highlighting the contradiction between police claims of a sudden illness and family allegations of severe physical assault, the BASL emphasised that every person in State custody has a fundamental right to life and bodily integrity. Invoking constitutional protections under Article 13(4), the legal body called upon the Inspector General and relevant authorities to conduct an immediate, impartial, and transparent investigation to ensure accountability and preserve public confidence in the administration of justice.
audit.body: The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) yesterday expressed grave concern over the death of 29-year-old Ishara Harshakumara, a father of two from Kiriwaththuduwa, while in the custody of the Homagama Police Station following his arrest on October 25. Highlighting the contradiction between police claims of a sudden illness and family allegations of severe physical assault, the BASL emphasised that every person in State custody has a fundamental right to life and bodily integrity. Invoking constitutional protections under Article 13(4), the legal body called upon the Inspector General and relevant authorities to conduct an immediate, impartial, and transparent investigation to ensure accountability and preserve public confidence in the administration of justice. The BASL statement further said: “The BASL views with grave concern the death of 29-year-old Ishara Harshakumara, a resident of Kiriwaththuduwa and a father of two, while in the custody of the Homagama Police Station following his arrest in connection with a drug-related investigation. It has been reported that members of the family, who visited the Homagama Police Station on October 25 morning to inquire about his condition, have expressed the view that they observed physical injuries which, in their opinion, indicated that he had been severely assaulted. In contrast, the Police Spokesman has stated that the suspect developed a sudden illness during an operation and died following hospital admission. In these circumstances, the BASL considers it imperative that the circumstances surrounding the death are fully and independently established, and that the differing accounts and concerns raised in relation thereto are subjected to a transparent and credible investigation. The BASL emphasises that a death in custody is a matter of the gravest concern, and that the State has a fundamental and non-delegable duty to safeguard the life, health and bodily integrity of every person in its custody. Any allegation of custodial violence or ill-treatment must therefore be treated with the utmost seriousness and, if established, dealt with strictly in accordance with the law. Article 13(4) of the Constitution and the jurisprudence of the higher judiciary affirm that deprivation of life cannot be imposed as punishment except by order of a competent court, underscoring the obligation of law enforcement authorities to ensure that the rights and dignity of persons in custody are fully protected. While noting that the Homagama Magistrate’s Court has ordered a post-mortem examination and that a preliminary inquiry has been initiated under the direction of the Homagama Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP). In a matter involving an allegation of custodial violence, public confidence requires that no reasonable question is left unanswered and that any person responsible for wrongdoing, if established, is held accountable in accordance with the law. Accordingly, the BASL calls upon the Inspector General of Police and all relevant authorities to ensure an immediate, impartial, transparent and comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of Ishara Harshakumara, with all relevant evidence properly preserved and examined and the investigation conducted without interference or prejudice. The BASL condemns any act of custodial violence or unlawful deprivation of life, if established through a proper investigation, while reiterating that the facts must be determined through a fair, independent and credible process. The BASL will take further steps if required in this regard and keep its membership and the public informed”.

audit.headline: Ceylon Chamber leads business promotion mission to Indonesia
audit.summary: The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce conducted a Business Promotion Mission to Jakarta, Indonesia, from 13 to 17 October 2026, to strengthen Sri Lanka–Indonesia business relations and explore opportunities for trade, investment and private sector collaboration. Led by Sheamalee Wickramasingha, Chairman and Group Managing Director, CBL Group, the delegation comprised representatives from CBL Global Foods Limited, Silvermill Group, Antler Fabric Printers (Pvt) Ltd, Dinamore (Pvt) Ltd, Macksons Holdings (Pvt) Ltd and The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce. During the mission, the delegation participated in Trade Expo Indonesia (TEI) 2026, engaging with potential business partners and exploring Indonesia’s export capabilities.
audit.body: The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce conducted a Business Promotion Mission to Jakarta, Indonesia, from 13 to 17 October 2026, to strengthen Sri Lanka–Indonesia business relations and explore opportunities for trade, investment and private sector collaboration. Led by Sheamalee Wickramasingha, Chairman and Group Managing Director, CBL Group, the delegation comprised representatives from CBL Global Foods Limited, Silvermill Group, Antler Fabric Printers (Pvt) Ltd, Dinamore (Pvt) Ltd, Macksons Holdings (Pvt) Ltd and The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce. During the mission, the delegation participated in Trade Expo Indonesia (TEI) 2026, engaging with potential business partners and exploring Indonesia’s export capabilities. The programme also included meetings with the Indonesian Ministry of Trade, the Indonesian Employers’ Association (APINDO) and the Indonesian Food and Beverage Association (GAPMMI) to discuss opportunities for closer business engagement and expanded trade. A key outcome of the visit was the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce and the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KADIN Indonesia). The agreement establishes a framework for closer cooperation between the two chambers, including facilitating business-to-business connections and promoting trade and investment opportunities in both markets. The delegation also attended Sri Lanka Connect 2026 in Jakarta on 16 October, where discussions included a meeting with Nurul Ichwan, Deputy Minister of Investment Promotion of Indonesia, to explore investment opportunities and strengthen economic cooperation. The mission concluded with a dinner hosted by Sashikala Premawardhana, Ambassador of Sri Lanka to Indonesia and ASEAN, providing a further opportunity to discuss bilateral business relations. The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce extends its appreciation to Sashikala Premawardhana and Dewi Gustina Tobing, Ambassador of the Republic of Indonesia to Sri Lanka, along with officials of both diplomatic missions, for their support in coordinating the programme and facilitating engagements with Indonesian institutions and business organisations. Through this mission, The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce continues to support Sri Lankan businesses in exploring overseas markets, establishing international partnerships and expanding trade and investment links with Indonesia and the wider ASEAN region.

audit.headline: Terrorisms impact on global security
audit.summary: Yemeni Houthi rebels have launched an escalating wave of missile, drone, and projectile strikes against Saudi Arabia, intensifying a renewed phase of cross-border conflict. Saudi Arabia has one of the largest defense budgets in the world, and its armed forces are equipped with advanced fighters and air-defense systems. But the Houthis have indigenous missiles and drones to effectively counter Saudi military strengths. G lobally, terrorism will add to instability and drive international security interventions, especially in the Middle East and Africa. The threat from terrorism will remain high and will worsen over the next five years, in spite of strong counter-terrorism measures.Extremists will continue to exploit fragile and violence-prone states, including in Southeast Asia.
audit.body: Yemeni Houthi rebels have launched an escalating wave of missile, drone, and projectile strikes against Saudi Arabia, intensifying a renewed phase of cross-border conflict. Saudi Arabia has one of the largest defense budgets in the world, and its armed forces are equipped with advanced fighters and air-defense systems. But the Houthis have indigenous missiles and drones to effectively counter Saudi military strengths. G lobally, terrorism will add to instability and drive international security interventions, especially in the Middle East and Africa. The threat from terrorism will remain high and will worsen over the next five years, in spite of strong counter-terrorism measures.Extremists will continue to exploit fragile and violence-prone states, including in Southeast Asia. New technologies could make it easier for terrorists to make advanced biological or chemical warfare agents.Extremist narratives will continue to inspire violence globally. The terrorism threat in Southeast Asia is increasing because of links between local extremists and terrorist groups.Terrorism significantly reduces foreign direct investment and capital formation, leading to economic instability. In 2023, the number of terrorist attacks worldwide surged to 3469. Yemeni Houthi rebels have launched an escalating wave of missile, drone, and projectile strikes against Saudi Arabia, intensifying a renewed phase of cross-border conflict. Saudi Arabia has one of the largest defense budgets in the world, and its armed forces are equipped with advanced fighters and air-defense systems. But the Houthis have indigenous missiles and drones to effectively counter Saudi military strengths. Pakistan and Egypt have condemned attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi movement on Saudi Arabia, reaffirming their support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, amid escalating regional tensions. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers have called for a return to dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the crisis involving Iran and safeguard regional security and stability, urging a political solution. Rather than a “war on terror,” what is needed is to transform security itself.Democracy provides opportunities for conflict prevention, conflict management and conflict resolution as well as opportunities of political participation. The word “terrorism” is politically and emotionally charged, and this greatly compounds the difficulty of providing a precise definition. What is terrorism, to one group may connote freedom fight to another group. Terrorism, in the modern sense, is violence against civilians to achieve political or ideological objectives by creating fear. Terrorists also attack national symbols to show their power and to shake the foundation of the country or society they are opposed to. This may negatively affect a government’s legitimacy. The United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy reaffirms the links between human rights and security, and places respect for the rule of law and human rights at the core of national and international counter-terrorism efforts. Terrorism is a transnational threat that cannot be addressed by a single country alone. The international order is also being contested in other ways. Some states have increased their use of ‘measures short of war’ to pursue political and security objectives. Such measures include the use of non-state actors and other proxies, covert and paramilitary operations and media manipulation. In parts of the Indo–Pacific, China’s power and influence are growing to match (in some cases exceed) that of the United States. The future balance of power in the Indo–Pacific will largely depend on the actions of the United States, China and major powers such as Japan and India.The quality and quantity of missile forces in the Indo–Pacific is rising, including ballistic missiles. Al-Qaeda operates from several safe havens around the world, one of which is Iran. Its alleged Iran directly supports al-Qaeda with weapons and funding. But their religious ideological differences, a Shia Iran and a Sunni al-Qaeda, limit direct commitment to each other’s political objectives. The core of their relationship is centred on disrupting US interests in the region. On the other side a threat has grown. Extreme Right-Wing Terrorism (ERWT) describes those involved in Extreme Right-Wing activity who use violence in furtherance of their ideology. These ideologies can be broadly characterized as Cultural Nationalism, White Nationalism and White Supremacism. Terrorist attacks can be broadly categorized into two categories: focused and indiscriminate. Historically, terrorism has largely fallen under the former category. In terms of the use of violence and force by terrorists, this also ranges across a wide spectrum- from individuals with military training and experience and “throwaway” operatives, who are sent untrained on suicide missions. Their use of violencealso illustrates the slow evolution of terrorist tactics and strategies, including traditionalassassination, bombings, arson, hostage-taking, hijacking sabotage and suicide bombings.More recent tactics include unconventional forms of terrorism,including nuclear terrorism (fabricating a dirty bomb, attacking a nuclear reactor etc) and high-tech terrorism involving cyberattacks. In spite of the apparent decline in Al Qaeda and ISIS in the Middle East, violent extremism linked to the two terrorist organisations continues to pose an ideological and security threat to Southeast Asia. ISIS’ growing footprint in this region can increasingly felt.Extremist networks in Southeast Asia often exploit policy gaps and security loopholes between nations to operate, recruit members and secure funding. The first is the significant growth in terrorist attacks by ISIS-inspired, self-radicalised individuals. The March 2021 ‘lone wolf’ attack on the Indonesian National Police Headquarters by a young female college student, shows the danger of radicalized domestic terrorists. She was reportedly radicalised online by ISIS propaganda. Since 2023, Indonesia has experienced a period with no large-scale terrorist attacks. Far from signaling the end of terrorism, it reflects an evolving threat which is moving online to radicalise lone-wolf actors. In 2020, the Philippines passed an anti-terrorism act. The act considerably expanded the definition of terrorism to include activities that incite terror and extremism, such as provocative speeches and proclamations.The Abu Sayyaf group, originally devoted to the establishment of a radical Islamic state in the Philippines through terrorism, has been fragmented by the bold Philippine military response. However by virtue of its maritime capability, it is an important part of the maritime terrorist threat facing Southeast Asia. The Abu Sayyaf Group (founded in 1991) remains a violent extremist and terrorist threat in the southern Philippines. Although ASG has historically aligned itself with al-Qa’ida and Jemaah Islamiyah, some ASG sub-groups have pledged allegiance to Islamic State.The continuous entry of foreign jihadists to the southern Philippines only compounds these issues, as radical foreigners subvert the minds of the locals. The strategic geographic location of India in foreign trade, combined with its natural resources spread across land and coastal areas, mandates a multi-faceted security apparatus. These long borders present multiple security challenges- illegal immigrants, insurgency, cross-border terrorism and illicit drug trade. India’s separatist landscape is shaped by a complex interplay of ethnic, religious and regional factors, particularly evident in regions such as Punjab, and Kashmir. India prudently subdivides terrorism into five major groups: ethno-nationalist terrorism, religious terrorism, ideological, narcoterrorism and state-sponsored terrorism. Europe could be more directly affected. Over the past decade, intelligence data collected shows that Iran increased its collaboration with criminal networks in Western countries to commit violence and target journalists, politicians, Jewish communities, and Iranian dissidents.Iran’s previous weaponization of criminal networks has targeted Jewish communities and synagogues, particularly in Europe, considering them legitimate extensions and representations of Israel.Iran also directly engages in state-led terrorism with agents deployed around the world that can be activated when necessary. Some of these agents act as interlocutors with Organised Crime Gangs (OCG) and terrorists in Europe. Recent attacks in the EU demonstrate the intent and capability of jihadist terrorists to inflict mass casualties on urban populations. The main concern of Member States is jihadist terrorism and the closely related phenomenon of foreign terrorist fighters who travel to and from conflict zones.The right-wing terrorism threat in Europe also remains a serious and evolving security challenge. Foreign terrorist fighters (FTFs) are individuals who travel to a state other than their state of residence or nationality to commit, plan, or receive training for terrorist acts. They continue to pose an evolving threat to global security. The European Parliamentary Research Service estimated 4,000 citizens from European Union (EU) member states (mostly from Belgium, France, Germany and the United Kingdom) left to participate in the Syrian civil war, with over 30 per cent having returned to Europe. In the past few years terrorist groups have begun employing drones. Both can be harnessed to respond effectively to multiple security challenges.Uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) have been identified as one of the key terrorist threats by the United Nations (UN) Security Council Counter-Terrorism Committee. UAS are remotely piloted airborne vehicles. They are also referred to as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), or more commonly drones.UAS are attractive for terrorists because they are affordable and require minimal training. Terrorists have deployed drones to attack state military assets, diplomatic sites, international trade, energy infrastructure, and civilian centres. State sponsorship of terrorist groups has also helped increase the number of drone attacks. Globally drones can travel up to 1,500 km, ideal for attacks on military targets deep within state territory.In 2015, a drone with radioactive sand targeted the roof of the Japanese Prime Minister’s office. Governments’ worldwide will also face a significant national security threat. Drones also perpetuate the psychological dimension of terrorism by spreading fear. Countries need extensive defence cooperation and intelligence sharing to mitigate terrorism.

audit.headline: Speaker should either resign or face charges – SJB
audit.summary: The Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) and Opposition parliamentarians state that the refusal to debate a No-Confidence Motion (NCM) brought by the Opposition against Speaker Dr. Jagath Wickramaratne constitutes a severe blow to the rights of the Opposition within a democracy. The SJB says that it will not be a party to any government scheme to amend or withdraw the serious allegations against the Speaker to suit the government’s own agenda and maintains that the Speaker should either resign from his post or face the 50 charges brought against him without fear by allowing a debate on the No-Confidence Motion against him to proceed. The motion has been signed by 44 Opposition Members of Parliament including Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa which is based on 50 allegations leveled against the Speaker.
audit.body: The Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) and Opposition parliamentarians state that the refusal to debate a No-Confidence Motion (NCM) brought by the Opposition against Speaker Dr. Jagath Wickramaratne constitutes a severe blow to the rights of the Opposition within a democracy. The SJB says that it will not be a party to any government scheme to amend or withdraw the serious allegations against the Speaker to suit the government’s own agenda and maintains that the Speaker should either resign from his post or face the 50 charges brought against him without fear by allowing a debate on the No-Confidence Motion against him to proceed. The motion has been signed by 44 Opposition Members of Parliament including Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa which is based on 50 allegations leveled against the Speaker. A statement issued by the media unit of the Office of the Leader of the Opposition yesterday (27) notes that this No-Confidence Motion was submitted to Parliament on October 9,2026, and included in the Order Paper on October 12. The Parliament Secretariat has announced that the revised No-Confidence Motion, set to be submitted by the Opposition, is scheduled for debate on Tuesday, November 3. The statement by the Opposition also notes that, according to legal experts, the government’s claim that this motion is subject to a judicial process (sub judice) is false. According to the statement, the allegations were based on a parliamentary report titled ‘Report of the Inquiry into the Leak of Confidential Information Regarding the Speaker’, which was prepared following a letter from the Speaker’s Private Secretary. Although it was previously agreed to seek a report from the Attorney General regarding whether the allegations contained in the motion might conflict with ongoing judicial proceedings, the government’s stance articulated during a party leaders’ meeting held on October 23, chaired by the Speaker was that consulting the Attorney General is unnecessary. The government further maintained that the matter could only be addressed if the Opposition were to amend the allegations and resubmit the motion. The Opposition points out that it is unethical for the Speaker to continue in his position while the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption is conducting an inquiry against him. Furthermore, they assert that the arguments presented by the government to reject this no-confidence motion lack any logical basis. The Opposition has further urged the public to take note of this situation, warning that the government’s unilateral decision poses a grave threat to the country’s democracy.

audit.headline: Isipathana edge St. Joseph Vaz to claim Under-15 Servo Hockey Title
audit.summary: Displaying grit, tactical discipline, and exceptional teamwork, the stick-wielding lads from Isipathana College put up a stellar campaign to capture the championship title at the recently concluded U-15 Servo Hockey Tournament held in Matale. The green shirts navigated a demanding tournament path featuring top-tier school hockey outfits from across the island, ultimately clinching the prestigious Servo Cup in thrilling fashion. Isipathana kicked off their group matches with a bang, blanking Mahinda Rajapaksha College 3-0. Though they faced minor setbacks in the preliminary rounds sharing honors in tightly contested 1–1 draws against Hindu College and Vijaya College, alongside a narrow 1–0 defeat to St. Joseph’s College, Wennappuwa they quickly rediscovered their rhythm. A commanding 3-0 victory over Ovilikanda Maha Vidyalaya firmly stamped their ticket into the knockout phases.
audit.body: Displaying grit, tactical discipline, and exceptional teamwork, the stick-wielding lads from Isipathana College put up a stellar campaign to capture the championship title at the recently concluded U-15 Servo Hockey Tournament held in Matale. The green shirts navigated a demanding tournament path featuring top-tier school hockey outfits from across the island, ultimately clinching the prestigious Servo Cup in thrilling fashion. Isipathana kicked off their group matches with a bang, blanking Mahinda Rajapaksha College 3-0. Though they faced minor setbacks in the preliminary rounds sharing honors in tightly contested 1–1 draws against Hindu College and Vijaya College, alongside a narrow 1–0 defeat to St. Joseph’s College, Wennappuwa they quickly rediscovered their rhythm. A commanding 3-0 victory over Ovilikanda Maha Vidyalaya firmly stamped their ticket into the knockout phases. The knockout stage tested the team’s mental fortitude to the absolute limit, requiring ice-cold composure under pressure. In the quarter-finals, Isipathana locked horns with host-city favorites St. Thomas’ College, Matale. After regular time ended deadlocked at 1–1, the Pathana stickmen kept their nerves intact during the penalty strokes, prevailing 2–0. The semi-final against Zahira College, Matale, proved equally tense. With neither side able to break the deadlock during regulation time, the match once again spilled into a dramatic penalty shootout. Demonstrating sharp defensive focus, Isipathana scraped through with a 1–0 stroke victory. Carrying their momentum into the grand finale against St. Joseph Vaz College, Wennappuwa, Isipathana delivered when it mattered most. A solitary, hard-fought goal separated the two sides at the final whistle, sealing a 1–0 win and sparking wild celebrations among the team and their traveling supporters as they hoisted the U-15 Servo Cup aloft. Isipathana’s collective triumph was further enriched by individual accolades, recognizing the standout performers who anchored their championship run: Best Player of the Tournament: M. Zaid, Best Goalkeeper of the Tournament: Sanuka Dilsara.

audit.headline: Transformation Committee curbs Franchise League play for Cricketers
audit.summary: Sri Lanka Cricket Transformation Committee has called on a press briefing at the SLC yesterday. Its member Sidath Wettimuny said Sri Lanka Cricket is set to introduce new restrictions on players’ participation in franchise Leagues, limiting them to three Leagues per year, including the Lanka Premier League (LPL). Wettimuny further said that under the proposed measures, players will also be required to return to Sri Lanka at least 10 days before an international commitment, ending their involvement in franchise cricket well ahead of national duty. He also said that the move is aimed at strengthening players’ commitment to the national team and ensuring Sri Lanka’s international commitments take priority over franchise cricket.
audit.body: Sri Lanka Cricket Transformation Committee has called on a press briefing at the SLC yesterday. Its member Sidath Wettimuny said Sri Lanka Cricket is set to introduce new restrictions on players’ participation in franchise Leagues, limiting them to three Leagues per year, including the Lanka Premier League (LPL). Wettimuny further said that under the proposed measures, players will also be required to return to Sri Lanka at least 10 days before an international commitment, ending their involvement in franchise cricket well ahead of national duty. He also said that the move is aimed at strengthening players’ commitment to the national team and ensuring Sri Lanka’s international commitments take priority over franchise cricket. SLC has previously introduced similar restrictions on franchise League participation but the regulations were not consistently enforced with several players participating in more franchise tournaments than permitted. Meanwhile the Transformation Committee also plans to strengthen the process of issuing No objection Certificates (NOCs) for overseas franchise Leagues with players fitness level becoming an important factor in granting permission. Wettimuny also pointed out that today too much of cricket for players has paved the way to more injuries. Injury management is also a key factor. All the proposed regulations are aimed at improving player fitness, managing workloads and ensuring national team commitments take first priority over franchise cricket. The Chairman of the SLC transformation committee Eran Wickramaratne said that Sri Lanka Cricket will have a new parliament approved constitution by the end of this year and If the legislative process continues smoothly regular elections can recommence at SLC in the early 2027 which would in turn pave the way for SLC reclaim it’s position as a fully operational member at the ICC,” said Chairman Eran. Meanwhile Roshan Mahanama, a member of the Transformation Committee pointed out that players discipline and fitness are paramount. The trainers, Physios have a big part and SLC is also looking on players short term and long term plans to develop cricket. The 2007 men’s ODI World Cup, next year’s under 19 boys and girls World Cup as well as women’s Champion Trophy in next March are part of short term plans and we are working on these assignments,” added Mahanama.

audit.headline: NCE Council reviews export sector barriers and forex opportunities
audit.summary: The National Chamber of Exporters of Sri Lanka (NCE) reviewed sectoral issues, export-market requirements and overseas trade plans at its Council meeting on 20 October 2026. Held in partnership with Prime Group and Melwa at the Prime Marina Sales Suite in Port City, the meeting considered matters the Chamber is taking up with authorities. The Council reviewed issues being pursued with government institutions. Among the matters discussed was the delay in implementing the Madrid Protocol. WIPO’s Madrid System provides trademark holders with a one-stop solution to secure and manage brand protection and covers 117 members representing 133 countries and over 80% of global trade, with more than 1.7 million registered trademarks. According to NIPO, the final draft is now to be submitted to Parliament for approval.
audit.body: The National Chamber of Exporters of Sri Lanka (NCE) reviewed sectoral issues, export-market requirements and overseas trade plans at its Council meeting on 20 October 2026. Held in partnership with Prime Group and Melwa at the Prime Marina Sales Suite in Port City, the meeting considered matters the Chamber is taking up with authorities. The Council reviewed issues being pursued with government institutions. Among the matters discussed was the delay in implementing the Madrid Protocol. WIPO’s Madrid System provides trademark holders with a one-stop solution to secure and manage brand protection and covers 117 members representing 133 countries and over 80% of global trade, with more than 1.7 million registered trademarks. According to NIPO, the final draft is now to be submitted to Parliament for approval. The council also discussed restrictions affecting the forest sector, and difficulties faced by electrical and electronic product exporters. During January–August 2026, Sri Lanka’s Electrical and Electronic Components (EEC) exports grew exceptionally, by 57.49% YoY to USD 440.31 Mn. For August 2026 alone, sector earnings reached USD 62.4 Mn, supported by a 30.83% rise in Insulated Wires & Cables. Overall, this performance highlights the industry’s expanding competitiveness and export potential. The NCE has been following up with the relevant authorities on these issues, including seeking a documented action plan from the Ministry of Environment. The Chamber has also requested further support from the Sri Lankan Commercial Officer in India in addressing trade difficulties arising from India’s BIS-QCOs and discussions with the Inland Revenue Department on VAT refunds are also being pursued. Changes to import procedures and new European Union regulations were mentioned in the meeting’s review of trade-related concerns. Following Customs’ shift to digital processing of import documentation on 1 October, the NCE is surveying exporters to identify difficulties with importing raw materials, machinery, packaging materials and other inputs. Meanwhile, the Chamber and other stakeholders are seeking technical assistance and training for exporters preparing to help Sri Lankan exporters comply with regulations, including EU’s new limits on mineral oil contaminants in food and agricultural products, due to take effect in January 2027. The EU’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation was also discussed, given its implications for exporters supplying that market. At the next sectoral discussions, members will address mineral-based products, chemicals, engineering, and electrical and electronic products. Topics include supply-chain bottlenecks, tariff barriers under bilateral free trade agreements, standardisation and raw-material costs. Conducting a presentation on Export & Beyond, entrepreneur, Chartered Engineer and inventor Lalith Kahatapitiya, Founder and Chairman of KIK Group of Companies, called for new foreign-exchange channels beyond existing sources. He emphasized the importance of several measures for the economy, including re-exports, local suppliers serving exporters, and the need for a new National Business Facilitation Centre. The Chamber’s overseas programmes are also taking shape, a visit to Italy and Sweden is planned for March 2027, with a trade show in Milan and business meetings in Stockholm. The council also discussed several upcoming plans, such as the NCE Budget Forum on 19 November and the 34th NCE Export Awards on 11 December.

audit.headline: New laws to prevent child exploitation on social media
audit.summary: Women and Child Affairs Minister Saroja Paulraj said new laws and regulations to prevent the growing trend of parents, adults involving children in various dangerous activities to earn money through social media will be enacted. A wide range of such activities are increasingly being reported on social media, including taking children to dangerous locations and high-risk areas, encouraging them to use obscene language, involving them in content or themes more appropriate for adults, and exposing them to sexually explicit content. The Minister pointed out that when parents put their own children at risk in pursuit of money or popularity, it raises serious questions about their suitability to fulfil their responsibilities as parents. The Minister further emphasised that even parents do not have the right to jeopardise a child’s privacy.
audit.body: Women and Child Affairs Minister Saroja Paulraj said new laws and regulations to prevent the growing trend of parents, adults involving children in various dangerous activities to earn money through social media will be enacted. A wide range of such activities are increasingly being reported on social media, including taking children to dangerous locations and high-risk areas, encouraging them to use obscene language, involving them in content or themes more appropriate for adults, and exposing them to sexually explicit content. The Minister pointed out that when parents put their own children at risk in pursuit of money or popularity, it raises serious questions about their suitability to fulfil their responsibilities as parents. The Minister further emphasised that even parents do not have the right to jeopardise a child’s privacy. She stated that it is not for parents to decide whether a child should seek popularity or public attention.Rather, this should be a personal decision made by the child when they have reached adulthood and attained sufficient maturity to make such choices independently. The Minister strongly stressed that children who are placed at serious risk due to their parents’ irresponsible use of social media may have to be considered children in need of protection. She further noted that, to safeguard their welfare and security, it may become necessary in the future to place such children under the care of protective guardianship arrangements. Meanwhile, the Women’s and Child Affairs Ministry in collaboration with the National Child Protection Authority (NCPA), has taken steps to develop a set of guidelines through a panel of experts, with the aim of fostering a child-friendly media culture. The preparation of these guidelines is currently in its final stage, and they are expected to be implemented in the near future. Countries around the world are also taking stricter measures to prevent the use of children on social media for commercial gain or personal fame, a practice commonly known as “kidfluencing.” Jurisdictions such as France and California in the United States have introduced legal requirements to ensure that income generated by children through social media is deposited into protected accounts for their future benefit. Laws have also been introduced to limit the amount of time children can be involved in such activities. Major global social media platforms are also introducing stricter policies to protect the privacy of minors. Through these new guidelines, Sri Lanka aims to establish a similar protective framework to safeguard children from exploitation on social media.

audit.headline: Rs.5 Mn compensation for dead, disabled officers
audit.summary: The Cabinet of Ministers approved payment of special compensation and relief to prison officers who were killed or injured on duty during clashes at the Negombo Prison on July 5 and 6, 2026, Cabinet Spokesman and Health and Mass Media Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said. Addressing the weekly Cabinet press briefing yesterday (27), the minister said that during the cabinet meeting on August 3, 2026, the Cabinet had decided to appoint a committee headed by the Justice and National Integration Ministry Secretary to make recommendations on the matter. The committee has since submitted its report, which was presented to the Cabinet, and approval was granted to implement its recommendations. “Under the approved proposal, special compensation will be paid in addition to the compensation provided under Public Administration Circular No. 22/93.
audit.body: The Cabinet of Ministers approved payment of special compensation and relief to prison officers who were killed or injured on duty during clashes at the Negombo Prison on July 5 and 6, 2026, Cabinet Spokesman and Health and Mass Media Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said. Addressing the weekly Cabinet press briefing yesterday (27), the minister said that during the cabinet meeting on August 3, 2026, the Cabinet had decided to appoint a committee headed by the Justice and National Integration Ministry Secretary to make recommendations on the matter. The committee has since submitted its report, which was presented to the Cabinet, and approval was granted to implement its recommendations. “Under the approved proposal, special compensation will be paid in addition to the compensation provided under Public Administration Circular No. 22/93. Rs.5 million will be paid for each officer who was killed, and Rs. 5 million to any officer who was totally disabled in the clashes. An officer who suffered partial disability with a 100% loss of maximum earning capacity will receive Rs. 4 million, while an officer who suffered temporary partial disability will receive Rs. 3 million. The Cabinet also approved amending the Prisons Ordinance to include appropriate provisions granting legal status to the Prisons Tactical Force. Measures will be taken to strengthen the force by recruiting a sufficient number of suitable officers, and to provide it with formal training in relevant fields and the necessary modern equipment. Steps will also be taken to establish a headquarters for the force at a suitable location.

audit.headline: CBSL marks 76th Anniversary with oration on AI and Public Trust
audit.summary: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) marked its 76th anniversary with a high-level oration on how artificial intelligence is reshaping central banking, held at the Central Bank Atrium on 23 October 2026. The oration was delivered by Shirin Hamid, Chief Information Officer and Director of the Information Technology Department at the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Her address, titled “The Intelligent Central Bank: Building Trust in the Age of AI,” explored both the promise and the pitfalls of deploying AI in monetary and financial institutions. Hamid said AI holds significant potential to strengthen how central banks carry out their mandates, but warned that the associated risks demand careful management. She stressed that building and sustaining public trust is essential as central banks increasingly weave AI-driven solutions into their operations and decision-making.
audit.body: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) marked its 76th anniversary with a high-level oration on how artificial intelligence is reshaping central banking, held at the Central Bank Atrium on 23 October 2026. The oration was delivered by Shirin Hamid, Chief Information Officer and Director of the Information Technology Department at the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Her address, titled “The Intelligent Central Bank: Building Trust in the Age of AI,” explored both the promise and the pitfalls of deploying AI in monetary and financial institutions. Hamid said AI holds significant potential to strengthen how central banks carry out their mandates, but warned that the associated risks demand careful management. She stressed that building and sustaining public trust is essential as central banks increasingly weave AI-driven solutions into their operations and decision-making. Responsible adoption, she argued, depends on systems that are explainable, secure and ethical, backed by robust governance frameworks. She also underlined the need for effective human oversight, to ensure AI enhances institutional accountability, sharpens decision-making and improves operational effectiveness. The occasion served as a platform for dialogue and knowledge-sharing on AI’s evolving role in central banking, with particular attention to its implications for institutional credibility, public trust and operational effectiveness. In a statement issued by its Secretariat Department on 27 October, the CBSL said the oration reaffirmed its commitment to fostering informed dialogue on emerging technologies and their responsible adoption. The bank said the aim is to strengthen institutional resilience, preserve public trust and prepare for the future of central banking. The anniversary oration comes as central banks worldwide weigh how to harness advanced technologies while safeguarding the credibility that underpins their work.

audit.headline: Coherence in qualifications frameworks
audit.summary: I n getting ready a book to celebrate the ninth decade of Lakmahal, the house in which I have lived for almost all my years, I thought I should go through the four previous books I wrote that were based on the house. They also covered various aspects of my life, even the very first book, though that started with a long account of how my grandparents had set up the place way back in 1937. That book had a little about my childhood and then went into greater detail about the years after I got back from Oxford, including the work I did at the British Council. I then went on to perhaps the most productive period of my life, the second book being entitled Lakmahal Justified: Taking English to the People.
audit.body: I n getting ready a book to celebrate the ninth decade of Lakmahal, the house in which I have lived for almost all my years, I thought I should go through the four previous books I wrote that were based on the house. They also covered various aspects of my life, even the very first book, though that started with a long account of how my grandparents had set up the place way back in 1937. That book had a little about my childhood and then went into greater detail about the years after I got back from Oxford, including the work I did at the British Council. I then went on to perhaps the most productive period of my life, the second book being entitled Lakmahal Justified: Taking English to the People. The third book was about my work at a national level, during the war and in pursuit of peace, while the fourth was about what I termed the Endgame, though there was still some useful work done then. I am pleasantly surprised, rereading all these, at how much I achieved. I am also saddened by what I did not achieve, despite intense efforts. Some of the drawbacks, with regard to both financial improprieties and culpable diffidence on the part of civil servants I looked at a couple of weeks back, in the context of the efforts to stop Mahinda Rajapaksa’s war effort. Today I want to look at problems I found in rereading the fourth book, which also covers my time as Chairman of the Tertiary and Vocational Education Commission. It was while there that I learnt about National Vocational Qualifications, of which there are seven levels. I found then that while there were many courses in the vocational training sector at levels 3 and 4, there were hardly any at levels 1 and 2, and these had been almost totally neglected. The idea of a ladder of progress began at the third level, though I managed to introduce English and Soft Skills courses at levels 1 and 2. These were immensely popular, though there was much resistance, led initially by the egregious Ranga Bandara whom Ranil had made Deputy Minister, who claimed that language did not come under vocational studies. This despite the fact that the training centres had long been offering English proficiency courses, though these were fundamentally wrongheaded, and not designed to develop communication skills, But I plan to look today not at NVQs but at another Qualifications Framework I discovered had also been developed, the Sri Lanka Qualifications Framework, which rejoices in 12 levels. This had been established by the universities, and its first level was the same as NVQ level 3. But the exclusive nature of our educational institutions was obvious in that the UGC had not bothered at all about defining their Levels 1 and 2 with the precision they brought to bear on the higher levels. I saw when I had a wider brief, being also on the National Education Commission, that the SLQF defined the skills and competencies at their Level 1 as being ‘Comparable to the holders of GCE (Ordinary Level) qualification’ and those at Level 2 as being ‘Comparable to the holders of GCE (Advanced Level) qualification’. But when we got to Level 3 they specified that ‘The qualification holders: -Should have an understanding of theory, practice, relevant methodology and recent developments in a particular area of study’. And they referred too to communication and problem solving skills as well as assuming responsibility and leadership. When I brought up the lacuna with regard to secondary schooling at the National Education Commission, my colleagues were horrified at the omission, though why none of them had noticed this previously is inexplicable if one assumes they were serious about their responsibilities. They agreed that this should be remedied and I prepared a draft, but unfortunately I was dismissed as TVEC Chair before the draft could be ratified. When I called the NEC a couple of months later to check on progress the Vice-Chairman told me they had more important things to consider. When I asked what these were, he said they had to finalise the criteria for recruitment to positions within the NEC. In short, the NEC had become a self-perpetuating entity that took little cognisance of what it was supposed to contribute to the nation, its own vegetable existence being a greater priority. I find that there has been a stab at suggesting the wider dimensions of education in the National Curriculum Framework produced by the Ministry of Education a few years back. This is a step forward, though the UGC has still not done anything about the basic levels of their SLQF when they might easily have extrapolated some requirements from what the MoE has produced. But as usual the MoE guidelines are verbose and will not be easy for teachers to comprehend. So I reproduce today the suggestions I made way back in 2017, which I trust makes clear what should be aimed at through the Ordinary Level curriculum, or rather what should have been achieved through the decade and more of schooling leading up to that examination. It said Students with a General Certificate of Education at Ordinary Level should have *Basic communication skills including the ability, in mother tongue and another language, to Express themselves politely and appropriately Frame and respond to simple questions Ask for and offer help Express likes and dislikes with reasons And, in mother tongue, to present and respond to reasons and arguments *Literacy in mother tongue and another language, as to reading and understanding and writing, with the capacity to Form letters and use basic punctuation correctly Find relevant information from a text Infer the meaning of words Scan for particular information and skim for general gist Understand basic notices, instructions and information Follow a simple story and answer questions about it Pay due attention to spelling and grammar And, in mother tongue, to read and write simple and coherent descriptions and narratives *Numeracy, with the ability to understand the concept of proportionality and calculate percentages be able to shop and pay and get the correct change calculate size and weight and area *The ability to read and extract information from maps and charts and tables organizational capacity, with the ability to divide up tasks for efficiency develop understanding of the needs of other people, and tolerance and the ability to empathise *Simple technical competencies, and the ability, while observing safety requirements, to use simple tools and instruments such as a hammer, screwdriver, spanner, needle and thread, computer, gas cooker *Basic aesthetic understanding including the ability to represent moods and feelings through colours or sounds *Understanding of concepts such as chronological order, sequencing, cause and effect, conditionality, and how to communicate these *Ability to work systematically and use tools or reasoning such as induction and deduction and comparison and contrasts and variables, so as to assess and analyse logically *Appreciation of social norms including the importance of Respecting other points of view Planning, prioritization and time management Entertainingly, if also very sadly, I was contacted a few years later by Prof Upali Mampitiya on behalf of the UGC Quality Assurance Council who asked me about the competencies he had seen in one of the textbooks I had produced while at the TVEC, about what Students with the GCE (Ordinary Level) should have. He said the Council wanted to ‘find out if that list is obtained from a government source since that would help us to use them as a benchmark’. I fear I was irritated enough to respond that ‘you must have realised that these are beyond government and it is what I formulated myself after I noticed that your lists in the Qualifications Framework had left out the lower levels, understandable since you had done that on behalf of the universities.’ Upali, who as I noted was instrumental in developing the SLQF framework, was a bright chap whom I had used way back in the early years of this century when I was trying to introduce some coherence into the mathematics curricula in school when I chaired the NIE Academic Affairs Board. I got in touch with him when I was at the TVEC about the SLQF and found he was now the AAB chairman. He claimed that that was because of me, since I had praised him highly at a meeting at which the Secretary to the Ministry of Education was present, when they desperately needed someone good for the task.

audit.headline: Symbolic gestures matter in Sri Lanka’s foreign relations
audit.summary: Ceylon had to subsidise and import massive quantities of rice, its staple food, from Burma, Thailand and Indo-China to provide its citizens with weekly rations. This placed considerable strain on government finances, particularly following the fall in export prices in the immediate aftermath of the Korean War. Rubber prices had also collapsed, leaving Ceylon in a difficult position. I n today’s intricate web of foreign relations, trade links matter because of their importance to the economic well-being of the global population. Economic ties can compel even inimical nations to act as partners, leaving their differences behind. China–U.S. relations can be cited as one of the most prominent examples in this regard. The same can be said of bilateral ties between India and China, two countries otherwise locked in a rivalry over their disputed border.
audit.body: Ceylon had to subsidise and import massive quantities of rice, its staple food, from Burma, Thailand and Indo-China to provide its citizens with weekly rations. This placed considerable strain on government finances, particularly following the fall in export prices in the immediate aftermath of the Korean War. Rubber prices had also collapsed, leaving Ceylon in a difficult position. I n today’s intricate web of foreign relations, trade links matter because of their importance to the economic well-being of the global population. Economic ties can compel even inimical nations to act as partners, leaving their differences behind. China–U.S. relations can be cited as one of the most prominent examples in this regard. The same can be said of bilateral ties between India and China, two countries otherwise locked in a rivalry over their disputed border. Amid these determinants of the foreign policies of different countries, symbolic gestures also matter considerably. They foster goodwill between countries and lay the foundations for the furtherance of ties in other fields. Recently, Sri Lanka witnessed such a symbolic gesture when Chinese Ambassador to Sri Lanka Wei Huaxiang visited the family members of R.G. Senanayake, the former Sri Lankan Minister of Trade and Commerce who played a pivotal role in negotiating and signing the historic 1952 Rubber-Rice Pact between Sri Lanka and China. During the meeting, Ambassador Wei reaffirmed China’s commitment to honouring its long-standing diplomatic and economic ties, emphasising that China would never forget its historic allies. He expressed his desire for the enduring bilateral friendship forged through early milestones such as the Rubber-Rice Pact to be preserved and passed down through generations. He met Chatuka Senanayake, a descendant of Mr. R.G. Senanayake. The Chinese Embassy released a photograph of the meeting into the public domain, apparently to drive home the message that China would not forget those who stood by it during trying times. It leaves room for interpretation that the gesture was also intended as a message for the current political dispensation in Sri Lanka. The historic pact is significant for several reasons. It was not merely a matter of Sri Lanka, then Ceylon, aligning itself with China, or vice versa. Rather, it was born out of the practical necessities of both sides. Ceylon desperately needed rice, which was in short supply, while China required rubber sheets. Against this backdrop, R.G. Senanayake, the then Minister of Commerce, discovered that China was prepared to sell rice to Sri Lanka in exchange for rubber under a barter-trade arrangement. At the time, China was unable to obtain rubber because of restrictions on rubber exports from Malaya following a United Nations resolution that prevented the sale of rubber to China. Out of practical necessity, the pact was born. Ceylon navigated the intricacies of global politics and withstood domestic pressure to press ahead with the historic agreement. Following the establishment of the People’s Republic of China on October 1, 1949, Sri Lanka recognised it on January 6, 1950. Since then, there have been many milestones in Sino-Sri Lankan relations. The development of Hambantota Port, the launch of Colombo Port City, the construction of the Bandaranaike Memorial International Conference Hall (BMICH) and the donation of the kidney hospital in Polonnaruwa are a few examples. However, the Rubber-Rice Pact stands out. It is not the only symbolic gesture that stands out in Sri Lanka’s relations with the rest of the world. At the San Francisco Peace Conference on September 6, 1951, J.R. Jayewardene, then Finance Minister of Ceylon, delivered a landmark speech that shaped post-World War II diplomacy and forged a lasting bond with Japan. Quoting the Dhammapada, “Hatred ceases not by hatred, but by love,” he argued that a free and independent Japan was essential for lasting peace in Asia. His words resonated with the Japanese people and became a cornerstone of the relationship between Sri Lanka and Japan. Japan remains grateful to Sri Lanka for the stance it took at a critical juncture in the country’s post-war history. In today’s complicated world, rivalries have intensified. For small and middle powers such as Sri Lanka, navigating these intricacies is difficult. For instance, elevating ties with one country may not sit well with another. Nevertheless, Sri Lanka must continue to extend symbolic gestures, particularly when geopolitical pressures limit its ability to deepen substantive ties with major powers. In its relations with Pakistan, Sri Lanka has much to draw upon in terms of symbolic gestures. Sri Lanka is the world’s largest donor of human eye corneas, and Pakistan is its single largest recipient. Following the mob lynching of Sri Lankan national Priyantha Kumara in Sialkot, Dr. Niaz Brohi, a leading Pakistani ophthalmologist, expressed his profound grief, saying, “We hang our heads in shame.” This is how symbolic gestures and shared humanitarian bonds matter in fostering relations between countries. Sri Lanka should never undermine the value of engaging in such diplomacy, particularly with the countries that stood by it during difficult times in the past. Of course, Sri Lanka has acted so in the past. What is now needed is to build on that legacy.

audit.headline: Namal indicted on 24 counts
audit.summary: The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) informed Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga Bodaragama yesterday (27) that an indictment containing 24 charges has been filed against Member of Parliament Namal Rajapaksa, who is currently in remand custody over the alleged acceptance of a bribe amounting to Rs.100 million in the controversial Airbus transaction. Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara, appearing on behalf of the Bribery Commission, submitted to the court that the indictment, comprising 59 witnesses along with attached documents and witness statements, has been filed before the Permanent Trial-at-Bar. Accordingly, Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga Bodaragama ordered that the suspect, Namal Rajapaksa, be produced before the Permanent Trial-at-Bar today (28). When the case was called, the suspect was produced in court by prison authorities.
audit.body: The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) informed Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga Bodaragama yesterday (27) that an indictment containing 24 charges has been filed against Member of Parliament Namal Rajapaksa, who is currently in remand custody over the alleged acceptance of a bribe amounting to Rs.100 million in the controversial Airbus transaction. Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara, appearing on behalf of the Bribery Commission, submitted to the court that the indictment, comprising 59 witnesses along with attached documents and witness statements, has been filed before the Permanent Trial-at-Bar. Accordingly, Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga Bodaragama ordered that the suspect, Namal Rajapaksa, be produced before the Permanent Trial-at-Bar today (28). When the case was called, the suspect was produced in court by prison authorities. Submitting further facts, Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara stated as follows: “According to the further report submitted to the court and as informed on a previous date, upon the conclusion of investigations related to this legal proceeding, the relevant dockets were submitted to the Attorney General by the Bribery Commission and the Criminal Investigation Department (CID). Following an examination of the dockets, the Attorney General instructed the Bribery Commission accordingly. Based on those instructions, it was the Attorney General’s position that this case should be tried before a Permanent Trial-at-Bar. Agreeing with that position, the Director General of the Bribery Commission, upon its directive, issued a letter to the Chief Justice pursuant to the Judicature Act requesting the appointment of a Three-Member High Court bench for this case. The Chief Justice has granted approval for that request. Pursuant to that approval, authorisation was granted to file the indictment relevant to this case before the existing Permanent Trial-at-Bar. Accordingly, the Bribery Commission has filed an indictment against the suspect under 24 charges, featuring 59 witnesses, alongside relevant annexures and witness statements before the Permanent Trial-at-Bar.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka Cakewalk into final
audit.summary: Paceman Dilshan Madushanka had his career best figures of 5 for 34 in his 8.3 overs spell as Sri Lanka made an easy 8 wickets win over host Pakistan in their fifth match of the Tri-Nation series played at Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore yesterday. With this victory Sri Lanka have qualified for the final alongside Pakistan to be played on October 31 at the same venue. The next match between Sri Lanka and England on October 29 has now become a dead rubber. Sri Lanka’s dominant bowling performance led by left arm seamer Dilshan Madushanka made it easy to restrict Pakistan for 110 in 25.3 overs. Babar Azam top scored 29 and Sri Lanka chasing an easy target reached it in only in 18.1 overs with opener Kamindu Mendis leading from the front scoring unbeaten 62 in 60 balls with 8 fours and 2 sixes.
