With this victory Sri Lanka have qualified for the final alongside Pakistan to be played on October 31 at the same venue. The next match between Sri Lanka and England on October 29 has now become a dead rubber. Sri Lanka’s dominant bowling performance led by left arm seamer Dilshan Madushanka made it easy to restrict Pakistan for 110 in 25.3 overs. Babar Azam top scored 29 and Sri Lanka chasing an easy target reached it in only in 18.1 overs with opener Kamindu Mendis leading from the front scoring unbeaten 62 in 60 balls with 8 fours and 2 sixes. Kamindu and Avishka Fernando (16) made a good tone adding 50 runs stand in 6.5 overs before Avishka was out off the bowling of skipper Shaheen Afridi, the first break through. Kusal Mendis (8) was bowled by leg spinner Arafat Minhas in the eighth over. However Kamindu and Pavan Ratnayake put the finishing touches adding 52 runs unbroken third wicket stand while Pavan Ratnayake hit the winning boundary in first ball of the 19th over bowled by Maaz Sadaqat. Sri Lanka have shown their batting power making record chase of 430 against England in previous game at Rawalpindi and their bowling strength was back to the fore against Pakistan yesterday at Lahore. Dilshan Madushanka bowled well and his bouncers made huge trouble to opponent batters while off spinner Sahan Arachchige bowled well to take 2 for 24 in his five overs spell to restrict opponents for 110 in just 25.3 overs. Dilshan Madushanka who was named Player of the Match said; “I always work hard in practice and happy about the match winning five-wicket haul. We had a plan for this match and it worked well to restrict them for a low score,” added Dilshan Madushanka. Sri Lanka came to this match with unchanged side while Pakistan made two changes with Saim Ayub and Razaullah made the way for Maaz Sadaqat and paceman Nassen Shah. Sri Lanka will meet England tomorrow but England are already out from the final.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka’s AML/CFT framework under international scrutiny as APG evaluation begins
audit.summary: Sri Lanka’s efforts to strengthen its financial system, combat money laundering and counter terrorist financing have entered a crucial phase with the commencement of the third Mutual Evaluation Conference of the Asia/Pacific Group (APG) on Money Laundering in Colombo. The inaugural event, held on Monday (26) under the patronage of Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya and Deputy Minister of Digital Economy Eranga Weeraratne, marked the beginning of an international assessment of the country’s Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (AML/CFT) framework. The evaluation is significant for Sri Lanka as its ability to prevent financial crimes, enforce laws and maintain transparent financial transactions has implications for international confidence, investment flows and the integrity of its financial system.
audit.body: Sri Lanka’s efforts to strengthen its financial system, combat money laundering and counter terrorist financing have entered a crucial phase with the commencement of the third Mutual Evaluation Conference of the Asia/Pacific Group (APG) on Money Laundering in Colombo. The inaugural event, held on Monday (26) under the patronage of Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya and Deputy Minister of Digital Economy Eranga Weeraratne, marked the beginning of an international assessment of the country’s Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (AML/CFT) framework. The evaluation is significant for Sri Lanka as its ability to prevent financial crimes, enforce laws and maintain transparent financial transactions has implications for international confidence, investment flows and the integrity of its financial system. Addressing the event, Prime Minister Amarasuriya stressed that the assessment would demonstrate the progress Sri Lanka has made in combating financial crimes and meeting international standards. She warned that the erosion of public trust in financial institutions and corruption posed serious threats to a country’s economic and political stability. Transparency, accountability, effective institutional coordination and strong law enforcement were essential to safeguarding the financial system and restoring public confidence, she said. The Prime Minister reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to strengthening the country’s AML/CFT framework and addressing emerging financial risks. Initial discussions during the conference focused on money laundering and terrorist financing risks, legal reforms and national strategies, involving the AML/CFT National Committee, its Task Force and relevant government institutions. The Attorney General’s Department, Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption, Sri Lanka Police, Customs and the Central Bank’s Financial Intelligence Unit also discussed ways to improve risk management and institutional coordination. Emerging threats, including fraud centres, human trafficking, offshore financial risks linked to the Colombo Port and Special Economic Zones, and the potential misuse of non-financial businesses, professions and non-profit organisations, received attention. The APG assessment visit, scheduled from October 25 to November 6, 2026, will examine Sri Lanka’s AML/CFT framework, National Risk Assessment and institutional performance. The findings will be important in identifying weaknesses, improving enforcement and strengthening safeguards against illicit financial flows, supporting Sri Lanka’s credibility in the global financial system. Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe and senior government officials attended the event.

audit.headline: Pine Labs and WEBXPAY bring the Indian payment experience to Sri Lanka
audit.summary: India is Sri Lanka’s largest and fastest-growing tourism source market. In 2025, over 5.3 lakh Indian travellers visited Sri Lanka, making India the country’s largest source of tourists by a wide margin, with this momentum continuing into 2026. Yet these travellers have continued to face friction at checkout, as the payment methods they use every day at home, including UPI, net banking and card options, are not always available in the seamless and familiar manner they expect. Indian consumers do not think twice when they see UPI at checkout. That familiarity, built through billions of domestic transactions, helps drive completion. Without it, even willing customers may hesitate, transactions may fail and merchants may lose revenue.
audit.body: India is Sri Lanka’s largest and fastest-growing tourism source market. In 2025, over 5.3 lakh Indian travellers visited Sri Lanka, making India the country’s largest source of tourists by a wide margin, with this momentum continuing into 2026. Yet these travellers have continued to face friction at checkout, as the payment methods they use every day at home, including UPI, net banking and card options, are not always available in the seamless and familiar manner they expect. Indian consumers do not think twice when they see UPI at checkout. That familiarity, built through billions of domestic transactions, helps drive completion. Without it, even willing customers may hesitate, transactions may fail and merchants may lose revenue. Pine Labs and WEBXPAY are solving this through a strategic cross-border payments partnership, the first Payment Aggregator-to-Payment Aggregator (PA-on-PA) collaboration of its kind in Sri Lanka under India’s RBI-authorised PA-CB framework. The PA-CB structure allows licensed Indian payment aggregators to partner directly with international aggregators, enabling Indian payment methods to be accepted abroad within a regulated, compliant framework. Through this partnership, WEBXPAY’s merchant network spanning hospitality, travel, retail and online commerce across Sri Lanka, can now accept UPI, UPI AutoPay, cards across major Indian issuers, net banking across 100+ banks, EMI conversions, and Credit on UPI, with T+1 settlement, embedded natively within existing integrations and available at scale from day one. For Sri Lankan merchants this is a meaningful commercial unlock. Indian travellers are already walking through their doors, now they can pay the way they do at home, on rails they trust, without any changes to their existing payment infrastructure. “India’s payment stack is one of the most sophisticated in the world and Indian consumers carry that expectation with them when they travel. At Pine Labs, we believe the next frontier of cross-border commerce is making that experience portable. Sri Lanka is our first activation under the PA-CB framework, and we intend to replicate this model across Southeast Asia and every market where Indian travellers and consumers are a meaningful commercial force,” said Tanya Naik, Sr. EVP & Head of Online Business, Pine Labs.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka’s 8% food myth: Bigger than it looks
audit.summary: By Sunil Gamage In Sri Lanka, ask a minister about farming and you will hear a small number: about 7 or 8 percent of GDP. That is the share of the economy officially credited to agriculture. It appears in budgets and speeches. But it is like judging a whole meal by the price of raw vegetables. It stops at the farm gate. It does not count the mill, truck, shop, restaurant or family meal. When you follow food from seed to plate, the picture changes. The food system is closer to a quarter of the economy—about 24.5 percent. The World Bank has said about one-sixth, or 16.7 percent. That is not a contradiction. It leaves out restaurants and much trade and transport. The problem is that only the smallest number guides decisions (8 percent of GDP). Official data put agriculture, forestry and fishing at 8.3 percent of the economy in 2024.
audit.body: By Sunil Gamage In Sri Lanka, ask a minister about farming and you will hear a small number: about 7 or 8 percent of GDP. That is the share of the economy officially credited to agriculture. It appears in budgets and speeches. But it is like judging a whole meal by the price of raw vegetables. It stops at the farm gate. It does not count the mill, truck, shop, restaurant or family meal. When you follow food from seed to plate, the picture changes. The food system is closer to a quarter of the economy—about 24.5 percent. The World Bank has said about one-sixth, or 16.7 percent. That is not a contradiction. It leaves out restaurants and much trade and transport. The problem is that only the smallest number guides decisions (8 percent of GDP). Official data put agriculture, forestry and fishing at 8.3 percent of the economy in 2024. Food, drink and tobacco manufacturing adds another 6.9 percent. Add trade, transport, restaurants, input suppliers and spending along the chain, and food reaches about 24.5 percent. Most wealth is made after the farm—yet most support goes to the farm. Processing sounds easy, but it needs care. Farm output creates about 1.20 rupees of wider activity for every rupee; food and drink manufacturing creates about 1.85. But processing imports machines, packaging and ingredients, so less value may stay in Sri Lanka. The sensible path is to process local produce and limit imports. Behind the numbers are 1.65 million small farmers—about 40 percent of the population—who grow 80 to 85 percent of the nation’s food. Most farm less than two hectares. Eighty-two percent must take extra work to survive. Around them, an informal economy takes money at every step. Fake seeds and fertilizer are common. Official supplies are expensive and far away, so farmers buy from neighbours. There are no receipts or refunds when crops fail. More than 90 percent of fertilizer is imported. The Rs. 10,000-per-acre subsidy does not cover real costs, so black markets grow. Police have seized illegal and tampered fertilizer; some sellers pass off ammonia as urea. Farmers pay high prices, lose harvests and borrow again. A handful of big rice millers control about 35 percent of the market. Farmers have little storage and credit, so they sell at harvest when prices are lowest. Official rice prices sit near Rs. 130 a kilo, while black-market Keeri Samba sells for Rs. 360. Farmers see almost none of that gap. The Northern Province Governor has compared paddy-market operators to a mafia. Gangs steal pepper, cinnamon and cardamom. One company reportedly spends Rs. 20 million over three months guarding a single crop. Youth unemployment is 43 percent, and young people are leaving the land. The results are visible. Tea output fell from 340 million kilograms in 2013 to 261 million in 2025. Smallholders harvest about 150 kilograms of green leaf per acre each month when the land could yield 600, earning roughly Rs. 23,000. For paddy, production costs Rs. 137 a kilo while farmers receive Rs. 120—a loss before household bills. About 19 percent of vegetables and 21 percent of fruit spoil each year because storage and roads are poor. Climate shocks are getting worse. In 2024/25, 18 percent of households reported severe welfare shocks, and 20 percent of farmers faced serious disruption. Cyclone Ditwah caused USD 814 million in farm losses, destroyed about a fifth of the Maha paddy harvest and affected over 227,000 farmers. Food insecurity has risen more than fivefold since 2019. One in three households now faces moderate or severe food insecurity. The World Bank estimates 24.5 percent of Sri Lankans lived below USD 3.65 a day in 2024. Food imports reached USD 2.5 billion in 2025, and all urea is imported. No single slogan will fix this. Import barriers raise prices; open borders can hurt local producers. A serious package would count the food system properly, link guaranteed paddy prices to real costs, target extension services better, invest in storage and rural roads, use targeted safeguards instead of blanket bans, and support cooperatives that let farmers process and sell their own rice. This is not really about statistics. It is about 1.65 million families who feed the nation but cannot feed themselves. When food producers are poor, indebted and leaving the land, food security passes to importers and middlemen. The 8 percent figure let governments treat farming as a welfare habit. The 24.5 percent figure says food is the backbone of the economy. Until the counting changes, funding will not—and farmers will keep walking away.

audit.headline: Apparel exports grow in September, but the year-to-date picture remains cautious: JAAF
audit.summary: Sri Lanka’s apparel exports returned to growth in September 2026, an encouraging sign for the sector. Although the nine-month total is still behind last year, the Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF) sees the latest result as a positive step. Apparel exports for the month came to US$ 416.99 million, up 3.47% from US$ 403.01 million in September 2025. The United States and the European Union, the sector’s two largest markets, led the gain. Exports to the US grew 7.17% to US$ 172.03 million, and exports to the EU (excluding the UK) grew 6.5% to US$ 132.46 million. Performance across markets was mixed. Exports to the UK fell 5.92% to US$ 47.33 million, and exports to other destinations slipped 3.89% to US$ 65.17 million. The cumulative figures tell a more sobering story.
audit.body: Sri Lanka’s apparel exports returned to growth in September 2026, an encouraging sign for the sector. Although the nine-month total is still behind last year, the Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF) sees the latest result as a positive step. Apparel exports for the month came to US$ 416.99 million, up 3.47% from US$ 403.01 million in September 2025. The United States and the European Union, the sector’s two largest markets, led the gain. Exports to the US grew 7.17% to US$ 172.03 million, and exports to the EU (excluding the UK) grew 6.5% to US$ 132.46 million. Performance across markets was mixed. Exports to the UK fell 5.92% to US$ 47.33 million, and exports to other destinations slipped 3.89% to US$ 65.17 million. The cumulative figures tell a more sobering story. Between January and September 2026, apparel exports totalled US$ 3,588.46 million, a decline of 5.52% from US$ 3,798.25 million in the same period last year. That is a shortfall of roughly US$ 210 million. One strong month, welcome as it is, does not close a gap of that size. The decline runs across all major markets over the nine months. The UK saw the steepest fall at 10.85%, followed by the EU at 5.44% and other markets at 5.43%. The US fell 3.69%, the smallest drop among the major markets. Changing trade flows of major trading countries, are also shaping the global picture. Chinese apparel shipments to the United States were around 34% lower in the first seven months of 2026, according to US import data. Industry representatives in competing countries note that China and India have been turning more of their attention to Europe following higher US tariffs, which has made the market more price-competitive. China’s share of EU apparel imports edged up from 26.9% to 28.6% between January and April 2026. For Sri Lankan manufacturers, this points to a busier European market at a time when overall demand remains soft, and it underlines the importance of competitiveness, reliability and diversification. “September’s growth in the US and EU is encouraging, and it shows our manufacturers can compete when demand is there. We’re still more than five percent behind where we were this time last year. What the industry needs now is steady, competitively priced energy and a supportive policy environment, so that this momentum lasts beyond a single month,” Yohan Lawrence, Secretary General, JAAF. JAAF sees September as an encouraging sign, particularly with the US and EU both growing, but not yet a turnaround. The industry will be watching closely whether this momentum carries through the remaining months of the year, and whether markets such as the UK can recover.

audit.headline: US intensifies focus on Colombo port
audit.summary: As the US pushes for new commercial opportunities for their businesses across the Indian Ocean, American Ambassador in Colombo Eric Meyer yesterday (27) addressed port stakeholders from Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, India, and Maldives at a U.S. Embassy-hosted regional workshop showcasing how trusted, secure American technology could transform maritime trade. Bringing together regional port decisionmakers and 11 American technology companies, the workshop highlights U.S. innovations that can streamline port operations, move cargo faster, reduce shipping costs, and strengthen supply chains, while opening new commercial opportunities for American businesses across the Indian Ocean. Sri Lanka’s Deputy Minister of Ports and Civil Aviation Janitha Kodithuwakku and Sri Lanka Ports Authority Chairman Dr. Parakrama Dissanayake joined the Ambassador for the opening.
audit.body: As the US pushes for new commercial opportunities for their businesses across the Indian Ocean, American Ambassador in Colombo Eric Meyer yesterday (27) addressed port stakeholders from Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, India, and Maldives at a U.S. Embassy-hosted regional workshop showcasing how trusted, secure American technology could transform maritime trade. Bringing together regional port decisionmakers and 11 American technology companies, the workshop highlights U.S. innovations that can streamline port operations, move cargo faster, reduce shipping costs, and strengthen supply chains, while opening new commercial opportunities for American businesses across the Indian Ocean. Sri Lanka’s Deputy Minister of Ports and Civil Aviation Janitha Kodithuwakku and Sri Lanka Ports Authority Chairman Dr. Parakrama Dissanayake joined the Ambassador for the opening. Building on the United States’ recent announcement of a $17 million grant to modernize the Port of Colombo, the two-and-a-half-day workshop, Advancing Maritime Single Windows and Port Community Systems, focuses on the digital infrastructure that keeps modern ports moving. The U.S. grant will support the development of two connected systems: a Maritime Single Window (MSW), allowing ships to submit arrival, departure, and regulatory information through one digital platform, and a Port Community System (PCS), connecting shipping companies, port operators, Customs, Immigration, and businesses to exchange cargo and logistics information in real time. Together, these systems will replace fragmented paperwork and processes with a more efficient, connected network—helping information move ahead of cargo, accelerating approvals, and reducing costly delays. “The Port of Colombo has earned its place as a major gateway for global trade, connecting American businesses to markets across South Asia and beyond,” said Ambassador Meyer. “American innovation can help write the next chapter of that story. When ports operate smarter, ships spend less time waiting, businesses spend less money moving goods, and families benefit from more reliable trade. We want U.S. companies at the forefront of this transformation, bringing world-class technology and expertise to strengthen the supply chains our economies depend on and open new doors for American businesses across the Indian Ocean.” “Behind every ship arriving in Colombo is a network of people, businesses, and systems that keeps global trade moving,” said Sri Lanka’s Deputy Minister of Ports and Civil Aviation Janitha Kodithuwakku. “By improving how our ports operate and how information is shared, we can reduce delays, lower costs for Sri Lankan exporters and importers, and make our businesses more competitive in international markets. Our partnership with the United States brings valuable technology and expertise to this effort, strengthening Colombo’s role as a regional trade hub and the supply chains connecting Sri Lanka to the world.” “The future competitiveness of the Port of Colombo will depend not only on how much infrastructure we build, but also how efficiently we utilize the infrastructure we already have. These two digital systems—PCS and MSW—will help us achieve precisely that,” said Sri Lanka Ports Authority Chairman Dr. Parakrama Dissanayake. The workshop is organized under the Quad Ports of the Future Partnership, an initiative supporting more efficient, secure, and digitally connected ports across the Indo-Pacific.

audit.headline: Death in police custody: Open verdict issued
audit.summary: Judicial Medical Officer at the Colombo South Teaching Hospital in Kalubowila issued an open verdict following the post-mortem examination of a 29-year-old person who died in the custody of the Homagama Police. He has been arrested in connection with a drug-related allegation. The open verdict was issued following post-mortem examination conducted at the Colombo South Teaching Hospital in Kalubowila. Police stated that the deceased’s body was handed over to his relatives following the examination. The deceased, a resident of Kiriwaththuduwa, was a father of two. He had been arrested by the Homagama Police and detained in a police cell when he suddenly fell ill according to police. He was subsequently admitted to hospital, where he died.

audit.headline: ‘Tertiary education advancement, key to producing workers with problem-solving skills’
audit.summary: By Hiran H. Senewiratne Tertiary education is vital for sustainable growth and for producing skilled workers with critical thinking, problem-solving and advanced tech skills, central to boosting productivity , competitiveness and innovation in the economy, said Dr. Nisha Arunatilake- Director of Research, Institute of Policy Studies (IPS). ‘STEM fields including science, technology, engineering and maths are key to fostering ongoing innovation- led growth, expanding economic activity and creating jobs for graduates and supporting industries, Dr Arunatilake said at a round table discussion held recently at the IPS auditorium in Colombo under the topic ‘Durable Growth in Sri Lanka: Advancing Human Capital for Inclusive Prosperity’. The event also marked the launching of the IPS flagship publication, ‘Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026.’ Dr.
audit.body: By Hiran H. Senewiratne Tertiary education is vital for sustainable growth and for producing skilled workers with critical thinking, problem-solving and advanced tech skills, central to boosting productivity , competitiveness and innovation in the economy, said Dr. Nisha Arunatilake- Director of Research, Institute of Policy Studies (IPS). ‘STEM fields including science, technology, engineering and maths are key to fostering ongoing innovation- led growth, expanding economic activity and creating jobs for graduates and supporting industries, Dr Arunatilake said at a round table discussion held recently at the IPS auditorium in Colombo under the topic ‘Durable Growth in Sri Lanka: Advancing Human Capital for Inclusive Prosperity’. The event also marked the launching of the IPS flagship publication, ‘Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026.’ Dr. Arunatilake added: ‘Population censuses reveal that the proportion of people aged 25 years and older within tertiary education in the country grew from 4 percent in 2012 to 6.9 percent in 2024, which trend was mainly driven by a significant rise in degree holders, who increased by 118 percent over this period. ‘However, the growth of the Gross Enrollment Ratio to Tertiary Education in Sri Lanka is much slower than that of other Asian peers. Further, ILO states that managers, professionals, technicians and associate professionals need higher education empowerment to enable them to work in an efficient and effective manner. ‘Countries such as Malaysia and Thailand which reached upper middle income status relied on a larger and more efficiently utilised pool of skilled professionals to maintain growth. Sri Lanka must double its tertiary enrollment ratio from 21 percent to 40 percent to be on par with other peers in the region.’ Research Fellow, IPS, Dr Pulasthi Amarasinghe said: ‘Sri Lanka’s post crisis economic recovery has not translated into a corresponding recovery in labour market outcomes. Improvements are needed in GDP growth and economy wide stability, employment, labour force participation while real earnings are yet to reach pre- crisis levels. He said that the ‘State of the Economy 2026 Report’ highlights several key findings on labour markets, which have not been matched by any labour market recovery, despite the unemployment rate returning to 4.4 percent in 2024. Dr. Amarasinghe said that the employment to population ratio also fell from 49.8 percent to 45.3 percent but the most important factor is that salaries of employees have remained below pre- crisis levels. He also said that a second structural shift in employment has constrained productivity growth. This crisis reinforced employment concentration in relatively low productivity activities, especially in agriculture and trade, while manufacturing and construction sectors have lost their share of employment. Dr Ganga Thilakaratne, Research Fellow attached to the IPS said, among other things, that Sri Lanka should address social protection needs urgently, such as those arising from the Covid 19 pandemic and from the 2022 economic crisis, besides issues from climate related disasters, such as floods and landslides.

audit.headline: Returns on ethics: A new compass for global finance in an age of debt and inequality
audit.summary: By Jayasri Priyalal MSc (NTU), MBA (Sri J) As the world moves closer to the 2030 deadline for achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), a troubling reality is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Global wealth continues to expand, financial markets reach record valuations, and technological innovation accelerates at an unprecedented pace. Yet millions of people are falling behind, public services are under strain, and environmental degradation continues unabated. The question confronting policymakers is no longer whether the global economic model is under stress, but whether the metrics guiding that model remain fit for purpose. For decades, economic success has been measured through indicators such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP), shareholder returns and Return on Equity (RoE).
audit.body: By Jayasri Priyalal MSc (NTU), MBA (Sri J) As the world moves closer to the 2030 deadline for achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), a troubling reality is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Global wealth continues to expand, financial markets reach record valuations, and technological innovation accelerates at an unprecedented pace. Yet millions of people are falling behind, public services are under strain, and environmental degradation continues unabated. The question confronting policymakers is no longer whether the global economic model is under stress, but whether the metrics guiding that model remain fit for purpose. For decades, economic success has been measured through indicators such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP), shareholder returns and Return on Equity (RoE). While these measurements have provided useful signals for investors and governments, they have often overlooked broader societal outcomes. Human well-being, environmental sustainability, equitable growth, and intergenerational justice rarely appear on traditional balance sheets. As a result, economic systems have rewarded financial extraction even when it undermines long-term development. Financial extraction was linked with the natural resources’ extraction led linear economic activities now contributing to the global warming led unprecedented natural disasters. Nowhere is this contradiction more evident than in the developing world. Over the past decade and a half, public debt across developing economies has risen dramatically. The consequences extend beyond accounting figures. Debt obligations increasingly determine national policy priorities, often forcing governments to devote scarce public resources to debt servicing rather than investments in healthcare, education, climate resilience, and employment creation. The result is a development paradox. Countries that need significant investments to achieve the SDGs are often transferring more resources to external creditors than they receive through development finance. Public budgets become instruments of repayment rather than vehicles for social progress. According to the analysis cited in the Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) Policy Brief, debt growth has substantially outpaced economic expansion in many developing nations, creating an unsustainable trajectory that threatens long-term prosperity. The implications are profound. Across numerous countries, debt-servicing costs are growing faster than spending on health and education. This creates a dangerous crowding-out effect, where investments in human development are sacrificed to maintain financial obligations. When nations are compelled to choose between servicing debt and funding schools, hospitals, or climate adaptation programmes, the sustainability of the prevailing financial architecture must be questioned. The challenge extends beyond debt alone. In recent years, I have argued that the traditional understanding of global development challenges as a “3D Crisis” comprising Deplorable Debt, Degraded Environment, and Depleted Natural Resources is no longer sufficient. A fourth dimension has emerged with enormous implications for economic governance: Data. The rise of digital platforms, artificial intelligence, and algorithm-driven business models has transformed the global economy. Data has become a strategic asset, often concentrated in the hands of a small number of corporations with unprecedented market power. While these technologies have generated efficiency gains and new opportunities, they have also contributed to widening inequalities, labour market insecurity, and economic concentration. The deeper problem is that technological progress has significantly outpaced the development of what may be called “social technologies” – the ethical frameworks, governance mechanisms, educational systems, and democratic institutions required to manage technological change in a socially responsible manner. Humanity has developed increasingly sophisticated physical technologies. We have artificial intelligence systems that process information in milliseconds and financial markets capable of moving trillions of dollars across borders instantly. Yet our institutions have struggled to ensure that these advances contribute to shared prosperity. Without corresponding social technologies, innovation can intensify existing inequalities rather than reduce them. This is precisely why we need a new framework for measuring economic performance. I propose the mainstreaming of Returns on Ethics (RoE) as a complementary indicator to traditional financial metrics. While Return on Equity evaluates financial profitability, Returns on Ethics asks a different and more fundamental question: what developmental, social, and environmental value is generated by every dollar invested? What is the use of wealth, without fresh air and water to survive. Returns on Ethics would evaluate investments through four interconnected dimensions. First, human capability restoration. Investments should be assessed according to how effectively they improve public health, strengthen education systems, enhance skills development, and support lifelong learning opportunities for workers. Human capital should be viewed not as a cost but as a strategic asset essential for sustainable development. Second, ecological and planetary integrity. Financial decisions should consider whether they contribute to environmental sustainability, biodiversity protection, carbon reduction, and responsible resource use. Economic growth that depletes natural capital cannot be regarded as genuine progress. It is high time that commercial enterprises focus on investment in the Circular Economy, withdrawing from the unsustainable environmental damaging linear economic activities. Third, decent work and labour agency . Technological innovation should be measured not only by productivity gains but also by its impact on employment quality, worker participation, data ownership, and social inclusion. Economic transformation must strengthen human agency rather than diminish it. Fourth, intergenerational justice . Financing arrangements should be evaluated according to their long-term effects on future generations. Policies that lock countries into perpetual cycles of debt dependence and austerity cannot be considered sustainable. Adopting such an approach would fundamentally change how governments, financial institutions, and investors evaluate success. A project generating attractive short-term returns but causing environmental damage, widening inequality, or weakening public services would score poorly under a Returns on Ethics framework. Conversely, investments in education, public health, green infrastructure, and climate resilience would be recognised as essential contributors to long-term economic value. Translating this vision into practice requires institutional reform. International financial institutions should modernise debt sustainability frameworks to incorporate development and resilience indicators alongside traditional debt metrics. Expenditures on health, education, and climate adaptation should be recognised as investments in productive capacity rather than discretionary spending. Debt-pause mechanisms should become standard features of sovereign lending agreements, enabling countries to respond to economic, health, or climate shocks without sacrificing development priorities. Similarly, debt-for-SDG and debt-for-climate swaps should be expanded to redirect resources toward measurable sustainable development outcomes. Developing economies should also strengthen regional financial cooperation, local-currency financing arrangements, and South-South partnerships to reduce excessive dependence on external financial centres and create more resilient development pathways. The challenge before us is not a lack of capital. Global financial resources are abundant. The real challenge is directing those resources toward outcomes that strengthen societies and preserve the planet. As 2030 approaches, the world faces a clear choice. We can continue measuring success primarily through financial returns while accepting widening inequalities and ecological decline, or we can embrace a broader vision of value creation rooted in human dignity, social justice, and environmental stewardship. Returns on Ethics offers a practical pathway towards that future. The time has come to place ethics at the centre of finance, not at its margins. Only then can global prosperity become truly sustainable and genuinely inclusive. audit.headline: Absence of political consensus 20 years after LTTE’s eradication: Whom to blame!
audit.summary: By Shamindra Ferdinando Last week’s Midweek piece, headlined ‘Nobel Peace Prize for Pillay draws global attention to Eelam War,’ prompted one of the writer’s ex-colleagues, now serving a foreign media group, to raise the failure on the part of Sri Lanka to achieve genuine post-war reconciliation and real development (https://island.lk/nobel-peace-prize-for-pillay-draws-global-attention-to-eelam-war/). He raised pertinent questions: But what next? … nearly two decades after the ‘liberation’ from terrorism, have we achieved economic progress like Singapore? Sri Lanka still exports poor women, mainly young Sinhala, Tamil and Muslim mothers, as vulnerable housemaids, to West Asia for menial wages.
audit.body: By Shamindra Ferdinando Last week’s Midweek piece, headlined ‘Nobel Peace Prize for Pillay draws global attention to Eelam War,’ prompted one of the writer’s ex-colleagues, now serving a foreign media group, to raise the failure on the part of Sri Lanka to achieve genuine post-war reconciliation and real development (https://island.lk/nobel-peace-prize-for-pillay-draws-global-attention-to-eelam-war/). He raised pertinent questions: But what next? … nearly two decades after the ‘liberation’ from terrorism, have we achieved economic progress like Singapore? Sri Lanka still exports poor women, mainly young Sinhala, Tamil and Muslim mothers, as vulnerable housemaids, to West Asia for menial wages. Another issue, he raised, was Sri Lanka’s pathetic response to the recommendations made by the Lessons Learnt and Reconciliation (LLRC) Commission, appointed by war-winning President Mahinda Rajapaksa. There is no doubt they were valid questions. What/Who made genuine reconciliation unachievable? Can war-winning Sri Lanka justify its catastrophic inability to deal with all post-war issues? But, perhaps, one of the most important issues is whether the government of Sri Lanka (GoSL) should be solely held responsible for the chaotic reconciliation efforts, amidst relentless hounding of the war- winning leaders and the government for defying the West and defeating the world’s most ruthless terrorist organisation, as identified by none other than the American Federal Bureau of Investigation. Having eradicated the battle-hardened Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), widely considered, by so called pundits, undefeatable, in the battlefield itself, war-winning President Mahinda Rajapaksa paved the way for genuine reconciliation by offering amnesty to all those who fought for the group. Although that amnesty quite rightly excluded LTTE cadres, who had been indicted for major crimes during the conflict, the general amnesty allowed them to be rehabilitated. Approximately 12,000 LTTE cadres benefited. It would be pertinent to mention that President Rajapaksa caused himself immense harm and also undermined the whole political party system by the enactment of the 18th Amendment for him to seek presidency for third time, in 2015, and the impeachment of CJ Dr. Shirani Bandaranayke in 2013. The international community, in general, supported Sri Lanka’s efforts to rehabilitate ex-LTTE cadres. IOM Chief of Mission Richard Danziger, in an interview with the writer, in late Nov. 2011, emphasised the pivotal importance of rehabilitation of ex-LTTE cadres. That exclusive interview, arranged by a friend of mine, Prabath Fernando, at the time on the IOM staff, gave an insight into what was happening on the ground (https://thuppahis.com/2011/12/01/iom-clarifies-role-in-reintegrating-tigers-into-society/). Interested parties reacted angrily to Danziger’s comments. They felt betrayed by the top IOM representative’s support to the military-led project. Obviously, they realised the danger to themselves in the international recognition for GoSL’s flagship project. The then Justice and Law Reforms Minister Milinda Moragoda played a significant role in the project. The former UNPer invited the All Ceylon Hindu Congress (ACHC) to participate in the GoSL effort, thereby giving confidence to the Tamil community and the Tamil Diaspora. Moragoda went to the extent of making special arrangements for married LTTE personnel. A section of the government may not have liked Moragoda’s status but no one else could have done a better job. On the invitation of Moragoda, the writer had the opportunity to visit Vavuniya where ex-LTTEers were undergoing rehabilitation. Top ACHC representatives were among those present. But, those who couldn’t stomach the LTTE’s defeat worked overtime to undermine the reconciliation process. They also couldn’t bear up the emergence of Mahinda Rajapaksa as the undisputed leader. As the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces, President Rajapaksa achieved the unthinkable. Under his leadership, the armed forces not only eradicated the LTTE’s conventional fighting capacity but implemented an unprecedented rehabilitation project that gave those who believed in a separate state confidence to start a new life. The rehabilitation of the LTTE should have been the foundation of the reconciliation process. A real consensus could have been achieved. But, the Tamil National Alliance (TNA) steadfastly refused to cooperate with the GoSL. The late R. Sampanthan-led TNA demanded that GoSL be hauled up before the international war crimes tribunal. Had the TNA accepted the rehabilitation of LTTE cadres as a key Confidence Building Measure (CBM), it could have quickly reached consensus with the GoSL. Instead, the TNA refused to acknowledge the rehabilitation project. The TNA despised the GoSL’s triumph over the LTTE so much, it conveniently forgot that the armed forces’ victory freed the party from the clutches of Velupillai Prabhakaran. The TNA remained under LTTE’s control since 2001 when Sampathan was compelled to recognise the LTTE as the sole representative of the Tamil speaking people. An unholy alliance The Nobel Peace Prize for Pillay prompted Dr. Jehan Perera, on behalf of one-time darling of the Norwegians, the National Peace Council (NPC), headed by him, to declare that the Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem Pillay is a reminder to Sri Lanka of unfinished commitments. Those demanding an explanation for GoSL’s post-war failure, and finding fault with successive governments, refuse to examine political developments that undermined the post-war reconciliation process. Having believed in the LTTE taking the upper hand in the northern theatre of operations, though the group vacated the East by June/July 2007, Western governments, the UN and the civil society groups struggled to cope up with the developing situation. The 2010 presidential election, the first national election after Sri Lanka’s triumph over the LTTE, placed the main Opposition UNP in an extremely embarrassing position. Having undermined the war effort, the UNP couldn’t have faced the electorate under any circumstances. The UNP’s US-backed move to entice war-winning Army Chief, retired General Sarath Fonseka, to contest the presidential election, delivered a knockout blow to the political party system. That utterly contemptible move had a ripple effect. It caused unlimited chaos and led to the overall deterioration of the political environment. The project involved the UNP, TNA and the JVP. They sank their differences to reach consensus under West’s prodding. At the behest of the TNA, the Tamil electorate voted for Fonseka who won all predominately Tamil-speaking electoral districts in the North and East, whereas Mahinda Rajapaksa won the vast majority of other districts. Fonseka lost by a staggering 1.8 mn votes. Fonseka’s superlative performance in the North and East should have brought an immediate end to war crimes accusations. The GoSL bashing at the Geneva-based United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) seemed nothing but a joke after the main Tamil party, with 22 parliamentary seats in the North and East, backed Fonseka after accusing him and his army of genocide. Surprisingly, President Mahinda Rajapaksa’s government never bothered to mention that at the right forum. Years later, in the run-up to the 2015 presidential election, Sampanthan acknowledged how the eradication of the LTTE, in 2009, saved his party. The veteran politician had no qualms in appreciating the LTTE’s defeat when the writer raised the issue with him. The late D.B.S. Jeyaraj posted The Island report on his website (https://dbsjeyaraj.com/dbsj/?p=36839) . But, the TNA continued to pursue what can be safely described as a destructive strategy. After Fonseka’s defeat, the UNP unceremoniously dropped him. A desperate defeated presidential election candidate had no option but to team up with the JVP at the 2010 April parliamentary polls. Under the JVP-Fonseka leadership, the Democratic National Alliance (DNA) won seven seats. Sri Lanka’s triumph over the LTTE further divided the country. Although Sampanthan had to acknowledge, years later, that his party was saved from the LTTE dictates, he was not at all willing to reach consensus with the GoSL. However, even the European Union publicly declared that the TNA had been able to win the lion’s share of seats, at the 2004 parliamentary polls, with the LTTE stuffing ballot boxes for TNA candidates. The EU made that shocking declaration in its final report on the 2004 parliamentary poll. The EU’s condemnation deeply embarrassed the TNA but the likes of Sampanthan had thick skins. The TNA increased hostilities following the 2010 parliamentary polls. The 2010 poll brought the TNA down to 14 seats, from 22 secured at the 2004 election. The drop in its popularity compelled the TNA to harden its stance against President Rajapaksa. It rejected the President’s efforts to kick start negotiations, with the backing of India. Instead, the TNA continued its alliance with the UNP and the JVP and reached consensus on Maithripala Sirisena as the common candidate at the 2015 presidential election. During President Mahinda Rajapaksa’s second term (2010 January to 2015 January) the government couldn’t make progress in the post-war reconciliation process. The TNA that directly benefited from LTTE terrorism directed at other political parties in the North and East, fully backed the group until the very end. Sampanthan never bothered to ask the LTTE to give up human shields or halt forcible child recruitment. In fact, none of those, now demanding accountability on the part of GoSL, asked the LTTE to give up resistance, at least after the LTTE suffered irreparable losses at the Anandapuram battle. The April 2009 battle effectively ended the LTTE capacity to wage conventional resistance. UN probe vs LLRC The TNA, in February 2012, accused the GoSL of failing to implement recommendations made by its own LLRC. The LLRC recommendations though failed to meet high expectations of the TNA and like-minded groups/parties gave the government some opportunity to address their grievances. But, the government failed to act on key recommendations. President Rajapaksa appointed the LLRC in response to the UN probe. He understandably refused to cooperate with the UN. Instead, the President appointed LLRC but still failed to implement its recommendations. For want of sound advice, President Rajapaksa rejected the UN probe fearing its bias, thereby deprived the country of an opportunity to set the record straight. There is no point in denying the fact that the war- winning government mishandled the issue. GoSL’s foolish approach allowed those propagating lies to advance their strategy. Years later, when Lord Naseby, through the Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA), obtained and disclosed classified dispatches from the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) regarding the final phase of the offensive (January to May 2009), exposed the utterly ill-informed decision to boycott the UN probe. The dispatches from the British High Commission, in Colombo, during that period when examined with public declaration by wartime US Defence Advisor, in Colombo, Lt. Colonel Lawrence Smith, in June 2011, strongly disputed the much touted unsubstantiated UN claim of at least 40,000 civilian deaths. Let me reproduce the paragraph, bearing No 137, verbatim: “In the limited surveys that have been carried out in the aftermath of the conflict, the percentage of people reporting dead relatives is high. A number of credible sources have estimated that there could have been as many as 40,000 civilian deaths. Two years after the end of the war, there is no reliable figure for civilian deaths, but multiple sources of information indicate that a range of up to 40,000 civilian deaths cannot be ruled out at this stage. Only a proper investigation can lead to the identification of all of the victims and to the formulation of an accurate figure for the total number of civilian deaths.” In fact, Lord Naseby’s disclosure, made in Oct. 2017, during the treacherous Yahapalana administration when considered with British and US position on the final phase of the offensive, in a way confirmed the UN findings that placed the number of dead, both civilians and LTTEers way below Marzuki Darusman’s 40,000 deaths figure. Darusman, one-time Indonesian Attorney-General in the notorious Suharto government, led the three-member UN accountability panel that unilaterally declared that the accusations couldn’t be investigated for 20 years from the date it was released. That report was released in March 2011. Successive governments owed explanations why a confidential UN report, that dealt with the Vanni offensive, had never been used in the defence of our armed forces. Although the UN publicly acknowledged the existence of the report, Sri Lanka never made an attempt to use it for our own defence. The UN acknowledged the report dealt with the situation in the Vanni during August, 2008, to May 13, 2009. The report placed the number of persons killed, and wounded, during this period, at 7,721 and 18,479, respectively. There cannot be a better detailed account than the UN report as it was based on information provided by NGOs, ICRC, as well as numerous other sources trapped in the war zone. Indian factor For some strange reason successive governments failed to use irrefutable available information to counter lies propagated against Sri Lanka by interested parties. As ground forces advanced steadily into LTTE-held territory, President Rajapaksa requested for immediate deployment of an Indian medical team to treat the wounded people evacuated from Puthumathalan. India responded swiftly. By the second week of March 2009, India stationed a medical team that treated several thousand men, women and children at Pulmoddai, north of Trincomalee. The writer was among a group of journalists allowed to visit the Indian medical facility after observing the transfer of the wounded from Puthumathalan to Pulmoddai from an Israeli built Fast Attack Craft (FAC). The transfer of the wounded and helpers took place under the direct supervision of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). If the GoSL planned to commit genocide, it wouldn’t have invited India to position a medical team, widely believed to be military/ex-military, at Pulmoddai. Once the LTTE collapsed, the Indian team moved to Menik Farm, the main displaced receiving centre where it remained busy until the situation was brought under control. Those who accused Sri Lanka of waging war, without witnesses, conveniently forgot that the ICRC and Indian team operated among the Tamil community throughout this period. But, Sri Lanka pathetically failed to build its defence on the basis of strong evidence to prove allegations wrong. The TNA and other Tamil parties disregarded developments on the ground. While they propagated blatant lies, including that GoSL held Tamil political prisoners, post-war Chief Minister of the Northern Province C.V. Wigneswaran suddenly alleged that GoSL had poisoned 104 LTTE cadres undergoing rehabilitation. The former Supreme Court judge made that preposterous accusation during the Yahapalana government when US troops were engaged in a training exercise with local counterparts in the Jaffna peninsula. That lie attracted international attention. The government did nothing. Wigneswaran enjoyed international media attention at the country’s expense. During the same time, TNA and other interested parties, backed by some Western embassies, particularly the British and German, threw their weight behind the Mannar mass grave accusations. They were proved utterly wrong when Sri Lanka got a US lab to conduct carbon dating testing on the finds. But by the time US results were released, Geneva had reiterated allegations and speculated about more mass graves. But no one asked for justice for thousands of people killed by the LTTE. Have you ever heard of them speaking of the 1989 assassination of TULF leader Appapillai Amirthalingam or Vettivelu Yogeswaran while having talks with President Ranasinghe Premadasa in Colombo? Or Neelan Thiruchelvam killed in late July 1999 in Colombo? All Tamils killed by the LTTE were discarded as traitors. But, those who threw their weight behind the separatist agenda, after having taken refuge overseas or played politics with the conflict, seemed hell-bent on taking revenge on the war-winning armed forces. In between the Indian withdrawal and the Gandhi assassination,the LTTE chased the Muslims out of the Northern Province. That influenced a Norwegian manic to killed several dozens children in Noway years later. Real post-war consensus can be achieved only if the Tamil community, and their representatives in Parliament, acknowledge the crimes perpetrated by the LTTE. Their insistence that the armed forces should be subjected to international legal mechanisms, while ignoring the atrocities perpetrated by the LTTE, made post-war national reconciliation impossible. That is the truth many refuse to acknowledge. Years after the May 1991 assassination of Gandhi, LTTE ideologue Anton Balasingham, a British national, in an interview with NDTV, declared: “As far as that event [Rajiv assassination] is concerned, I would say it is a great tragedy, a monumental historical tragedy for which we deeply regret and we call upon the government of India and the people of India to be magnanimous to put the past behind and to approach the ethnic question in a different perspective.” This declaration was made in late June 2006 as Sri Lanka was preparing for the final onslaught. The assassination of Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar, in August 2025, the abortive bid to assassinate Army Commander Lt. Gen. Sarath Fonseka, in April 2006, and the Mavil-aru challenge three months later compelled President Mahinda Rajapaksa to take that monumental decision to eradicate the LTTE. The LTTE was brought down to its knees in two years and 10 months (August 2006 to May 2009). The LTTE had the opportunity to accept surrender soon after the Anandapuram debacle, in the first week of April 2009. None of those jubilant over Nobel Peace Prize for Pillay dared to ask the LTTE to at least give up human shields and allow child soldiers to surrender. Geneva Human Rights chief Pillay herself failed to urge the LTTE to accept the ground situation. But to be fair to Pillay, Prabhakaran wouldn’t have surrendered as he remained confident of external intervention on his behalf, even at the last moment. An unholy alliance The Nobel Peace Prize for Pillay prompted Dr. Jehan Perera, on behalf of one-time darling of the Norwegians, the National Peace Council (NPC), headed by him, to declare that the Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem Pillay is a reminder to Sri Lanka of unfinished commitments. Those demanding an explanation for GoSL’s post-war failure, and finding fault with successive governments, refuse to examine political developments that undermined the post-war reconciliation process. Having believed in the LTTE taking the upper hand in the northern theatre of operations, though the group vacated the East by June/July 2007, Western governments, the UN and the civil society groups struggled to cope up with the developing situation. The 2010 presidential election, the first national election after Sri Lanka’s triumph over the LTTE, placed the main Opposition UNP in an extremely embarrassing position. Having undermined the war effort, the UNP couldn’t have faced the electorate under any circumstances. The UNP’s US-backed move to entice war-winning Army Chief, retired General Sarath Fonseka, to contest the presidential election, delivered a knockout blow to the political party system. That utterly contemptible move had a ripple effect. It caused unlimited chaos and led to the overall deterioration of the political environment. The project involved the UNP, TNA and the JVP. They sank their differences to reach consensus under West’s prodding. At the behest of the TNA, the Tamil electorate voted for Fonseka who won all predominately Tamil-speaking electoral districts in the North and East, whereas Mahinda Rajapaksa won the vast majority of other districts. Fonseka lost by a staggering 1.8 mn votes. Fonseka’s superlative performance in the North and East should have brought an immediate end to war crimes accusations. The GoSL bashing at the Geneva-based United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) seemed nothing but a joke after the main Tamil party, with 22 parliamentary seats in the North and East, backed Fonseka after accusing him and his army of genocide. Surprisingly, President Mahinda Rajapaksa’s government never bothered to mention that at the right forum. Years later, in the run-up to the 2015 presidential election, Sampanthan acknowledged how the eradication of the LTTE, in 2009, saved his party. The veteran politician had no qualms in appreciating the LTTE’s defeat when the writer raised the issue with him. The late D.B.S. Jeyaraj posted The Island report on his website (https://dbsjeyaraj.com/dbsj/?p=36839) . But, the TNA continued to pursue what can be safely described as a destructive strategy. After Fonseka’s defeat, the UNP unceremoniously dropped him. A desperate defeated presidential election candidate had no option but to team up with the JVP at the 2010 April parliamentary polls. Under the JVP-Fonseka leadership, the Democratic National Alliance (DNA) won seven seats. Sri Lanka’s triumph over the LTTE further divided the country. Although Sampanthan had to acknowledge, years later, that his party was saved from the LTTE dictates, he was not at all willing to reach consensus with the GoSL. However, even the European Union publicly declared that the TNA had been able to win the lion’s share of seats, at the 2004 parliamentary polls, with the LTTE stuffing ballot boxes for TNA candidates. The EU made that shocking declaration in its final report on the 2004 parliamentary poll. The EU’s condemnation deeply embarrassed the TNA but the likes of Sampanthan had thick skins. The TNA increased hostilities following the 2010 parliamentary polls. The 2010 poll brought the TNA down to 14 seats, from 22 secured at the 2004 election. The drop in its popularity compelled the TNA to harden its stance against President Rajapaksa. It rejected the President’s efforts to kick start negotiations, with the backing of India. Instead, the TNA continued its alliance with the UNP and the JVP and reached consensus on Maithripala Sirisena as the common candidate at the 2015 presidential election. During President Mahinda Rajapaksa’s second term (2010 January to 2015 January) the government couldn’t make progress in the post-war reconciliation process. The TNA that directly benefited from LTTE terrorism directed at other political parties in the North and East, fully backed the group until the very end. Sampanthan never bothered to ask the LTTE to give up human shields or halt forcible child recruitment. In fact, none of those, now demanding accountability on the part of GoSL, asked the LTTE to give up resistance, at least after the LTTE suffered irreparable losses at the Anandapuram battle. The April 2009 battle effectively ended the LTTE capacity to wage conventional resistance. The LLRC recommendations though failed to meet high expectations of the TNA and like-minded groups/parties gave the government some opportunity to address their grievances. But, the government failed to act on key recommendations. President Rajapaksa appointed the LLRC in response to the UN probe. He understandably refused to cooperate with the UN. Instead, the President appointed LLRC but still failed to implement its recommendations. For want of sound advice, President Rajapaksa rejected the UN probe fearing its bias, thereby deprived the country of an opportunity to set the record straight. There is no point in denying the fact that the war- winning government mishandled the issue. GoSL’s foolish approach allowed those propagating lies to advance their strategy. Years later, when Lord Naseby, through the Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA), obtained and disclosed classified dispatches from the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) regarding the final phase of the offensive (January to May 2009), exposed the utterly ill-informed decision to boycott the UN probe. The dispatches from the British High Commission, in Colombo, during that period when examined with public declaration by wartime US Defence Advisor, in Colombo, Lt. Colonel Lawrence Smith, in June 2011, strongly disputed the much touted unsubstantiated UN claim of at least 40,000 civilian deaths. Let me reproduce the paragraph, bearing No 137, verbatim: “In the limited surveys that have been carried out in the aftermath of the conflict, the percentage of people reporting dead relatives is high. A number of credible sources have estimated that there could have been as many as 40,000 civilian deaths. Two years after the end of the war, there is no reliable figure for civilian deaths, but multiple sources of information indicate that a range of up to 40,000 civilian deaths cannot be ruled out at this stage. Only a proper investigation can lead to the identification of all of the victims and to the formulation of an accurate figure for the total number of civilian deaths.” In fact, Lord Naseby’s disclosure, made in Oct. 2017, during the treacherous Yahapalana administration when considered with British and US position on the final phase of the offensive, in a way confirmed the UN findings that placed the number of dead, both civilians and LTTEers way below Marzuki Darusman’s 40,000 deaths figure. That report was released in March 2011. Successive governments owed explanations why a confidential UN report, that dealt with the Vanni offensive, had never been used in the defence of our armed forces. Although the UN publicly acknowledged the existence of the report, Sri Lanka never made an attempt to use it for our own defence. The UN acknowledged the report dealt with the situation in the Vanni during August, 2008, to May 13, 2009. The report placed the number of persons killed, and wounded, during this period, at 7,721 and 18,479, respectively. audit.headline: Disaster management: Need for radical rethink
audit.summary: Wednesday 28th October, 2026 Sri Lanka takes disaster management for granted, paying it the attention it deserves only when the fear of disasters looms. Cyclone Arnab is intensifying over the Bay of Bengal and moving towards India’s eastern coast, causing heavy rainfall here. The Irrigation Department has warned of floods in several parts of the country, and the National Building Research Organisation has issued warnings of landslides, covering eight districts, and red-level evacuation warnings for high-risk areas in Ratnapura, Kalutara and Nuwara Eliya. audit.body: Wednesday 28th October, 2026 Sri Lanka takes disaster management for granted, paying it the attention it deserves only when the fear of disasters looms. Cyclone Arnab is intensifying over the Bay of Bengal and moving towards India’s eastern coast, causing heavy rainfall here. The Irrigation Department has warned of floods in several parts of the country, and the National Building Research Organisation has issued warnings of landslides, covering eight districts, and red-level evacuation warnings for high-risk areas in Ratnapura, Kalutara and Nuwara Eliya. Disaster management must be a continuing process even when there are no immediate threats of floods and landslides. The success of a country’s disaster management strategy hinges on proactive planning and prevention rather than reactive responses to emergencies. Floods claim lives and destroy property year after year. But many people continue to live in landslide-prone areas facing the constant fear of being buried alive only to be evacuated when heavy rains trigger warnings. The challenge is not merely to evacuate people when danger looms but also to relocate them to safer areas. Prof. Ranjith Bandara, in a well-argued article, From the Tsunami to Cyclone Ditwah: Who is responsible for Sri Lanka’s persistent failures in disaster management? published on the opposite page today, calls for a rethink of Sri Lanka’s disaster management strategy. He has identified what is wrong with the country’s disaster preparedness. Prof. Bandara has highlighted several reasons why Sri Lanka’s disaster management strategy has not yielded the desired results. They include chronic institutional failures from the 2004 tsunami to Cyclone Ditwah in 2025; inadequate disaster preparedness while climate change, unplanned construction, deforestation and blocked waterways are increasing disaster risks; weak implementation and coordination with special emphasis on the failure of the National Council for Disaster Management to meet between April 2018 and August 2025; unclear responsibilities with bureaucratic delays and underutilised funds hampering risk-reduction projects; neglected research and community needs; non-incorporation of scientific findings and local knowledge into planning; lack of effective communication of early warnings, and accountability issues. He argues that Sri Lanka must prioritise prevention, enforce safety standards, ensure transparent spending and review whether recommendations are implemented, rather than measuring success by relief efforts. It is shocking that the National Council for Disaster Management did not meet for a seven-year period, and the country’s lack of disaster preparedness has come as no surprise. One may recall the National Security Council did not meet regularly during the UNP-led Yahapalana government. It did not meet at all during the month before the Easter Sunday terror attacks in 2019. Meanwhile, there are disturbing reports about cities across the world gradually sinking, threatening millions of residents with flooding, damaged infrastructure and displacement. Excessive groundwater extraction, rapid urbanisation, heavy construction and rising sea levels are aggravating the problem. Jakarta is among the worst affected, while Mexico City, Bangkok, Ho Chi Minh City, Shanghai, Lagos and Tehran also face serious land subsidence. Colombo, a Ramsar wetland city, is also threatened. Experts have pointed out that Colombo’s relatively flat terrain, proximity to the Indian Ocean and exposure to heavy monsoon rainfall increase its vulnerability. Rapid, unplanned urban development, the loss of wetlands and inadequate drainage further aggravate flood risks. Sri Lanka must brace itself for environmental, economic, social, architectural and engineering challenges that accompany the sinking-city phenomenon. Several areas in and around Colombo have been built on natural floodplains, former marshes, paddy fields and other low-lying land. Research by Sri Lankan universities and the World Bank identifies urban expansion into flood-prone areas as a significant contributor to Colombo’s flood vulnerability. These urban centres experience floods almost every year, but unplanned urban development continues unabated. Inadequacies in emergency responses, a lack of proactive planning and chronic institutional weaknesses point to the need for a radical rethink of Sri Lanka’s disaster management strategy, and the establishment of an empowered central coordinating authority with a cross-sectoral mandate to address the challenges posed by climate change and natural disasters.

audit.headline: Palm-leaf manuscript digitisation project launched at Gangaramaya with Indian assistance
audit.summary: India International Centre (IIC), Delhi in collaboration with the Gangaramaya Temple, Colombo launched the SAMHiTA (South Asian Manuscript Histories and Textual Archive) Palm-Leaf Manuscript Digitisation Project at the Gangaramaya Temple, on Friday, October 23. The Project is undertaken with the financial assistance from the Indian government. Indian High Commissioner Santosh Jha attended the launch ceremony and a site visit at the Temple. Venerable Dr. Kirinde Assaji Thera, the chief incumbent of Gangaramaya Temple, Venerable Dr. Pallegama Rathnasara Thera, trustees of the Temple, and Prof. Gamini Ranasinghe, Project Adviser, and his team of local experts, were present. Project SAMHiTA seeks to preserve the rich intellectual and cultural heritage of South Asia by digitising ancient manuscripts and safeguarding the knowledge they contain, for future generations.
audit.body: India International Centre (IIC), Delhi in collaboration with the Gangaramaya Temple, Colombo launched the SAMHiTA (South Asian Manuscript Histories and Textual Archive) Palm-Leaf Manuscript Digitisation Project at the Gangaramaya Temple, on Friday, October 23. The Project is undertaken with the financial assistance from the Indian government. Indian High Commissioner Santosh Jha attended the launch ceremony and a site visit at the Temple. Venerable Dr. Kirinde Assaji Thera, the chief incumbent of Gangaramaya Temple, Venerable Dr. Pallegama Rathnasara Thera, trustees of the Temple, and Prof. Gamini Ranasinghe, Project Adviser, and his team of local experts, were present. Project SAMHiTA seeks to preserve the rich intellectual and cultural heritage of South Asia by digitising ancient manuscripts and safeguarding the knowledge they contain, for future generations. These manuscripts are repositories of civilisational wisdom, documenting languages, philosophies, religious traditions, rituals, customs and artistic practices. During the site visit, Project Adviser and team demonstrated the work of preservation of manuscripts and the process of digitisation. Gangaramaya Temple is the first institution in Sri Lanka to partner with IIC under Project SAMHiTA. IIC and the Temple signed an MoU in July 2026 for the digitisation of ancient manuscripts preserved at the Temple. The digitisation is currently underway, led by a team of Sri Lankan experts, and is expected to be completed by the end of November 2026. Speaking at the ceremony, the High Commissioner expressed appreciation to Venerable Dr. Kirinde Assaji Thera, for his leadership and guidance and Prof. Gamini and his team of experts for their commitment to the initiative. He noted that the Government of India is honoured to support this effort. The project reflects the deep and enduring Buddhist heritage shared by India and Sri Lanka, rooted in centuries of spiritual, intellectual and cultural exchange. The High Commissioner recalled the exposition of the sacred Devnimori Relics of Lord Buddha from India, hosted at the Gangaramaya Temple in February 2026, which brought the peoples of the two countries together in reverence and devotion. The High Commissioner invited other institutional partners in Sri Lanka that are pursuing the digitisation of ancient manuscripts to collaborate with Project SAMHiTA, where the Government of India provides grant assistance for such efforts. He wished the Project every success at the Gangaramaya Temple and expressed the hope that it will be expanded to include more manuscript collections for preservation.

audit.headline: Airbus deal: Namal among four indicted
audit.summary: Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara yesterday (27) informed the Colombo Magistrate’s Court that indictments had been filed, in respect of the Airbus case, before the Permanent Trial-at-Bar, against four persons, including SLPP MP Namal Rajapaksa. On behalf of the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) Bandara brought the matter to the notice of Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga S. Bodaragama. The court was told that the indictments consisted of 24 charges against the defendants. Bandara said that he expected yesterday to be the last date this particular case was taken up at the Colombo Chief Magistrate’s court. SLPP National List MP Rajapaksa has been held in remand since 4 September this year over the Rs 100 mn bribery allegation pertaining to the 2013 procurement of 10 aircraft from Airbus company.
