audit.headline: Norochcholai unit goes offline again, raising fresh questions over power security
audit.summary: By Ifham Nizam Sri Lanka’s electricity supply security has come under renewed scrutiny after a generating unit at the Norochcholai Lakvijaya coal power plant complex was taken offline for maintenance, just two days after all three units were reported to have returned to the national grid, following the October 17 countrywide blackout. The latest shutdown of Unit 2, reported on October 26, has raised questions about maintenance planning, the reliability of the country’s largest coal-fired power station and the adequacy of public disclosures on the availability of critical generating capacity. As of Tuesday (27), no confirmed date for Unit 2’s return to service was available in the reports reviewed.
audit.body: By Ifham Nizam Sri Lanka’s electricity supply security has come under renewed scrutiny after a generating unit at the Norochcholai Lakvijaya coal power plant complex was taken offline for maintenance, just two days after all three units were reported to have returned to the national grid, following the October 17 countrywide blackout. The latest shutdown of Unit 2, reported on October 26, has raised questions about maintenance planning, the reliability of the country’s largest coal-fired power station and the adequacy of public disclosures on the availability of critical generating capacity. As of Tuesday (27), no confirmed date for Unit 2’s return to service was available in the reports reviewed. Nor had the authorities publicly explained the precise nature of the maintenance, whether it had been scheduled before the blackout or whether it was connected to inspections or remedial work following the incident. The absence of a clear timeline is significant because the restoration of Unit 2 to its full 270-megawatt capacity, on October 22, enabled the National System Operator (NSO) to discontinue electricity demand-management measures imposed from October 19 to 21. The Unit 3 was subsequently reconnected, with all three units reportedly contributing to the grid by October 24. The renewed shutdown, therefore, comes at a sensitive moment, when the power sector is attempting to restore confidence in the reliability of electricity generation following a countrywide system failure. The sequence of events warrants a clear explanation from the authorities. A unit returning to full capacity and subsequently being taken offline for maintenance does not, by itself, establish a breakdown or negligence. However, the public needs to know whether the work was planned, why it became necessary, at this particular time, and how long the country must operate without that generating capacity. Critics have alleged that substandard coal shipments brought in since this government came to power led to breakdowns at Norochcholai. The three Norochcholai units, each rated at 300 MW, have a combined installed capacity of 900 MW. At the operating output reported during the recent restoration, the loss of Unit 2’s 270 MW represents a substantial reduction in available generation from the plant. The NSO has reportedly assured consumers that the latest maintenance will not interrupt electricity supplies. That assurance, however, needs to be considered alongside the system’s available reserves, demand levels, hydropower output and the availability of other generating plants. All three Norochcholai units were disconnected from the national grid following the nationwide blackout on October 17, when instability in the electricity system resulted in a total system failure. The shutdown was described as a safety measure while the system was being stabilised. On October 20, Cabinet Spokesperson Nalinda Jayatissa said Unit 1 remained offline following a technical failure associated with the blackout. He also said that Unit 1 had undergone maintenance from July 30 to September 30 and rejected allegations linking the incident to substandard coal. The restoration process subsequently proceeded in stages. On October 22, the NSO announced that Unit 2 had reached its full 270 MW output, allowing demand-management measures to end. Unit 3 was then brought back to the grid, with all three units reported to be operating by October 24. The latest maintenance shutdown has reopened questions about the distinction between units being reconnected after a system-wide event and their sustained availability under normal operating conditions. Were the units subjected to comprehensive inspections before returning to service? Was the maintenance now being undertaken on Unit 2 already scheduled, or did the need emerge during the restoration process? Have engineers identified any common technical issues requiring further attention? These questions are particularly relevant because the plant plays a central role in meeting Sri Lanka’s baseload electricity demand. The recurring difficulties associated with Norochcholai have financial as well as technical implications. When coal-fired generation becomes unavailable, the system operator may have to rely more heavily on other sources, including thermal plants using imported fuel, depending on prevailing system conditions. Such substitution can increase generation costs and place additional pressure on the finances of the electricity sector. The actual cost of the latest shutdown, however, cannot be established without information on replacement generation, fuel consumption and the duration of the outage. Norochcholai has also experienced repeated breakdowns and maintenance-related shutdowns over the years. Earlier reporting documented major overhauls being postponed amid power shortages and other constraints, raising concerns about the long-term consequences of deferred maintenance. The current episode makes it important to establish whether the latest work forms part of a properly planned maintenance programme or reflects an issue that could have been identified and addressed earlier. It would be premature to conclude that the latest shutdown is connected to the October 17 blackout. The available information does not establish such a link. Equally, the authorities should not leave consumers to speculate about the reason for the shutdown or its expected duration. The Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka has published a page containing communications relating to the October 17 total system failure, including a preliminary report submitted by the NSO on October 23. The findings and recommendations of the investigation, and the extent to which they address the generation and transmission failures, remain important to public understanding of the incident. The immediate issue is the restoration deadline. Neither a confirmed completion date nor sufficient technical details about the current maintenance were available in the reports reviewed by this newspaper. The NSO and plant management need to clarify the work being undertaken, whether the shutdown was scheduled in advance, the expected return-to-service date and the precautions being taken to prevent further disruption. They should also disclose the present output of Units 1 and 3, the available reserve margin and the contingency arrangements should another major generating unit become unavailable. For a country still rebuilding confidence after a nationwide blackout and several days of demand management, assurances that there will be no interruption to supply are important. But reliable public communication also requires specific information on generation availability, maintenance schedules and restoration deadlines. The central question is not simply whether electricity can be supplied today. It is whether Sri Lanka’s power system can maintain a dependable supply without repeated emergency measures or costly recourse to alternative generation. Norochcholai’s latest shutdown makes that a question the authorities need to answer with facts, a clear timeline and a credible account of the maintenance programme. audit.headline: BASL demands comprehensive probe into latest death in police custody
audit.summary: Condemning the latest death in police custody, the Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) yesterday (27) requested the Inspector General of Police, and all relevant authorities, to ensure an immediate, impartial, transparent and comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of Ishara Harshakumara, The text of the statement: “BASL views with grave concern the death of 29-year-old Ishara Harshakumara, a resident of Kiriwaththuduwa and a father of two, while in the custody of the Homagama Police Station, following his arrest in connection with a drug-related investigation. It has been reported that members of the family, who visited the Homagama Police Station on the morning of 25th October, 2026, to inquire about his condition, have expressed the view that they observed physical injuries which, in their opinion, indicated that he had been severely assaulted.
audit.body: Condemning the latest death in police custody, the Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) yesterday (27) requested the Inspector General of Police, and all relevant authorities, to ensure an immediate, impartial, transparent and comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of Ishara Harshakumara, The text of the statement: “BASL views with grave concern the death of 29-year-old Ishara Harshakumara, a resident of Kiriwaththuduwa and a father of two, while in the custody of the Homagama Police Station, following his arrest in connection with a drug-related investigation. It has been reported that members of the family, who visited the Homagama Police Station on the morning of 25th October, 2026, to inquire about his condition, have expressed the view that they observed physical injuries which, in their opinion, indicated that he had been severely assaulted. In contrast, the Police Spokesman has stated that the suspect developed a sudden illness during an operation and died following hospital admission. In these circumstances, the BASL considers it imperative that the circumstances, surrounding the death, are fully and independently established, and that the differing accounts and concerns raised in relation thereto are subjected to a transparent and credible investigation. The BASL emphasises that a death in custody is a matter of the gravest concern, and that the State has a fundamental and non-delegable duty to safeguard the life, health and bodily integrity of every person in its custody. Any allegation of custodial violence or ill-treatment must therefore be treated with the utmost seriousness and, if established, dealt with strictly in accordance with the law. Article 13(4) of the Constitution and the jurisprudence of the higher judiciary affirm that deprivation of life cannot be imposed as punishment except by order of a competent court, underscoring the obligation of law enforcement authorities to ensure that the rights and dignity of persons in custody are fully protected. While noting that the Homagama Magistrate’s Court has ordered a post-mortem examination and that a preliminary inquiry has been initiated under the direction of the Homagama Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP). In a matter involving an allegation of custodial violence, public confidence requires that no reasonable question is left unanswered and that any person responsible for wrongdoing, if established, is held accountable in accordance with the law. Accordingly, the BASL calls upon the Inspector General of Police and all relevant authorities to ensure an immediate, impartial, transparent and comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of Ishara Harshakumara, with all relevant evidence properly preserved and examined and the investigation conducted without interference or prejudice. The BASL condemns any act of custodial violence or unlawful deprivation of life, if established through a proper investigation, while reiterating that the facts must be determined through a fair, independent and credible process. The BASL will take further steps if required in this regard and keep its membership and the general public informed.”

audit.headline: Opposition alleges govt. move to arm military with police powers
audit.summary: … questions Defence Secretary’s controversial role Former External Affairs Minister Prof. G. L. Peiris has warned that the NPP government plans to grant police powers to the armed forces and confer sweeping powers on the Secretary to the Ministry of Defence under the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill. Addressing the media at former President Ranil Wickremesinghe’s office at Flower Road, Colombo, Prof. Peiris explained how the proposed legislation could be used to silence the democratic Opposition and suppress the media. The former parliamentarian said the Bill posed a grave threat to civil liberties because it lacked a sufficiently clear definition of terrorism.
audit.body: … questions Defence Secretary’s controversial role Former External Affairs Minister Prof. G. L. Peiris has warned that the NPP government plans to grant police powers to the armed forces and confer sweeping powers on the Secretary to the Ministry of Defence under the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill. Addressing the media at former President Ranil Wickremesinghe’s office at Flower Road, Colombo, Prof. Peiris explained how the proposed legislation could be used to silence the democratic Opposition and suppress the media. The former parliamentarian said the Bill posed a grave threat to civil liberties because it lacked a sufficiently clear definition of terrorism. Although the Opposition accepted the need to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA), which has been in force since 1979, he stressed that the proposed legislation could criminalise legitimate political activities. A person conducting a political campaign to pressure the government to abandon a project, or even distributing leaflets opposing a government initiative, could face terrorism charges, he warned. Prof. Peiris also expressed concern over provisions empowering the Defence Secretary to issue detention orders and restrict access to certain places. He argued that these powers could be used to curtail the activities of the media and restrict people’s movements. Questioning the need to authorise the armed forces to exercise police powers in the absence of a state of emergency, he warned that the provisions could undermine democratic practices and weaken judicial safeguards. He also criticised provisions allowing suspects to be detained for extended periods under orders issued by the Defence Secretary. Under the proposed law, an initial detention order could be issued for up to two months, with the possibility of an extension, potentially exposing individuals to prolonged detention. Prof. Peiris alleged that the government was creating an environment in which the Defence Secretary could authorise detention without adequate judicial oversight, paving the way for the suppression of democratic opposition. The proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill have drawn criticism from political parties and civil society groups concerned about their implications for fundamental rights and civil liberties. (SF)

audit.headline: Cannabis and Hashish Worth Rs. 157 Million Seized at Peliyagoda
audit.summary: COLOMBO (News1st); Sri Lanka Customs has seized a stock of cannabis and hashish meticulously smuggled into the country from Thailand. The drugs were discovered during an inspection at a Peliyagoda Customs warehouse of suspicious items fashioned as components of a table imported into the country as a gift. Furthermore,Sri Lanka Customs stated that they confiscated hidden stocks of cannabis valued at Rs. 24 million and hashish valued at Rs. 133 million inside those components. Moreover, a 29-year-old resident of the Ragama area has also been arrested in connection with the incident. Sri Lanka Customs further stated that steps have been taken to hand over the suspect and the contraband to the Police Narcotic Bureau for further investigation.

audit.headline: Customs Probes Illegal Import of Over 80kg of Gold
audit.summary: COLOMBO (News1st); Sri Lanka Customs has launched a wide-ranging investigation into an incident involving the illegal importation of gold into the country using funds belonging to Jeffrey Mohamed, who was accused of siphoning off large sums of US dollars abroad. Sri Lanka Customs stated that the investigation is currently being conducted regarding a gold jewelry shop owner in Pettah. Moreover, Initial investigations have revealed that he had brought over 80 kilograms of gold into the country. Police stated that several teams have now commenced investigations to locate the gold. Furthermore, Jeffrey Mohamed, accused of setting up 36 shell companies to illegally transfer dollars abroad under the guise of imports, is currently in remand custody.

audit.headline: Rain and strong winds to persist in several parts of the island
audit.summary: The influence of Very Severe Cyclonic Storm Arnab on Sri Lanka’s weather has gradually weakened as the storm makes landfall along the coast of Andhra Pradesh, India, the Department of Meteorology said. Several spells of showers are expected in the Western and Sabaragamuwa provinces and the Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Galle and Matara districts. Showers or thundershowers may occur at a few places in the Uva Province and the Batticaloa and Ampara districts after 1.00 p.m. Strong winds of 40–50 kmph may occur at times over the western slopes of the Central Hills, the Northern, North-Central and North-Western provinces, and the Trincomalee and Hambantota districts. The public has been advised to take precautions against possible damage from temporary localised strong winds and lightning during thundershowers.

audit.headline: No clear winner in Israel as exit polls suggest rebuke for Netanyahu
audit.summary: Exit polls indicate there is no clear winner in Israel’s elections, with both incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, appearing to fall short of an outright path to victory. According to Israel’s Channel 12 News, Netanyahu’s bloc is projected to collapse from 68 seats in the previous Knesset to 50 seats. Eisenkot’s bloc had 52 seats, while the exit polls suggest the Arab parties have a record 18 seats. Even though Netanyahu’s coalition, including far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties, is expected to be smaller, his Likud party is projected to have the largest share of seats in the next Knesset with 24 seats to Eisenkot’s Yashar party’s 22 seats. An outright victory requires a coalition to have at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot appear short of that mark, based on the exit polls.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked many of his supporters in his speech early Wednesday, among whom he counted US President Donald Trump and God. “Together with our great friend President Trump, we are determined to eliminate this threat once and for all,” he said, referring to Iran and the ongoing war. He also thanked members of his Likud party, other government and coalition partners, his wife and children, and Israel’s soldiers. “Finally I’d like to thank the creator of the world, which is giving me the power to continue to act for the eternity of Israel and our beloved nation and state – our only state,” he said at the end of his speech. “I’d like to say to you, we made it against our enemies and we will form the future … do not be afraid, Israel, do not be afraid. The lion will roar … The people of Israel is alive.” CNN

audit.headline: Namal Rajapaksa to be produced before Trial-at-Bar today over Airbus deal
audit.summary: Member of Parliament Namal Rajapaksa, who is in remand custody over allegations relating to the acceptance of a Rs. 100 million bribe in connection with the SriLankan Airlines Airbus purchase deal, is scheduled to be produced before the Colombo Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar today (28). Meanwhile, his bail application in connection with the Krrish deal is also scheduled to be taken up at the Colombo Chief Magistrate’s Court today. The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption informed the Colombo Chief Magistrate’s Court yesterday (27) that indictments had been filed against Namal Rajapaksa and other defendants before the Colombo Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar over the Airbus transaction. Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara, appearing for the Commission, informed the court that a 24-count indictment had been filed against the MP.

Meanwhile, his bail application in connection with the Krrish deal is also scheduled to be taken up at the Colombo Chief Magistrate’s Court today. The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption informed the Colombo Chief Magistrate’s Court yesterday (27) that indictments had been filed against Namal Rajapaksa and other defendants before the Colombo Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar over the Airbus transaction. Deputy Solicitor General Janaka Bandara, appearing for the Commission, informed the court that a 24-count indictment had been filed against the MP. The prosecution requested that he remain in remand custody until he was produced before the High Court and the indictment was served. However, Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga S. Bodaragama stated that the Magistrate’s Court no longer had jurisdiction to issue further orders in the case following the filing of indictments before the High Court. The Magistrate accordingly ordered the Superintendent of Prisons to produce Namal Rajapaksa before the Permanent High Court Trial-at-Bar today and directed that the matter be reported back to the Magistrate’s Court on October 30.

audit.headline: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in US after Brazil cancels his passports
audit.summary: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has left Brazil and arrived in Florida, United States, following his defeat in Sunday’s presidential runoff election. Flávio, 45, is the eldest son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and has served as a senator since 2019. A trained lawyer, he contested the presidential election as the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party (PL), losing to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday. Although Flávio is considered less confrontational than his father, he appealed to a similar support base during the election campaign, pledging to pursue a comparable political agenda. He had also sought to strengthen ties with Washington, actively courting US President Donald Trump and members of his administration. During a meeting at the White House in May, Flávio presented himself as a loyal ally of Trump.

Flávio, 45, is the eldest son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and has served as a senator since 2019. A trained lawyer, he contested the presidential election as the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party (PL), losing to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday. Although Flávio is considered less confrontational than his father, he appealed to a similar support base during the election campaign, pledging to pursue a comparable political agenda. He had also sought to strengthen ties with Washington, actively courting US President Donald Trump and members of his administration. During a meeting at the White House in May, Flávio presented himself as a loyal ally of Trump. Following his election defeat, Flávio left Brazil and travelled to the United States on Tuesday. Even before his arrival was confirmed, the Trump administration had indicated that it would grant visas to the senator and his family, allowing them to enter the country. Flávio has reportedly met his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, in Florida. However, details of the route he took to leave Brazil and whether he intends to settle in the United States remain unclear. Like his father, Flávio refused to recognise his election defeat, describing the result as “impossible” and calling for it to be annulled. Meanwhile, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has described Flávio Bolsonaro’s alleged departure from Brazil as “shameful”. Addressing the matter in a speech, Lula also stated: “Those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear.” BBC

audit.headline: Sri Lanka and Türkiye Sign New Air Deal
audit.summary: COLOMBO (News 1st); A new chapter in relations between Sri Lanka and Türkiye took shape in Ankara on Tuesday (27), as the two nations signed an amended air transport agreement aimed at expanding connectivity and unlocking fresh opportunities in tourism, trade and investment. The protocol amending the existing Air Transport Agreement was signed by Sri Lanka's Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Arun Hemachandra together with Enver İskurt, Deputy Minister of Transport and Infrastructure of Türkiye. Beyond aviation, the agreement reflects a broader ambition to bring the two nations closer together through stronger economic and people-to-people links. Improved air connectivity is expected to create new opportunities for travellers, businesses and investors, while making it easier for citizens of both countries to engage in tourism, commerce and cultural exchange.

audit.headline: A vision for SriLankan Airlines
audit.summary: SriLankan Airlines has spent far too long being treated as a national asset whose losses can be excused in the name of tourism, connectivity and national pride. That approach has failed taxpayers, drained public resources and allowed the airline to operate without the commercial discipline expected of a sustainable business. If the national carrier is to have a future, its first priority must be to become profitable. Everything else must follow from that objective. Recent reports that SriLankan Airlines is exploring opportunities to expand its network to Perth, China and Africa have once again raised questions about the airline’s strategic direction. The newly appointed CEO of the airline has argued that the airline must take the lead in developing routes that support Sri Lanka’s tourism industry, including destinations other airlines might initially consider commercially unattractive.
audit.body: SriLankan Airlines has spent far too long being treated as a national asset whose losses can be excused in the name of tourism, connectivity and national pride. That approach has failed taxpayers, drained public resources and allowed the airline to operate without the commercial discipline expected of a sustainable business. If the national carrier is to have a future, its first priority must be to become profitable. Everything else must follow from that objective. Recent reports that SriLankan Airlines is exploring opportunities to expand its network to Perth, China and Africa have once again raised questions about the airline’s strategic direction. The newly appointed CEO of the airline has argued that the airline must take the lead in developing routes that support Sri Lanka’s tourism industry, including destinations other airlines might initially consider commercially unattractive. The argument sounds attractive on the surface. More flights could bring more visitors, stimulate economic activity and strengthen Sri Lanka’s international connections. But it also reveals the fundamental confusion that has plagued the national carrier for years. Is SriLankan Airlines a commercial enterprise, or is it an instrument of government tourism policy? The distinction matters because SriLankan Airlines is not an independent business operating with unlimited capital. Its losses ultimately burden the Treasury, diverting public money from healthcare, education, infrastructure and other essential services. Every rupee used to sustain an unprofitable route is a rupee that must be justified to taxpayers. Tourism is undoubtedly vital to Sri Lanka’s economy. But developing tourism is not the airline’s primary responsibility. Its responsibility is to operate a viable airline, generate revenue, control costs and deliver a return on the capital invested in it. Tourism promotion can be a welcome secondary benefit, but it cannot serve as a permanent excuse for commercial failure. If the government believes that a particular route is essential to national tourism policy despite being commercially unviable, it should make that decision transparently and establish whether the wider economic benefits justify the cost. The airline should not be expected to conceal the price of public policy within its operating losses. The first task, therefore, is to establish a clear commercial strategy. SriLankan Airlines must determine what kind of carrier it can realistically become, given its finances, fleet, competitive position and access to markets. Can SriLankan be a smaller regional carrier connecting selected destinations? Can the airline profitably sustain a broader international network? Which routes generate adequate returns, and which merely consume scarce resources? These questions require evidence, not ambition. Expansion into Perth, China or Africa should proceed only where rigorous commercial assessments demonstrate a credible path to profitability. Opening a route simply because it might attract tourists is not a strategy. It is a gamble with public money. The airline must also examine its ancillary businesses. Ground handling, catering, cargo and aircraft engineering may offer opportunities to generate independent revenue and improve operational efficiency. These activities should have transparent accounts, measurable performance targets and clear management responsibilities. Where practical, their performance should be assessed separately so that profitable operations are not obscured by losses elsewhere. Any restructuring must, of course, account for shared costs and operational dependencies. Once SriLankan Airlines has demonstrated sustained operational improvement, the government should seriously consider strategic partnerships with credible international aviation companies. Such partnerships could bring capital, technical expertise, management discipline and access to wider commercial networks. But partners will be difficult to attract on favourable terms if the airline remains burdened by political interference and an unclear business model. Ultimately, SriLankan Airlines needs a strategic vision that survives changes of government. That vision must identify its core markets, define its competitive advantage, establish realistic financial targets and hold management accountable for results. National pride cannot be measured by the number of destinations on a route map. Nor can the value of a national carrier be judged by the flag painted on its aircraft. SriLankan Airlines deserves the opportunity to recover. But recovery requires an end to the comfortable assumption that taxpayers will always pay for its failures. The airline must learn to fly on its own wings and prove that it can do so profitably.

audit.body: - Subscription list for debentures opens 3 Nov. with Rs. 10 b initial offer and option to increase up to Rs. 30 b in two tranches - Four options: 5-year debentures offer fixed coupon of 12.75% or a floating rate of 1.5% above the 12-month Treasury Bill rate, while 7-year debentures offer 13% fixed or 1.75% above the Treasury Bill rate Bank of Ceylon (BOC), Sri Lanka’s leading state-owned commercial bank, is set to create another milestone in the country’s capital market with the launch of Sri Lanka’s largest-ever listed debenture issue, with a maximum issue size of Rs. 30 billion. The bank proposes to initially raise Rs. 10 billion, with an option to increase the issue to Rs. 20 billion in the event of an oversubscription of the initial tranche and a further option to increase the total issue size up to Rs. 30 billion, making it the largest listed debenture issue undertaken in Sri Lanka. The proposed issue comprises Basel III compliant, Tier 2, Listed, Rated, Unsecured, Subordinated, Redeemable debentures with a non-viability write-down feature. The debentures carry an issue rating of AA (Stable) from Lanka Rating Agency, while BOC’s issuer rating stands at AA-(lka)/Stable from Fitch Ratings Lanka Ltd. The debentures will be offered with five-year and seven-year maturities, providing with medium to long-term fixed income investment opportunities. The issue is confined to qualified investors and the minimum subscription for qualified investors is Rs. 10,000, while individual investors are required to apply for at least Rs. 5 million. The debentures are offered in four different types to meet diverse requirements of qualified investors. The fixed coupon rate of the five-year debenture will be 12.75% per annum while the floating coupon rate will be 1.50% above the applicable twelve-month Treasury Bill rate. The Fixed coupon rate of the seven-year debenture will be 13% per annum while the floating coupon rate will be 1.75% above the applicable twelve-month Treasury Bill rate. BOC’s largest debenture issue comes at a significant juncture for the Sri Lankan economy, at a time when the country is prioritising sustainable, investment-led and inclusive economic growth. Against this backdrop, a stronger capital base will further enhance BOC’s capacity to mobilise and channel funds towards productive sectors of the economy, thereby supporting Sri Lanka’s next phase of economic development. This landmark issue therefore represents more than a significant capital-raising exercise for the bank. BOC, as the country’s leading state-owned commercial bank, remains well positioned to play a pivotal role in financing businesses, facilitating investment and supporting the broader development priorities of the country. BOC is a Corporate Finance Advisor licensed by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka. This largest Basel III Debenture issuance was exclusively structured and managed by the Investment Banking team who possess a wealth of expertise in structuring innovative capital market instruments. The issue follows BOC’s pioneering Sustainability Bond issuance, another landmark transaction structured and managed by the bank’s Investment Banking Division, reflecting BOC’s continued leadership in developing innovative capital-market solutions while advancing sustainable finance in Sri Lanka. The Legal Department of BOC acts as the lawyers to the issue, while the Corporate Branch of the bank acts as the bankers to the issue. The Investment Banking Division will also continue to act as the Registrar to the proposed issue, while Hatton National Bank PLC will be the trustee to the issue. The bank is opening the subscription list of the BASEL III Debenture Issue at 9.30 a.m. on 3 November 2026 and will remain open for 14 market days unless the bank decides to close it earlier based on subscription levels. Applications for the debentures will be accepted from qualified investors in accordance with the terms and conditions set out in the Prospectus. The Prospectus and application forms can be downloaded from the web sites of the CSE; www.cse.lk and BOC; www.boc.lk. Duly completed application forms should be enclosed in an envelope marked “BOC Debenture Issue” together with the remittance for the full amount payable on application and delivered to the Investment Banking Division at 7th Floor of BOC Head Office or collection points mentioned in the prospectus. With a long-standing presence in Sri Lanka’s banking industry, Bank of Ceylon has played a significant role in the country’s economic development by mobilising savings, extending credit and supporting individuals, businesses and major economic sectors. The proposed debenture issue is expected to further enhance the bank’s capacity to support corporate, SME, retail and institutional customers while maintaining prudent regulatory capital buffers. Investors are advised to carefully read the Prospectus, including the terms of the debentures, risk factors, non-viability write-down provisions and eligibility requirements, before making an investment decision. Bank of Ceylon invites eligible local and foreign investors to participate in this landmark issue and be a part of the bank’s continuing journey of financial strength and contribution to Sri Lanka’s economic development. At a time when the country is entering a new phase of investment-led growth, the issue represents an opportunity for investors to participate in the growth journey of the nation’s leading state-owned commercial bank while contributing to the broader economic progress of Sri Lanka.

audit.headline: Binod Chaudhary signals plans to further expand investments in Sri Lanka
audit.summary: Binod Chaudhary Nepalese business leader and investor Binod Chaudhary is looking to further expand his investment footprint in Sri Lanka, building on his group’s existing interests in the country, including its investment in Union Bank and its presence in the hospitality sector. Chaudhary, Chairman of the Chaudhary Group, has indicated continued confidence in Sri Lanka’s long-term economic potential and is exploring opportunities to increase investments across key sectors, with particular interest in financial services, hospitality and other areas with strong growth potential. The Group’s investment in Union Bank and its interests in Sri Lanka’s hotel and tourism industry reflect its existing commitment to the country.
audit.body: Binod Chaudhary Nepalese business leader and investor Binod Chaudhary is looking to further expand his investment footprint in Sri Lanka, building on his group’s existing interests in the country, including its investment in Union Bank and its presence in the hospitality sector. Chaudhary, Chairman of the Chaudhary Group, has indicated continued confidence in Sri Lanka’s long-term economic potential and is exploring opportunities to increase investments across key sectors, with particular interest in financial services, hospitality and other areas with strong growth potential. The Group’s investment in Union Bank and its interests in Sri Lanka’s hotel and tourism industry reflect its existing commitment to the country. Further investments could strengthen the group’s presence while contributing to capital formation, employment and the development of Sri Lanka’s tourism and services sectors. “We believe Sri Lanka has tremendous long-term potential. Our existing investments, including in banking and hospitality, have given us valuable experience in the market, and we remain open to expanding our investments where we see the right opportunities,” said Binod Chaudhary. The potential expansion comes as Sri Lanka continues to attract renewed interest from international investors seeking opportunities in tourism, financial services, infrastructure, consumer businesses and other growth sectors. Chaudhary said Sri Lanka’s strategic location, tourism potential, talented workforce and access to regional markets continue to make the country an attractive destination for long-term investment. The Chaudhary Group will continue to evaluate new investment opportunities and potential partnerships in Sri Lanka, with a focus on projects capable of generating sustainable economic value.

audit.headline: Bond market yields open steady to higher on selected tenors
audit.summary: By Wealth Trust Securities The secondary Bond market yesterday kicked off the fresh trading week with yields holding broadly steady across majority of the yield curve. However, selective selling pressure on the 2033 and 2034 tenors saw yields push higher. Market activity and transaction volumes remained at moderate levels, ahead of an auction packed week. The week will see back-to-back primary auctions, with a Rs. 100 billion Treasury Bill auction scheduled for tomorrow (28), followed by a Rs. 100 billion Treasury Bond auction on Thursday (29). The 15.02.28 maturity traded at the rate of 10.45%. The 01.08.30 and 15.10.30 maturities traded at the rates of 11.50% and 11.55%-11.54% respectively. The 01.12.31 maturity traded at the rate of 11.85%. The 15.12.32 maturity traded at the rate of 12.00%.

audit.headline: CSE starts week in red, down 0.23%
audit.summary: The Colombo stock market yesterday opened the week in red, extending losses into a sixth consecutive session. The ASPI was down 0.23% or 44.35 points at 19,640.56 and the active S&P SL20 fell 0.21% or 11.76 points to 5,601.87. Market turnover was nearly Rs. 666.3 million on 29.7 million shares traded. Foreign investors were net sellers on a net outflow of Rs. 6.6 million. With 123 counters ending in red against 80 gainers, the top contributors to the ASPI decline were CARS, COMB, LAMB, DIST and HAYL. First Capital Research said the bourse opened on a positive note but failed to sustain its early momentum, with continued fluctuations throughout the first half of the session before ultimately closing in negative territory. HNW participation remained subdued, while retail participation was relatively higher, driven by margin selling.
audit.body: The Colombo stock market yesterday opened the week in red, extending losses into a sixth consecutive session. The ASPI was down 0.23% or 44.35 points at 19,640.56 and the active S&P SL20 fell 0.21% or 11.76 points to 5,601.87. Market turnover was nearly Rs. 666.3 million on 29.7 million shares traded. Foreign investors were net sellers on a net outflow of Rs. 6.6 million. With 123 counters ending in red against 80 gainers, the top contributors to the ASPI decline were CARS, COMB, LAMB, DIST and HAYL. First Capital Research said the bourse opened on a positive note but failed to sustain its early momentum, with continued fluctuations throughout the first half of the session before ultimately closing in negative territory. HNW participation remained subdued, while retail participation was relatively higher, driven by margin selling. The banking sector led the daily turnover with a share of 28%, followed by the capital goods, and diversified financials sectors collectively contributing 35%. NDB Securities said high net worth and institutional investor participation was noted in Access Engineering, Commercial Bank and John Keells Holdings. Mixed interest was observed in Sampath Bank, Panasian Power and Hayleys whilst retail interest was noted in Waskaduwa Beach Resort, Muller and Phipps and SMB Leasing. Foreign participation in the market activity remained at subdued levels with foreigners closing as net sellers. The banking sector was the top contributor to the market turnover due to Commercial Bank and Sampath Bank whilst the sector index edged up by 0.09%. The share price of Commercial Bank decreased by 75 cents to close at Rs. 195.25 and Sampath Bank ended flat at Rs. 138.50. The capital goods sector was the second highest contributor to the market turnover due to Access Engineering and John Keells Holdings whilst the sector index edged up by 0.11%. Access Engineering ended down 20 cents to Rs. 74.50 and John Keells Holdings gained 10 cents to Rs. 17.70. Panasian Power was also included amongst the top turnover contributors. The share price of Panasian Power fell 10 cents to close at Rs. 10.

audit.headline: Cargills Bank introduces Sri Lanka’s first ocean plastic debit card
audit.summary: - Initiative to support marine conservation Cargills Bank has launched the Cargills Bank Ocean Plastic Debit Card, marking the first time such a product has been introduced to the Sri Lankan market. This initiative is a key part of the bank’s commitment to sustainable banking and serves as a practical step toward addressing the global challenge of marine pollution. The cards are produced using recycled ocean-bound plastic specifically sourced from the Indian Ocean region, including the Maldives, as well as the Dominican Republic. By transitioning to these recycled materials, Cargills Bank aims to raise meaningful awareness about the impact of plastic waste on our oceans while supporting the protection of coastal ecosystems.
audit.body: - Initiative to support marine conservation Cargills Bank has launched the Cargills Bank Ocean Plastic Debit Card, marking the first time such a product has been introduced to the Sri Lankan market. This initiative is a key part of the bank’s commitment to sustainable banking and serves as a practical step toward addressing the global challenge of marine pollution. The cards are produced using recycled ocean-bound plastic specifically sourced from the Indian Ocean region, including the Maldives, as well as the Dominican Republic. By transitioning to these recycled materials, Cargills Bank aims to raise meaningful awareness about the impact of plastic waste on our oceans while supporting the protection of coastal ecosystems. This move aligns the bank’s operations with circular economy principles, providing customers with a way to support environmental sustainability through their everyday financial choices. Commenting on the launch, Managing Director/CEO Senarath Bandara said: “This sustainability initiative is a continuation of the bank’s Corporate Sustainability Goals (CSG), reflecting a deep-seated commitment to reducing the environmental footprint of traditional banking operations. The successful realisation of this eco-friendly product was made possible through the technical and production expertise of Lake House Printers and Publishers PLC, alongside the global payment technology leadership of Mastercard. Together, these partners have ensured that the Ocean Plastic card meets the highest international standards of durability and security while remaining an emblem of environmental responsibility.” Chief Manager - Cards Services Shihan Pathiraja added: “From an operational standpoint, transitioning to ocean-bound plastic was a meticulous process to ensure that sustainability did not compromise functional excellence. We have integrated this eco-friendly material into our existing debit card infrastructure seamlessly, ensuring that our customers enjoy the same high-speed transaction capabilities and global acceptance they expect from Cargills Bank. This product allows our cardholders to carry a piece of our conservation mission in their pockets, turning every point-of-sale interaction into a statement of environmental advocacy.” To further drive awareness and community engagement, Cargills Bank will be providing extensive visibility for this initiative across its social media channels, inviting customers to become active participants in the bank’s journey toward a greener future. This launch underscores the bank’s belief that modern financial services must not only be innovative but also ethically aligned with the preservation of the planet for future generations.

audit.headline: Corrugated carton industry under growing cost pressure
audit.summary: Sri Lanka’s corrugated carton industry is facing mounting financial pressure as the cost of paper and other essential inputs continues to rise. For many manufacturers, the challenge is no longer simply maintaining profitability; it is ensuring the industry’s sustainability. While several packaging sectors have adjusted their prices in response to rising costs, corrugated carton manufacturers initially took a more cautious approach. Many held prices steady, expecting global supply-chain disruptions, geopolitical tensions and commodity-price increases to ease. That relief has yet to arrive. Instead, the prices of key paper grades used in carton production, including Kraft Liner, White Liner, Test Liner and Medium, have continued to climb by 30-50% across different paper grades.
audit.body: Sri Lanka’s corrugated carton industry is facing mounting financial pressure as the cost of paper and other essential inputs continues to rise. For many manufacturers, the challenge is no longer simply maintaining profitability; it is ensuring the industry’s sustainability. While several packaging sectors have adjusted their prices in response to rising costs, corrugated carton manufacturers initially took a more cautious approach. Many held prices steady, expecting global supply-chain disruptions, geopolitical tensions and commodity-price increases to ease. That relief has yet to arrive. Instead, the prices of key paper grades used in carton production, including Kraft Liner, White Liner, Test Liner and Medium, have continued to climb by 30-50% across different paper grades. Manufacturers are also contending with higher costs for energy, transport, chemicals, starch, inks, labour, maintenance and other operating needs in line with growing inflation and global market realities. Together, these increases are placing the sector under severe strain. Manufacturers have worked to absorb as much of the additional cost as possible while continuing to serve customers at competitive prices. They have reduced waste, improved machine efficiency, managed energy use, optimized transport and strengthened production productivity. These efforts have helped, but they cannot offset rising costs indefinitely. Paper accounts for a substantial share of the cost of producing corrugated cartons. Even a modest increase in paper prices can significantly affect the final cost of a carton; when prices rise across all major grades, the cumulative impact is considerable. This leaves manufacturers caught between escalating costs and intense competition. Customers need affordable packaging, while producers must recover enough to maintain quality, invest in machinery, retain skilled employees and deliver reliably. The consequences could extend well beyond the carton industry. Corrugated cartons are an essential part of Sri Lanka’s manufacturing and export supply chain. Food and beverage producers, tea exporters, agricultural businesses, apparel manufacturers, pharmaceutical companies and many others depend on a reliable supply of quality cartons. If carton manufacturers face growing financial difficulties, the effects may spread across these industries. Higher packaging costs could also weaken Sri Lanka’s export competitiveness, particularly when local exporters are already competing with producers that may have better access to raw materials or lower production costs. The sector is therefore calling for a realistic understanding of the pressures it faces. Manufacturers did not rush to raise prices when costs first began to rise. They waited, hoping conditions would improve and paper prices would return to more sustainable levels. Instead, the pressures have persisted. A responsible adjustment to carton prices may now be necessary, not simply to improve margins, but to help ensure that manufacturers can continue operating sustainably. The challenge is to balance customers’ need to manage costs with the need for carton manufacturers to remain financially viable. The industry is not asking for an easy solution; it is asking for recognition of the realities facing the sector. A sustainable corrugated carton industry is essential to Sri Lanka’s manufacturing and export sectors. Preserving it will require cooperation among paper suppliers, manufacturers, customers, exporters and policymakers. Without appropriate market adjustments, continued cost pressures could have consequences far beyond the carton industry itself.

audit.headline: Digital VAT in Sri Lanka: Why platform liability and reverse charge are essential to avoid costing households and Treasury
audit.summary: Executive summary Sri Lanka’s VAT on cross-border digital services, in force since July 2026, is a necessary and overdue reform, but its design is incomplete. It relies only on registration by non-resident suppliers and fully carves out supplies to VAT-registered businesses. Without platform liability and a B2B reverse charge, it will likely under-collect and place the entire new burden on households. Key points Background: The reform was IMF-backed, with a modest expected yield (0.04-0.08% of GDP). Its stronger case is equal treatment of local and foreign suppliers. It was delayed twice before Act No. 14 of 2026 confirmed the July start. Weak enforcement: The Inland Revenue Department would have to chase foreign vendors with no local presence. Large brands may register, but smaller providers likely won’t.
audit.body: Executive summary Sri Lanka’s VAT on cross-border digital services, in force since July 2026, is a necessary and overdue reform, but its design is incomplete. It relies only on registration by non-resident suppliers and fully carves out supplies to VAT-registered businesses. Without platform liability and a B2B reverse charge, it will likely under-collect and place the entire new burden on households. Key points Background: The reform was IMF-backed, with a modest expected yield (0.04-0.08% of GDP). Its stronger case is equal treatment of local and foreign suppliers. It was delayed twice before Act No. 14 of 2026 confirmed the July start. Weak enforcement: The Inland Revenue Department would have to chase foreign vendors with no local presence. Large brands may register, but smaller providers likely won’t. B2B carve-out: (Supplies made to local VAT registrants): Reverse charge would raise real revenue from banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, which are exempt from invoice-credit VAT and therefore cannot claim input tax credits under that mechanism, while also creating an audit trail. The carve-out forgoes this, loses visibility, and leaves local providers at a disadvantage. Equity: Individuals pay digital VAT while businesses buying the same services pay nothing, which undercuts the aim of base broadening and any future cut to the 18% rate. Global practice: Simplified registration for B2C supplies and reverse charge for B2B supplies are widely used internationally. Platform liability is also increasingly adopted, including in the EU, UK, Australia, Canada and Singapore, but its scope varies. OECD guidance presents platform liability as an effective policy option. Recommendation: Keep simplified registration for B2C supplies, add platform liability for marketplaces, app stores, and replace the B2B carve-out with reverse charge. Support these with clear location-indicator guidance, proportionate penalties and data-sharing with financial institutions. Completing the framework with platform liability and reverse charge Sri Lanka’s decision to tax cross-border digital services represents a necessary and overdue modernisation of the Value Added Tax system. It responds to the reality that value is increasingly created and consumed online, often without any physical presence in the country of consumption. Local providers have long charged VAT on comparable services while many non-resident suppliers have not. The reform aims to correct that imbalance, broaden the tax base, and support the eventual possibility of reducing the high 18% standard rate. Yet the framework that has been enacted relies almost exclusively on vendor registration by non-resident suppliers and contains a complete carve-out for supplies to VAT-registered businesses. This design is incomplete. Without the addition of platform/marketplace liability and a reverse charge mechanism for business-to-business supplies, the regime risks delivering only a fraction of its potential revenue while placing the entire incremental tax burden on individuals and households. Policymakers still have the opportunity to strengthen the legislation and the accompanying administrative rules so that digital VAT becomes a genuine instrument of base broadening rather than a limited and largely symbolic measure. A record of ambition tempered by repeated delay The intellectual and policy origins of digital VAT in Sri Lanka are well documented. The International Monetary Fund’s June 2024 staff report identified the taxation of digital services as one element of a broader package intended to raise revenue and improve neutrality. The expected yield was modest, approximately 0.04% of GDP in the first full year, with some estimates ranging up to 0.08%. The stronger argument was never the absolute size of the revenue but the principle of equal treatment: a Sri Lankan consumer purchasing streaming, software or cloud services from a foreign provider should face the same VAT treatment as one purchasing from a local supplier. Legislative progress followed a familiar pattern of announcement, enactment and postponement, further prolonged by a Supreme Court challenge that delayed the regime’s finalisation and exacted a real opportunity cost in foregone revenue. The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2025 was certified on 11 April 2025. Gazette Notification 2443/30 of 1 July 2025 set an original effective date of 1 October 2025. Cabinet subsequently deferred implementation to 1 April 2026. A further postponement moved the start to 1 July 2026. The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Act No. 14 of 2026, certified on 30 June and published in gazette on 3 July 2026, finally placed the regime on a firm statutory footing and confirmed the July 2026 commencement. Although Sri Lanka’s digital-services VAT provisions came into effect on 1 July 2026, with section 25L principally governing registration and section 25N providing that VAT is not charged where the recipient is VAT-registered, the regime remains non-operational in practice because the prescribed registration form has yet to be made available, preventing non-resident digital service providers from completing the registration process. The mechanics that emerged are conventional in outline but incomplete in substance. Non-resident suppliers of digital services through electronic platforms must register once their supplies to persons in Sri Lanka exceed Rs. 60 million in any twelve-month period or Rs. 15 million in a quarter. A recipient is treated as located in Sri Lanka if at least two of the following indicators are present: a billing or residential address in Sri Lanka, payment through a Sri Lankan bank or financial institution, a payment instrument issued in Sri Lanka, or a Sri Lankan IP address. Registration, return filing and payment are electronic; payment may be made in Rupees or an approved foreign currency, either directly or through a representative. Supplies to VAT-registered resident businesses are entirely carved out. No obligation is placed on platforms, marketplaces or app stores to collect or remit VAT on the underlying supplies they facilitate. Digital VAT: Real revenue, not a compliance checkbox This sequence of delays and the final design choices invite a sober assessment. Digital VAT should not be reduced to a compliance checkbox required by an external program. It should raise meaningful revenue, follow the proven architecture used by successful jurisdictions, and contribute to the larger project of base expansion that can eventually support a lower standard rate. Features that work elsewhere should not be discarded because of lobbying pressure, administrative convenience or incomplete understanding of implementation options. More than one hundred countries already collect VAT on non-resident digital services. The tax base belongs to the country of consumption. Sri Lanka is entitled to collect it fully. Introducing marketplace liability and reverse charge would convert a half-measure into a credible instrument of fiscal policy, one capable of raising revenue, promoting fairness between local and foreign suppliers, and supporting the longer-term objective of reducing the high standard VAT rate of 18% that currently weighs on consumers. The tools exist. International experience demonstrates that they work. The remaining question is whether Sri Lanka will choose to use them OECD recommendations and the global standard The OECD International VAT/GST Guidelines, together with subsequent practical toolkits, provide the clearest international consensus on how to tax cross-border supplies of services and intangibles. For business-to-consumer supplies the recommended approach is to require the non-resident supplier to register and account for the tax under a simplified regime. For business-to-business supplies the preferred mechanism is reverse charge: the local business customer accounts for the VAT as if it were the supplier. This arrangement relieves the foreign supplier of registration obligations on those particular supplies while ensuring that the tax is reported and, where the customer cannot claim full input credit, that revenue is actually collected. Where digital platforms facilitate the transactions, the OECD strongly encourages jurisdictions to impose liability on the platform itself—the “deemed supplier” or full platform liability model. Platforms already possess customer location data, control payment flows and can scale compliance far more efficiently than a tax administration attempting to locate and compel thousands of individual foreign vendors. International practice is not uniform. Simplified vendor registration for B2C supplies and reverse charge for B2B supplies are widely used across jurisdictions. Platform liability is also increasingly adopted, including in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Singapore, but its scope differs. OECD guidance identifies platform liability as an effective policy option. Australia’s extension of GST to imported digital services and the European Union’s progressive introduction of deemed-supplier rules illustrate the practical advantages of concentrating collection at the platform level. Enforcement becomes realistic, the long tail of smaller suppliers is captured, and revenue leakage is substantially reduced. Sri Lanka’s exclusive reliance on vendor registration, the absence of platform liability, and the substitution of a full B2B carve-out for reverse charge constitute the weakest available combination of collection methods. Large, reputation-conscious global brands may eventually register. The multitude of smaller software providers, freelance platforms, content creators and niche applications almost certainly will not. The Inland Revenue Department will be left to pursue entities that have no local presence, no local bank account and little commercial incentive to comply. When the same administration already faces well-documented challenges in securing full compliance from resident taxpayers, the expectation that it can effectively police non-residents who simply ignore registration or under-declare values is unrealistic. Platform liability reverses the burden of enforcement: a limited number of large, visible platforms become the collection points, using systems and data they already maintain. The revenue and equity cost of the B2B carve-out The decision to exempt supplies to VAT-registered businesses rather than apply reverse charge carries particularly serious consequences for both revenue and fairness. Under a reverse charge mechanism a local VAT-registered recipient self-assesses the tax. For a fully taxable business the net cash effect is neutral because the output tax is matched by an equal input credit. Banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit are subject to the separate VAT on financial services but are exempt from invoice-credit VAT; accordingly, they cannot claim input tax credits under the invoice-credit mechanism. The same concern may arise for other businesses whose ability to recover input tax is restricted. Those sectors are significant purchasers of foreign cloud computing, software licenses, digital advertising, data analytics and related services. Reverse charge would therefore generate genuine additional revenue from a rapidly growing category of imports. It would also create a complete audit trail that allows the tax authority to monitor the volume and nature of cross-border digital purchases. Under the B2B carve-out, the foreign supplier does not charge VAT and the VAT-registered recipient does not self-assess it. However, the enacted framework may still require the foreign supplier to furnish prescribed information concerning such supplies to the Inland Revenue Department. The carve-out therefore does not necessarily leave these transactions entirely unreported, but it does not create the same recipient-level self-assessment and audit trail that a reverse charge would provide. This limits visibility and may make misclassification, for example, a private consumer presenting as a business is more difficult to detect. Local digital service providers continue to charge VAT while their foreign competitors do not on B2B sales, recreating the competitive distortion the reform was intended to eliminate. This outcome stands in direct contradiction to the stated policy objective of base broadening. Broadening the tax base cannot mean capturing only individuals, households and non VAT registrant businesses, while excluding businesses that are exempt from invoice-credit VAT, including banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, from the reverse-charge net. Yet that is the practical effect of the present design. Individuals, households and non VAT registrant businesses pay digital VAT on streaming subscriptions, applications, software and online services. Businesses purchasing comparable or identical services from non-resident suppliers face no corresponding liability. The entire additional burden of expanding the VAT base in the digital sphere therefore falls on ordinary consumers. Such an arrangement is inequitable. It is also fiscally short-sighted. Every Rupee of revenue left uncollected from B2B digital imports is a Rupee that cannot contribute to the fiscal space required for a future reduction in the standard 18% rate. Fairness, administrative capacity and the question of influence The present design raises uncomfortable questions of fairness. Domestic VAT registration thresholds have been subject to repeated adjustment; more local small and medium enterprises face compliance obligations and the associated costs. At the same time the largest global platforms face only a registration form that they may or may not complete, with no marketplace liability to enforce collection on the many underlying suppliers they host. Local providers charge VAT; foreign providers of B2B digital services do not. The competitive playing field remains tilted. It is legitimate to ask whether the abandonment of reverse charge and the omission of platform liability reflect purely technical judgment or the successful representation of interests that prefer the current, limited arrangement. Reverse charge, by its ordinary operation, would have brought businesses exempt from invoice-credit VAT, including banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, into the collection mechanism and produced revenue that the carve-out simply forgoes. Administrative convenience is not a sufficient justification for forgoing that revenue. Other countries with larger digital markets and more complex economies have implemented the fuller OECD package. Sri Lanka does not need to invent new systems. It can adapt existing models and begin with the largest platforms. The alternative, proceeding with vendor registration alone and a full B2B carve-out, almost guarantees modest receipts, persistent non-compliance among smaller foreign providers, zero contribution from the B2B segment, and, within a relatively short period, another round of legislative amendments to correct what could have been designed correctly from the outset. A practical and proven path forward A more robust framework is available and does not require radical innovation. It would retain simplified electronic vendor registration for business-to-consumer supplies, introduce platform liability for major marketplaces, app stores, and replace the B2B carve-out with a reverse charge mechanism. Supporting measures, clear guidance on the application of location indicators, proportionate penalties, and structured information exchange with financial institutions would complete the architecture. These are precisely the tools that have proven effective in other jurisdictions. They align with OECD recommendations, protect the competitive position of local providers, generate revenue from purchases by businesses exempt from invoice-credit VAT, including banks, financial institutions, life insurance companies and other VAT registered companies who are prevented from claiming full VAT input credit, and ensure that base expansion is not borne solely by households. Sri Lanka cannot afford a digital VAT regime that exists primarily to satisfy an external checklist. The digital economy is one of the few expanding tax bases available to the country. Confining collection to vendor registration while carving out the entire B2B segment is, in effect, planning for underperformance. Policymakers still possess the authority and the time to strengthen the regime before it settles into underwhelming practice. Introducing marketplace liability and reverse charge would convert a half-measure into a credible instrument of fiscal policy, one capable of raising revenue, promoting fairness between local and foreign suppliers, and supporting the longer-term objective of reducing the high standard VAT rate of 18% that currently weighs on consumers. The tools exist. International experience demonstrates that they work. The remaining question is whether Sri Lanka will choose to use them. (The author was awarded Tax Practice Leader of the Year 2024 (ASPAC) by International Tax Review (ITR) and was a top-four finalist for Tax Litigation and Disputes Practice Leader of the Year (ASPAC))

audit.headline: Exports hit record in Sept., nine-month earnings at all-time high
audit.summary: - September total exports up 17.23% to $ 1.69 b; YTD earnings up 5.04% YoY to $ 13.61 b - Jan.-Sept. merchandise exports up 5.35% YoY to $ 10.76 b; services rise 3.88% YoY to $ 2.85 b - EDB Chief Mangala Wijesinghe expresses confidence in recording over $ 18 b export target by year-end Sri Lanka’s export sector posted its highest-ever monthly performance in September 2026, with total earnings surpassing $ 1.69 billion and reflecting a 17.23% year-on-year (YoY) growth driven by strong merchandise shipments, despite the challenges faced by the tensions in the Middle East and its direct impact on overall costs. The latest data released by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB) showed that merchandise exports shipped in September were up 21.66% YoY to over $ 1.38 billion, though estimated service earnings in the month showed a moderate growth of 0.67% YoY to $ 306.17 million.
audit.body: - September total exports up 17.23% to $ 1.69 b; YTD earnings up 5.04% YoY to $ 13.61 b - Jan.-Sept. merchandise exports up 5.35% YoY to $ 10.76 b; services rise 3.88% YoY to $ 2.85 b - EDB Chief Mangala Wijesinghe expresses confidence in recording over $ 18 b export target by year-end Sri Lanka’s export sector posted its highest-ever monthly performance in September 2026, with total earnings surpassing $ 1.69 billion and reflecting a 17.23% year-on-year (YoY) growth driven by strong merchandise shipments, despite the challenges faced by the tensions in the Middle East and its direct impact on overall costs. The latest data released by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB) showed that merchandise exports shipped in September were up 21.66% YoY to over $ 1.38 billion, though estimated service earnings in the month showed a moderate growth of 0.67% YoY to $ 306.17 million. The September exports registered a 5.6% month-on-month (MoM) increase compared to August 2026. Cumulative exports during the first nine months of 2026 rose by 5.04% YoY to over $ 13.61 billion, also marking the highest recorded level for the period. Merchandise export earnings during January-September increased by 5.35% YoY to over $ 10.76 billion, whilst services exports during the same period were estimated to have surged by 3.88% to $ 2.85 billion. Services exports include sectors such as ICT/BPM, construction, financial services, and transport and logistics. Addressing the media, EDB Chairman and CEO Mangala Wijesinghe described the September outcome as a resilient way towards achieving the country’s annual merchandise export target of over $ 18 billion, whilst commending exporters for navigating external shocks and yet contributing to economic development. “This performance demonstrates the potential of Sri Lankan exporters to strengthen their presence in international markets despite an increasingly competitive global trading environment. As we move forward, our priority must be to sustain this growth momentum by strengthening the competitiveness of existing export sectors while accelerating the development of new products, services and markets,” he said. For 2026, Sri Lanka has set an ambitious export revenue target of $ 20 billion, reflecting an anticipated YoY growth of 10-12%. Merchandise exports are expected to exceed $ 15.7 billion in 2026, while services exports are projected to rise to $ 4.3 billion. The EDB noted that the merchandise exports growth in September was driven largely by improved demand across the agricultural and industrial product categories, while services lagged. Apparel and textile exports rose 3.46% YoY to $ 439.78 million in September 2026, from $ 425.07 million a year earlier. Exports to the US rose 6.33%. Rubber and rubber-based product exports surged 33.68% to $ 99.31 million, up from $ 74.29 million in September 2025. Industrial and surgical rubber glove exports grew 34.38% to $ 31.70 million, while pneumatic and retreaded tyres and tubes increased 39.57% to $ 54.95 million. Exports of spices, essential oils and oleoresins climbed 73.19% to $ 74.73 million. Pepper exports jumped 165.38% to $ 23.46 million, while cinnamon exports rose 68.27% to $ 42.59 million. Coconut fibre-based product exports recorded a 2.99% increase. Activated carbon exports grew 43.52% YoY to $ 25.26 million, reflecting stronger earnings from value-added coconut-based products. Food and beverage exports increased 27.92% to $ 63.77 million in September 2026, compared with $ 49.85 million a year earlier. Electrical and electronic component exports surged 88.35% YoY to $ 68.54 million, supported by a 114.62% increase in insulated wire and cable exports. Seafood exports rose 4.01% to $ 23.61 million, from $ 22.70 million in September 2025. Frozen fish exports increased 15.85% to $ 13.96 million, while shrimp exports surged 207.27% to $ 3.38 million. Meanwhile, transport and logistics services exports were estimated at $ 167.9 million, up 23.32% from $ 136.15 million in September 2025. Cumulative export earnings from key value-added sectors recorded YoY growth during January–September 2026. Rubber-based products rose 8.44%, coconut-based products 3.68%, processed food and beverages 20.9%, electrical and electronic components 61.05%, and spices and concentrates 30.53%. However, apparel and textile exports declined 5.68% YoY to $ 3,783.76 million. Apparel exports fell 5.36% to $ 3,513.37 million, while textile exports dropped 9.66% to $ 270.39 million. Exports to the US, European Union (EU) and the UK decreased by 3.83%, 5.54% and 10.41%, respectively, amid subdued demand in key markets. Tea export earnings fell 6.83% to $ 1,083.58 million. Tea packet exports declined 4.42%, while bulk tea earnings dropped 11.13%. Growth in tea bag exports of 53.39% and instant tea exports of 9.85% was insufficient to offset the overall contraction. Weaker demand in the Middle East further affected performance, with tea exports to the region falling 34.22%. Shipments to the United Arab Emirates, Iran and Iraq declined by 59.66%, 65.80% and 47.72%, respectively. The US, Sri Lanka’s largest export market, accounting for 20.3% of merchandise exports, recorded an 18.06% YoY increase in September 2026, with earnings reaching $ 281.84 million. Cumulative exports to the US rose marginally by 0.05% to $ 2,252.99 million during January–September 2026. India overtook the UK to become Sri Lanka’s second-largest export destination, with cumulative exports increasing 12.3% to $ 889.84 million during the first nine months of 2026. September exports to India surged 29.65% YoY to $ 113.22 million. In contrast, exports to the UK fell 3.17% to $ 71.71 million in September, while cumulative earnings declined 9.33% to $ 654.36 million. Exports to the EU, accounting for 20.12% of Sri Lanka’s merchandise exports, increased 1.92% YoY in September 2026. However, cumulative exports to the bloc declined marginally by 0.15% during January–September 2026, indicating broadly stable performance in the key market.

audit.headline: Fitch assigns ‘A-(EXP)(lka)’ rating to Asia Asset Finance’s proposed debentures
audit.summary: Fitch Ratings yesterday assigned Asia Asset Finance PLC’s (AAF) proposed Sri Lankan rupee-denominated subordinated listed debentures of up to Rs. 3 billion an expected National Long-Term Rating of ‘A-(EXP)(lka)’. AAF is rated ‘A+(lka)’ with a Stable Outlook. The debentures are likely to have a five-year maturity and will be listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE). AAF plans to use the proceeds to strengthen its Tier 2 capital base, the secondary layer of regulatory capital, and to support loan-book expansion. The final rating is subject to Fitch receiving final documentation that conforms to information already received. The proposed debentures are rated two notches below AAF’s National Long-Term Rating. Fitch said it applied its Bank Rating Criteria in rating the instrument, as it believes the prudential capital framework for Sri Lankan finance companies is closer to that for banks.
audit.body: Fitch Ratings yesterday assigned Asia Asset Finance PLC’s (AAF) proposed Sri Lankan rupee-denominated subordinated listed debentures of up to Rs. 3 billion an expected National Long-Term Rating of ‘A-(EXP)(lka)’. AAF is rated ‘A+(lka)’ with a Stable Outlook. The debentures are likely to have a five-year maturity and will be listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE). AAF plans to use the proceeds to strengthen its Tier 2 capital base, the secondary layer of regulatory capital, and to support loan-book expansion. The final rating is subject to Fitch receiving final documentation that conforms to information already received. The proposed debentures are rated two notches below AAF’s National Long-Term Rating. Fitch said it applied its Bank Rating Criteria in rating the instrument, as it believes the prudential capital framework for Sri Lankan finance companies is closer to that for banks. The expected rating reflects Fitch’s baseline notching for loss severity for this debt class and its expectation of poor recoveries in the event of default. Fitch applied no additional notching for non-performance risk, as the debentures do not contain going-concern loss-absorption features, meaning they cannot be written down or converted to equity while the company continues to operate. AAF’s own National Long-Term Rating reflects Fitch’s expectation that its majority shareholder, India-based Muthoot Finance Ltd (MFL), rated ‘BB+’ with a Stable Outlook, would provide extraordinary support to AAF if needed. Fitch based this view on MFL’s 78.4% shareholding, its record of ordinary equity support, and the strategic and operational alignment between parent and subsidiary in their core product, gold-backed loans.
