audit.headline: Mango Tree test of Arahat Mahinda
audit.summary: Before preaching Buddhism to King Devanampiya Tissa, Arahant Mahinda used a logical puzzle — often described as the world’s first recorded intelligence or wisdom test — based on a mango tree to check if the king had the intellectual capacity to understand the Dhamma - Modern daydream of an ancient envoy's return Age and a frail heart keep me confined to my home, yet an alert mind keeps me voraciously curious. Two private TV channels—both epitomising the vulgarity of free-market capitalism—keep me updated on the Sangha mischief in our public square. Pensive in my armchair, far removed from the calibrated, boorish ‘Bana’ at the Satyagraha sit-in at Viharamahadevi Park, my mind drifted into a desperate daydream. I closed my eyes and wondered: What if?
audit.body: Before preaching Buddhism to King Devanampiya Tissa, Arahant Mahinda used a logical puzzle — often described as the world’s first recorded intelligence or wisdom test — based on a mango tree to check if the king had the intellectual capacity to understand the Dhamma - Modern daydream of an ancient envoy's return Age and a frail heart keep me confined to my home, yet an alert mind keeps me voraciously curious. Two private TV channels—both epitomising the vulgarity of free-market capitalism—keep me updated on the Sangha mischief in our public square. Pensive in my armchair, far removed from the calibrated, boorish ‘Bana’ at the Satyagraha sit-in at Viharamahadevi Park, my mind drifted into a desperate daydream. I closed my eyes and wondered: What if? What if the time warp separating antiquity from today’s chaos were ripped open, and Arahat Mahinda Thero himself stepped out of the third century BC and onto the soil of twenty-first-century Sri Lanka? What if the legendary missionary son of Dharmasoka walked among us today, only to find that his pristine, liberating message of the Buddha had been weaponised, commodified, and reduced to pageantry and ritual, making the cry of ‹Sadhu’ an agitational refrains of hired hooligans? It was a mind-boggling possibility: the architect of Sinhala Buddhism surveying how a capricious, power-hungry priestly class had traded the profound logic of the Mihintale mango tree for luxury SUVs, political contracts, and televised circuses. In this mental theater, the ancient sage Arahat Mahinda had come to interrogate, wielding the sharp intellect that once founded a nation to utterly dismantle the pious fraud of its modern guardians. Arahat Mahinda Thero stood at the Satyagraha protest site. Under a canvas canopy, a group of saffron-clad figures sat in a single row, striking poses of deep, meditative exhaustion for a cluster of television cameras. This was the grand satyagraha, orchestrated at the behest of a defunct political dynasty whose members are currently adrift, desperate to reclaim their lost turf. Shrouded in simple, earth-toned robes, my imaginary Arahat Mahinda stepped straight out of the third century BC and into the chaotic theater of this modern political circus. He had no entourage, no media coordinator to assist him; he walked directly to the enclosure where the main architects of this spectacle sat. The test There sat Ulapane Sumangala, adjusting his microphone with practiced ease; Balangoda Kassapa, frantically checking his smartphone under the fold of his robe to see if his latest TikTok live-stream was trending; and Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna, the High Priest of Mihintale, looking noticeably uncomfortable so far from his mountain rock sanctuary and so close to actual public scrutiny. The trio blinked, squinting through the camera glare. There was something terrifyingly authentic, something fiercely primordial about the visitor that rendered their haughty air of entitlement suddenly very fragile. Hoping to capture a viral moment of monastic solidarity, Ulapane Sumangala cleared his throat, assumed a pose of pious pain, and bellowed into the microphone: “Welcome, Most Venerable Arahath Therun-wahanse, to our sacred struggle!” The transient political circuses built by greed are nothing more than passing shadows on the ever-changing landscape of time. They do not define our beautiful island, nor can they ever truly compromise the pristine core of the Dhamma. For twenty-three centuries, the true light brought by Arahat Mahinda has endured—not through golden fences, luxurious pageants, or the patronage of powerful politicians, but because the pristine Dhamma resides quietly and immovably within the hearts of ordinary, virtuous people Sumangala proclaimed, his voice booming through the speakers: “We sit here in noble sacrifice to save our nation, our heritage, and our Sasana from the treacherous hands of those who demand accountability and transparency!” The imaginary Arahat Mahinda looked at the elaborate sound system, the stock of bottled mineral water tucked behind the cushions on which the ‹Satyagrahis› sat, and the fleet of SUVs parked on the roadside behind the marquee. A faint, razor-sharp smile touched his lips. He did not recite a stanza, nor did he offer a conventional blessing. Instead, he pointed a calm, steady finger toward a large, leafy tree standing nearby.” “Monks,” Arahat Mahinda said, his voice carrying a thunderous, resonant clarity that dwarfed the loudspeakers. “What tree is that?” he intoned. Monk Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna, recognising the opening lines of the famous logic test that his own monastic perch had on our free-market economy, perked up. He saw an immediate opportunity to demonstrate his scriptural authority. “That, Most Venerable One, is a mango tree.” “Are there other mango trees besides this one?” Arahat Mahinda inquired, his demeanor glistening with sharp, deductive intensity. Age and a frail heart keep me confined to my home, yet an alert mind keeps me voraciously curious. “Yes, Most Venerable Arahath Therun-wahanse,” Balangoda Kassapa chimed in, eager to display his intellect to his digital followers. “There are many other mango trees in this park, and indeed, across the entire island.” “And are there trees here that are not mango trees?” asked Arahat, his voice tightening like a bowstring. “Of course, of course!” Ulapane Sumangala joined the fray, sensing a rhetorical victory. “There are Mara trees, Na trees, and many majestic banyans. There are countless trees that are not mango trees.” Arahat Mahinda paused. A sudden, dramatic silence overwhelmed the entire park. The wind ceased to blow. The birds stopped chirping. Then he leaned forward, his gaze flashing like lightning: “Apart from those other mango trees, and the trees that are not mango trees, does this specific mango tree itself remain?›” “Naturally, Venerable Sir!” Monk Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna answered confidently. “If you set aside all other mango trees and all non-mango trees, this solitary tree still stands right where it is. It is elementary!” responded the Mihintale custodian. Arahat Mahinda’s face hardened, shifting from calm inquisitor to Cosmic Arbiter. “An excellent grasp of basic botany. Now, let us apply this same rigorous line of reasoning to the political forest you have planted here today. Tell me, Sumangala, who are the people currently funding, supplying, and cheering for this noble satyagraha of yours?” Sumangala puffed out his chest, adopting a fiercely theatrical posture. “These are the righteous guardians of the old order, Sir! The visionary leaders who built great expressways, the generous patrons who gave us unchecked power, and the elite statesmen currently unjustly sidelined by the ungrateful masses!” “I see,” Arahat Mahinda, the Ashokan envoy, replied smoothly, his tone dripping with sarcasm. “And are there other corrupt, discredited politicians in this country besides the ones who paid for your tents, your cheer squads, and your ears today?” Kassapa shifted uneasily, his phone buzzing violently in his palm as the live comments started flying in. “Well... yes. History is full of them. There are many political opportunists across the land who have plundered the public purse.” “And are there people in this country who are not corrupt, discredited politicians?” Arahat pressed further, his voice rising to a crescendo. Portly Monk Walanhanduwe Dharmaratna coughed into his hand, looking nervously at the cameras that were now capturing his sudden panic. “Yes, technically. The vast majority of the citizenry are ordinary, hardworking people who simply wish to live in peace, feed their children, and see justice prevail.” The imaginary Arahat Mahinda of my daydream stepped onto the stage, his presence making the Satyagraha space feel suffocatingly small. ‘Then tell me, wise monks,’ Arahat Mahinda roared, his authoritative voice shaking the very poles of the makeshift tent. ‘If we set aside all those other corrupt politicians roaming elsewhere, and if we set aside the entire population of honest, hardworking citizens who want nothing to do with your theater... who is left sitting under this tent?!’” “An absolute, terrifying silence stilled the air. Television cameras zoomed in on the sweat breaking out on Sumangala’s brow. Arahat Mahinda’s deductive trap had snapped shut with the force of a steel jaw. By their own logic, the only entities remaining in the equation were the handful of compromised oligarchs pulling their strings, and the monks who consented to act as their spiritual human shields. ‘You see,’ Arahat Mahinda continued, his voice dropping to a devastatingly sharp whisper that cut deeper than a blade, “Twenty-three centuries ago, I used this very riddle to ensure that a king possessed the logical capacity to govern for the welfare of all living beings. I taught him that the land belongs to the people, and that the ruler is merely its temporary guardian. But you three have completely inverted Dhamma! You have become the vanguard of brazen rogues, using the sacred robes of the Enlightened One to protect the hordes of the greedy!›” “Venerable Sir!” Walanhanduwe protested, his face turning an angry shade of crimson as he clutched his relic casket for comfort. “We are protecting our traditional privileges! If the elite fall, who will sponsor our grand pageants? Who will build our golden fences? Who will pay for our luxury hybrid SUVs?!” “The Dhamma does not require a golden fence built with stolen public funds!” the resonant voice of the Arahat replied, firm as the Mihintale rock. “A true sanctuary is built on virtue, not on the patronage of a discredited court. Look at yourselves! You call this a satyagraha firm adherence to truth. Yet your truth is bought by the plateful, your fasting is a comedic illusion staged between television commercial breaks, and your devotion is a transactional lease signed with politicians currently adrift in the turbulent currents of their own bad karma!” Balangoda Kassapa quietly slipped his phone into his bag, suddenly very aware of how utterly ridiculous his live-stream looked to a nation laughing hysterically in the comments section. Ulapane Sumangala tried to rally his thoughts to launch a fierce counteroffensive about external conspiracies and threats to their heritage, but the words withered in his throat, completely vaporised under the cool, blinding light of the Arahat’s gaze. “The mango tree in Mihintale still bears fruit because its roots were planted in honest soil,” Arahat Mahinda said, turning his back on the stage with a dramatic sweep of his robes. “But this plastic garden of corruption you have built in the park will wither before the sun sets. Go back to your temples! Wash the political soot from your robes! And remember that the people of this island are no longer the naive subjects of a bygone era, they have passed the intelligence test, even if their supposed teachers have failed it miserably!” With that final, earth-shattering declaration, the imaginary Arahat stepped away from the soiled site of the fraudulent protest. Light that endures Vivid figures of my daydream faded back. I returned to the dull stillness of my quiet room. The heavy sorrow that had weighed so deeply on my eighty-four-year-old heart began to lift, replaced by a gentle, enduring conviction. The transient political circuses built by greed are nothing more than passing shadows on the ever-changing landscape of time. They do not define our beautiful island, nor can they ever truly compromise the pristine core of the Dhamma. For twenty-three centuries, the true light brought by Arahat Mahinda has endured—not through golden fences, luxurious pageants, or the patronage of powerful politicians, but because the pristine Dhamma resides quietly and immovably within the hearts of ordinary, virtuous people. As long as there are those who remember the simple, compassionate logic of that ancient mango tree—who seek truth, practice kindness, and guard their minds against hatred—the light of the Buddha remains undiminished. Governments rise and fall. Interim illusions invariably crumble into dust. The timeless path of virtue stands unshakeable, offering its eternal sanctuary of peace and ultimate hope to a waiting nation. As the Blessed One declared in the Dhammapada: ‘Selo yathā ekaghano vātena na samīrati, Evaṃ paṇḍitā nindāpasaṃsāsu na samiñjanti.’ “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so, the wise remain unmoved by praise or blame.”

audit.headline: Mark Surgenor wins historic BCC International President’s Award 2026
audit.summary: Council for Business with Britain in Sri Lanka President Mark Surgenor In a groundbreaking achievement on the global business stage, Mark Surgenor, President of the Council for Business with Britain (CBB) in Sri Lanka (2023–2025), has been named the winner of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) International President’s Award 2026. Out of a competitive international network of more than 75 British Chambers of Commerce and Business Councils worldwide, this recognition marks a monumental milestone as the first time ever that Sri Lanka has received this prestigious award. The annual Chamber Awards celebrate the individuals and organisations that strengthen the global Chamber Network and drive international commerce. Mark...
audit.body: Council for Business with Britain in Sri Lanka President Mark Surgenor In a groundbreaking achievement on the global business stage, Mark Surgenor, President of the Council for Business with Britain (CBB) in Sri Lanka (2023–2025), has been named the winner of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) International President’s Award 2026. Out of a competitive international network of more than 75 British Chambers of Commerce and Business Councils worldwide, this recognition marks a monumental milestone as the first time ever that Sri Lanka has received this prestigious award. The annual Chamber Awards celebrate the individuals and organisations that strengthen the global Chamber Network and drive international commerce. Mark... Surgenor was specifically honored for modernising the CBB during his two-year presidency (2023–2025), successfully transforming it from a traditional networking group into a high-value platform for commercial insight, trade access, and strategic connections. His tenure included hosting high-impact forums, engaging with over 200 member organisations, and founding CBB NextGen - a structured platform empowering the next generation of business leaders and entrepreneurs. Surgenor is CEO of HSBC Sri Lanka and Maldives. Additionally, he significantly strengthened bilateral partnerships with the British High Commission, the UK Department for Business and Trade, the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, and peer councils. Commenting on the award, Surgenor said: «I›m honoured to receive the President›s Award and hugely grateful to everyone across the Council who has contributed to what we›ve achieved. Together we›ve worked to strengthen UK-Sri Lanka business links, bringing the next generation into our work and ensuring the Council offers real value to its members.» British Chambers of Commerce President Andy Haldane, CBE added: «Mark›s leadership shows the difference one individual can make to an entire business community. He has modernised the Council and created stronger practical connections between firms in the UK and Sri Lanka. This award is thoroughly deserved recognition of his energy, integrity and lasting contribution to the global Chamber Network.» Award supporter Quest CEO Des Shaw said: «Mark has combined strategic vision with practical delivery, creating lasting value for members and ensuring the Council is well placed for the future. We warmly congratulate him on his achievements.» To read the official announcement from the British Chambers of Commerce, visit: British Chambers of Commerce News

audit.headline: Mercy, robes and the rule of law in Sri Lanka
audit.summary: Ven. Gnanasara Thero, Father Mathew Peiris, Ven. Somarama Thero Presidential pardons and the disrobing of imprisoned Buddhist monks may appear to belong to distinct legal domains. Yet both bring into focus a fundamental question of constitutional governance: how should public power be exercised when it intersects with criminal accountability, religious authority and public trust? Two controversies, one constitutional question The relationship between religion and the State in Sri Lanka is frequently examined through the constitutional recognition accorded to Buddhism under Article 9 and the general guarantee of religious freedom under Article 14. These provisions raise enduring questions about the relationship between the State’s special constitutional obligations towards Buddhism and the protection of religious freedom.
audit.body: Ven. Gnanasara Thero, Father Mathew Peiris, Ven. Somarama Thero Presidential pardons and the disrobing of imprisoned Buddhist monks may appear to belong to distinct legal domains. Yet both bring into focus a fundamental question of constitutional governance: how should public power be exercised when it intersects with criminal accountability, religious authority and public trust? Two controversies, one constitutional question The relationship between religion and the State in Sri Lanka is frequently examined through the constitutional recognition accorded to Buddhism under Article 9 and the general guarantee of religious freedom under Article 14. These provisions raise enduring questions about the relationship between the State’s special constitutional obligations towards Buddhism and the protection of religious freedom. These questions have recently assumed renewed public significance, with a large gathering reported around Viharamahadevi Park in protest against State decisions concerning Buddhism. Against this backdrop, two developments invite closer constitutional scrutiny: the Supreme Court’s decision invalidating former President Maithripala Sirisena’s 2019 pardon of Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thero, and the introduction of new prison regulations governing the removal of the robes of imprisoned Buddhist monks. Although the two controversies concern different exercises of State authority, they converge on a common constitutional question: what limits should govern the exercise of public power when it intersects with criminal accountability, religious status and the rule of law? The two developments are legally distinct. Article 34 of the Constitution confers a power of presidential clemency, whereas the removal of monastic robes engages prison administration and the rules governing religious discipline. Nevertheless, both reveal the importance of distinguishing the existence of a power from the legitimacy of its exercise. A constitutional power may be broad without being arbitrary. Equally, respect for religious self-governance does not require the State to surrender its responsibility to administer criminal justice. The central challenge is to determine how these forms of authority can coexist without undermining the rule of law. The significance of these controversies becomes clearer when considered against the historical development of the pardon power, the political role of Buddhist clergy in Sri Lanka, and the symbolic and institutional significance of the monastic robe. The prerogative of mercy: historical origins and constitutional tensions The power to pardon has historically served as an exceptional mechanism for tempering the rigidity of criminal law in the interests of justice, equity and public welfare. It may provide a remedy for miscarriages of justice, mitigate disproportionate sentences, recognise rehabilitation, or respond to compelling humanitarian circumstances. Although wrongful convictions are ordinarily addressed through appellate remedies, clemency retains significance where judicial remedies are inadequate and in capital cases, where mitigating circumstances may warrant the commutation of a death sentence or longer prison sentences. Nevertheless, its exceptional nature demands that the power be exercised consistently with the rule of law. In England, the royal prerogative of mercy became concentrated in the Crown and was subsequently inherited, in modified constitutional forms, by several jurisdictions influenced by English common law. The historical association between clemency and sovereign authority explains its unusual constitutional character. Whereas courts determine criminal liability and impose sentences according to law, the power of mercy permits the executive to intervene after conviction. This intervention may serve legitimate humanitarian purposes, but it also creates the possibility of political favouritism and arbitrary interference with the administration of justice. The United States Constitution provides a useful comparison. Article II, Section 2 empowers the President to grant reprieves and pardons for federal offences, except in cases of impeachment. Although clemency may correct injustice or mitigate excessive punishment, its exercise has raised concerns about impartiality and accountability, particularly where beneficiaries have personal or political connections to the President, as illustrated by President Joe Biden’s controversial pardon of his son, Hunter Biden, in December 2024. However, American history also reveals a striking counterpoint: in United States v. Wilson (1833), George Wilson refused to accept a pardon granted by President Andrew Jackson for mail robbery. The case established that a pardon must be accepted to take effect, illustrating that even the extraordinary power of presidential mercy cannot necessarily be imposed upon its intended beneficiary. These examples expose an enduring dilemma. The pardon power may operate as an instrument of compassion, reconciliation and correction, but its exceptional breadth can also make it vulnerable to political manipulation. The appropriate response is not necessarily to abolish executive discretion. It is to identify the constitutional and institutional safeguards that distinguish legitimate mercy from arbitrary favour. Presidential clemency under Article 34: discretion as a constitutional trust Article 34(1) of the Sri Lankan 1978 Constitution authorises the President, in the case of an offender convicted of an offence by a court within Sri Lanka, to grant a free or conditional pardon, grant a respite, substitute a less severe punishment, or remit all or part of a punishment or penalty. The provision confers substantial discretion. However, the breadth of the language does not resolve the question of how that discretion should be exercised. In a constitutional democracy, the powers of public institutions derive their legitimacy from the Constitution and must be exercised consistently with its governing principles. The distinction between a constitutional power and a personal prerogative is therefore fundamental. A pardon is not a private act of generosity by the officeholder. It is an exercise of public authority capable of affecting the administration of justice, the interests of victims and the public’s confidence in the legal system. The constitutional position also requires a distinction between a pardon and the judicial determination of guilt. Clemency may relieve an offender from the execution of a sentence to the extent authorised by the pardon, but it does not empower the President to set aside the judicial determination itself. Otherwise, the executive would effectively assume a judicial function and disturb the constitutional allocation of powers. Although a pardon may lawfully affect the punishment imposed, an unexplained or arbitrary exercise of clemency in such circumstances may raise serious concerns about judicial independence and the authority of the courts. The question is therefore not simply whether the President possesses the power to pardon. It is whether the particular decision represents a lawful exercise of that power. Padron for Gnanasara Thero: judicial review and executive accountability These issues came into sharp focus in Centre for Policy Alternatives and Dr. Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu v. Maithripala Sirisena and Others, SCFR 256/2019, considered together with Sandhya Ekneligoda v. Attorney General and Others, SCFR 257/2019. In its judgment of 10 September 2026, the Supreme Court invalidated the pardon granted to Ven. Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thero in May 2019. Gnanasara Thero had been convicted by the Court of Appeal in 2016 on counts of contempt of court arising from his conduct at the Homagama Magistrate’s Court. The convictions concerned conduct that interfered with the authority and proceedings of the court. President Sirisena subsequently granted him a full pardon under Article 34(1). The petitioners challenged the pardon on constitutional grounds, arguing that it undermined the rule of law, judicial independence and the separation of powers and violated the guarantee of equality under Article 12(1). The Supreme Court’s decision is significant for reasons extending beyond the identity of the beneficiary. It affirmed that the exercise of presidential clemency is capable of judicial scrutiny under the fundamental rights jurisdiction of the Court. The constitutional discretion conferred by Article 34 does not place a presidential decision beyond review where the applicable constitutional requirements for such review are satisfied. A particularly important aspect of the judgment concerned the absence of a contemporaneous record adequately explaining the decision. The Court also examined the circumstances in which the pardon was processed, the treatment of requests both supporting and opposing clemency, and the apparent reliance on a recommendation prepared by the Additional Secretary (Legal), without a documented independent assessment by the President of the relevant considerations. The Court concluded that the decision was arbitrary and invalid. It declared the pardon, as recorded in the presidential minute dated 21 May 2019, null and void and of no force or avail in law. At the same time, it clarified that the decision did not permanently prevent a future pardon, provided that any subsequent decision was made lawfully and after proper consideration of the relevant material. The judgment thus drew a distinction between the existence of the pardon power and the legality of its exercise. The President retained the constitutional authority to grant mercy, but that authority could not be exercised in disregard of the constitutional framework. Presidential immunity and the possibility of judicial review and accountability in the exercise of clemency Presidential immunity under Article 35 of the Constitution is a qualified protection against personal civil and criminal proceedings, rather than an absolute exemption from constitutional accountability. It rests on the need to protect the functioning of the highest executive office, premised on the expectation that presidential powers will be exercised in the interests of the State and its people, and not to their detriment. The question of prison attire in previous cases does not appear to have provoked the same controversy as it has in the case of Ven. Gnanasara Thero. Neither Father Mathew Peiris’s case nor that of Ven. Somarama Thero appears to have raised any contestation over the clothing worn following conviction. The approach appeared to have upheld equality among prisoners and at the same time never intended to diminish their religious faith or prevent personal religious observance. Indeed, Peiris was reportedly seen wearing a cross bearing a figure of the crucified Christ even within prison premises The proviso to Article 35(1) preserves the right to institute fundamental rights proceedings under Article 126 against the Attorney-General in respect of acts or omissions of the President in the exercise of official functions. Significantly, the Nineteenth Amendment strengthened this safeguard by permitting such proceedings even while the President remains in office. Accordingly, proceedings challenging the legality of a former President’s official acts reinforce the principle that the exercise of executive power remains subject to constitutional scrutiny and that the rule of law does not cease to operate at the highest levels of government. The possibility of judicial scrutiny, in turn, raises the question of how the exercise of presidential clemency can be meaningfully assessed. Recording reasons for a pardon can help establish whether the decision was based on relevant considerations and exercised for a proper purpose, rather than for arbitrary or improper reasons. Such considerations may include the gravity and circumstances of the offence, the sentence imposed, the offender’s conduct and rehabilitation, the interests of victims, and the wider public interest. Their relative significance will depend on the circumstances of each case. The objective is not to replace presidential discretion with a rigid checklist, but to ensure that the exercise of this exceptional power remains reasoned, defensible and consistent with the rule of law. The monastic robe: religious status, prison administration and institutional competence The second controversy concerns a different form of authority. On 24 October 2026, an Extraordinary Gazette notification amended the Department of Prisons’ Standing Orders to establish procedures governing the removal of robes worn by Buddhist monks when they are imprisoned. Under the newly inserted Standing Order 356A, the Commissioner of Prisons is required to consult the Department of Buddhist Affairs concerning the removal of a monk’s robes. The Department must inform the relevant Nikaya or chapter and communicate its position on the proposed action within ten days. The amendments also address the clothing that a monk may wear when taken outside prison, including circumstances in which the relevant Nikaya or chapter has not permitted the wearing of robes. The significance of these provisions lies in the institutional distinction they recognise. Imprisonment is a matter for the State’s criminal justice and prison administration systems. The question of whether a monk should be disrobed, however, may also concern the disciplinary authority of the Buddhist monastic order to which the monk belongs. The robe is not merely an item of clothing. It signifies membership of the Sangha, a symbol of religious vocation and an institutional identity governed by religious traditions and disciplinary rules. Its removal can therefore have implications beyond the practical administration of imprisonment. The new procedures establish a formal channel between prison authorities, the Department of Buddhist Affairs and the relevant monastic institution. They recognise the relevance of ecclesiastical authority without displacing the State’s responsibility to enforce lawful sentences and maintain prison administration. This does not mean that the robe provides immunity from criminal law. A monk remains subject to investigation, prosecution, conviction and imprisonment in accordance with the law. Nor does imprisonment automatically establish that the monk has been formally disrobed. These are distinct questions requiring attention to their respective legal and institutional frameworks. The underlying issue is one of institutional competence: which authority is entitled to make which decision, and within what limits? The State must not surrender its responsibility for criminal justice, but it should also distinguish the administration of a prison sentence from the determination of religious status where the governing rules allocate a role to the relevant religious institution. Nevertheless, the involvement of religious authorities should not be confused with an exemption from criminal law. A monk remains subject to the law of the State. The robe cannot confer immunity from arrest, prosecution, conviction or imprisonment. The amendment is therefore best understood as an attempt to regulate the point of intersection between State authority and monastic discipline, rather than as a transfer of criminal jurisdiction to religious authorities. These principles extends to the clergy of other faiths, with appropriate regard for their respective religious traditions and institutional practices. Somarama Thero: the robe and criminal accountability The relationship between Buddhist monastic identity and political power has a long history in Sri Lanka. The assassination of Prime Minister S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike in 1959 provides a particularly revealing example. The political mobilisation associated with Bandaranaike’s rise to power was popularly described through the phrase “Sanga, Veda and Guru” - the Buddhist clergy, medical practitioners and teachers. The phrase captured the political significance of these groups in the social and electoral transformation of the 1950s. The irony of the assassination was that Ven. Somarama Thero, a Buddhist monk who was also an Ayurvedic practitioner and associated with teaching at an Ayurvedic institution, became the central figure in the criminal proceedings arising from Bandaranaike’s death. The religious and professional identities that carried social and political authority did not place him beyond criminal accountability. The historical record also contains an episode directly related to the symbolism of religious attire - the question of robes. During his trial, Somarama stopped wearing his yellow robes when appearing in court. Justice T.S. Fernando reportedly observed that Somarama had “a streak of conscience” because he did not attend court in his saffron robes. The episode should not be mistaken for a legal determination that Ven. Somarama had been formally disrobed by his monastic institution. The robe may communicate a symbol of religious vocation and social authority, but it cannot determine criminal liability. Nor should the wearing or removal of robes become a substitute for examining the conduct of the individual concerned. The distinction matters: personal conduct, institutional discipline and State-imposed punishment are separate matters, even when they intersect. The historical example illustrates the political significance of religious identity and the limits of the authority it confers. A comparative perspective: religious office and the limits of State authority The distinction between criminal punishment and religious status extends beyond Buddhist monastic life. The case of Anglican priest Father Mathew Peiris offers a useful, albeit institutionally distinct, comparison. Following his conviction for the murders of his wife, Eunice Peiris, and Russel Ingram, Peiris spent approximately twelve years in prison before his release in October 1997 under a general amnesty. He was reportedly permitted to wear clerical attire during his initial court proceedings and remand custody but wore ordinary prison clothing following his conviction. Upon release, he was again seen in clerical attire and continued to be addressed as “Father”. Contemporary reporting, however, indicated that he no longer held his Bishop’s licence and could participate in church activities only in the capacity permitted to lay members. His case illustrates the distinction between religious identity, ordination and institutional authorisation to exercise the functions of a religious office, particularly when a person is outside prison. While the State determined his punishment through its criminal jurisdiction, it also implies his attire during imprisonment in accordance with the principle of equality before the law. Contrasting fates Significantly, the question of prison attire in previous cases does not appear to have provoked the same controversy as it has in the case of Ven. Gnanasara Thero. Neither Father Mathew Peiris’s case nor that of Ven. Somarama Thero appears to have raised any contestation over the clothing worn following conviction. The approach appeared to have upheld equality among prisoners and at the same time never intended to diminish their religious faith or prevent personal religious observance. Indeed, Peiris was reportedly seen wearing a cross bearing a figure of the crucified Christ even within prison premises. Also, it was Father Peiris who baptised Somarama Thero in Welikada Prison, giving him the name “Peter” just two days before he was hanged for the assassination of Prime Minister S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike. Father Peiris, by contrast, left Welikada Prison following his release under a general amnesty in October 1997. (The author is an Attorney-at-Law, and Senior Lecturer in Law, Asia Pacific Institute of Information Technology (APIIT), Sri Lanka)

audit.headline: OPA presents collective professional proposals for Budget 2027
audit.summary: The Organisation of Professional Associations of Sri Lanka (OPA), under the leadership of OPA President Jayantha Gallehewa, presented its proposals and recommendations for the Budget 2027 to Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma at a meeting held on 6 October, 2026. The proposals represent the collective voice and professional expertise of the OPA’s 52 member associations, bringing together knowledge and perspectives from across Sri Lanka’s professional community. The initiative was undertaken through the National Issues Committee (NIC), chaired by OPA Vice President and NIC Chairman Bhanu Wijayaratne, with the active contribution of its members.
audit.body: The Organisation of Professional Associations of Sri Lanka (OPA), under the leadership of OPA President Jayantha Gallehewa, presented its proposals and recommendations for the Budget 2027 to Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma at a meeting held on 6 October, 2026. The proposals represent the collective voice and professional expertise of the OPA’s 52 member associations, bringing together knowledge and perspectives from across Sri Lanka’s professional community. The initiative was undertaken through the National Issues Committee (NIC), chaired by OPA Vice President and NIC Chairman Bhanu Wijayaratne, with the active contribution of its members. The proposals were developed through consultations with the OPA’s member associations and focused on key areas of national importance, with the objective of providing constructive and evidence-informed recommendations to the national Budget process. Among the key areas addressed were fair taxation, export financing, elder care and social protection, research and innovation, the circular economy, the built environment and heritage, and measures to address the country’s professional brain drain. The proposals also reflected wider professional perspectives on strengthening economic resilience, improving productivity, encouraging investment and supporting sustainable national development. The OPA delegation was led by OPA President Jayantha Gallehewa and included General Secretary Eng. Ravi Rupasinghe, Vice President and NIC Chairman Bhanu Wijayaratne, NIC Member B.A.H.S. Preena, OPA Assistant Secretary Indika Ranaweera, Vice President and Career Guidance and Skills Development Committee Chairman V. Rameshkumar, NIC Member and Career Guidance and Skills Development Committee Convener Udesh I.W. Seneviratna and OPA Editor Priyantha Wickramarathna. Speaking on the occasion, Gallehewa emphasised the organisation’s commitment to placing the knowledge, experience and collective expertise of Sri Lanka’s professional community at the service of the nation. He noted that the OPA’s role extends beyond representing individual professions and includes contributing constructively to national policy and decision-making. The presentation of the Budget proposals marks another important step in the OPA’s continuing engagement with the Government. Through the NIC and its 52 member associations, the OPA continues to provide a platform for translating professional knowledge and experience into practical recommendations on matters of national importance. The OPA expressed its appreciation to the Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry for providing the opportunity to present its proposals and reaffirmed its readiness to continue contributing professional expertise to the national development and Budget process.

audit.headline: PDMO rejects all Domestic Dollar Bond bids; market says bid rates too high
audit.summary: - Turns down every bid at 23 Oct. auction for $ 100 m issue, which had option to raise up to $ 300 m - Notice cites only issuer’s right to accept or reject any application; no other details given The Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) has rejected all bids received at its Domestic Dollar Bond auction held on 23 October, with market sources indicating that demand was encouraging, but the rates bid were too high. The issue was for $ 100 million, with the option of raising up to $ 300 million. “Pursuant to Section 6 of the Offer Document, which reserves the Issuer’s right to accept or reject any application, in whole or in part, the Issuer has decided not to accept any bids received under this auction,” the PDMO said in its notice, giving no further details.
audit.body: - Turns down every bid at 23 Oct. auction for $ 100 m issue, which had option to raise up to $ 300 m - Notice cites only issuer’s right to accept or reject any application; no other details given The Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) has rejected all bids received at its Domestic Dollar Bond auction held on 23 October, with market sources indicating that demand was encouraging, but the rates bid were too high. The issue was for $ 100 million, with the option of raising up to $ 300 million. “Pursuant to Section 6 of the Offer Document, which reserves the Issuer’s right to accept or reject any application, in whole or in part, the Issuer has decided not to accept any bids received under this auction,” the PDMO said in its notice, giving no further details. The fixed rate of interest payable on the bonds, which are US dollar-denominated debt securities issued in the domestic market, was to be determined through competitive bidding. Market sources said the PDMO probably believed the bids did not factor in Fitch Ratings’ recent upgrade of Sri Lanka. In September, Fitch upgraded Sri Lanka’s Long-Term Issuer Default Rating to ‘B-’ from ‘CCC+’, with a Stable outlook. A higher rating typically lowers the risk premium investors demand over benchmark US Treasury yields, which together determine dollar bond pricing. Given the availability of funds and current global uncertainties, the PDMO may be willing to wait before returning to the market, the sources said. Accepting costlier bids could also have set a higher benchmark for future foreign currency borrowing. This was the second Domestic Dollar Bond issue since the debt crisis. In the first, in December 2025, the PDMO raised $ 50 million under a fixed-rate arrangement, recording firm demand for one- and two-year maturities. The one-year tranche drew $ 45.5 million in bids, of which $ 33 million was accepted at a weighted average fixed rate of 5.7%. The two-year tenor received $ 42.5 million in bids, with $ 17 million accepted at a weighted average rate of 6.1%. Only $ 1 million was bid for the three-year maturity, and no bids were accepted.

audit.headline: Resus Energy becomes first Sri Lankan corporate to list Green Bonds on Luxembourg Stock Exchange
audit.summary: The Damana solar power project Resus Energy PLC has announced the dual listing of its Rs. 1 billion Green Bond on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange (LuxSE) and its display on the Luxembourg Green Exchange (LGX), effective 19 October 2026. With this milestone, Resus Energy becomes the first non-financial corporate issuer from Sri Lanka to be featured on LGX, the sustainable finance platform operated by LuxSE. The dual listing follows the issuance and listing of the Bond on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in July 2025 and marks Sri Lanka’s first-ever Green Bond issuance by a non-banking and finance company and the first by a local energy company, with NDB Investment Bank Limited acting as the Financial Advisor and Manager to the transaction. The listing is a significant step for the company and for Sri Lanka’s growing sustainable finance market.
audit.body: The Damana solar power project Resus Energy PLC has announced the dual listing of its Rs. 1 billion Green Bond on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange (LuxSE) and its display on the Luxembourg Green Exchange (LGX), effective 19 October 2026. With this milestone, Resus Energy becomes the first non-financial corporate issuer from Sri Lanka to be featured on LGX, the sustainable finance platform operated by LuxSE. The dual listing follows the issuance and listing of the Bond on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in July 2025 and marks Sri Lanka’s first-ever Green Bond issuance by a non-banking and finance company and the first by a local energy company, with NDB Investment Bank Limited acting as the Financial Advisor and Manager to the transaction. The listing is a significant step for the company and for Sri Lanka’s growing sustainable finance market. Launched by the Luxembourg Stock Exchange in 2016, LGX was the world’s first platform dedicated exclusively to green, social and sustainable securities. Being displayed on LGX increases the international visibility of Resus Energy PLC’s Green Bond among ESG-focused investors and demonstrates how a Sri Lankan renewable energy company can meet international expectations for green finance disclosure. Sri Lanka’s presence on LGX has grown steadily, led primarily by financial institutions. Resus Energy PLC’s listing marks the entry of a company directly involved in developing and operating renewable energy assets into this group, providing international investors with an opportunity to support capital investment in clean power generation. “Bringing our Green Bond to the Luxembourg Stock Exchange and the Luxembourg Green Exchange is a proud milestone for Resus Energy PLC and for Sri Lanka. It confirms that a Sri Lankan renewable energy company can meet the highest international standards of sustainable finance. It also connects the projects powering our national grid with investors around the world who want their capital to make a measurable climate impact,” saidManaging Director Kishan Nanayakkara. Managing Director Kishan Nanayakkara The listing comes as Sri Lanka works toward ambitious national targets. Under its updated Nationally Determined Contributions, the country has committed to generating 70% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030 and to making electricity generation carbon neutral by 2050. The Green Bond issue comprised up to 10 Million Listed, Rated, Unsecured, Senior Redeemable Green Bonds of Rs. 100 each, in two tenors: Type A, four years at a fixed annual coupon of 11.55%; and Type B, five years at a fixed annual coupon of 11.75% Fitch Ratings Lanka Limited rated the bond A-(lka). The bond was structured in line with international sustainability standards, and all of its proceeds are committed to developing renewable energy projects. More than 55% of the proceeds are allocated to developing 8 MW of new solar capacity, expected to deliver approximately 15 GWh of clean electricity annually to the national grid and avoid approximately 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions.

audit.headline: Sajith discusses proposed anti-terrorism, organised crime laws with diplomatic corps
audit.summary: Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa has met representatives of diplomatic missions and international organisations in Colombo to discuss concerns over proposed legislation targeting terrorism and organised crime. According to a statement issued by the Opposition Leader's office on 25 October, the discussions focused on the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, with particular attention to their potential impact on fundamental rights, judicial independence and constitutional protections. Former parliamentarian M.A. Sumanthiran, along with serving and former lawmakers, also expressed concerns about the proposed laws during the meeting.
audit.body: Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa has met representatives of diplomatic missions and international organisations in Colombo to discuss concerns over proposed legislation targeting terrorism and organised crime. According to a statement issued by the Opposition Leader's office on 25 October, the discussions focused on the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, with particular attention to their potential impact on fundamental rights, judicial independence and constitutional protections. Former parliamentarian M.A. Sumanthiran, along with serving and former lawmakers, also expressed concerns about the proposed laws during the meeting. Premadasa said legislation to combat terrorism and organised crime was necessary, but stressed that such measures must be accompanied by effective judicial oversight and safeguards to prevent the misuse of executive powers. The discussions also addressed objections raised by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka (HRCSL), which warned in a statement issued on 21 October that the proposed Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill was “wholly incompatible” with the fundamental rights provisions of the Constitution and the country’s international human rights obligations. The Commission cautioned that the proposed law could be more draconian than the Prevention of Terrorism Act of 1979 and called for its withdrawal and substantial revision. Key areas of concern included; provisions permitting confessions to senior Police officers, detention authorised by the executive, broad definitions of serious offences and limitations on judicial discretion in decisions concerning remand and bail. The HRCSL has separately called for revisions to the proposed terrorism legislation, urging the authorities to adopt a narrower definition of terrorism, ensure judicial supervision of detention orders, guarantee access to legal representation and strengthen safeguards governing bail. The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) has also called for the withdrawal of the proposed organised crime legislation and the withdrawal or amendment of the terrorism Bill in its current form. Premadasa urged the Government to make the recommendations of expert committees’ public and conduct broader consultations with the HRCSL, the BASL and other relevant stakeholders before proceeding with the legislation. He said constitutional safeguards were important not only for politicians and activists, but also for ordinary citizens who might come into contact with the criminal justice system.

audit.headline: Sumathi Holdings celebrates 70 years of success
audit.summary: - From a single betting shop on Maliban Street in 1956 to 11 principal businesses and over 2,000 people Sumathi Holdings marked its 70th anniversary on 9 October, with a celebration at the Sangam Ballroom of ITC Ratnadipa, Colombo, attended by over 500 guests from Sri Lanka’s business, government, financial and media communities. Held under the theme “70 Years of Sumathi Legacy”, the evening looked back to 1956, when founder Mr. U.W. Sumathipala opened Sporting Star’s first betting shop on Maliban Street, Pettah – the business from which the Group grew. The evening opened with a drone show and fireworks over Galle Face.
audit.body: - From a single betting shop on Maliban Street in 1956 to 11 principal businesses and over 2,000 people Sumathi Holdings marked its 70th anniversary on 9 October, with a celebration at the Sangam Ballroom of ITC Ratnadipa, Colombo, attended by over 500 guests from Sri Lanka’s business, government, financial and media communities. Held under the theme “70 Years of Sumathi Legacy”, the evening looked back to 1956, when founder Mr. U.W. Sumathipala opened Sporting Star’s first betting shop on Maliban Street, Pettah – the business from which the Group grew. The evening opened with a drone show and fireworks over Galle Face. The program that followed included an address and toast by Chairman Jagath Sumathipala, the unveiling of the 70th anniversary logo, and addresses by Directors Chadu Sumathipala and Chathula Sumathipala, accompanied by a live orchestra and performances by vocalist Umara Sinhawansa, pianist and music director Soundarie David Rodrigo, and composer and singer Nadeeka Guruge. U.W. Sumathipala built Sporting Star into one of the country’s leading bookmakers and established it as the market leader. He also expanded into cinema, supporting the growth of the Sri Lankan film industry and into gems, representing the business at The World Gem and Jewellery Exhibition in Milan. His values of “Honesty and Integrity” remain the Group’s guiding principles today. After U.W. Sumathipala’s passing in 1979, Jagath Sumathipala joined the business at the age of 19, supported by his maternal uncle, Dharmasiri, who guided him in the horse racing operations. His first assignment was to create the Group’s own race paper, which he turned into a commercial printing company. He moved the main office from Maliban Street to Chatham Street and carried forward his father’s gem business. When his brother, Thilanga Sumathipala, returned from his studies in 1986, Jagath Sumathipala handed the racing operations over to him, and Thilanga Sumathipala built them further. In 1987 took a new step, Jagath Sumathipala opened Sri Lanka’s first race-by-race live commentary betting shop. Building on this, the Group began broadcasting races in 1992 and by 1998 was showing every race live across all its outlets. Today Sporting Star operates more than 200 outlets across the island and, since 2019, the online platform BetSS.com. Milina Sumathipala’s influence reached well beyond the business. She gave the entire profit of her film Ganga Addara (1980) to build a Neurosurgery Unit at the Colombo General Hospital, today’s National Hospital. In 1981, she began the blood donation drives and support for the Cancer Hospital through which more than 20,000 pints of blood have since been donated, and in 2001 she became the first woman President of the All Ceylon Buddhist Congress. Following a restructuring in 2017, Jagath Sumathipala, together with the third generation, has shaped Sumathi Holdings into a Group of 11 principal businesses employing more than 2,000 people, across betting and gaming, healthcare, information technology, restaurants, security, printing, renewable energy, investments and film. Much of today’s Group began as an answer to something Sporting Star needed. Security for its outlets became Lokx Security Services; printing for its racing papers became InPrint Solutions; and the technology behind its betting systems is now developed by Mainframe. Three Group companies mark milestones of their own this year: Great Wall Restaurants turns 35. Jagath Sumathipala set it up in 1991 on Chatham Street to bring authentic Chinese food to Colombo. Sumathi IT turns 25. It provides network infrastructure, data communications and geospatial engineering across Sri Lanka, and introduced DJI’s enterprise drones to the country. LifeServ turns 25. The healthcare distributor has been a leader in Sri Lanka’s drug-eluting stent market for two decades and opened an oncology division in 2025. A third generation now leads the Group alongside the Chairman. Chadu Sumathipala leads the Group’s IT sector: he founded Mainframe, brought the Group’s key systems in-house, built BetSS.com, and set up Sumathi IT’s drone division and its first research and development centre. Chathula Sumathipala leads the Group’s services cluster and grew LifeServ built Sumathi Energy, whose projects include the 5MW Wewila solar plant and battery storage at Monaragala and Wewila. The celebrations extended to the Group’s people. On 8 October, Sporting Star’s head office celebrated with its staff and presented long-service awards to more than 200 employees with ten or more years’ service, 31 of whom have been with the company for over 30 years. The longest-serving, R.V. Ghanasena of Anuradhapura, has been with Sporting Star for 40 years. On 10 October, Sporting Star outlets across the island held celebrations of their own for staff from Great Wall Restaurants and commemorative gifts for customers. Sumathi Holdings Chairman Jagath Sumathipala said: “Seventy years ago, my father opened a single shop on Maliban Street, built on his word and the trust of his customers. Honesty and integrity built this Group, and the more than 2,000 people who stand with us today carry those values forward. As we enter our eighth decade, our commitment is to build the businesses that will serve Sri Lanka for the next seventy years.”

audit.headline: Supreme Court enters decisive judgement in relation to jurisdiction of Commercial High Court
audit.summary: A bench of the Supreme Court comprising Justices Mahinda Samayawardhena, Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna, and K.M.G.H. Kulatunga delivered judgement overturning an order of the Commercial High Court on 21 October, by which the Commercial High Court had dismissed an action at the pre-trial stage on the basis that there was insufficient evidence to establish the claim to satisfy the minimum monetary threshold of the Commercial High Court to hear a case. According to the order of the Commercial High Court which was challenged, the position taken up by the Defendant that the Plaintiff’s claim had been artificially inflated to meet the jurisdictional threshold of the Commercial High Court was upheld by the Commercial High Court also with a finding that there was no evidence placed to support the claim.
audit.body: A bench of the Supreme Court comprising Justices Mahinda Samayawardhena, Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna, and K.M.G.H. Kulatunga delivered judgement overturning an order of the Commercial High Court on 21 October, by which the Commercial High Court had dismissed an action at the pre-trial stage on the basis that there was insufficient evidence to establish the claim to satisfy the minimum monetary threshold of the Commercial High Court to hear a case. According to the order of the Commercial High Court which was challenged, the position taken up by the Defendant that the Plaintiff’s claim had been artificially inflated to meet the jurisdictional threshold of the Commercial High Court was upheld by the Commercial High Court also with a finding that there was no evidence placed to support the claim. The Defendant in the case had initially raised a jurisdictional objection on the basis that the dispute was not a commercial dispute as there was no written contract or agreement between the parties. However, at the pre-trial stage, the Defendant had altered its objection and contended that the monetary threshold had not been met. Having considered the objections raised by the Defendant, the Commercial High Court dismissed the Plaintiff’s entire case in 2024. The Plaintiff-Appellant, Kish International Ltd., thereafter preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court, contending that the transaction between the parties was intended to be in USD and that, cumulatively, the sums claimed in the Plaint including demurrage, loss of profits, and interest exceeded the statutory threshold required to file the case in the Commercial High Court as demonstrated in the Plaint. It was the Plaintiff-Appellant’s position that the Commercial High Court could not lawfully dismiss the action at the pre-trial stage on the ground of an alleged lack of evidence as the pre-trial hearing is not the stage at which evidence is led or evaluated. The Appellant further contended that the High Court Judge ought not to have permitted the Defendant to reformulate a jurisdictional objection that had not been pleaded in the original defence. Justice Samayawardhena, in the judgement of the Supreme Court, specifically addressed, inter alia, the role of the pre-trial conference, which constitutes a pivotal stage in civil proceedings: “The purpose of the pre-trial conference is not to provide an opportunity for a party to introduce a new case outside the scope of the pleadings, to expand the scope of the dispute, or to prepare the case for a full-fledged trial.” The Supreme Court further held that “jurisdiction cannot ordinarily remain in suspense throughout the proceedings and ultimately depend upon the result of the very adjudication which the Court assumed jurisdiction to undertake. If jurisdiction is properly attached when the action was instituted, a subsequent finding on the merits that the Plaintiff has proved an amount less than that claimed does not, for that reason, retrospectively divest the Court of jurisdiction.” In addition, the Supreme Court, in its judgment, held that Parliament had used the word ‘including’, which should be given a wider interpretation, encompassing ‘commercial transactions’, and providing guidance as to the nature and breadth of the transactions that Parliament intended to bring within the jurisdiction of the Commercial High Court. It was held that the expression ‘commercial transactions’ must be given a broad and purposive interpretation, rather than being confined to the particular categories expressly enumerated in item 1 of the enacting act. The Supreme Court observed in its judgement that the Commercial High Court Judge had required the Plaintiff, at the pre-trial stage and before the action had even been fixed for trial, to establish by evidence the several components of its claim which the Supreme Court contended was a matter for determination upon the evidence at the trial. It was held that the absence of evidence establishing a particular component of the claim at the pre-trial stage could not justify the conclusion that such amount should be excluded in determining the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court. The Supreme Court through this extensive judgement proceeded to set aside the impugned order of the Commercial High Court and awarded costs against the Defendant-Respondent in respect of both the proceedings before the Commercial High Court until the dismissal and the Supreme Court appeal. The Supreme Court further directed the Commercial High Court to proceed with the matter and to hear and conclude the case expeditiously. On behalf of the Plaintiff-Appellant, Kish International Ltd., Counsel Nishan Premathiratne appeared with Vikum Jayasinghe and Manith Dasanayake on the instructions of Gamindu Karunasena. The Commercial High Court was firstly established in 1996 by an Act of Parliament and it is presently holden in the Western Province to hear and determine disputes of a commercial nature above Rs. 50 million, including matters relating to intellectual property, admiralty, debt recovery and arbitral referrals.

audit.headline: UNP demands immediate presidential pardon for Gnanasara Thera
audit.summary: The United National Party (UNP) yesterday demanded an immediate presidential pardon for Ven. Galagodaaththe Gnanasara Thera, facilitated by the intervention of the Maha Nayake Theros of the Three Chapters, to resolve the ongoing crisis. In a statement, the party said the Sathyagraha, a non-violent sit-in protest, demanding the Thera’s release had been suspended following a notification by the Maha Nayake Theros. Citing former Chief Justice Sarath N. Silva, the UNP said the maximum prison sentence for contempt of court was 18 months, and that Gnanasara Thera had already served more than 10 months in prison for the offence. The party said steps had previously been taken to secure a presidential pardon for the Thera at the request of the Maha Nayake Theros, and claimed that the Supreme Court ruling had indicated another presidential pardon could be considered.

audit.headline: A preventable threat
audit.summary: T he continuous rainfall is affecting most parts of Sri Lanka, with severe weather warnings expected to remain in force until at least the end of this week. The current weather system is being driven by the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), combined with a low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal. Dengue is an unwelcome visitor whenever rainfall increases in the country. According to statistics from the National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU), the country has recorded around 105,000 dengue cases, with approximately 80 dengue-related fatalities. The latest dengue outbreak remains heavily concentrated in urban areas characterised by dense populations and rapid construction. The Western Province is the worst affected, accounting for more than 52 per cent of all reported cases nationwide.
audit.body: T he continuous rainfall is affecting most parts of Sri Lanka, with severe weather warnings expected to remain in force until at least the end of this week. The current weather system is being driven by the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), combined with a low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal. Dengue is an unwelcome visitor whenever rainfall increases in the country. According to statistics from the National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU), the country has recorded around 105,000 dengue cases, with approximately 80 dengue-related fatalities. The latest dengue outbreak remains heavily concentrated in urban areas characterised by dense populations and rapid construction. The Western Province is the worst affected, accounting for more than 52 per cent of all reported cases nationwide. With the onset of the northeast monsoon, health officials continue to stress the importance of community involvement, urging residents to clean gutters, empty water containers weekly and seek immediate medical attention for high fevers that persist beyond two days. Yet, some people in continue to ignore fever, regardless of its severity or the underlying cause. It is sheer ignorance that has repeatedly landed Sri Lanka in difficult situations when it comes to dengue. This ignorance takes two forms. People remain woefully unaware of potential dengue mosquito breeding sites, while also neglecting their own health, particularly when they develop a fever. Some simply swallow a couple of tablets and carry on with their daily work. Others send their children to school despite their fever. Nearly a decade later, many still fail to understand that dengue can be fatal. There are four distinct serotypes of the dengue virus: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4. All four can be transmitted to humans by infected female Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which acquire the virus by biting infected people. Infection with one serotype generally provides lifelong immunity against that particular serotype, but not against the other three. A person can therefore contract dengue more than once. In fact, a subsequent infection with a different serotype can increase the risk of severe dengue. Infection with all four serotypes is not a safe or recommended way to acquire immunity; it can have serious consequences. If one member of a household contracts dengue, the other family members and their neighbours can be protected by taking measures to prevent mosquitoes from biting the infected person. Keeping the patient under a mosquito net throughout the day and night, particularly during the first week of illness, can help prevent mosquitoes from acquiring the virus and subsequently transmitting it to others. This is neither impractical nor impossible. Mosquito nets are used in healthcare settings for this very reason. When a mosquito bites an infected person, it can acquire the virus, which then multiplies inside the mosquito before the insect becomes capable of transmitting it to other people. Unfortunately, many Sri Lankans remain unaware of this important aspect of dengue prevention. Even in healthcare settings, the consistent use of mosquito nets for dengue patients deserves greater attention. Ensuring that patients are protected from mosquito bites is an important component of dengue control, alongside eliminating mosquito breeding sites and preventing mosquito bites in the wider community. Mosquito repellents are another important line of defence. However, the duration of protection varies according to the product’s active ingredient, concentration and formulation. Some repellents may need to be reapplied every few hours, while others provide protection for longer. Therefore, applying repellent once or twice a day may not be sufficient, particularly in areas where dengue transmission is high. People should follow the product label’s instructions and take additional precautions to avoid mosquito bites. There are several other crucial aspects of dengue prevention that many people remain unaware of. Fogging is one method used to control adult mosquitoes, but it is not the only way to eliminate them. Its effectiveness depends on factors such as the insecticide used, the method of application and whether mosquitoes are exposed to it. Mosquitoes that are not adequately exposed to the insecticide may survive. Moreover, fogging provides only temporary relief unless it is accompanied by measures to eliminate breeding sites and prevent mosquitoes from multiplying. Adult Aedes mosquitoes, the primary vectors of dengue, typically live for two to four weeks in nature, although their lifespan varies depending on environmental conditions. Dengue mosquitoes generally have a limited flight range, often remaining within a few hundred metres of their breeding sites. Although they can travel farther under certain circumstances, there is little justification for automatically blaming properties 500 metres or even a kilometre away without evidence. One of the most effective ways to protect ourselves is to thoroughly inspect and clean our own homes, gardens and surrounding areas, while working with our neighbours to eliminate potential breeding sites. Families must also pay close attention to the health of all their members, particularly those who may be vulnerable to severe dengue. Rather than assuming that one sex is necessarily at greater risk of dying from the disease, public health measures should ensure that women and men alike receive timely medical attention and appropriate care. Fathers, husbands, sons and brothers have an important role to play in protecting their daughters, wives, mothers, grandmothers and sisters, just as every family member should look out for the others.

audit.headline: Afghanistan-Pakistan trade declines sharply as border crossings remain closed
audit.summary: Trade between Afghanistan and Pakistan has declined sharply amid rising tensions between the neighbouring countries and the continued closure of border crossings. Mohammad Younus Mohmand, Vice President of the Afghan Chapter of the Pakistan-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said that the bilateral trade has fallen by about 95 percent. “We no longer have trade with Pakistan. Our transit via Pakistan and Pakistan’s transit via Afghanistan to Central Asia have come to a complete halt,” Mohmand said. Pakistani newspaper Dawn reported on Monday that the figures released by the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan in August showed that bilateral trade between the two neighbouring countries fell 95 percent in 2026-27 compared with the previous year.
audit.body: Trade between Afghanistan and Pakistan has declined sharply amid rising tensions between the neighbouring countries and the continued closure of border crossings. Mohammad Younus Mohmand, Vice President of the Afghan Chapter of the Pakistan-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said that the bilateral trade has fallen by about 95 percent. “We no longer have trade with Pakistan. Our transit via Pakistan and Pakistan’s transit via Afghanistan to Central Asia have come to a complete halt,” Mohmand said. Pakistani newspaper Dawn reported on Monday that the figures released by the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan in August showed that bilateral trade between the two neighbouring countries fell 95 percent in 2026-27 compared with the previous year. The TDAP also reported that bilateral trade fell to US$ 358 million in fiscal year 2025-26, down from US$ 1.3 billion in fiscal year 2024-25, a decrease of about 74 percent. Pakistan closed the main border crossings with Afghanistan on Oct. 12, 2025, after deadly clashes between the Pakistani Forces and the Afghan Taliban. In September, Pakistani Government said that it was ready to re-open the border crossings if the Taliban took measures against the militant groups operating from Afghanistan. Relations between Pakistan and the Taliban deteriorated as Pakistani authorities accused the Taliban of harbouring the militant group, Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has taken responsibility for attacks inside Pakistan. The Taliban publicly deny harbouring any militant group, but a U.N. report, released in August, said that the Taliban continue to support TTP.? The closure of the border crossings has hurt Pakistani industries, particularly pharmaceuticals, according to Government data. Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper, citing Pakistan’s Bureau of Statistics, said pharmaceutical exports declined 25.53 percent in the first quarter of 2026-27, which is primarily attributed to the disruption of trade with Afghanistan. (VOA)

audit.headline: Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by students
audit.summary: Aleksandar Vucic, who has shaped Serbia’s political life for more than a decade, has lost snap Parliamentary Elections to a student-led movement that led protests against him for almost two years. After a heated race, Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List in Sunday’s elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years. “It is clear that we have lost these elections,” the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) told supporters after a sample of votes showed his electoral list was expected to win 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member Parliament, compared with 135 to 140 for the Student List. The student movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024.
audit.body: Aleksandar Vucic, who has shaped Serbia’s political life for more than a decade, has lost snap Parliamentary Elections to a student-led movement that led protests against him for almost two years. After a heated race, Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List in Sunday’s elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years. “It is clear that we have lost these elections,” the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) told supporters after a sample of votes showed his electoral list was expected to win 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member Parliament, compared with 135 to 140 for the Student List. The student movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024. The youth-led protests grew into a broader wave of social unrest and evolved into the Student List political platform, which promised to tackle corruption, depoliticise public institutions and restore citizens’ rights. During the election campaign, the movement was led by Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad. Vucic referred to the demonstrators, who included university professors, doctors and workers, as “blockaders” and accused them of seeking to destabilise Serbia. A former ultranationalist, Vucic cultivated an image of a pragmatic leader who maintained ties with the European Union, Russia and China as well as, increasingly, with Israel in recent years. (Aljazeera)

audit.headline: Any Police officer in uniform can enforce traffic rules, spokesman says
audit.summary: Police Spokesman ASP F. U. Wootler stated that any single Police officer who is on duty, wearing the official uniform, is authorised to make a traffic detection and take legal action against traffic rule offenders. He said that according to the Motor Traffic Act, any Police officer who is in official uniform is a member of the Police force and that there is no need for him to be a traffic Police officer to detect any motor traffic violations and take legal action. He further clarified that under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance, that one traffic Police officer can make a traffic detection and take legal action against a traffic offender, and that no particular number of witnesses is required to prove the truth of any fact in any court case.
audit.body: Police Spokesman ASP F. U. Wootler stated that any single Police officer who is on duty, wearing the official uniform, is authorised to make a traffic detection and take legal action against traffic rule offenders. He said that according to the Motor Traffic Act, any Police officer who is in official uniform is a member of the Police force and that there is no need for him to be a traffic Police officer to detect any motor traffic violations and take legal action. He further clarified that under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance, that one traffic Police officer can make a traffic detection and take legal action against a traffic offender, and that no particular number of witnesses is required to prove the truth of any fact in any court case. Addressing the media yesterday (26), the Police Spokesman said that the authority to take action over traffic violations is not limited to officers attached to the Traffic Police and explained that any Police officer in official uniform can initiate legal action over traffic offences, even when carrying out duties alone. Clearing the misguided perceptions about the Police traffic officers and at times when motorists not wanting to stop their vehicles when one Police officer would stop the vehicle, he requested all motorists to abide by the traffic rules, laws and regulations of the country and ensure that they assist the Police officers on duty by following their instructions even if one Police officer on duty would instruct to stop a vehicle. Responding to concerns about Police officers hiding to catch traffic offenders, Wootler said that the IGP has informed all Police officers in the country that it is not necessary to conceal themselves when detecting traffic violations. The Police Spokesman made these clarifications in response to questions circulating on social media regarding the authority of Police officers to enforce traffic laws.
