audit.headline: Proposed laws threaten FR, Opposition reiterates
audit.summary: Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa during a consultation with foreign diplomats and representatives of international organisations at his office in Colombo on Sunday raised serious concerns regarding Government’s newly proposed security legislation. The talks focused on the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, with former MP M.A. Sumanthiran alongside current and former Parliamentarians joining Premadasa in warning that the proposed laws threaten fundamental rights, judicial independence, and the rule of law. Premadasa stressed that while tackling terrorism and organised crime is essential, decisive State action must be balanced with strict judicial oversight and respect for civil liberties.
audit.body: Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa during a consultation with foreign diplomats and representatives of international organisations at his office in Colombo on Sunday raised serious concerns regarding Government’s newly proposed security legislation. The talks focused on the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, with former MP M.A. Sumanthiran alongside current and former Parliamentarians joining Premadasa in warning that the proposed laws threaten fundamental rights, judicial independence, and the rule of law. Premadasa stressed that while tackling terrorism and organised crime is essential, decisive State action must be balanced with strict judicial oversight and respect for civil liberties. The Opposition highlighted recent critical assessments from key oversight bodies, including the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka (HRCSL), which declared the Prevention of Organised Crime Bill “wholly incompatible” with the Constitution’s fundamental rights’ safeguards and international obligations. Concurrently, the Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) called for the withdrawal of the Organised Crime Bill and major amendments to the Anti-Terrorism Bill, demanding the public release of the underlying expert committee report and its recorded dissents. In response, Premadasa outlined the Opposition’s demands for transparent reform, including the publication of expert recommendations, proportionate definitions of offences, restored judicial discretion over bail, protection against coerced confessions, and mandatory consultations with legal bodies before proceeding. Reaffirming Sri Lanka’s national sovereignty, Premadasa noted that resolving domestic legal questions remains the primary responsibility of Parliament and national courts, while emphasising the value of constructive dialogue with international partners to safeguard constitutional democracy.

audit.headline: Public servants briefed on next steps of Prajashakthi Movement
audit.summary: A programme to brief District Secretaries, Divisional Secretaries and District Planning Directors on the next steps of the Prajashakthi National Movement was held at Temple Trees recently under the leadership of the President’s Secretary Dr Nandika Kumanayake. Kumanayake emphasised to those who were present that proper coordination among officials was essential to carry out all development activities, including those under the Prajashakthi programme. He also stressed that any issues obstructing development should be resolved systematically. He pointed out that public officials should cultivate certain qualities and that development work could be facilitated by working efficiently and as a team. He also explained the importance of developing personally as an official who acts without corruption.
audit.body: A programme to brief District Secretaries, Divisional Secretaries and District Planning Directors on the next steps of the Prajashakthi National Movement was held at Temple Trees recently under the leadership of the President’s Secretary Dr Nandika Kumanayake. Kumanayake emphasised to those who were present that proper coordination among officials was essential to carry out all development activities, including those under the Prajashakthi programme. He also stressed that any issues obstructing development should be resolved systematically. He pointed out that public officials should cultivate certain qualities and that development work could be facilitated by working efficiently and as a team. He also explained the importance of developing personally as an official who acts without corruption. Speaking further Kumanayake said one of the key demands that emerged during the ‘aragalaya’ was that corrupt politicians should be removed. ‘The issue of public servants also being responsible emerged alongside that demand. At the last election, the people had an opportunity to send corrupt politicians home and bring a new force to power. However, they cannot transfer public officials or send them home. There is no mechanism for that. When people visit a Government institution to obtain a service and experience irregularities, injustice or wrongdoing, there must be a place where they can report it. That is why we established Internal Affairs Units in Government institutions’. ‘What is corruption’? asked Kumanayake. ‘Even among public servants, there is no clear understanding of this. If an official uses the authority entrusted to them to perform their duties in any way for their personal benefit that is corruption. If such practices are not addressed at the outset, and if they are followed by those at the top, they become the normal way of doing things. That was the system that existed in our country. Why should we reject such practices? Ultimately, they can lead to an economic crisis. Investors will be reluctant to come to the country. Essential projects were not implemented, while unnecessary projects were undertaken. As a result, the country accumulated debt and eventually reached a point where it did not have sufficient foreign exchange to import fuel. Taxes were imposed at levels the public could not bear, and poverty increased. Corruption was the reason for this. These practices also destroy human relationships and lead to an increase in crime. They have now spread even to the private sector. As a result, our country fell to one of the lowest positions in the world in terms of preventing corruption’’. Kumanayake pointed out how people had no place to report these matters. ‘They were concerned about what would happen to their safety if they spoke out. Therefore, no one revealed what they knew. Eventually, these issues erupt somewhere, and the ‘aragalaya’ was one such result. We have to encourage people to come forward and report these matters. Through this, we expect to strengthen integrity among public servants. Internal Affairs Units were established in Government institutions for this purpose. Report any wrongdoing or injustice you experience to these units. We will intervene,’ he said. The President’s Senior Additional Secretary Kapila Janaka Bandara briefed the gathering on five areas: the rural road development database planned for 2027, the introduction of an Innovation Hub, the preparation of a strategic plan, the collection of data for an online information system relating to tanks and the Ellanga cascade irrigation system, as well as the introduction of an entrepreneurship development database.

audit.headline: Rains to pound most provinces today
audit.summary: Cyclonic Storm Arnab intensifies in Bay of Bengal No direct impact on SL Heavy rainfall between 100 mm and 150 mm is expected across most provinces today (27) and tomorrow (28) as Cyclonic Storm Arnab intensifies in the Bay of Bengal, Deputy Defence Minister Major General (Rtd.) Aruna Jayasekara stated yesterday (26). Addressing a press conference at the Disaster Management Centre (DMC), he said there is no direct impact on Sri Lanka, but the public should remain vigilant without being unnecessarily alarmed. Intermittent rain or thundershowers may occur in the Northern, Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern, North Western, Central and North Central Provinces and around Trincomalee, with southwesterly winds of 30 to 40 kmph.
audit.body: Cyclonic Storm Arnab intensifies in Bay of Bengal No direct impact on SL Heavy rainfall between 100 mm and 150 mm is expected across most provinces today (27) and tomorrow (28) as Cyclonic Storm Arnab intensifies in the Bay of Bengal, Deputy Defence Minister Major General (Rtd.) Aruna Jayasekara stated yesterday (26). Addressing a press conference at the Disaster Management Centre (DMC), he said there is no direct impact on Sri Lanka, but the public should remain vigilant without being unnecessarily alarmed. Intermittent rain or thundershowers may occur in the Northern, Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern, North Western, Central and North Central Provinces and around Trincomalee, with southwesterly winds of 30 to 40 kmph. The Deputy Minister said the DMC has informed all District and Divisional Secretaries and the District Disaster Management Committees, and its Emergency Operations Centre has been operating for the past few days. The ‘117’ unit is gathering information and passing it on to the public at district level. The Armed Forces have been placed on standby, and the Police, Civil Security Department (CSD) and Coast Guard are monitoring districts at risk. He urged the public to follow all risk advisories. Met Department Director General A.L.K. Wijemannage said the system was centered near Latitude 15.4°N and Longitude 88.5°E at 8.30 am yesterday, about 1,100 km northeast of Kankesanturai. It is expected to become a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by 5.30 pm yesterday and a severe cyclonic storm today (27). It is forecast to make landfall on the Indian coast through Andhra Pradesh around 11.30 am tomorrow (28). Winds over the Bay of Bengal may reach 80 to 100 kmph, and up to 120 kmph in some areas. Rainfall is expected to intensify in the southwestern parts of the island and is expected to ease slightly after today. Winds of 40 to 50 kmph may occur at times in the Northern, North Central and North Western Provinces and the Trincomalee District. The Met Department’s forecast issued at 2.00 pm yesterday also mentioned the western slopes of the Central hills and the Hambantota District and said rainfall above 75 mm is likely in some places. The Met Department also said the El Niño phenomenon is developing and that it causes cyclones in the Bay of Bengal to intensify. It added that flash floods could occur in some places. DMC Director and Media Spokesperson Pradeep Kodippili said a person was injured when a tree fell in Ingiriya, Kalutara, and falling trees were reported in Galle, Matara and Ratnapura. The DMC and the State Timber Corporation have begun a programme to address hazardous trees. Irrigation Director L.S. Sooriyabandara said a minor flood is likely in low-lying areas of the Kalu Ganga floodplain within 24 hours. The areas at risk are the Pelmadulla, Nivitigala, Ratnapura, Kuruwita, Ayagama and Elapatha Divisional Secretariat Divisions in Ratnapura, and the Ingiriya, Horana, Dodangoda, Millaniya, Bulathsinhala, Madurawala and Palindanuwara Divisions in Kalutara. Water is being released from the Deduru Oya, Rajanganaya, Thabbowa and Inginimitiya reservoirs. Residents of low-lying areas along the Kala Oya and Mee Oya were also urged to be vigilant. Level 3 (Red) landslide warnings were issued for the Ratnapura, Ayagama, Pelmadulla, Kuruwita, Elapatha and Opanayake areas in the Ratnapura District. Several areas in the Galle, Gampaha, Kalutara, Kandy, Kegalle, Kurunegala and Nuwara Eliya Districts are under Level 1 or Level 2 warnings.

audit.headline: SC imposes travel ban on Keheliya, four others
audit.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) yesterday imposed a travel ban on former Health Minister Keheliya Rambukwella and four others in contempt of court proceedings arising from their alleged failure to comply with payment orders issued by the Court in a judgement delivered on March 27, 2026. The Controller General of Immigration and Emigration was directed to implement the travel ban forthwith. A Supreme Court three-judge bench comprising Chief Justice Preethi Padman Surasena and Justices Achala Wengappuli and Gihan Kulatunga also granted the five respondents three months from yesterday to pay the respective sums ordered to be paid to the State. Four of the respondents, including Rambukwella, were ordered to be released on bail upon furnishing bonds of Rs. 50 million each, with two sureties.
audit.body: The Supreme Court (SC) yesterday imposed a travel ban on former Health Minister Keheliya Rambukwella and four others in contempt of court proceedings arising from their alleged failure to comply with payment orders issued by the Court in a judgement delivered on March 27, 2026. The Controller General of Immigration and Emigration was directed to implement the travel ban forthwith. A Supreme Court three-judge bench comprising Chief Justice Preethi Padman Surasena and Justices Achala Wengappuli and Gihan Kulatunga also granted the five respondents three months from yesterday to pay the respective sums ordered to be paid to the State. Four of the respondents, including Rambukwella, were ordered to be released on bail upon furnishing bonds of Rs. 50 million each, with two sureties. The contempt proceedings were initiated by Transparency International Sri Lanka (TISL) over the alleged failure of the respondents to comply with the Supreme Court’s directions in case No. SC/FR/65/2023. In that judgement, the Court had ordered Rambukwella to pay Rs. 75 million to the State, while the other four respondents, including former National Medicines Regulatory Authority (NMRA) Chairman S. J. S. Chandraguptha, former NMRA Chief Executive Officer Prof. S. D. Jayaratne and former Medical Supplies Division Director Dr. Vijith Gunasekara, were each directed to pay Rs. 50 million. Appearing for Rambukwella, President’s Counsel Eraj de Silva tendered a receipt confirming a cash deposit of Rs. 20 million and undertook to pay the balance within two weeks. The second respondent, Chandraguptha, undertook to pay Rs. 5 million within a week and settle the remaining amount within two months. Prof. Jayaratne tendered a receipt as proof of payment of Rs. 50 million and sought to have the proceedings against him discharged. However, the Court said it would consider the application on the next hearing date, as the relevant payment documents had not been filed in the case. Dr. Gunasekara informed Court that Rs. 20 million would be paid within two weeks. He also undertook to dispose of other properties and settle the balance within three months. Counsel for the fifth respondent, Dr. A. T. Sudharshana, informed Court that Rs. 2 million would be paid within a week, followed by steps to dispose of other assets within three months to settle the outstanding amount.

audit.headline: SC nullifies Ranil Wickremesinghe’s remission
audit.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has invalidated the remission of the prison sentence granted to a man by former President Ranil Wickremesinghe under a General Amnesty in September 2024, ruling that the decision violated the Fundamental Right to equality and equal protection of the law. A three-judge bench comprising Justices Janak De Silva, Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna and Sampath Wijeratne held that the man had received preferential treatment compared to another person jailed for the same offence. The Court found that the difference in the wording of their warrants of commitment, one referring to default in payment of a “fine” and the other to default in maintenance payments did not constitute a valid ground for granting substantially different remissions.
audit.body: The Supreme Court (SC) has invalidated the remission of the prison sentence granted to a man by former President Ranil Wickremesinghe under a General Amnesty in September 2024, ruling that the decision violated the Fundamental Right to equality and equal protection of the law. A three-judge bench comprising Justices Janak De Silva, Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna and Sampath Wijeratne held that the man had received preferential treatment compared to another person jailed for the same offence. The Court found that the difference in the wording of their warrants of commitment, one referring to default in payment of a “fine” and the other to default in maintenance payments did not constitute a valid ground for granting substantially different remissions. The judgement was delivered on a fundamental rights petition filed by Ahamend Jaleel Farmilla Begum, whose former husband had been sentenced to 29 months’ imprisonment after failing to pay maintenance arrears amounting to Rs. 1.74 million. The petitioner had obtained a maintenance order from the Colombo East Quazi Court directing her former husband to pay maintenance totalling Rs. 60,000. Following his failure to comply with the order, the Magistrate’s Court of Negombo issued an enforcement certificate for the arrears, and he was subsequently imprisoned in July 2024. However, following a recommendation by the then Justice Minister to grant a General Amnesty to mark Prisoners’ Day, the remainder of his sentence was remitted, and he was released on September 12, 2024. Challenging the decision, the petitioner argued that the remission was arbitrary and had adversely affected her ability to recover the outstanding maintenance payments. She also pointed out that another person, Mohamed Faizal Mohamed Nawshad, who had been imprisoned for defaulting on maintenance payments, had not received a similar benefit. The Supreme Court observed that Nawshad had served approximately eight months of a 27-month prison sentence by the time the amnesty was granted but received only a one-week remission. In contrast, the petitioner’s former husband had served less than two months of his 29-month sentence before the remainder was remitted. The Court held that both men were, in substance, in the same position, as their imprisonment arose from defaults in meeting maintenance obligations. The difference in the terminology used in their respective warrants could not justify the unequal treatment. Accordingly, the Court declared that the former President, the Justice Ministry Secretary and the Commissioner General of Prisons had violated the petitioner’s fundamental right to equality and equal protection of the law guaranteed under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The respondent parties had justified the difference on the basis that the former husband’s warrant recorded his sentence as being in default of payment of a fine, whereas Nawshad’s warrant referred to default in maintenance payments. Rejecting that justification, the Court explained that the relevant legal provisions permitted maintenance arrears to be recovered in the same manner as fines. The terminology used in a warrant could not therefore justify treating the two men differently. The judgement further stated that the exercise of executive power must be directed towards the public interest and cannot be based on arbitrary distinctions.

audit.headline: Sixty percent of SLPP electorate-level branch committees established – D.V. Chanaka
audit.summary: Over 60 percent of the Sri Lanka Podujana Peramuna’s (SLPP) electorate-level branch committees nationwide have now been established under the guidance of National Organiser MP Namal Rajapaksa, according to party National Convener D. audit.headline: Sri Lanka–Romania expand co-operation on employment, trade and investment
audit.summary: Sri Lanka and Romania have taken further steps to strengthen bilateral cooperation in employment, trade and investment following a business forum held in Timisoara, Romania. The forum, on 24 October, was organised by the Chambers of Commerce of Timis and Arad and attended by Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra and Sri Lanka’s Ambassador to Romania, Samantha Pathirana, and representatives of the Romanian business community. Discussions focused on expanding suitable employment opportunities for Sri Lankan workers, promoting ethical recruitment practices, strengthening worker protection, and identifying new avenues for bilateral trade and investment. More than 28,000 Sri Lankans are currently employed in Romania, contributing to various sectors of the country’s economy.
audit.body: Sri Lanka and Romania have taken further steps to strengthen bilateral cooperation in employment, trade and investment following a business forum held in Timisoara, Romania. The forum, on 24 October, was organised by the Chambers of Commerce of Timis and Arad and attended by Deputy Minister Arun Hemachandra and Sri Lanka’s Ambassador to Romania, Samantha Pathirana, and representatives of the Romanian business community. Discussions focused on expanding suitable employment opportunities for Sri Lankan workers, promoting ethical recruitment practices, strengthening worker protection, and identifying new avenues for bilateral trade and investment. More than 28,000 Sri Lankans are currently employed in Romania, contributing to various sectors of the country’s economy. During the discussions, Florica Chirita, the Timis Chamber of Commerce President, expressed satisfaction with the performance and commitment of Sri Lankan workers, highlighting their reliability, dedication and contribution to Romanian businesses. The contribution of Sri Lankan workers was also recognised as an important element of Romania’s workforce. A key proposal emerging from the discussions was an initiative by the Timis Chamber of Commerce to organise a business delegation visit to Sri Lanka in 2027. The proposed mission is expected to bring together Romanian entrepreneurs interested in recruitment, trade and investment opportunities, creating further avenues for cooperation between the two countries. The engagement marks another step towards developing stronger economic ties between Sri Lanka and Romania, with an emphasis on creating decent employment opportunities, ensuring fair and ethical recruitment, safeguarding the rights and welfare of Sri Lankan workers, and encouraging mutually beneficial trade and investment. Sri Lanka remains committed to strengthen international economic partnerships that deliver practical benefits to its people while fostering sustainable cooperation with partner countries.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka’s First Agri-PV Pilot Demonstrator opens in Kandy
audit.summary: A new approach to combining renewable energy with agriculture was showcased in Kandy when the Agri-Solar Pilot Demonstrator for Training & Research opened at the National Seminary of Our Lady of Lanka, Ampitiya, on October 23. The project introduces agrivoltaics , or Agri-PV, an approach that integrates solar photovoltaic (PV) electricity generation with agricultural cultivation on the same land. By allowing farming to continue beneath elevated solar panels, Agri-PV offers an opportunity to make more effective use of land while exploring how renewable energy generation and agricultural production can complement one another. The initiative is supported by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE) under the Renewable Energy Solutions (RES) Programme of the German Energy Solutions Initiative, with support from the German Energy Agency (dena).
audit.body: A new approach to combining renewable energy with agriculture was showcased in Kandy when the Agri-Solar Pilot Demonstrator for Training & Research opened at the National Seminary of Our Lady of Lanka, Ampitiya, on October 23. The project introduces agrivoltaics , or Agri-PV, an approach that integrates solar photovoltaic (PV) electricity generation with agricultural cultivation on the same land. By allowing farming to continue beneath elevated solar panels, Agri-PV offers an opportunity to make more effective use of land while exploring how renewable energy generation and agricultural production can complement one another. The initiative is supported by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE) under the Renewable Energy Solutions (RES) Programme of the German Energy Solutions Initiative, with support from the German Energy Agency (dena). It brings German renewable-energy expertise to Sri Lanka while promoting technology transfer, practical training and applied research. SUNfarming International GmbH, Germany, contributes its Agri-PV technology and engineering expertise, while SUNfarming Lanka (Pvt) Ltd coordinates local implementation in collaboration with the National Seminary, which hosts the facility. The installation has a total solar PV capacity of 51.48 kWp, comprising elevated Agri-Solar structures and a separate modular installation designed for practical PV training. The elevated structures incorporate SUNfarming-branded bifacial glass-glass solar PV modules, allowing agricultural activities to continue beneath them. The system incorporates a specially designed panel arrangement intended to protect crops from heavy rainfall and intense sunlight, while potentially helping to reduce soil moisture loss and crop stress. The demonstrator provided a practical platform for researchers and agricultural specialists to investigate which crops and cultivation methods are best suited to Agri-PV under Sri Lankan conditions. It also enabled agricultural performance to be monitored and assessed over time, building evidence on crop suitability, growing conditions and the practical application of Agri-PV in Sri Lanka. Technical training is another central component. During installation, 26 trainees from the Ceylon German Technical Training Institute (CGTTI) gained hands-on experience alongside the German engineering team. The facility is intended to support further practical training, technology demonstration and applied learning in solar PV and Agri-PV. For Sri Lanka, the project provides a practical starting point for exploring innovation at the intersection of agriculture and renewable energy. By combining technology demonstration, skills development and local assessment, it could help strengthen technical capacity and generate knowledge to inform future Agri-PV initiatives. As a pilot demonstrator dedicated to training and research rather than commercial-scale development, its longer-term value will lie in the lessons learned and the evidence generated under local agricultural and climatic conditions.

audit.headline: Sri Lanka’s exports top US$13.6 Bn in first nine months
audit.summary: Sri Lanka’s export earnings rose 5.04% year-on-year to US$13.61 billion in the first nine months of 2026, supported by growth in merchandise and services exports, with electrical and electronic components, spices and processed food among the strongest-performing sectors. Total exports during January–September increased from US$12.96 billion in the corresponding period last year, according to the latest figures released by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB). Merchandise exports grew 5.35% to US$10.76 billion, while services exports increased 3.88% to US$2.85 billion, reflecting continued expansion across both segments. September recorded particularly strong growth, with total exports rising 17.23% year-on-year to US$1.69 billion. Merchandise exports surged 21.66% to US$1.39 billion, while services exports edged up 0.67% to US$306.17 million.
audit.body: Sri Lanka’s export earnings rose 5.04% year-on-year to US$13.61 billion in the first nine months of 2026, supported by growth in merchandise and services exports, with electrical and electronic components, spices and processed food among the strongest-performing sectors. Total exports during January–September increased from US$12.96 billion in the corresponding period last year, according to the latest figures released by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB). Merchandise exports grew 5.35% to US$10.76 billion, while services exports increased 3.88% to US$2.85 billion, reflecting continued expansion across both segments. September recorded particularly strong growth, with total exports rising 17.23% year-on-year to US$1.69 billion. Merchandise exports surged 21.66% to US$1.39 billion, while services exports edged up 0.67% to US$306.17 million. Among the key sectors, electrical and electronic components recorded the strongest growth during the first nine months, with earnings increasing 61.05% to US$508.86 million. Exports of spices, essential oils and oleoresins rose 30.53% to US$430.53 million, while food and beverages grew 20.90% to US$526.31 million. Rubber and rubber-based products generated US$773.88 million, up 8.44%, while coconut-based products increased 3.68% to US$942.5 million. ICT and business process management exports also expanded 3.69% to an estimated US$1.24 billion. However, apparel and textile exports declined 5.68% to US$3.78 billion, while tea exports fell 6.83% to US$1.08 billion. Seafood exports recorded a 2.03% contraction during the period. The United States remained Sri Lanka’s largest merchandise export destination, accounting for approximately 20.3% of total merchandise exports. India overtook the United Kingdom to become the second-largest destination, with exports rising 12.3% to US$889.84 million. EDB Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Mangala Wijesinghe said sustaining growth would require greater competitiveness, value addition, innovation, technology adoption and market diversification. The National Export Development Plan 2026–2030 targets annual export earnings of US$36 billion by 2030, providing a framework to expand market access, promote investment and strengthen the country’s export sector.

audit.headline: Temple elephant kills man
audit.summary: A 34-year-old unmarried tour guide, Piyasantha Jayalath, residing in Middaramulla, Ahungalla, was killed yesterday (26) after he was attacked by an elephant at the Kande Viharaya in Aluthgama. The incident occurred when the man had gone to visit the Kande Viharaya in a van with tourists and attempted to offer a fruit basket to the temple elephant. The elephant had struck him with its trunk and trampled him. Hospital doctors said the man was already dead on admission to the Balapitiya Hospital. His body is currently at the Balapitiya Hospital mortuary pending further investigations.

audit.body: COLOMBO (News 1st); A new generation of Indian naval leaders arrived in Colombo as three vessels from the Indian Navy's First Training Squadron made a formal visit to Sri Lanka, bringing with them 135 officer under-trainees and a renewed focus on maritime cooperation between the two neighbouring nations. The visiting flotilla includes INS Tir, a 107-metre training ship commanded by Captain Tijo K. Joseph, INS Sujata, a 103-metre Offshore Patrol Vessel under the command of Commander Jishnu Madhavan, and ICGS Sarathi, a 105-metre Offshore Patrol Vessel commanded by Commandant Kundan Singh. The Commanding Officers of the three vessels called on Commander Western Naval Area Rear Admiral Harsha De Silva at the Western Naval Command Headquarters, where mementoes were exchanged to mark the occasion and reaffirm the cordial relationship between the two navies. During their stay in Sri Lanka, the officers and trainees are scheduled to participate in a range of programmes organised by the Sri Lanka Navy aimed at enhancing bilateral ties, professional engagement and mutual cooperation. Sri Lankan naval personnel will also have the opportunity to board the visiting vessels, observe training operations and exchange professional expertise with their Indian counterparts, providing valuable opportunities for learning and collaboration. Beyond official engagements, the visiting officers and trainees are expected to tour several key locations and places of interest across the island, allowing them to experience Sri Lanka's culture, heritage and maritime significance while further strengthening people-to-people connections between the two countries.

audit.headline: Nearly Perfect GPA, International Awards, and a Mission to Serve Sri Lanka
audit.summary: COLOMBO (News 1st); A Sri Lankan Navy officer who has spent years breaking barriers is celebrating yet another milestone, this time on the international stage, after graduating with a near-perfect GPA and multiple prestigious awards from a leading United States military university. U.S. Ambassador Eric Meyer presented a Master's degree from the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) to Lieutenant Commander Piyumi Kathriarachchi of the Sri Lanka Navy at the American Center in Colombo, marking the completion of an academic journey that has earned recognition both in the United States and Sri Lanka. The ceremony was attended by Rear Admiral Rohan Joseph, Director General of Training, and Commander C.R.P. Walakuluge, Director of Media of the Sri Lanka Navy.
audit.body: COLOMBO (News 1st); A Sri Lankan Navy officer who has spent years breaking barriers is celebrating yet another milestone, this time on the international stage, after graduating with a near-perfect GPA and multiple prestigious awards from a leading United States military university. U.S. Ambassador Eric Meyer presented a Master's degree from the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) to Lieutenant Commander Piyumi Kathriarachchi of the Sri Lanka Navy at the American Center in Colombo, marking the completion of an academic journey that has earned recognition both in the United States and Sri Lanka. The ceremony was attended by Rear Admiral Rohan Joseph, Director General of Training, and Commander C.R.P. Walakuluge, Director of Media of the Sri Lanka Navy. Praising her achievement, Ambassador Meyer said Lieutenant Commander Kathriarachchi's success highlights both individual excellence and the long-term value of professional military education. "Lieutenant Commander Kathriarachchi's achievements reflect both her exceptional dedication and the value of world-class American military education. Through U.S.-funded training, she has gained knowledge and skills that she is now bringing home to strengthen Sri Lanka's Navy. Her success demonstrates how investing in the professional development of our partners strengthens our defense cooperation and contributes to a safer, more secure Indian Ocean region," Ambassador Meyer said. Graduating near the top of her class at the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School in Monterey, California, Lieutenant Commander Kathriarachchi completed the Defense Logistics Management programme with honours, achieving an outstanding 3.98 Grade Point Average out of a possible 4.0. Her academic success was accompanied by two major honours: the NPS Outstanding Thesis Award and the Kiwanis Club of Monterey Outstanding International Student Award, an accolade presented to only two international students at the institution each year. Her studies were funded through the U.S. International Military Education and Training (IMET) programme, which supports the professional development of Sri Lankan military personnel while strengthening defence cooperation between Sri Lanka and the United States. Beyond the classroom, her research focused on spare parts procurement challenges faced by the Sri Lanka Navy, producing practical recommendations aimed at improving operational readiness and strengthening naval capabilities. Following the degree presentation, Lieutenant Commander Kathriarachchi engaged with Sri Lankan youth at the American Center, encouraging them to pursue education, develop new skills and seize opportunities that can contribute to the country's future. Reflecting on her experience in the United States, she said: "My time in the United States gave me new tools to tackle real challenges facing our Navy. I look forward to putting that knowledge to work in service of Sri Lanka and hope my experience encourages other young Sri Lankans to pursue opportunities that can make a difference for our country." For Lieutenant Commander Kathriarachchi, international recognition is the latest chapter in a career already defined by historic achievements. A past pupil of Taxila Central College, Horana, she made history in 2013 by becoming the first female midshipman in Sri Lanka Navy history to receive the prestigious Sword of Honour. (Image Provided By U.S. Embassy in Sri Lanka)

audit.headline: Baila scene this 31st Night!
audit.summary: Features Published on By Share Tweet Dear Mr. Alvis, Please publish this at your earliest convenience. This has reference to some of the articles you have published regarding the setup at a New Year’s Eve dance. Going by what is on social media, I believe the baila will be quite prominent on 31st Night as some of the bands that have been highlighted are more into the Sinhala music setup. I can’t see them bringing into their repertoire those nostalgic favourites, generally associated with a New Year’s Eve dance. What makes a New Year’s Eve dance extra special are those perennial favourites, especially during the lead up to the dawning of the New Year.
audit.body: Features Published on By Share Tweet Dear Mr. Alvis, Please publish this at your earliest convenience. This has reference to some of the articles you have published regarding the setup at a New Year’s Eve dance. Going by what is on social media, I believe the baila will be quite prominent on 31st Night as some of the bands that have been highlighted are more into the Sinhala music setup. I can’t see them bringing into their repertoire those nostalgic favourites, generally associated with a New Year’s Eve dance. What makes a New Year’s Eve dance extra special are those perennial favourites, especially during the lead up to the dawning of the New Year. As mentioned by you in your articles, I don’t think some of the bands advertised have ever heard of songs like ‘This Land Is Your Land,’ ‘You Are My Sunshine,’ ‘When The Saints Go Marching In,’ ‘Roll Out The Barrel,’ ‘Celebration,’ ‘She’ll Be Coming Round The Mountain,’ ‘Happy Days Are Here Again,’ ‘Auld Lang Syne,’ etc. A New Year’s Eve event, without those songs, would be just another dance, and we have such dances right throughout the year, with the baila dominating the scene at these dances. I have absolutely nothing against baila music and I love what Wally Bastianz created, M.S Fernando, Anton Jones, Nihal Nelson, and also Desmond De Silva and Sunil Perera. However, at every event in the country the baila is there in a big way, so let’s make New Year’s Eve an exception. Let the baila come into the scene, immediately after the dawning of the New Year, and then again for the final set. Thank you, Benny J.

audit.headline: Beyond recovery: Policy priorities to achieve durable growth in Sri Lanka
audit.summary: By Rashmi Anupama and Kalani Kiriveldeniya, Research Assistants, Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) Sustaining Sri Lanka’s post-crisis macroeconomic stability requires productivity-enhancing reforms to achieve durable and inclusive growth. Against this backdrop, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) hosted a roundtable discussion on 14 October 2026 on its flagship publication, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026, to discuss policy priorities to rebuild the country’s economic foundations amidst ongoing domestic and global uncertainties.
audit.body: By Rashmi Anupama and Kalani Kiriveldeniya, Research Assistants, Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) Sustaining Sri Lanka’s post-crisis macroeconomic stability requires productivity-enhancing reforms to achieve durable and inclusive growth. Against this backdrop, the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka (IPS) hosted a roundtable discussion on 14 October 2026 on its flagship publication, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026, to discuss policy priorities to rebuild the country’s economic foundations amidst ongoing domestic and global uncertainties. IPS Research Fellows Dr Asanka Wijesinghe and Dr Lakmini Fernando presented key findings, followed by interventions from Dr Yashodha Senadheera, Deputy Director of the Economic Research Department of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL); Dr Liliya Aleksanyan, Senior Country Economist for Sri Lanka at the Asian Development Bank (ADB); Sanjaya Ariyawansa, Senior Economist at Sampath Bank; and other invited parties. Growth Has Returned, but Can Sri Lanka Sustain It? Dr Asanka Wijesinghe discussed Sri Lanka’s macroeconomic performance, external sector competitiveness, and policy priorities for durable growth. He highlighted that while the economy’s recovery has been satisfactory, sustained annual growth of approximately 8.3% between 2026 and 2030 would be required to regain the pre-crisis growth trajectory. Against this background, Sri Lanka needs to accelerate reforms towards achieving stated medium-term growth target of 7% or above. Rising global fuel prices and the resulting external sector pressures pose an immediate challenge to Sri Lanka’s economic growth. Sri Lanka recorded a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of 4.2% in the second quarter of 2026, with increased contribution of investment to economic output. However, the increased import bill has been a drag on output growth. The merchandise trade deficit widened considerably during January–August 2026, when compared to 2025. Improvements in fiscal consolidation and debt management have given Sri Lanka breathing space amidst a hostile external sector. Dr Wijesinghe stressed the need to maintain fiscal discipline, strengthen external competitiveness, and continue engagement with international financial institutions as the country rebuilds its resilience. Strengthening Export Competitiveness Dr Wijesinghe emphasised that expansion of exports is essential for achieving 7% economic growth, as growth driven primarily by domestic demand has its limitations. Sri Lanka’s reliance on non-reciprocal preferential market access faces growing challenges as competing economies negotiate reciprocal trade agreements. For example, Indonesia’s preferential access to the European Union (EU) and India’s trade agreement with the United Kingdom (UK) could weaken Sri Lanka’s competitiveness. This challenge could be further compounded by the potential loss of existing preferential arrangements for Sri Lanka, including the Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+). Securing more predictable tariff regimes in major export markets is a necessary precondition, and it requires accelerating tariff reforms and simplifying the tariff structure. However, these reforms must be carefully sequenced, as sudden reductions in tariff protection could adversely affect domestic industries, particularly Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs). He also recommended a dedicated fund to support trade adjustment. Reorienting Fiscal Policy Towards Long-Term Growth Building on these discussions, Dr Lakmini Fernando explained how fiscal policy could support durable growth beyond the current International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme. During the adjustment period, government capital expenditure declined to historically low levels, constraining the scope for public investment to support long-term growth and development. Achieving 7% economic growth could require gross fixed capital formation equivalent to approximately 30–42% of GDP, depending on investment efficiency. Mobilising such investment also requires a supportive environment for private investment alongside productive public expenditure. She also highlighted the need to prioritise education, healthcare, skills development, social protection, climate-resilient infrastructure, and green investment to meet evolving future demand. Improving public financial management, strengthening project implementation capacity, and ensuring transparent and competitive procurement were also identified as essential reforms. On debt sustainability, Dr Fernando stressed adhering to a medium-term debt management strategy, strengthening fiscal institutions, and exploring innovative financing. Continued engagement with international financial institutions could ease financing pressures. She also highlighted the importance of long-term planning and consistent implementation. Expert Perspectives: Monetary Stability, Economic Resilience, and Emerging Shocks Dr Yashodha Senadheera elaborated on the Central Bank’s monetary policy response to external supply-side shocks. She explained that although monetary policy has limited capacity to directly address supply-driven inflation, intervention may become necessary when such shocks generate persistent inflationary pressures or threaten inflation expectations. Maintaining price stability while considering broader economic conditions therefore requires careful, data-driven policy decisions. Dr Liliya Aleksanyan highlighted the lasting effects of successive crises and global energy-price volatility, emphasising the need for greater energy security through renewable energy. She also encouraged Sri Lanka to explore Asian export markets like India, alongside traditional markets such as EU and the United States of America (USA). Additionally, she highlighted the importance of preparing for emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence Sanjaya Ariyawansa focused on revenue mobilisation and climate risks. He called for improvements in tax administration, integration of SMEs into the tax system, and independent fiscal oversight. He also urged closer assessment of how climate-related shocks could affect agriculture, energy, public expenditure, and banking sector stability to strengthen preparedness and resilience. From Policy Recommendations to Implementation The subsequent roundtable discussion further explored several themes raised during the presentations and expert interventions. Participants discussed the assumptions underlying growth projections, the investment required to achieve higher growth, and opportunities to strengthen revenue mobilisation. To overcome the persistent gap between budgetary allocations and actual expenditure, participants also focused on improving the efficiency and timely utilisation of public investment. The discussion also explored fiscal responses to energy price shocks, the importance of supporting industries affected by tariff reforms, and the potential contribution of innovative climate financing instruments. Participants underscored that strengthening institutional capacity and anticipating risks are equally important as designing appropriate policies. The Way Forward The growth trajectory demands complementary reforms across macroeconomic management, international trade, public investment, fiscal institutions, and climate resilience. Ultimately, Sri Lanka’s long-term economic prospects will depend both on identifying the right policy priorities and implementing them consistently. As emphasised throughout the discussion, durable growth requires a forward-looking development strategy that strengthens the country’s capacity to withstand future shocks while delivering sustained improvements in economic well-being.

audit.headline: Darley Butler- HelpAge partnership helps to conduct free mobile medical camps
audit.summary: On of Sri Lanka’s oldest commercial enterprises Darley Butler Company recently donated Rs. 2.5 million to HelpAge Sri Lanka (HASL)- to support its’ Mobile Medical Units (MMU) that provide free medical and eye care facilities to disadvantaged elderly citizens in the country. audit.headline: Dengue far from beaten: over 105,000 cases, 79 deaths so far
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet Dengue cases exceed 105,000; death toll rises to 79 The National Dengue Control Unit said yesterday that 105,097 dengue cases had been reported across Sri Lanka so far this year, while the death toll had risen to 79. The Western Province accounted for the highest proportion of cases, with 54,673 infections, representing 52.02 per cent of the national total. Gampaha recorded the highest number of cases at 22,053, followed by Colombo with 20,384, Kandy with 8,378 and Kalutara with 6,592. Meanwhile, 4,377 cases were reported during the first 25 days of October, highlighting the continuing spread of dengue across the country.

audit.headline: ECCSL celebrates 30 years of resilience, achievement and a new chapter
audit.summary: The European Chamber of Commerce of Sri Lanka (ECCSL) marked its 30th Anniversary at its Annual General Meeting (AGM) and Members’ Night held at Cinnamon Lakeside Colombo, bringing together distinguished members, business leaders, industry representatives, stakeholders and partners to celebrate three decades of strengthening economic and commercial relations between Sri Lanka and Europe. The occasion marked an important leadership transition, with Past President John Wilson handing over the presidency to newly appointed President Ahamed ur Rahman. The transition signals a new chapter for ECCSL, building on the Chamber’s achievements while placing renewed emphasis on collaboration, innovation, sustainability and creating greater opportunities for its members.

He also acknowledged the dedication of the Chamber’s team and members whose collective contribution has been central to its continued growth and resilience.

audit.headline: Flood threat intensifies as Cyclone Arnab drives heavy rain and rising river levels
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet By Ifham Nizam Sri Lanka’s immediate flood risk is worsening as rivers rise, reservoirs release water and Cyclone Arnab strengthens over the Bay of Bengal, bringing the threat of torrential rain, strong winds and rough seas to several parts of the country. While Arnab is not expected to make landfall in Sri Lanka, its effects could aggravate flooding before the storm reaches India’s eastern coast tomorrow (28). Director of the Irrigation Department’s Hydrology and Disaster Management Division, L. S. Sooriyabandara, said on Monday that water levels in several reservoirs and rivers had risen, although no widespread flooding had been reported at that stage. The Kalu Ganga had risen considerably, while water levels in the Kelani Ganga and several other river basins had also increased.
audit.body: News Published on By Share Tweet By Ifham Nizam Sri Lanka’s immediate flood risk is worsening as rivers rise, reservoirs release water and Cyclone Arnab strengthens over the Bay of Bengal, bringing the threat of torrential rain, strong winds and rough seas to several parts of the country. While Arnab is not expected to make landfall in Sri Lanka, its effects could aggravate flooding before the storm reaches India’s eastern coast tomorrow (28). Director of the Irrigation Department’s Hydrology and Disaster Management Division, L. S. Sooriyabandara, said on Monday that water levels in several reservoirs and rivers had risen, although no widespread flooding had been reported at that stage. The Kalu Ganga had risen considerably, while water levels in the Kelani Ganga and several other river basins had also increased. Heavy rainfall in Anuradhapura, Trincomalee, Puttalam and Kurunegala districts had prompted the opening of spill gates at the Deduru Oya and Rajanganaya reservoirs. The Deduru Oya Reservoir was releasing approximately 5,300 cubic feet of water per second, while Rajanganaya was releasing around 2,300 cubic feet per second. The Irrigation Department warned that sudden, intense rainfall could inundate low-lying areas, urging residents near rivers and in flood-prone locations to remain vigilant. Meanwhile, the Meteorology Department forecast showers or thundershowers in the Northern, Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern, North-Western, Central and North-Central provinces and Trincomalee District, with rainfall exceeding 75 mm possible at some locations. Winds of 40–50 kmph were also expected in several areas, including the western slopes of the Central Hills and parts of the Northern and North-Western provinces. Arnab was forecast to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm before reaching the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday. A red warning has been issued for fishing and naval communities operating in affected parts of the Bay of Bengal, where winds could reach 80–100 kmph and waves rise to 3–4 metres. Authorities have urged the public to follow official weather and flood advisories as the situation develops.

Galagodaaththe Gnanasara Thera, has been temporarily suspended. Organisers said the decision had been taken following an assurance from the Mahanayake Theras of the three Nikayas that they would take stepts to resolve the issue through discussions. The government has maintained that Ven. Gnanasara, who was returned to prison in October after the Supreme Court invalidated the presidential pardon granted to him by former President Maithripala Sirisena in May 2019, will not be released through a fresh pardon. The “Justice for the Robe – Freedom March” began in Kandy on 10 October and proceeded to Colombo.

audit.headline: Growing anger in Jaffna over Indian poaching and proposed Fisheries Bill
audit.summary: News Published on By Share Tweet Jaffna fishermen protest Indian trawling, proposed Fisheries Bill Fishermen’s organisations in Jaffna have distributed leaflets demanding an end to Indian trawlers plundering fishing grounds off the Northern and Eastern provinces and the withdrawal of a proposed Fisheries Bill which, they claim, would pave the way for companies to take over marine resources. The leaflets were distributed jointly by Jaffna fishermen’s organisations and the Jana Aragala movement, with Frontline Socialist Party activist Vasantha Mudalige among those taking part. Taxes imposed on fishing nets and equipment have pushed prices beyond the reach of ordinary fishermen, the leaflet states, adding that buying a boat has become unthinkable. Although a fuel subsidy has been announced for the fishing industry, fishermen continue to pay market prices for fuel, it says.
audit.body: News Published on By Share Tweet Jaffna fishermen protest Indian trawling, proposed Fisheries Bill Fishermen’s organisations in Jaffna have distributed leaflets demanding an end to Indian trawlers plundering fishing grounds off the Northern and Eastern provinces and the withdrawal of a proposed Fisheries Bill which, they claim, would pave the way for companies to take over marine resources. The leaflets were distributed jointly by Jaffna fishermen’s organisations and the Jana Aragala movement, with Frontline Socialist Party activist Vasantha Mudalige among those taking part. Taxes imposed on fishing nets and equipment have pushed prices beyond the reach of ordinary fishermen, the leaflet states, adding that buying a boat has become unthinkable. Although a fuel subsidy has been announced for the fishing industry, fishermen continue to pay market prices for fuel, it says. The government has failed to fulfil its promises, the leaflet alleges. “We still try to console ourselves that they will do it today, that they will do it tomorrow,” it states. Indian trawlers continue to plunder local fishing grounds, while the failure of successive governments to intervene effectively has compounded the problem, according to the leaflet. It further accuses the present administration, like its predecessors, of failing to develop the fisheries sector on a scientific basis. The demands include lower fuel prices, concessionary fuel supplies for the fishing industry, affordable quality fishing equipment, effective action against Indian incursions and the withdrawal of the proposed Fisheries Bill. Indian bottom trawlers entering Sri Lankan waters off the North-East have long been accused of damaging fishing nets, depleting fish stocks and destroying seabed habitats, undermining the livelihoods of Tamil fishing communities. Fishermen in the region also face restrictions on access to coastal areas because of military-held land and naval controls. The protest comes amid continuing difficulties in resolving the long-running fishing dispute between Sri Lanka and India. Bilateral talks on bottom trawling have been postponed, with no new date fixed as of early October, according to contemporary reports.
